en: The Glorious Āyurveda Sūtra with Commentary
I bow to that one with the face of a sea-monster, whose own self shines as if enveloped by the great rays emerging from the strikes of tusks uprooting mountain ridges during his playful sport.

The Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause, bestowed upon Prajāpati Brahmā the Āyurveda, which is beneficial to all living beings. Both the syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha* emerged from the throat of Brahmā in ancient times; therefore, both are auspicious.
Having thus performed the supreme auspicious rite by means of the word *atha* according to the manner described, he favors the first aphorism with the words: *atha*.
"Now, therefore, one should eat substances that are age-prolonging and which cause the non-alteration of the humors (*dhātu*) located within the body. (1)

The meaning of this is as follows: "Dhātusthā" means those that reside within the *dhātus* (tissues). "Gati" refers to the movement of the *doṣas* (humors), a movement preceded by the causes of the absence of pathological change (*vikāra*). One should eat substances suitable for food—substances that serve as the cause for those movements, or rather, those that prevent their provocation—this is the meaning of the aphorism. Regarding "in the *dhātus*": the *dhātus* are stated to be "chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. They are called "dhātusthā" because they reside there for the purpose of circulation. These [residences] and the *doṣas* form a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*).

Vāyu, pitta, and kapha—these are the three doṣas in brief. If the activity [of medicine] were directed solely toward the result of increasing those substances that cause the increase of the bodily constituents (dhātus), it would yield only a minor fruit; however, keeping in mind the intention that the activity of Āyurveda bestows many human goals (puruṣārthas), he says: "For long life...
The activity arising from the desire for long life brings about the human goals that constitute the purpose of Āyurveda.

By the word "long" (*cira*), it is meant that when the accomplishment of an effect and the consumption of substances have occurred, there arises for one desiring longevity an activity; specifically, for a person who desires it, there is an activity directed toward the object of the wish, "May I have a long life. For one who possesses such expertise—consisting of experience regarding the subjects taught in the scriptural tradition and manual skill—this activity has as its object the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) of this [longevity]. Thus, the purpose (*prayojana*) is that [the science] establishes the human goals contained within the meaning of Āyurveda. Regarding this, the statement from the *Sūtrasthāna* says: "By one desiring longevity, [this is] the means for achieving dharma, artha, and sukha."
One should exercise the highest degree of respect toward the instructions of Āyurveda.

Now, one might object: "In this treatise, it was stated that the purpose (*prayojana*) is that which establishes the goals of man through the meaning of Ayurveda; if that were so, then the causality of the absence of disease as an effect would not constitute a [separate] cause. Anticipating this objection, he says: "taddhetu... (the cause of that).
One should protect the object that serves as the cause for that [attainment]. || 3 ||

The meaning of "that which has become the cause" (*taddhetubhūtārtha*) is the meaning of that which has become the cause for the effect of freedom from disease. That itself is the purpose (*prayojana*). The preservation of that very [body] is the meaning of "the state of being the fruit" (*phalībhūtārtha*); the sense is that its cause must be brought about. Regarding this, there is a statement in the Sūtra: "Having examined all [factors], constantly observing the body, and having observed it as free from disorder, one should treat it with wholesome [regimen] alone."
The inability to distinguish between what is digested and what is undigested exists in the tongues of men.

Having recognized the disorder through such a manifestation, one must cultivate the consumption of wholesome food as the means to its removal. Indeed, this very object which serves as the cause for that [wholesome state] must be protected. The meaning is that the intake of food in deficient or excessive amounts is the cause of disorder; therefore, the object that serves as the cause for its removal must be protected.

Anticipating the objection that over-indulgence or over-oppression of the senses might not be causes of disorder, he says "no"—neither the over-indulgence nor the over-oppression of the senses [is a cause of disorder]. (4)

The sense organs (*indriya*) are hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell; their objects (*viṣaya*) are sound, touch, form, taste, and odor. The organs of action (*karmendriya*) are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ. The meaning is that one should engage these with regard to wholesome and moderate objects. Now, it has been established that both under-eating and over-eating are causes of disease. Regarding this, there is a statement: "Food in deficient measure does not lead to strength, growth, or vigor; however, food in excessive measure quickly provokes all the bodily humors (*doṣa*)."

In accordance with this statement, it is established that these two alone possess the nature of causes, and not the excessive pampering or excessive affliction of the sense organs. Therefore, [anticipating the objection] that this sūtra would be redundant, he says: "Doṣa..."—meaning they are the factors that bring about the increase and decrease of the *doṣas*. (5)

The increase of the *doṣas* is also a cause for *doṣa*-related diseases; likewise, the decrease of the *doṣas* is also a cause for the provocation (*prakopa*) of the *doṣas*. "Being caused by the *doṣas*" means being caused by the provocation of the *doṣas*. The causal relationship between the increase and decrease of the *doṣa*-disorders has been specified, but not so for the excessive pampering or excessive affliction of the sense organs. Regarding this, there is a saying: "One should not afflict the sense organs, nor should one over-indulge them. [The reason for this is that] these two [excessive pampering and affliction] serve as the basis for the increase and decrease of the *doṣas*, because they bring about such increase.
For all beings, there is growth through those who are equal and the opposite through those who are contrary;
the relationship between cause and effect exists precisely between these two. The meaning is that it is possible to describe their causality as being mediated through a succession.

Is it not the case that the increase and decrease of the *doṣas* occur spontaneously, and not due to the excessive pampering or excessive affliction of the sense organs? Furthermore, the causal relationship between those two [pampering/affliction and the *doṣas*] is established solely by the power of time (*kāla*). Regarding this, there is a statement in the *Sūtrasthāna*:
"The accumulation (*caya*), provocation (*prakopa*), and pacification (*praśama*) of *vāyu* occur during the three seasons beginning with summer;
those of *pitta* during the three beginning with the rainy season; and those of *śleṣman* during the three beginning with winter."

Based on this statement, one might ask how the relationship of cause and effect between these two can be asserted; anticipating this objection, he says: "The characteristics also are likewise" (lakṣaṇāny api tathā). //6//

Where the characteristics of what has not reached its time appear as having reached it, and where the absence of those characteristics appears when the time has arrived, there is a fixed rule. For the establishment of a thing occurs through characteristic and means of knowledge (*lakṣaṇa-pramāṇa*). In this regard, the statement of the Sūtra is: "The applications of time, purpose, and action—whether deficient, perverse, or excessive, as well as correct application—are to be known as the sole cause of disease and health."
Disease is the disharmony of the humors; the equilibrium of the humors is health.

He designates the appropriate effect that brings about the cessation of disease, which is produced by the knowledge of the cause and the statement of its specific characteristics—by means of the words "by the fit" (yogya).
And that [disease] he should cause to cease by means of those who are fit. (7)

The meaning is that one should prepare substances whose tastes are suitable for the purpose of inducing *recaka* (therapeutic purgation) to alleviate the pain produced by the disease of trauma (*abhighātāmaya*). The referent of the word "that" (*tat*) is the extent of the disease of trauma; one should purge that [disease] with a substance that brings about its cessation. Regarding this, there is a statement in the Sūtra:
"One should avoid the extremely terrible *āmadoṣa* which is designated as 'poison' (*viṣa*), because it acts rapidly like poison and because its treatment is contradictory."

Now, it may be objected that the statement made to demonstrate that the sense organs have disease as their cause—namely, that it arises from excessive pampering or excessive affliction of the senses—is not acceptable. [For] eating in excess has undigested matter (*āma*) as its cause, and the accumulation of *āma* alone is the cause of all diseases. Because it is more logical to consider the removal of *āma* as the remedy, the author says "free from *āma*" (*anāma*), out of dissatisfaction with the previous view:
one should practice the preservation of that which is free from *āma*. (8)

Since the very absence of the accumulation of *āma* constitutes the causal complex for the absence of disease, therefore, the daily practice of "preserving what is not *āma*" (*anāmapālana*) is the prescribed rule. "Preserving what is not *āma*" means that one should perform the act of non-preservation of *āma*. Here, the statement of the reason for performing the action of preserving what is not *āma* appears in the aphorism: "One should always be a consumer of measured food, for measure is the stimulator of the digestive fire.
Substances, whether heavy or light, depend upon measure."

Now, one might object: "The causal complex that prevents the onset of fever and other diseases is the same causal complex that promotes the digestive fire; therefore, the avoidance of *āma* would be unnecessary. To this, he says: "*Āmam* [is the root]";
for *āma* is indeed the source of all diseases. (9)

"Undigested matter (*āma*) alone is the cause"—here, the word *hi* indicates well-known fact. On this point, there is the statement of the Sūtra: "The dosha, residing in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), having destroyed the digestive fire and obstructed the channels, brings about fever; therefore, one should perform fasting (*laṅghana*)."

It can be said that whoever possesses the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) for activating the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) has the capacity to consume all things, and even longevity is attained. Now, while it must be stated that the cessation of *āma* (undigested matter) is indeed the remedy for all diseases, the failure to effect the cessation of *āma* in cases such as fever (*jvara*) becomes caused by a fault. Furthermore, since the cessation of *āma* must be brought about through fasting (*laṅghana*) and other means, the performance of fasting is also essential; this was established by Brahmā, as he says with the word "first" (*ādi*).
Brahmā declared that which is primary. || 10 ||

The meaning is that Brahmā stated that both [methods] are indirect causes for performing *laṅghana* (fasting/lightening therapy) for the purpose of drying up the *āma*, because they both establish the means for removing the disease. Regarding this, there is a statement in the Sūtra: "In the case of *āma*, fasting should be performed; in the case of constipation (*viṣṭambha*), sudation (*svedana*) should be applied vigorously. Since it is said that *āma* is removed by fasting, he asks what was the resulting fruit of that [removal], and therefore says: "That... (*tad*).
The cessation of that is health. || 11 ||

Only through the cessation of the *āmadoṣa* does one become free from disease, which is the goal of human endeavor. Defects that have been subdued by fasting (*laṅghana*) and digestive treatments (*pācana*) may sometimes flare up again;
however, for those who have been purified by thorough cleansing therapies (*saṃśodhana*), there is no recurrence.

Thus it has been stated that for one whose body has been conquered through fasting and digestive treatments, diseases do not recur. This being so, since the five sense organs have all objects as their domain, by what means or for what reason can the mind be brought to have the Self as its object? To this he says: "The healthy one" (anāmayī). The healthy one regards the Self [as his own]. (12)

Having brought about the health of the body according to the method previously described, the individual soul experiences supreme bliss through the yoga of self-reflection and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). Regarding this, there is a saying: "Defects that have been gradually accumulated and virtues that have been gradually accumulated, once they have passed away and returned to their original state, become unshakable."

The meaning is that by performing actions free from affliction (*anāmaya*), one becomes healthy and experiences the very bliss of heaven. In this manner, the health of the body has been established. However, by that much alone, the causal complex for the contemplation of the Self (*ātma-manana*) has not been set forth. Is it being argued that one becomes healthy simply by virtue of possessing a powerful digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) such that all the sense organs become enjoyers of all objects? Since health is not produced solely by the causal complex for the contemplation of the Self, the author states "I" (*aham*) out of this underlying dissatisfaction.
The notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*) is the agent of action. (13)

The cognition "I" is the object of such notions as "I am red" or "I am dark," which are based solely upon the substrate of the ego (ahaṃkāra). Likewise, one who is capable of being known through the reflective awareness (anuvyavasāya), "I am a possessor of knowledge," becomes qualified for virtuous action (satkarman). It is possible to perform self-contemplation (ātma-manana) by means of good action;
for it was indeed by action alone that Janaka and others attained perfection.

Thus, by virtue of being the object of knowledge regarding the category of *dharma*, the Supreme Brahman is established as the object of knowledge regarding the mind. This Self, who is established as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), is indeed the individual soul (*jīvātman*). Both of these are situated within the body alone. To designate that one of the two possesses the status of the enjoyer of all, he says: "In the place," etc. The ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is the possessor of the place. || 14 ||

The meaning is that the intention is this: it is not possible for the Supreme Self to be the locus [of the body], whereas it is possible for the individual selves (jīvātman) to be so; thus he says [the following]. Since health is established by its own nature for whomever yoga operates for a certain duration, he says "as long as" (yāvat).
As long as one considers oneself free from disease. || 15 ||

The meaning is that immediately after the discernment of substances that cause depletion and nourishment, one is able to conceive the determination "I am healthy" by partaking in the causal totality (sāmagrī) for the effect of health. It has been stated that he who is healthy and fit for the yoga of self-reflective meditation (nididhyāsana) should, having joined the five sense organs—which have their respective external objects as their domain—to the body, contemplate the Supreme Self with the internal organ, the mind, which has the self as its object.
To the objection that the external objects being the domain of the external senses would be irrelevant [to the realization of the Self], he says: "He alone enjoys. (16)
For the Unborn is the presiding controller. || 17 ||
The individual soul (*jīva*), which experiences all objects, enjoys everything. On this point, there is a scriptural passage (*śruti*):
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree."
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit of the fig tree,
while the other looks on without eating.

Thus, scripture itself is the authority in this matter. From the statements "he desires," "he knows," and "he exerts effort," it is understood that the conjunction of the self and the mind is the cause of every action. Therefore, the individual soul (jīvātman) is the experiencer of all objects, as this is perceived through cognition. Consequently, he says "he experiences" (bhuṅkte) to indicate that [the object] is experienced by the Supreme Self.
He experiences the enjoyments of sense-objects. (18)

The intended meaning is that the Supreme Self (paramātman), whose nature is self-luminous, is the object of the experience of existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda). According to the scriptural passage, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," the Supreme Self is the infinite knowledge of truth, whose essence is the bliss of its own object.

[Objection: But surely the one [the individual soul] experiences the enjoyment of all objects. [Response: Enjoyments are dependent upon karma. While it must be stated that the soul’s status as an enjoyer of karma is its essential nature (*vidhi*), the soul appears as an enjoyer of only those objects present before it, whereas the Supreme Self appears as the enjoyer of all objects because of His omniscience. Since it would follow that both possess the status of being enjoyers of karma, the author says "another" (*anya*) to resolve this inconsistency: "Another enjoys the karma. (19)

The meaning is that the individual soul (*jīvātman*), being subject to the authority of *karma*, experiences objects of enjoyment dependent upon its own actions. Through good action (*sukarman*), it experiences the fruit consisting of objects that bestow happiness; through evil action (*duṣṭakarman*), it experiences the fruit consisting of objects of suffering. Since experience (*bhoga*) consists of the nature of pleasure and pain, experience—defined as the perception of pleasure and pain—is presented as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the individual soul. The implication is that the soul would then result in experiencing all possible objects.
The meaning is that while the body produced by evil action exists, one should always perform only virtuous action.

The injunction (*vidhi*) is the Supreme Self’s performance of action regarding virtuous deeds (*satkarma*). However, because it would follow that even the Lord (*Īśvara*) possesses the qualification for performing actions that generate any particular karma, the author states "He who" (*yaḥ*) out of this unease:
"He who is the agent is the enjoyer of the fruits of action. (20)

It is said that [the Lord] bestows upon the agent of action—distinguished by ego—the fruits of pleasure and pain arising from the consumption of substances that serve as causes for yielding results characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*. This is because there is a scriptural conclusion (*nigama*) that the fruit of action necessarily follows directly [from the act]. To this, he says: "The agent" (*kartā*).
The agent is the embodied being (*śarīrī*). (21)

The meaning is that as long as there is an agent of action, one who possesses a body is the agent here. It has been stated that whoever performs an action with a view toward some fruit is called "one who possesses a body. Because of the absence of a body, it is not possible for the Self to eat food; therefore, due to this underlying dissatisfaction, he says—"one who is bodiless.
One who is bodiless does not eat food. 22.

The relationship between action and its fruit is one of cause and effect, established by necessity, like that of food and eating. One obtains a fruit corresponding to one's own action; the meaning is that it bestows that fruit upon the embodied being. Day after day, humans desire food. If, for the sake of daily sustenance, an action conducive to that fruit has been performed in this world, no absence of that fruit is observed there. Yet, even in that case, the body exists. Therefore, he says "no," [denying] that there is no causal relationship between action and its fruit;
for the body alone is not fit for experience, due to its connection with the self. || 23 ||

The meaning is that, at the very time of the body's initial production, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from previous births provide results such as the drinking of breast milk for infants and others.

Now, one might object: "Infants and others certainly possess bodies, yet no karma has been performed therein, because they lack the capacity [to act]. The result of drinking breast milk and so forth is provided by the mother; therefore, it is impossible to assert a causal relationship between karma and its fruit. To this, he says: "capable of experience" (*bhogayogya*). Even though there is an absence of visible karma at that moment, the performance of karma in a previous birth is postulated, because the self possesses a body.

If it is argued that because maintaining the body is appropriate, the mother provides breast milk and so forth to infants and others, we say no. It is postulated that the maintenance of the body and such functions are the results of karma from previous births. Since the Self possesses a body, and since maintaining the body is appropriate for the Self, it is understood that the individual soul (jīva) is the locus of experience for the embodied being who is the cause of the conjunction with the body. Therefore, the capacity to preside over the body belongs to none other [than the Self]; thus he says: "The two unborn ones" (ajau), for they are the presiding entities. || 24 ||

"Unborn" (aja) means that which is not born. The meaning is that those two—the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)—are situated within the body. The meaning is that the experience of objects is possible for only one of these two, namely for him who has the cognition "I am the knower of the pot. Therefore, he says: "The other eats the food" (25).

The limbs of the body are the sense organs, and the possessor of the limbs is the embodied self (*śarīrin*). For the sake of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) experiencing objects within the range of the senses, it brings about the connection with those sense organs that constitute its limbs; thus, through the otherwise inexplicable nature of such cognitions as "I know," "I desire," and "I exert effort," the individual soul consumes food. In response to the doubt—namely, what is experienced by a self distinct from that [body]—he says: "He does not eat. Another [self] indeed does not eat. (26)

Since it is well known that another, the Supreme Self, possesses the experience of all objects, and because [the individual self] is not distinct from Him in respect to the fruit [of action], the meaning is that He "eats" (anatti) such a fruit of this purpose; that is to say, He Himself experiences it, because His nature is self-luminous. Lest one should think that the body—being an effect produced by modifications and caused by a collection of causal factors—might be the locus for the experience of this Self and thus suitable for its enjoyment, he says: "When existing" (sati). This means:
when the body exists, for the sake of enjoyment. || 27 ||

The meaning is that it is stated that while the body exists, the capacity for the enjoyment of all objects is accomplished by the self. What are the limbs of the embodied one? It has been demonstrated that even the five sense organs are limbs. Since the mind is beyond the range of the [other] senses and is an internal organ, it is taught that there are six; for these six serve as the means for the self to obtain the objects of enjoyment. Therefore, the body's fitness for enjoyment is established by its very nature.

Cognition of objects is dependent upon the sense organs, and the sense organs are themselves established in the body; the meaning is that all objects of experience are dependent upon the body. Now, activity is indeed twofold: for the attainment of the desired and for the avoidance of the undesired. One form of activity is the necessity of protecting the body experienced as one's own substratum. Thus, this twofold activity is appropriate for the self.

In that case, how can the five sense organs be constituent parts of the body? How is the fruit consisting of the attainment of the desired obtained through them? Is the fruit consisting of the attainment of the desired also obtained through the avoidance of the undesired? Since it must be understood that both fruits belong to the embodied being (śarīrin) by way of the avoidance of the undesired, he says: "Eightfold. The embodied being possesses eight limbs. (28)

The collection of eight branches is the "eightfold" (*aṣṭāṅga*). One who possesses a body is a "possessor of a body" (*śarīrī*). Regarding this, there is a statement from the Sūtra: "They say that its eight branches—Kāya, Bāla, Graha, Ṛtvaṅga, Śalya, Daṃṣṭrā, Jara, and Vṛṣa—are those upon which medical treatment (*cikitsā*) is based."

Diseases that act as the cause for bodily afflictions are "incidental" (*aupādhika*); even the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) caused by the aggravation of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha* do not increase [independently]. Thus, it is established that the eight diseases constitute the limbs [of the body]. Such are the diseases of bodies; it is established that those *dhātus* are the limbs. The meaning is that since the body consists of the seven *dhātus*, it is established that the diseases which cause afflictions to the limbs are, through a causal succession, themselves the limbs.

[Objection: "If it must be stated that substances which increase the *dhātus* are auxiliary (*aṅga*) [to the body], then that is easily established; however, how could those things which cause the destruction of the *dhātus*—that is, the destroyers of the body—be auxiliary? [Response: This is not so, because it is possible to state a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between diseases and the effect, which is the absence of the body. He specifies the characteristics and measures of the eight diseases that serve as the causes for the destruction of the body with the words beginning with "yāvat": "The body [remains] as long as there is the performance of [the prescribed] rites. (29)

The object to be accomplished (*kārya*) is that which is to be brought about by the activity (*kṛti*) of those factors—both those that establish and those that remove—which are produced by the knowledge of the scope of the knowledge of the causes (*nidāna*). In this regard, the instruction is that "whenever there is a rule" (*yāvad-vidhi*), that body alone is the object to be accomplished for whom the remover is capable of enduring the rituals prescribed in the scriptures (*yāvac-chāstroktakarman*). On this point, the statement of the Sūtra is:
"Purification (*śodhana*) and pacification (*śamana*): thus medicine is twofold in brief;
it is the supreme medicine for the disorders born of the body, applied in due order."

Since even the body of a child is one with respect to the delimitation of "bodily-ness," the term *krama* (sequence) is intended here because it is meant to be distinguished by the different branches of medicine, namely *kāyacikitsā* (internal medicine) and *bālacikitsā* (pediatrics), as the "supreme medicine" for each. Now, one might object: since it is observed that when the causal complex for curing diseases caused by *āma* is present, the diseases produced by it are indeed cured, those diseases born from *āma* are designated as *kāya* and *bāla*. What then is the status of other types of diseases, such as those born of planetary influences (*graha*)? With this intention, he says: "Āma... [and so forth].

A *graha* is that which causes the agitation of the mind through fear arising from the causes of natural diseases, artificial poisons, and improper actions, and which brings about suppression and conflict. || 30 ||

Regarding this, some [object]: "Diseases are born of *āma*. For them, a certain action induced by a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the remedy. Since it is impossible to perform an action that removes *āma* in the case of diseases caused by the possession of spirits (*graha*), because such a causal complex for their removal has not been experienced here, and because it is not seen in the scriptures, this aphorism is therefore inappropriate. To one who speaks thus, the author, desiring to provide a rebuttal, explains the aphorism with the word "āma."

The remedy in that regard consists of the removal of those diseases and the subduing of those planetary influences (*graha*). Mantras, ritual procedures (*tantra*), the offering of oblations (*bali*), and so forth, are the means of removal. The meaning is that when the planets are favorable, even the diseases arising from the planets—which follow the path of a single *doṣa*—can be easily removed through such means as the offering of oblations, mantras, and ritual procedures. In that context, the suppression of fear occurs through the mantras and rituals that constitute the totality of conditions; the meaning is that there is an absence of disease produced by the totality of conditions caused by *āma*.

The numerous diseases arising in the upper parts of the body, which are to be cured by the methods previously described, have been observed to be many. Their causation (*nidāna*) pertains to a different domain, because the causation of these [upper-body diseases] also pertains to a domain distinct from that [of the previous ones]. Those factors which cause the provocation of *vāta*, *pitta*, and *āma* residing in the ears, eyes, head, nose, and tongue, and which constitute the causes of effects produced by those [provocations], are born of such causes; thus he specifies the diseases of the upper body with the term "āmaja" (born of *āma*).

These [diseases] are caused by *āma*, are the causes of effects produced by *āma*, are caused by other [factors], and are the removers of diseases caused by other [factors]; they have as their cause the upper parts of the body. || 31 ||

The meaning is that because the causes of diseases arising from the anterior part of the body and those produced by the causal complex of the posterior part of the body have been demonstrated, those diseases residing in the posterior part of the body—which arise from desire and are established through their own causal effects—become capable of being cured by remedial measures. Anticipating the doubt that these might be incapable of being cured by means such as *recaka* (exhalation) or fasting (*laṅghana*), the remedies for those ailments are now revealed: "Doṣa...

etc. Diseases of the joints of the bones, ears, nose, and so forth, which arise from the absence of the movement of the *doṣas*, are cured by some [remedies] using a surgical instrument (*śastra*). || 32 ||

The humors—Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha—become aggravated. The meaning is that surgical instruments, caustic applications (kṣāra), and thermal cautery (agni-karma) are the remedies for the pains arising from vitiated blood (duṣṭa-rakta) and foreign bodies (śalya) produced by the movement caused by the factors of morbidity at the junctions of the ears, nose, and so forth; they release the blood from the head and bones. Regarding this, there is a statement:
"The disease is difficult to cure when it is treated with instruments and the like, and even more so when there is a combination [of humors];
by the word 'one' (eka), the predominance of certain [factors] is established."

The phrase "remedies for that" means they are not remedies for many types of diseases. Those ailments caused by the *doṣas* are destroyers of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). Remedies for those [poisons] consist of medicinal herbs and the like. On this point, there is a statement:
"One should employ nasal drops, collyrium, and potions for the pacification of poison;
and one should give them to the one who has consumed poison after purging both upwards and downwards."
At the time [of treatment], one should administer fine copper dust mixed with honey to purify the heart;
once the heart is purified, one should then give a *śāṇa* measure of gold powder.
Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, poison does not adhere to one whose heart is marked by gold.
Because of this statement:
"One should protect food and drink from poison, especially that of a lord of the earth; for his security and well-being depend upon them, as do dharma and other virtues which are rooted therein."

Thus, by this other statement as well, the meaning of the Sūtra is made known: that for those whose diseases have arisen from the consumption of substances caused by illness, the very result is the cessation of disease through the application of medicines that remove them; for it is observed that activity toward a result occurs even for the sake of avoiding the undesirable. Therefore, he asks: "How can there be the state of being an enjoyer of all things that increase one's physical constitution? To this, he says: "prakāśamāna... (The one who is free from disease and undecaying [is so] because of consuming the delicious juices that nourish the bodily constituents, which are obtained through the withdrawal of the nectar that issued forth upon attaining the first departure while it was still manifest). 33. [The one who is free from disease and undecaying is so] because of consuming the delicious juices that nourish the bodily constituents, which are obtained through the withdrawal of the nectar that issued forth upon attaining the first departure while it was still manifest.

One who practices yoga—illuminated by the heat produced by the breath-wind arising from the Kuṇḍalinī which is the very nature of the fire (*agni*), having drawn up the nectar descended from the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*) at the first departure [of breath], and having nourished the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*) as appropriate—becomes long-lived. Furthermore, because of consuming the pure essence (*rasa*), the fruit arises; thus, the state of agelessness (*ajaratva*) is well-established. Regarding this, there is a verse by a poet:
"Employing the sixfold qualities (*ṣāḍguṇya*) according to his capacity, he utilizes the elixir (*rasāyana*);
thus his limbs become stable and strong."

It was stated previously that we shall hereafter explain the procedure for the sequence of yoga concerning the body (*śārīra*). Now, in order to describe the fruit consisting of the attainment of the desired goal, the author—intending to show that what was established as "one desiring long life should practice yoga" is difficult for all people because of the abundance of their respective sins and because this [practice] causes suffering—states another aphorism beginning with "kāya":
"One should perform *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac therapy) using substances that increase the vital fluid (*caramadhātu*) during the appropriate time for the body. (34)

"One should employ elixirs (rasāyana) which bestow nourishment upon the bodily constituents (dhātu) and strength to the sense organs," according to this statement. [One should use] those substances that are the best within their respective groups, as measured by their primary qualities.
To that extent, the city of opposing tastes is said to be that elixir (rasāyana).

Thus ends the definition of *rasāyana*. Regarding the sequence in the procedure for *rasāyana* and the procedure for its application: among the substances mentioned in the section on gems (*ratnavarga*), diamond (*vajra*) is the most excellent because it is a metallic substance (*rasadravya*). Among the substances mentioned in the section on jewels (*maṇivarga*), the magnet-stone (*kāntamaṇi*) is the most excellent because it is a metallic substance. Among the categories of minerals (*pāṣāṇavarga*), mica (*abhra*) possesses excellence because it is a metallic substance. Among the categories of substances containing *sattva*, the *sattva* of *bhūnāga* possesses excellence because it is a metallic substance.

Among substances distinguished by the attribute of possessing flavor, mercury (*rasendra*) attains preeminence because it is itself a substance possessing flavor. Among ritual acts such as consecration (*saṃskāra*), the seed-substance (*bīja*) attains preeminence because it is a substance possessing flavor.

In this context, the purpose (*prayojana*) is stated as: "The object of activity arising from the desire for long life, which accomplishes the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) that are the subject matter of Āyurveda. Thus, everything is subsumed, since the knowledge of the causal relationship of each individual factor is the motivator for the knowledge directed toward its respective object. He says "yaḥ" (he who) to indicate that one should know [this] as being thus accomplished through human goals:
"He who knows thus. (35)
The meaning is that it should be understood in the manner thus described.

By this much, the knowledge of the object to be removed (nivartya) and the remover (nivartaka) has arisen. To the question, "How is the fruit, which consists of the supreme human goal (uttama-puruṣārtha), obtained by that? he says: "She" (sā).
He becomes long-lived. || 36 ||

Surely there are many things in the world that bring about cessation. The meaning is this: at one time, the knowledge of all objects of experience must be accomplished; the knowledge that brings about the cessation of all bodies is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Following the knowledge of these categories, the human goal of a long life—which is the effect and cause regarding knowledge—is attained.
He says "that" (*tad*) to show that the very knowledge of these categories is itself the medicine:
"That alone is the medicine. (37)
Immediately after the knowledge of medicine, he explains the act of medical treatment—namely, "that very [knowledge] is the treatment. (38)

Various diseases arise in the bodies of humans, horses, elephants, and so forth. The remedial substances—such as trees, creepers, and other suitable materials—are beneficial through the six types of tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*). He says "tāvat" (to that extent) to indicate that one should observe the subject matter set forth in Āyurveda; that is, one should examine those substances to that extent. || 39 ||

One should examine substances that increase the sense organs, which have as their scope all objects that cause the corruption of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*)—the causes for the non-occurrence of the provocation of the humors (*doṣa*).
He explains the substances consisting of the six tastes: "The tastes...
The tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent; they are the protectors of those [constituents]. (40)

Since the body consists of the seven constituent elements (dhātus), those tastes protect the seven constituent elements respectively; thus, because they preserve the seven constituent elements every day, they are called "protectors" (paritrāṇaka). Regarding this, there is a statement:
"Those tastes are indeed variations of taste according to their essence, and through the conceptualization of degrees of intensity."
Exceeding all calculation, they arise and are to be employed according to the specific faults and their remedies.

The *rasas* (tastes/flavors) are the protectors of that [body], for they pacify the defects (*doṣas*) residing in the body and thus act as its guardians. Since it is inappropriate to state that the *rasas* and so forth are the causes of the manifestation of the provocation (*prakopa*) of the *doṣas*, the *doṣas* themselves are well-known for that purpose. Therefore, because the relationship of cause and effect between the three [humors] and the six [tastes] is established, he says: "It may be... (*syād iti*).
May the tastes—sweet, sour, and pungent—protect you. || 41 ||
Just as those who have balanced humors and those who activate the digestive fire [attain health]. || 42 ||

Those tastes become sweet, sour, and pungent upon digestion. If the tastes are in equilibrium, the *doṣas* are likewise in equilibrium; meaning that those *doṣas*, being free from provocation due to the correspondence with the tastes and other factors, are the stimulators of the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*). On this point, the statement of the Sūtra is: "The post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) of a substance is threefold, consisting of sweet, sour, and pungent."

The threefold classification of the six tastes during digestion has been established. Now, one might object: among the six, this threefold classification appears to indicate that only the three *doṣas* stand in a relationship of cause and effect with the six tastes. What, then, is the status of the other three? To this, he says: "Established. Three [of the tastes] are established in the sixfold digestion. (43)

It has been established that the six tastes, becoming threefold, do not cause the provocation of the *doṣas*. That very point is further specified: "Bitter [taste] is sweet in its post-digestive transformation (*pāka*). (44)
A substance of bitter taste attains sweetness when digestion is performed by the digestive bile (pācaka-pitta).
He states that even an astringent taste, becoming sour like that [bitter] taste, removes the provocation of phlegm and bile—thus he says: "The astringent...
Astringent is a sour taste. (45)

Having become astringent and sour, it imparts the qualities of the substances combined with it during digestion; the meaning is that there exists a causal relationship between the provocation of *kapha* and *pitta* and the astringent-acid taste (*rasa*).

Even the pungent taste (ūṣaṇa-rasa), having become a salty taste (lavaṇa-rasa) during digestion, acts as a cause for the provocation of phlegm (kapha) and wind (pavana); thus, the relationship of cause and effect exists by virtue of its counteracting that [provocation]. He states this with the words: "Pungent is salty in digestion" (ūṣaṇaṃ lavaṇaḥ pāke). || 46 ||
The meaning is that pungent taste, having become a saline substance, removes wind and phlegm (*pavana-kapha*).

Now, it may be asked: the six tastes, beginning with sweet, nourish the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*) specifically increases the blood constituent (*asṛg-dhātu*); for the blood constituent itself is designated as "taste-blood" (*rasa-asṛk*). Thus, the single constituent nourished by astringent taste becomes one; therefore, because it functions as a nourisher by initiating a single taste, it is designated as "one constituent" (*ekadhātu*) in its function of nourishing.

Since it is commonly held that only the six tastes (ṣaḍrasa) nourish the bodily tissues (māṃsadhatu), and because in the world no substance possessing taste is ever seen apart from substances containing the six tastes—and because the absence of such substances is a matter of observed experience—it might be argued: "If disease-producing substances are not observed, and thus the substances that cause them are non-existent, how could there be the application of medical treatises for the purpose of curing those diseases? Anticipating this objection, he says: "By permutation" (vyutkrama). "Substances with permuted tastes are the causes of disorders. (47)

Sweetness and bitterness are friends; astringent and sour tastes are friends; salty and pungent tastes are friends. In the mutual combination of substances other than these with those other than these, there exists the presence of contrary tastes. Therefore, the meaning is that only the two contrary tastes are the causal factors. Consequently, when digestion occurs by virtue of being dependent on karma, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) alone is the regulator therein. The Lord, who is omniscient, He alone bestows the fruit corresponding to one's own karma.

Since it is possible that all types of food might be consumed daily by all bodies, one should therefore station a highly trustworthy scholar near oneself, distinguish between edible and inedible substances, and inform him of everything; then, acting while knowing the causal relationship regarding health through that scholar, one should proceed. On this matter, there is a saying: "A king should station a physician near his palace;
thus he remains ever-watchful in all matters."

The consumption of food that is irregular in its sequence or possesses conflicting tastes is indeed "unequal food" (viṣamānna). Therefore, nothing remains that does not require protection [by the digestive fire]. It is digested by the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni). Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the food eaten day after day is digested by the digestive fire? Through that digestion, the consumed food is reduced to ashes; how then, by differentiating everything into essence (sāra) and waste (kiṭṭa), is the nourishment of the bodily constituents (dhātu) performed? To this, he says: "By the digestive bile" (pācaka). The digestive bile (pācakapitta) digests the food. || 48 ||

Food consumed by the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) is not digested; therefore, it must be processed by the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*). By means of that [bile], having distinguished between the essence (*sāra*) and the waste (*kiṭṭa*), it is capable of performing the function of the waste; this is the meaning. Regarding this, there is a statement:
"In that regard, bile is fivefold in nature and resides between the receptacle of the digested food (*pakvāśaya*) and the receptacle of undigested food (*āmāśaya*)."
Even though it consists of the five elements, it is so called because of the emergence of the qualities of fire.

But surely, the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*) does not digest food alone by separating it into essence (*sāra*) and waste (*kiṭṭa*). Since the humors (*doṣas*), when vitiated, corrupt the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), they must necessarily also digest the humors themselves. Regarding this, there is a saying: "The fire digests the food; it digests the humors, excluding the food; upon the depletion of the humors, it digests the constituents; and indeed, upon the depletion of the constituents, it consumes the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)."

In accordance with this statement, since it appears that only the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) acts as the assistant to the cooker and not that *pitta*, the author states "doṣa... out of dissatisfaction [with that view]:
"Likewise, it is born from the *doṣas*, *dhātus*, *malas*, and heat. (49)

The meaning is that [the digestive fire] digests by differentiating between the humors (*doṣa*) arising from the heat of impurities (*mala-uṣman*) and the bile (*pitta*) along with its disorders. Now, one might ask: "Is the digestion of the humors the cause for the cessation of disease? By means of the digestive bile (*pācaka-pitta*), which dries up the humors through fasting at the edge of the undigested matter (*āmānta*), it digests the disorders situated within those humors. In this regard, the designation "digestive bile" refers specifically to the heat produced by the two coiled [fires] consisting of wind (*anila*) and fire (*anala*); otherwise, it would not be suspected to belong to pure fire alone. With the intention that when the pair [of wind and fire] has removed the humor, they bestow qualities contrary to it, he says:
"The *grahaṇī*. The *grahaṇī* constituent (*kalā*) sustains life-force (*āyus*) and vital energy (*tejas*). || 50 ||

Pācaka-pitta is capable of gathering the qualities of external objects while suppressing and restraining the base qualities residing within the [dosic] constituents; it is thus able to bestow favor upon its own acquired qualities. Because Pācaka-pitta alone possesses the capacity for both suppression and favoring, the term *grahaṇī* is specifically designated as a portion (*kalā*) of pitta. That *kalā* sustains life-force and vital energy. Regarding this, the statement from the *Śārīra-sthāna* says: "The function of the fire of the bodily elements derived from food has been defined as follows:
the digester of food is considered superior to all other digesters."
For they are rooted in that [wind], and their increase or decrease consists of its increase or decrease.
Therefore, one should carefully protect it with wholesome food and drink, properly prepared and appropriate; for when it is stable, life and strength remain stable.

There are many such statements. The term *śikhin* (fire) is well known in the context of the "blazing digit" (*kalājvalana*) precisely because it arises from the bile produced by the wheel of wind and fire generated by the breath rising from the *kuṇḍalinī*. It is established in all schools of thought that *Kuṇḍalinī* consists of fire and wind, and that she possesses bile. That digit is the digit of blazing; as for the claim that she burns the body, that is incorrect. For as long as the food that has been eaten is being thoroughly consumed after being divided into its essential and waste components, [the process continues].

The meaning is that, by virtue of being merely the agent of cooking food, it establishes the function of burning for the wind of the breath arising from Kuṇḍalinī; thus, while residing within the entire body, it performs the service of sustaining life.

Now, it may be argued that what was stated—that the *grahaṇīkalā* maintains the vitality of life—is not tenable; for it is precisely the consumption of wholesome and unwholesome food that effects the maintenance of the body’s firmness. For instance, when one partakes of food and drink after discerning the rules regarding what is salutary and what is unsalutary, satisfaction and nourishment arise; in the absence of such [discernment], emaciation is observed. Therefore, through these two alone—positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—the relationship of cause and effect is established.

If it is argued that when there is a disease that suppresses the consumption of food, that [disease] itself [is the cause], [the author] says "food" (bhakta), because of the lack of satisfaction [in that view]:
by eating food, the *kalā* becomes weak due to the non-obstruction of the *āmāśaya*. || 51 ||

*Bhakta* means food. When the stomach (*āmāśaya*) becomes excessively full by the eating of food, the *pitta-kalā* (the portion of bile) situated within the *kuṇḍalinī* becomes weak; being unable to pervade the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) with the nutrient essence (*rasa*) produced by the digestion resulting from the intake of food, that *kalā* consequently becomes weak. Regarding this, there is the statement of the Sūtra:
"The consumption of both wholesome and unwholesome food mixed together is considered 'equal eating' (*samaśana*).
One should know 'overeating' (*adhyaśana*) to be eating again after having already eaten."
Eating too much or too little at the improper time constitutes irregular diet;
all three of these produce either death or terrible diseases.

The meaning is that for such reasons as these, the *kalā* becomes weak; that very state is called "incompatible diet" (*viruddhāhāra*). Being weak, the *kalā* does not digest food. That disease becomes eightfold. Due to the diversity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces various effects, and because indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) is the primary factor, there arise the complications of fever (*jvaropadrava*) as its subdivisions. He states this with the word "āma": from the excessive filling of the stomach (*āmāśaya*), due to the weakness of the *kalā*, and from the obstruction of the movement of the wind (*pavana*) situated in the stomach, there indeed occurs an aggravation of the wind (*anilaprakopa*).

Due to the weakness of the bodily constituents (*kalā-daurbalyāt*), fevers manifest; the meaning is that fevers do not arise without indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). On this point, the statement from the *Nidāna* is as follows:

"That [fever] arises in eight ways through the humors (*doṣa*)—individually, in combination, or all together—and the external (*āgantuka*) [factors]; therein, the impurities (*mala*) are corrupted by their respective specific causes of corruption."
Having entered the stomach, followed the undigested food (āma), and blocked the channels,
it casts the fire outside from its position in the row of openings.
Moving along with that [fever], causing the entire body to burn and making the limbs excessively hot, they bring about the fever.

Although that fever is one, the causes that produce its complications take various forms; therefore, the meaning is that it manifests in many forms among humans, horses, cattle, elephants, and so forth. The meaning is that fevers arising from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) due to the consumption of food prescribed for each respective species become eightfold according to the distinctions of those complications. As for the claim that "fever born of indigestion is manifested in eight ways," that is incorrect because of the absence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that generates such a distinction; with this in mind, he says: "Of whatever kind... (verse 53). Of whatever kind the *doṣas* are, of that same kind are the fires produced by the provocation of *vāyu*, and of that same kind are the fevers.

The meaning is that those five types of *doṣa*, such as the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*), which arise from causes that provoke the *doṣas* and are produced from tastes contrary to them, become displaced from their own locations and manifest in many forms. Regarding this, there is a statement:
"The cruel one exists in various wombs under diverse names."

By demonstrating the distinction between causes that indicate characteristics contrary to those [of other fevers], once the specific differentiator is known, one can state that fever is indeed a single entity which assumes various forms through its diverse effects. With the underlying sense that "once its characteristics are known, its respective distinctions can also be understood," he says—beginning with "the eyes":
"It burns, setting ablaze the eyes, ears, nose, head, burning sensation, tongue, mouth, and stomach. (54)

In the eyes, ears, nose, and so forth, as well as headache, burning of the tongue, and dryness of the mouth; "in the belly" means an internal heat. From the feet to the head, it burns like fire—this is the meaning of *jvara* (fever). Regarding its prodromal symptoms, the statement in the *Nidāna* is: "Its premonitory signs are lethargy, restlessness, heaviness of the limbs, a bad taste in the mouth, loss of appetite, yawning, and eyes clouded with tears."
Pain in the limbs, indigestion, diminished vitality, excessive sleepiness,
horripilation, stooping, cramps in the calves, and exhaustion [are the symptoms].
In this [body], there is intolerance for wholesome advice,
a fondness for pungent and sour flavors, aversion toward delicious foods, and likewise an intense thirst for children;
and there is an uncaused agitation toward sound, fire, cold, wind, water, shade, and heat.
Following that, desire and aversion arise, and the manifestation of fever occurs.
The meaning is that when one who has developed a fever from consuming incompatible tastes (*viruddharasa*) is characterized by such symptoms, [the specific type of fever] must be recognized.

Although an effect produced by a single cause is unitary, he designates the fever as being conditioned (*aupādhika*) by the distinct increases in *āmadoṣa* generated by the vitiation of the respective *doṣas* through unwholesome tastes—beginning with "limbs" (*aṅga*).

Vāta-fever is characterized by pain in the limbs, obstruction and excessive pressure in the channels of waste, displacement from the pathways of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), and a sensation of the fire moving within the site of the wind (*anilasthala*).

It causes excessive oppression of all the limbs; it causes oppression by excessively obstructing all the channels of impurity (*mala*); and by blocking the movement through the channels of the *dhātus*, it produces disorders such as restlessness and heaviness—this is the meaning. Regarding this, the statement from the *Nidāna* is as follows:
"Due to the irregularity of the coming and going, agitation, softness, sensation, and heat in various parts of the body, various shifting pains arise there."
Numbness in the feet, stiffness, cramps in the calves, fatigue,
a peculiar sensation in the joints, exhaustion in the thighs, and a seizing pain in the waist.
The back feels as if it were being ground to powder, the belly as if it were being squeezed;
the bones seem to break, especially the ribs and limbs.
There is a seizing and piercing pain in the heart, as if by a goad in the chest;
there is a churning in the shoulders, a splitting in the arms, and a pressing sensation in the shoulder-blades.
Inability to chew, yawning of the jaws, ringing in the ears,
piercing pain in the temples, headache, and a bad taste in the mouth [are the symptoms].
Astringent taste in the mouth, or the non-excretion of impurities;
dryness, and reddish discoloration of the skin, face, eyes, nails, urine, and feces.

Excessive salivation, loss of appetite, lack of faith in food, perspiration, sleeplessness, dryness of the throat and lips, thirst, parchedness, vomiting, cough, and despondency are the results of digestion.
In fever caused by Vāta (wind), there is horripilation, tingling in the teeth, trembling,
suppression of sneezing, giddiness, delirium, a desire for warmth, and stooping of the body.

In *pavanapitta* (wind-bile), there is "affliction of the limbs," meaning a crushing pain throughout all the limbs. Due to the channels being filled with wind, there is "obstruction of the pathways of waste," meaning that because all the orifices for waste products are filled with air, the functioning of feces, urine, and so forth becomes difficult. There is "deviation from the natural path of the tissues" (*dhātu*), which means movement in a contrary direction caused by disease. From the wind, there occurs "movement in the place of wind," that is, movement in the place of the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*). Because the site of the fire has shifted, the meaning is that it becomes impossible to digest food.

In that regard, it can be said that when indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arises from the consumption of food whose *rasa* has become vitiated due to the provocation of the *doṣas*, fevers become threefold according to the differentiation of those *doṣas*. There is one fever common to all, which, by becoming threefold through internal differentiation of the *doṣas*, results in four types of fever. Beyond this, it cannot be said that there is a fifth type, "vāta-pitta fever," for the purpose of completing the count of eight fevers.

Apart from the fever explained here, its effect cannot arise because the causal complex (sāmagrī) for its production is absent; for it has been stated that an effect cannot exist without its cause. Due to this underlying intention, he says: "pavana... etc. The disease characterized by the symptoms of both [wind and bile], arising from the vitiation of the rasa-tissue (rasa-dhātu) caused by undigested food (ajīrṇa) born from the discordance of tastes due to wind (pavana) and bile (pitta), and which moves through the blood-tissue (rakta-dhātu) and so forth, is the fever of the provocation of wind and bile (pavanapittaprakopajvara). || 56 ||

Is it not the case that in the aphorism "nanu pavanapittajvaro'sti," the word "asti" (is) is understood as the explanation? One should not express dissatisfaction with the meaning of the aphorism by suggesting that its explanation should be done otherwise because it is not seen in the *Nidāna* treatise. Rather, three types arising from dual combinations appear: fever caused by wind and bile (*pavanapittajvara*), fever caused by wind and phlegm (*pavanaśleṣmajvara*), and fever caused by bile and phlegm (*pittaśleṣmajvara*). This being so, the meaning is that the eightfold nature of fever—including exogenous fever caused by trauma—is clearly elucidated in this authoritative source.

In the *Nidāna*, there is no mention of a dual fever (*dvandvaja-jvara*) characterized primarily by *vāta* and *pitta*, nor are its specific symptoms observed. Rather, eight types of fever are established: one fever of wind and phlegm (*pavana-kapha*), fever of phlegm and bile (*śleṣma-pitta*), and accidental fever due to injury (*āgantuka-abhighāta*). In Āyurveda, the dual fever of wind and bile (*pavana-pitta*) is indeed established as a *dvandva*.

The purport of the Ayurvedic statement is that fever is of eight forms: the common fever (sāmānyajvara) taught by the Supreme Brahman, the three fevers arising from the three doṣas individually, and the three fevers born from combinations of two doṣas. This is because the wind element (*pavana*) is essential for its association with the other two *dhātus*. ... Wind is the master of the other two, due to its pervasiveness (*vibhutva*), its rapid action (*āśukāritva*), its strength (*balitva*), and its tendency to provoke the others.

"One should indicate the predominance of a disease by means of its independence (svātantrya) or dependence on another (pāratantrya). Therefore, the meaning is that those arising from the combination of two [humors] possess three forms. Even in that case, it is logical that *pavana* (vāta), when combined with two others, assumes two forms; the meaning is that because *kapha* and *pitta* are light, they do not possess such strength. Regarding this, there is a statement: "In every way, through the purification or impurity of the *rasas* and so forth, in their respective order..."
Due to the predominance of wind, bile, or phlegm, it generally follows the limit of seven, ten, or twelve days for both liberation and death.

According to this statement, the general meaning is that there are three types born from dual combinations (*dvandvaja*), which, together with the exogenous (*āgantuka*) type, become eightfold. This is because a common fever (*sāmānyajvara*) is liberated from its respective causes at the time when indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) has ceased. Each fever is liberated after seven days once a particular *dhātu* (tissue element) predominates. For fevers born from wind-pitta (*pavanapitta*), wind-kapha (*pavanakapha*), and the dual combinations, the limit is ten or twelve days. For a fever born from phlegm-pitta (*kaphapittajvara*), the limit is one day.

The limit for [fevers] caused by wind-pitta and wind-kapha is ten days; within that time the fever subsides. This cessation occurs when the rasa and other tissues (dhātus) have returned to their normal state. The meaning is that if the rasa and other elements become vitiated (virasa) while residing in the tissues, they abandon the body without exceeding the previously mentioned periods.

Thus—a fever born of wind-kapha disorders, arising from the vitiation of rasa caused by indigestion (ajīrṇa), which moves through the rasa, blood, flesh, and fat tissues, and is accompanied by the symptoms of both [wind and kapha]. || 57 ||

The explanation of this [term] should also be made according to the manner previously stated. He states another defect of the *dvandva* [compound]: "kaphapitta... etc. A disease characterized by both [sets of symptoms], arising from a disorder of phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*), produced by a loss of taste in the bodily fluids (*rasa*) caused by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), and affecting the tissues (*dhātu*) such as bone and marrow, is a fever born of a disorder of phlegm and bile (*kaphapittavikārajātajvara*). || 58 ||

The meaning is that these various modifications arise due to their respective temporal causes. Now, one might object: how is the number of the eight types of fever completed? There are three fevers produced by the three *doṣas* individually; there are three fevers born from combinations of those respective pairs of *doṣas*; and there is one fever born solely from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). Indeed, all fevers are produced precisely from indigestion arising from the vitiation of the *rasa*. This is because the causal relationship between the absence of indigestion and the absence of fever can be stated, as the concomitance (*vyāpti*) between the presence of indigestion and the presence of fever is observed. Furthermore, there exists an authoritative scripture that establishes this rule: "There is no fever without indigestion."
Since it would not be logical for there to be eight types [of fever] together with that [innate fever] as an adventitious state distinct from it, he says—out of this dissatisfaction—"the mind":

"Adventitious fevers are those arising from desire, fear, spirits, injury, and time; their internal burning, dyspnea, wheezing, intoxication, vertigo, fainting, vomiting, diarrhea, grief, anger, and fear are their qualities, while the remedies for those [qualities] are the remedies for these adventitious fevers. (59)

A fever born of mental trauma is a mental fever; the very means of curing it is the attainment of firmness of mind. *Kāma* (lust) is a fever produced by the arising of mental states directed toward objects of pleasure. A fever produced by fear is a fever generated by a contrary cognition regarding an object of constant knowledge—the experience of other things that is not overwhelmed by [the pursuit of] material ends. Such a fever is a "fever of trauma" (*abhighātajvara*). These are indeed fevers born of time and inherent nature (*svabhāva*). There are many such fevers.

Therefore, the meaning is that because even an adventitious fever (āgantuka-jvara) is preceded by the presence [of the doshas], the completion of the number eight is effected by the Sūtra. In that regard, the statement on the etiology is as follows: "In the rainy season, autumn, and spring, the natural (prākṛta) fevers arise respectively from Vāta and the other doshas; any other is unnatural (vaikṛta) and difficult to cure, and the natural fever is generally caused by Vāta."
During the rainy season, the vitiated wind (vāta), combined with bile (pitta) and phlegm (kapha), produces fever;
and in autumn, the bile causes it, followed by the phlegm as its secondary strength.
Due to that [season] being of such a nature and because of the discharge [of humors], there is no danger from fasting therein;
yet in spring, phlegm arises, and subsequently wind and bile may also occur.
Fever that arises from strong [doshas] with only slight defects and is free from complications is curable;
however, it is declared incurable in every respect when there is knowledge of [the presence of] morbid transformation (vikṛti).

The meaning is that thus the symptoms of the eight types of fever have been designated. The diseases—consisting of the humors (doṣas) such as phlegm and bile in their dual combinations, and the tastes produced by those causes which result in a lack of relish—reach as far as the bone and marrow tissues; through a very firm circulation together with the aforementioned humors, and accompanied by the collection of symptoms that cause destruction, the humors become capable of taking away life. This is the meaning.

In that context, when the *grahaṇī* (the digestive faculty) becomes weak, then the *rasas* (nutrient essences), becoming altered in taste (*virasa*) during digestion, produce various diseases caused by their respective factors. In this case, the remedy consists precisely in the absence of the power of the *kalā* (the digestive transformation stage), which serves as the cause for the non-occurrence of the effect. It is stated that "fasting (*laṅghana*) should be practiced until the *doṣas* are digested"; however, this does not logically follow, because the preservation of the absence of *āma* (undigested matter) cannot be the remover of those diseases produced by the cause of the absence of the effect [of *āma*], since there exists the presence of the effect caused by *āma*. To address the doubt as to what the regulating factor (*niyāmaka*) is here, he says: "pavana... etc.
The sequence of treatment, by nourishing the strength of the digestive fire, prevents the initial provocation of the wind and other humors.

Through remedial measures such as medicines, the *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha* become unagitated. By nourishing the strength of the digestive fire (*agni-bala*) with these, one performs whatever action is prescribed; this indeed is the sequence of treatment (*kriyā-krama*).
When the *doṣas* have been diminished by fasting (*laṅghana*), the digestive fire is kindled, and lightness is achieved;
then health, hunger, thirst, relish, digestion, strength, and vitality arise.

Such is the statement. Herein, the sequence of actions consists of performing the treatment that prevents the provocation of the *doṣas* and maintaining the function of the digestive fire (*agni*). He explains precisely what was stated [above] with the verse beginning "pathyāt":

"When the *doṣas* have been diminished by wholesome diet (*pathya*) and the strength of the digestive fire has arisen, one becomes free from hunger, thirst, aversion to food, and exhaustion; and through the proper application of emetics and purgatives according to the division of strength and time, one becomes happy, being freed from the fear of dyspnea, asthma, heart disease, irregular fever, and diarrhea. (61)

By consuming food that is wholesome, moderate, and beneficial, when the *doṣas* have been diminished, one prevents the occurrence of their provocation; therefore, when the requisite conditions are firmly established, one gains strength of the digestive fire (*agni*), as well as hunger, thirst, relish for food, and vitality. If one becomes capable of sustaining the bodily tissues (*dhātus*), then, by subsequently performing the procedures of emesis and purgation, one becomes free from the fear of dyspnea, cough, heart disease, and irregular fevers, and thus attains happiness. The meaning is that such a person attains longevity.

But is this not also untenable? It is incorrect to say that the bodily constituents (dhātus) nourish themselves by consuming wholesome food, for it is possible to describe a relationship of cause and effect between the consumption of food and the indigestion arising from it. Therefore, since it is possible to describe a relationship of cause and effect between the stomach and the fire (analena) which has performed its function through the process of digestion into essence and waste, he says: "Āma... [Verse 62]:
"The *āma* situated in the stomach (*āmāśaya*) is the producer of the strength of all the bodily constituents."

The food produced from the consumption of eatables and drinks, by transforming the constituent elements (*dhātu*) according to their respective natures, nourishes them and discards the waste; by that [waste], it fills the stomach. When the stomach is full by that means, it nourishes the constituent elements—this is the meaning. Regarding this, there is a statement in the Sūtra:

"When feces and urine have been discharged, when the heart is perfectly clear, when the humors (*doṣa*) follow their own paths, when belching is purified, when hunger has arrived, and when the wind moves in its proper direction..."
Likewise, when the digestive fire is stimulated, the sense organs are clear, and the body is light, one should take food according to the prescribed rules; for that is considered the proper time.
One should consume food that is regulated by rules, timely, and wholesome for the purpose of completely filling the stomach (*āmāśaya*).

Now, one might object: "Since the six tastes of substances, upon digestion, establish their respective tastes within the tissues (*dhātus*), and the tissues, being satisfied, fill the stomach with that flavorful liquid—then, because the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*) would be weak and thus incapable of performing its function, how could there be a causal relationship between those two? Anticipating this objection, he says: "By the *samāna* wind...
"The *samāna* wind, inflaming the organs located therein, performs the act of digestion. (63)

When the fire is ignited by the *samāna* wind, that *kalā* digests everything consumed. The point is that it is easy to explain the relationship of cause and effect between the action of drying up the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and the body, and the function of the stomach (*āmāśaya*). On this matter, there is a statement from the Sūtra:
"The *samāna* moves everywhere within the abdominal cavity situated near the fire;
it supports, it digests, it differentiates, and it releases."
The meaning is that while the digestive fire (*rasa*) moves within the stomach (*koṣṭha*), he [the physician] should thus release the weakness of the *kalā* (the digestive faculty).

Now, one might object: if the weak fire is incapable of digesting the food situated in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), then the statement that "they kindle it with the *samāna* wind" is inconsistent; for in the case of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arising from overeating, how can the weakness of the *grahaṇī-kalā*—which resides in the stomach and holds the food—be removed by the pure *samāna* wind alone, without a substance that has become ignited by fire? To this, he says: "When vitiated," etc. (*duṣṭa*).
This is the ritual procedure for the disease of malignant grahaṇī. || 64 ||
On the contrary, the meaning is that when the *grahaṇīkalā* is vitiated, it becomes the cause of disease;
having entered that very [organ] along with the corrupted food (*āma*),
they produce effects by causing constipation (*viṣṭambhana*) leading to *alasaka*, and by inducing downward displacement (*cyāvana*) leading to *viṣūcikā*.

Thus says the scriptural statement (*sūtra*). By the consumption of incompatible food, the *grahaṇīkalā* becomes vitiated; being thus corrupted, it is incapable of performing its function of assimilating the food consumed and nourishing the constituent elements (*dhātu*). Since the morbid state of the *grahaṇīkalā* and the diseases arising from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) stand in a relationship of cause and effect, the meaning is that the vitiated *grahaṇī* is established as the producer of disease.

Now, surely the kindling of the mild digestive fire must occur through the gastric fire (*jaṭharānala*). Since an external fire is inappropriate here, it must be manifested by the *samāna* wind. Thinking that this [fire] alone is not capable [of digestion] without the consumption of remedial substances, he mentions the remedial substance: "liquid" (*drava*).
Dividing the food from time to time with liquid substances, the *samāna* wind, having reached the stomach, causes the fire residing there to blaze and thus digests it. (65)

In reality, however, one who eats food together with liquid substances consumes it after having turned those condiments into a liquid state. That consumed food, being situated near the fire and acted upon by the *samāna* wind—which is ignited and divides the food into essence (*sāra*) and waste (*kiṭṭa*)—causes it to reach the heart; then, by means of the *prāṇa* wind, it causes it to enter the stomach (*āhārakoṣṭha*), and subsequently causes it to go to the region of the navel. Therefore, that *kalā*, being excessively ignited, does not possess the quality of nourishing the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).

On the contrary, it causes the drying up of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). When the *grahaṇīkalā* is excessively inflamed, it vitiates the constituents; therefore, that organ digests [the food] leaving only a residue of burning. It also becomes a cause of the depletion of the constituents. Likewise, it may digest the internal organs (*āśaya*). That too is designated as "indigestion" (*ajīrṇa*). Because its capacity to nourish the constituents has fallen away, that digestion is not considered a state of fire (*anagnikṛti*); this is what is meant by "it is not pleasing. On this point there is a saying: "The humors (*doṣa*) reach the state of accumulation (*caya*) and so forth either immediately or even not at all within the body;
yet they suddenly pervade the entire body from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head."
But when provoked, the *mala* recedes only slightly, like a torrent of water;
the various and innumerable transformations of the provoked *malas* do not leave the body. Therefore, one must apply the remedy according to their causes, symptoms, and therapeutic means.

Now, if one has eaten liquid substances until the elements (dhātus) are satisfied, and if that food is then digested by the excessive fire among the five types of digestive bile (pācakapitta), that food so digested will not provide nourishment for the elements. Furthermore, its digestion will not even be completed. Consequently, the internal receptacles (āśayas) become empty and, like indigestion (ajīrṇa), cause a provocation of the food. Anticipating this objection, he says: "When empty, [the wind] becomes provoked. "When empty, the wind (vāyu) becomes provoked. (66)
Regarding this, there is a statement in the Sūtra:
"When it is weak, the food releases itself even while raw;
for the strength of the *grahaṇī* is indeed the digestive fire (*agni*), and that fire is also dependent on the strength of the *grahaṇī*."
Therefore, when the fire is vitiated, the grahaṇī becomes corrupted and becomes the cause of disease;
for food is that which nourishes the humors, tissues, vitality, strength, and complexion.

Thus says the *Śārīra*: Due to the excessive heat of the fire, food becomes liquefied; because of this, even when the food is digested without remainder, the receptacles (āśayas) become empty. Within those empty receptacles, the wind (vāyu) increases, because wind possesses the quality of dryness (*rūkṣa*). The meaning is that when a receptacle is empty, the wind becomes aggravated. In this regard, wind is dry, light, white, rough, subtle, and mobile. Just as combustion occurs when there is contact with fuel that serves as the cause for the kindling of fire, so too does [the wind] flare up.

Because the *āśayas* (receptacles) have become empty, and because there is an absence of liquid substances that serve as the fuel for the fire, the *grahaṇīkalā* cannot remain due to its inherent quality of self-ignition; for this reason, he says "analā" [in the verse], meaning:
the fire becomes diminished. || 67 ||

In reality, however, even this is untenable; for when the stomach (*āmāśaya*) is empty, no cause for the provocation of the wind (*pavana*) is observed. Furthermore, the state of being the cause of the effect of health (*anāmaya*) is the state of preserving health, since that [health] has non-disease as its cause. Consequently, the aphorism "when [the stomach] is empty, the wind becomes provoked" would be rendered meaningless. This is because the *grahaṇīkalā* (the digestive tract) is situated near the *samāna* wind, and thus the causal complex for combustion is present there.
