If it is argued that the sūtra "the fire becomes small" would also be redundant, [we reply: because of the consumption of food which benefits the five vital breaths (prāṇas), there is an increase in what benefits the humors (doṣas); moreover, there is specifically an excess of waste products such as feces and urine.

Wherever the causality of the provocation of *pavana* (vāyu) is observed when the *āśaya* (receptacle) is empty, there this rule applies: when a disease is seen to have arisen from the suppression of feces and urine, and the *āśaya* has been emptied by a purgative substance that removes that [suppression], then the causality of the provocation of *pavana* is observed therein; such is the intended meaning, because it is so observed. Due to the emptiness of the *āmāśaya*, there is dryness (*rūkṣatā*) of the *vāta*.

The quality of dryness (*rūkṣaguṇatva*) was first acquired [by the body], and due to the consumption of incompatible tastes, indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arises; because of this, the food is not digested by being separated into its essential nutrient (*sāra*) and waste (*kiṭṭa*), and thus the liquid portion, such as feces and urine, appears abnormal. In that state, because the *siddhakalā* has not been ignited, digestion occurs through a fire that has arisen [from that abnormality]; when disease is observed resulting from this, it would be caused by the provocation of the humors (*doṣaprakopa*) due to the emptiness of the internal organs (*āśaya*) created by that opposing movement.

Therefore, the meaning is that the aphorism, "When [the stomach] is empty, the wind becomes aggravated," has been correctly established. Regarding the aggravation of disease born of indigestion, since there is a necessity to kindle the digestive fire arising from the emptiness of the *āmāśaya* (stomach), he first explains the substance of *rasa* (nutrient fluid) which is the cause of an action free from the aggravation of *pavana* (wind): "The sweet...
[Verse 68]. Food that has become sweet, when consumed, removes the aggravation of *pavana*.

By means of its inherently established sweet taste, which—conditioned by the specific substances and actions involved—prevents the occurrence of wind (vāyu) provocation, it renders the food consumed sweet and thereby removes the provocation of the wind; thus, it is called "hāraka" (the remover). When there is provocation of that site due to the emptiness of the stomach (āmāśaya), one should first eat a substance possessing a sweet taste that counteracts that [provocation], because there is no room for the digestive fire (agni) to cook the food already eaten. Similarly, a substance that becomes sweet at the end [of digestion] is a remover of wind provocation. In this regard:

The post-digestive transformation (*vipāka*) of a substance is of three kinds, consisting of sweet, sour, and pungent. According to this statement, does a substance that becomes sweet upon digestion remove the *doṣas*, or is it a substance that is inherently possessed of a sweet taste? It cannot be the first case, because all substances undergo these three types of transformation during digestion; thus, there would be no regulating factor to determine that only a specific substance removes the *doṣas*. Nor can it be the second case, for if it were simply a substance possessing a sweet taste that removes all *doṣas*, then the following statement would be contradicted:
"Buttermilk and the like destroy Vāta, while the three [groups] beginning with the bitter (bitter, astringent, and pungent) destroy Kapha."
Those that are astringent, bitter, and sweet produce pitta, while others produce it as well.

According to this statement, since there is no delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*), the status of being a regulator belongs to the one alone; therefore, the claim that "this is a unity" is incorrect. For instance, when one first eats food together with sweet-tasting condiments (*vyañjana*), that food becomes sour upon reaching the heart. Then, having entered the heart, it subsequently moves to the stomach (*pakvāśaya*). Thereafter, it becomes pungent in taste and is digested. Therefore, the substance that was sweet...

The meaning is that this sutra is purposeful because it is understood to remove the provocation of the wind (*pavana-prakopa*) in that same manner. Indeed, the emptiness of the stomach (*āmāśaya-riktatva*) alone is the cause for the provocation of the wind, since no other cause for the effect of the provocation of bile (*pitta-prakopa*) is observed. It must be stated that the food consumed day after day, while being digested, nourishes the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) by way of eliminating the three humors (*doṣa*).

In that regard, since the cause of the provocation of *pitta* is not perceived, it must be stated that the food consumed day after day, while being digested, effects the removal of the three *doṣas*. Since the knowledge of the effect does not arise without the knowledge of the cause, and because there is a lack of perception regarding the cause of that *pitta*-provocation, [the author], expressing a sense of dissatisfaction, says: "Situated in the heart...
[Verse 69]: Food soaked in the *kapha* located in the heart becomes sour and destroys the provocation of *pitta*.

The meaning of this is as follows: the fact that the stomach (*āmāśaya*) is a cause for the provocation of wind (*pavana*) has been established. However, keeping in mind the underlying dissatisfaction—that it could be argued that indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) is the cause for the provocation of bile (*pitta*), yet its effect (the provocation) is not observed as the cause [of indigestion]—an alternative explanation is offered by some; he states this alternative dissatisfaction with the words "the heart" (*hṛd*).

The meaning of this is as follows: for one who has consumed substances that have become sweet, that [substance], having entered the throat by means of the *udāna* wind and reached the heart, becomes saturated with *kapha* and turns sour due to the defect of its association. That taste (*rasa*) causes the provocation of *pitta*. On this point, there is a sūtra:
"Sour [taste] stimulates the digestive fire, is unctuous, beneficial for the heart, digestive, and appetizing;
it is hot in potency (*vīrya*), cold in touch, pleasing, laxative, and light."
It alleviates phlegm, bile, and blood, and facilitates the downward movement of obstructed wind.

According to this statement, since no cause for the provocation of *pitta* is observed, the meaning is that the sweet taste (*svādurasa*), which counteracts *pitta*, removes the provocation of *pitta*. In this regard, the statement of the Sūtra—"Buttermilk and similar substances destroy wind (*māruta*)"—has been established.
Following this statement, the fact that the sweet taste produces an absence of *pitta*-provocation has been demonstrated. The meaning of these two statements from the Sūtra is easy to understand.

But surely, by way of pacifying the provocation of the *doṣas*, the sweet and sour tastes nourish the *dhātus* and thereby cause the provocation of *vāta*. Therefore, [the author], feeling that [the previous statement] might not preclude that [provocation], says: "The sweet...
The sweet and sour tastes produce *kapha*. (70)

Both sweet taste (*madhurasa*) and sour taste (*amlarasa*) cause the provocation of phlegm (*kapha*). Sweet taste is a rasa that counteracts wind (*pavana*) and bile (*pitta*); having become those respective substances, it enters within. Its very function of counteracting them is its human purpose (*puruṣārtha*). Nevertheless, it is said to be a cause of phlegm. Bitter (*tikta*), pungent (*uṣaṇa*), and astringent (*kaṣāya*) tastes are the counteractors of phlegm. Thus, the sixfold group of tastes possesses the capacity to counteract the humors (*doṣa*). Among these tastes, sweet and sour tastes become the causes for the provocation of wind and bile.

For it is said that these two indeed cause an increase in *kapha*. Yet, both of them—the sweet taste (*svādurasa*) and the acid taste (*amlarasa*), which is a derivative taste (*aupādhikarasa*)—are causes for the provocation of digestive bile (*pacanapitta*). On the contrary, they also become causes for the provocation of *vāta*. To address the doubt as to how they can be eliminators of *kapha*, he says: "The heart... (verse 71).
[The acid taste] removes the *kapha* located in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), which has been dried by the fire after the food has descended from the heart.

It removes the phlegm located in the stomach (*āmāśaya*) that has been consumed as food and dried by the digestive fire. That very food, having been consumed and remaining sequentially in the receptacles (*āśaya*) and so forth, performs the separation of the essence (*sāra*) and waste (*kiṭṭa*); while it is being digested and situated in the stomach, that very food becomes pungent in taste (*kaṭurasa*). Regarding this, there is a statement in the Sūtra:
"The digestion (*vipāka*) of a substance is threefold, consisting of sweet, sour, and pungent."

In accordance with this statement, even that which is sweet by its own nature becomes sour through the influence of an adjunct (*aupādhika*) and thereby generates bile (*pitta*). Following that, the functional activity of the sour taste must be described: residing in the stomach (*āmāśaya*), it becomes pungent and acts as a remover of phlegm (*kapha*); such is the meaning. The intention is that the capacity of the pungent taste to remove phlegm is well-known. "The pungent [taste] agitates the tip of the tongue, causing a tingling sensation;
it causes discharge from the eyes, nose, and mouth, and seems to burn the cheeks."

Now, it has been stated that the Sūtra teaches that a single substance performs a threefold division; however, this is questionable. First, the efficacy of the sweet taste alone must be explained. Immediately thereafter, the efficacy of the sour taste must be explained, because the pungent taste likewise possesses such efficacy. Therefore, it is the equilibrium of the sweet, sour, and pungent tastes that is established [in the Sūtra], and not the totality of factors that merely alleviate disease. Regarding this, the statement of the Sūtra is as follows:
"Disease is the disharmony of the *doṣas*; the equilibrium of the *doṣas* is health."

The statement "this word is the authority here" refers to the fact that the totality (sāmagrī) observed as the equilibrium of the three defects (doṣas) must be produced by those three alone. With the intention of addressing the question, "If that is so, what becomes of the other tastes?", it was stated that "that must be considered. In this regard, the statement from the *Śārīra* is:
"First, one should consider that which is born of the six tastes and has become sweet;
having turned into foam, it reaches phlegm (kapha), and then, through burning (vidāha), it attains acidity."
Bile, falling from the stomach and having fallen further,
is dried by the fire, becomes cooked, condensed, and turns pungent and windy.

The meaning is that a substance possessing a single taste alone undergoes a threefold division during digestion. Food is consumed there in order to bring about the non-disordered state of the digestive fires (*dhātu*) and the humors (*doṣa*)—wind, bile, and phlegm—since those [humors] consist of many tastes. Those tastes yield their respective fruits as impelled by their specific rules; whatever tastes a person perceives, the fruit is bestowed through the power of experiencing those perceived tastes. Thus one should understand tastes.

Therefore, because the result prescribed by the respective rules is obtained only from the consumption of substances possessing many flavors, he says "sweet," etc., out of a sense of dissatisfaction [with the previous view]: "Sweet, sour, and pungent—these flavors, when cooked, are balanced in their humors (doṣas) and bestow the fruit of their combination according to their respective natures. (72)

All tastes, through the process of digestion, become sweet, sour, and pungent; thus, the tastes as they truly exist are themselves the givers of their respective fruits. He provides the resolution with the word "ya" (those which):
those tastes which are the causes thereof, from which the fires are produced, and which nourish the bodily constituents (dhātus) produced by those fires. || 73 ||

The meaning of this is as follows: "Those which have that as their cause" means those which have become the causes for the effects produced by that [pitta]. The state of being fire (*analatva*)—which arises from the various effects of consuming substances with specific tastes—is indeed the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*). The meaning of the aphorism is that the tastes, once digested by the fire, perform the nourishment of the respective elements beneficial to each of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Regarding this, there is a statement: "The five heats—earthy, watery, fiery, airy, and ethereal—successively digest the five qualities of food, such as the earthy and so forth, according to their own nature."
And when matured, those elements residing in the body nourish their own respective elemental qualities separately:
the earthly ones nourish only the earthly, and the remaining ones nourish the remaining qualities.

Since every substance that constitutes the body consists of the five elements, food containing a predominance of the earth element nourishes the earth and wind constituents of a body desiring to eat such food. Food containing a predominance of the water element brings about an increase in the water constituents of a body desiring to eat such food. Likewise, food containing a predominance of the fire element brings about an increase in the fire constituents of a body desiring to eat such food; and the same applies to air.

The meaning is that even the ethereal element (*nābhasa*) likewise causes growth. Whatever substance a rasa is associated with, it bestows the qualities of that very substance. From substances in which the five elements predominate, the constituent parts that manifest those respective substances increase. Therefore, to the question of what the relationship of cause and effect was for rasa and the others, he says:
"From rasa [comes] blood" (verse 74).

The meaning is that the astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*) is the cause for the nourishing activity that increases the blood produced from the blood-element (*rakta-dhātu*). For it is said, "The essence (*rasa*) is indeed the blood; the essence is truly that. Therefore, because of the identity between the essence and the blood, the six tastes are the nourishers of the seven elements (*dhātu*). Regarding this, there is a statement from the *Śārīra*: "From the essence comes blood, from that flesh, from flesh fat, and from that bone;
from bone marrow, from that semen, and from semen the embryo is born."

Thus, it is made known that there exists a cause-and-effect relationship between the seven *dhātus* and the six [tastes], beginning with *rasa*. While it may be granted that a substance possessing *rasa* generates the blood *dhatu*, what is the specific rule governing the statement that the astringent (*kaṣāya*) taste generates the blood *dhatu*? It has been established that the *doṣas* and other factors act as causes for the state of health (*aroga*); furthermore, it is intended here that they generate the *dhātus* through the process of nourishing them by way of a succession of stages.

The point is that once the causal relationship between the absence of disorders of the *doṣas* and *dhātus*, and [the presence of] *rasa* and the other elements, is understood, it is well-established that the effect of bodily health exists only when *rasa* is present. By consuming food with an astringent (*kaṣāya*) taste, the *rasa-dhātu* and *rakta-dhātu* flourish. The meaning is that the pungent (*ūṣaṇa*) taste, having nourished the blood element (*rakta-dhātu*), becomes the cause for the growth of the flesh element (*māṃsa-dhātu*). From *rasa* comes blood; from that, flesh; from flesh, fat (*medas*); from fat, bone (*asthi*); from bone, marrow (*majjā*); from marrow, semen (*śukla*); and from semen, the embryo (*garbha*) arises.

The taste arising from the element of space (*ākāśa*) is sweet (*madhura*), it nourishes the white constituent (*śukladhātu*), and its contrary taste destroys it. The taste arising from the element of earth (*pṛthivī*) nourishes the marrow constituent (*majjādhātu*), and its contrary taste destroys it. The pungent taste arising from the element of fire (*tejas*) nourishes the bone constituent (*asthidhātu*), and its contrary taste destroys it. Saline taste is a sub-variety of the pungent taste. The bitter taste arising from the element of wind (*pavana*) increases the flesh and fat constituents; since fat is also of the nature of flesh, no distinction is intended here.

The bitter taste (kaṣāya-rasa) originates from the ether element (gaganabhūta) and provides the tissues of plasma and blood, because plasma and blood constitute a single tissue. Therefore, one designates the body as being composed of the five elements—namely, "five"—meaning the body consists of the five elements. || 75 ||

It is not tenable that the five elements exist separately within this body, because the body consists of defects (*doṣa*), constituents (*dhātu*), impurities (*mala*), and receptacles (*āśaya*). Since each [element] is a single great substance (*mahādravya*), there is no commingling; nor is there a partial commingling of each one, because it is impossible to separate them, and because in each individual body no substance endowed with the specific characteristics of those [elements] is perceived.

Keeping in mind the intention that the statement "the body consists of the five elements" is not capable of withstanding scrutiny, [the author] first designates the characteristic of the connection with the space-element (gagana-bhūta) and its effect, stating: "The ear...
[Verse 76]. It is heard by means of the two channels (sirā) that convey the quality of sound situated within the ear.

The meaning of this is as follows: "Antasthitau" means those two which abide within (*antasthitau*). "Śabdaguṇakau" means those two for which sound is the quality; the suffix *kap* is used here in the sense of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. [Sound] is heard by means of the two channels (*sirā*) that inform one of objects present and suitable [for perception]. Regarding this, there is a statement from the *Śārīra*:
"Each limb has six parts, and its sub-limbs include the eyes, heart, and so forth.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their qualities, respectively."
In the subsequent [elements], there is a sequence of the increase of one quality each for air, fire, water, and earth.

A substance possessing eleven qualities pervades the body. That which has smell as its quality is perceived in the nose. That characterized by the qualities of water is perceived in the tongue. A substance possessing the qualities of fire appears in the eyes; in this regard, the cognition that perceives form is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The substance of air possesses the quality of touch. The substance of space possesses the quality of sound, because sound is perceived in the space delimited by the ear-cavity.

Therefore, the statement that "the body consists of the five elements" is well-established. The meaning is that the definition of space (*ākāśa*) as "that which possesses sound as its quality" is well-known. [Objection: Sound is heard through the two channels located within the ear. To what extent, then, does the fact that space constitutes the body cohere with this? [Response: "When X exists, Y exists."

By the maxim "in the absence of which there is the absence of which," the apprehension of sound—which is perceived by the auditory organ—does not, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), prove that the body is composed of ether (*ākāśa*). Therefore, the refutation given against the statement that "the body consists of the five elements" would be unavoidable; anticipating this objection, he says: "Sound. Ether has sound as its quality. (77)

That substance which has sound as its quality is ether (*ākāśa*), possessing the quality of sound; the suffix *kap* is used here in the sense of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because ether has sound as its quality. When there is contact with another substance, cognition having that [contact] as its object arises. By the principle of "otherwise it would be inexplicable" (*anyathānupapatti*), the pervasiveness of air (*vāyu*) is understood. (Because it is perceived as a substance devoid of qualities, like ether) the fact that air is cognizable solely through touch is established, since air is experienced as possessing the quality of touch—that is, "air possesses the quality of touch. That which has touch as its quality is "possessing the quality of touch."

When there is contact with another substance, a cognition having that as its object arises; for, while it is not an object for other senses, it possesses that [specific] objectivity. Furthermore, the fact that the wind—which is the object of the cognition whose object is the cognition dependent on that [skin]—pervades a portion of the body is well-known. The skin is produced from the elements of rasa (plasma) and blood. It is established that the skin, which does not serve as a substrate for the other elements, sustains the wind in the form of inhalation and exhalation—thus [it is said]:
"The skin, produced from the elements of rasa and blood, carries inhalation and exhalation."
The wind, enveloped by the seven layers of skin and elements, is born from space. || 79 ||

In both cases, with respect to the effect pervaded by the nature of being a *dhātu*, a single body possesses the relationship of cause and effect. By this much, it is established that the skin alone is produced from the *rasa* and *asṛj* *dhātus*, and that it is the pervader of the skins of bodies belonging to all species; such is the meaning. That air (*vāyu*) is produced from space (*ākāśa*), because it is established by valid cognition through the scriptural statement, "From space, air [is born]. Now, it must be stated that the body possesses the property of holding air, and, in the absence of an obstacle to burning, the property of holding fire; otherwise, it would behave like the air in the sky.

It should not be said that [the body] is unfit for the practice of *dhāraṇā* on account of the wind (*anila*), because the function of digesting food by the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) is not observed to be caused by the absence of an obstacle to burning; rather, the bile located in the *kuṇḍalinī* is useful for performing functions like fire. The digestive faculty (*grahaṇīkalā*) performs the function of digestion as its specific action. Therefore, since it is improper to say that the body is composed of fire alone, he says "six" out of this underlying intention.
The fire residing in the eye, enveloped by fifty-six vessels, digests food endowed with five forms; this fire, born of wind, perceives its own object. || 80 ||
The meaning of this is as follows:

the fire (*anala*)—that is, the fire in the form of *tejas*—which resides within the eye-spheres enveloped by fifty-six channels (*sirā*), acts as an obstacle to the burning of the constituent parts of substances enveloped by flames because it is situated in the middle of the eyeball surrounded by such channels. Having thus become the digestive faculty (*grahaṇī-kalā*) for the purpose of digesting consumed food, that fire remains pervading the body. It perceives even objects located at a great distance, provided they belong to its own class (*sajātīya*).

Therefore, that which sees while situated in the center of the eyeball is indeed the fire (*analas*) that pervades the entire body. The fire born of wind (*anilaja-analas*) makes even a distant object its domain by means of the substance of the fire born of wind residing within itself. Even though the wind is extremely distant, it is grasped as an object by the eye. However, the bile (*pitta*) located in the *kuṇḍalī* is for the purpose of digesting all consumed food; because that *kuṇḍalī* has the nature of a deity, that bile also becomes like fire (*taijasa*).

For the purpose of perceiving objects within its range, the ocular faculty (*cakṣus*), which consists of the fiery element (*taijasa*), makes even a distant object its domain. This means that this faculty is capable of digesting everything.

The gustatory faculty (*rasanendriya*) is conceptualized for the purpose of distinguishing between tastes (*rasa*) and other qualities; the substance arising from that [faculty] is for the purpose of distinguishing those very qualities, because it is impossible to perceive anything distinct from what has arisen there by means of that [faculty]. Keeping this intention in mind, he explains the nature of the gustatory faculty with the word "saliva" (*lālā*):
by means of saliva, which takes the form of taste, one perceives taste through the tongue while distinguishing the various differences among tastes and so forth. || 81 ||

The saliva, which has the form of taste (*rasa*), resides at the tip of the tongue and grasps objects; its meaning is that it performs the differentiation of consumed food. Now, one might object: "It is understood according to the rules that the *grahaṇī* organ, when undamaged, performs the differentiation of tastes and so forth. Even though that [organ] is undamaged, the knowledge of such differentiation is not experienced. If the causal relationship between the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) and the knowledge of that differentiation is apprehended, then how can the causal relationship between the water of saliva situated at the tip of the tongue and that [differentiation] be apprehended? For the differentiation of those [tastes] is established through other means (*anyathāsiddha*).

Therefore, because its nature as something not produced from anything else is not perceived, he says—out of this very unease—"the tongue": "The tongue, situated in two vessels, is the perceiver of all tastes. (82)

In the case of the gustatory organ (*rasanendriya*), which is of the nature of fire (*analaja*), tastes and so forth are experienced by making various manifest flavors (*vyañjana*) through the mere contact of taste and touch. This is because it is established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The meaning is that its support by two channels, its capacity to perceive all tastes, and its being produced from fire are perceived only of this [organ] and not of any other. The definition of earth is "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*). Earth, possessing odor, is that which perceives the odors of the entire body.

The body is composed of earth (*pārthiva*), because the quality of odor (*gandha*) is perceived therein; that which is not so is not thus, like a body of air (*vāyavya*). The phrase "like" provides the example of those who dwell in the world of air (*vāyuloka*). However, in this [body], all odors are perceived due to the presence of earthly constituents. Therefore, [the opponent] says "four," out of dissatisfaction with the claim that the body consists of the five elements (*pañcabhūtātmaka*). There are twenty-four channels (*sirā*) originating at the tip of the nose; the earth [element] awakens one to the twenty-four principles (*tattva*). (83)
All the principles (tattvas) appear at the tip of the nose. Therefore, with the underlying dissatisfaction as to how the body could be a composite of earthy elements, he says:
"That which is enveloped by veins. From food, beings are born; once born, they grow through food; it is eaten and it eats beings; therefore, it is called "food" (anna). (84)

All bodies are composed of earth; the other elements—water, fire, air, and space—are present merely to fulfill their function as the means for perceiving the effects of that [earth]. Therefore, one might suspect that a body could consist of other constituent parts as well—this is raised by the word "nāsikā" (nose).
Those [elements] which have become modifications through the excess of the nose are perceived at the tip of the nose.

Each of those possesses qualities fixed to it, namely the qualities of the form of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*), and they serve as the supports for the twenty-four channels (*sirā*). All the constituent parts abound in qualities such as fragrance. Therefore, since it is established by all people that the body is composed of earth (*pārthiva*), it can be said that this body is enveloped by these channels.

The aphorism stating that the body consists of the humors (*doṣa*), elements (*dhātu*), and wastes (*mala*), and is composed of the five elements preceded by the cognition of perceiving odors, is untenable; it is not appropriate to say that [the soul] exists having entered the body while remaining in a location distinct from that body. Furthermore, the statement "beings are born from food" is also not logically consistent, for if that were so, there would be the birth of offspring at all times for everyone—if this objection is raised, we reply as follows:

Because all defects reside within the causal complex of eating food, such an effect [as a pure body] is not possible. However, when there is union between a woman and a man through the medium of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), offspring are produced. Therefore, among the seven constituents (*dhātu*) situated within the body, three are derived from the mother and three from the father; the union of these two is the *yoni*. Regarding the statement that "the *yoni* is the conjunction of semen and blood," it is the father’s semen that is to be joined. This conjunction occurs when there is a combination of many [particles] through the power of this semen.

The white element (*śukla*) is derived from the father; it is the final constituent (*dhātu*) consisting of a single essence. Since the singular number would otherwise be inappropriate, the characteristic of the womb (*yoni*) is the combination of the paternal elements of bone, marrow, and semen. Likewise, blood, flesh, and fat are derived from the mother; the womb is the combination of these. Therefore, when there is union between a woman and a man, the designation "womb" refers specifically to the convergence of the causal complex that produces the seven constituents (*dhātu*).

Regarding the term "blood" (*rakta*), there is an identity between the nutrient fluid (*rasa*) and the blood; that they constitute a single constituent element (*dhātu*) has already been established previously. Thus, there are four elements derived from the mother and three derived from the father. He explains that the union of these two sets of elements is the *yoni* (the womb/source): "derived from the mother."
The body consists of blood, flesh, and fat derived from the mother; marrow, bone, and semen derived from the father; and it is composed of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. || 86 ||

Women possess four elements (*dhātu*), while men possess three elements. This is because, due to the influence of the combination of fewer or more [elements], the female state was mentioned first. Therefore, there is a union of woman and man. Regarding this, they say: "I bow to the Mother and Father, the parents of the world, Pārvatī and Parameśvara;
they are the female and male portions of that single form, manifested through the desire to create."
At the time of birth, those two alone are remembered as the parents of everyone.

The singular term [for "parents"] is used to represent either one of the two; therefore, the meaning is that the *yoni* (womb/source) consists of the union of the elements (*dhātu*) of both. Furthermore, it is stated that there are four female elements (*strī-dhātu*) in order to indicate that the *yoni* alone is the cause for the production of the world. Although the father and the mother are both manifold causes, it is *prakṛti* (primordial nature) itself that is the cause for the origin of the world.

Since the scriptural authority exists—namely, "From *prakṛti* comes the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One, the Ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); from the Ego-sense, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)"—the mother, being the most excellent, is mentioned first. Regarding this, there is the statement of the *Śārīra*:
Accompanied by the subtle primary elements (mahābhūtas) which are of the nature of seeds and follow the sentient being,
it gradually grows within the mother's womb through the nourishment derived from her food.

[Objection: Surely there are four elements derived from the mother and three derived from the father; by that much alone, the production of the body is established. Beyond this, of which substance are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* the qualities (*guṇa*)? Only in such a case could the relationship of cause and effect between quality and the possessor of quality (*guṇin*) be asserted. Since no substance in the form of a possessor of these qualities is observed, qualities cannot exist without a possessor of qualities. Therefore, the portion of the aphorism stating that "the body consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*" would be rendered meaningless. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Life-span" (*āyuḥ*).
It produces a body characterized by long life, health, splendor, strength, and purity, as well as the qualities of sattva. || 87 ||

It has been established that such are the characteristics of the quality *sattva*. Now, since substance (*dravya*) is the substratum of qualities, it follows that being the substratum of qualities is the defining feature of substance. The qualities belong to the five elements; thus, they reside in their respective substances and are therefore established as distinct from them. Consequently, one might designate these qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* as belonging to this [particular] substance. Among those [qualities], smell and the rest—namely, smell, taste, form, touch, and sound—are the individual delimiters of the five elements.

Because those three qualities (*guṇas*) cannot serve as limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*), and because it is not logically possible for a quality to exist apart from its possessor (*guṇin*), he states "longevity" (*āyuḥ*) due to another underlying intention:

longevity, health, luster, and strength—these are the essential forms that manifest from the body; for since the cause must otherwise be untenable, one is required to postulate these specific effects. On this point, there is a statement from the *Śārīra*:
"Just as the luster of the sun's rays is refracted by a crystal..."

As a sentient being enters the womb, it is seen to be accompanied by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Because the causal factors that produce these respective qualities follow along with their effects—since the state of being caused is governed by its causes—the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* arise from the consumption of various causal substances and reside within the individual soul (*jīvātman*). For this very reason, its possession of qualities (*guṇitva*) has been established. It is just like the light residing in a crystal: when the sharp rays of the sun appear, fire is perceived therein; in that case, the conjunction of the crystal and the solar rays is the cause.

When the causal complex for the production of an effect is present, this rule must be understood: wherever an effect is observed due to the immediate proximity of the causal complex, [that is the case]. In that regard, when the entire causal complex—including the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) and other factors—is present within a portion of the living being, and upon the entry of wholesome or unwholesome food brought by the mother and father, it nourishes the constituent elements (dhātus) based in the digestive faculty (grahaṇīkalā); the aggregate of chyle (rasa), blood (asṛj), flesh (māṃsa), and fat (medas) is then designated as the "blood-element" (raktadhātu).

The paternal portion, however, is white (*śukla*). The combination of bone, marrow, and semen is designated as "white. Otherwise, it would be impossible to state that the blood and semen alone are the causes for the production of the effect, which is the body composed of the seven constituents (*dhātu*). Therefore, this is for the purpose of making known that the body consists of the seven constituents.
In this context, that which is derived from the mother is soft—the blood, flesh, marrow, semen, and so forth;
whereas that which is derived from the father is firm—the semen, the vessels, the bones, the hair, and so forth.
According to this statement,
there is a verse from the *Kāvyavacana*:
"Woman and man are the two portions of your own self, O you whose form is divided by the desire to create."
At the time of birth, those two alone are remembered as the parents of everyone;

therefore, the union of semen and blood is called the *yoni*. By the power of the term *sānnipātya*, the confluence of the elements consisting of the seed is what is meant by *sānnipātya*. Regarding this, there is a statement from the *Śārīra*:
"The consciousness of the trees of the mind [arises] in births within various *yoni*s."

The meaning is that in those various wombs, consciousness manifests as a mind (citta) of such a kind. Now, an objection is raised: since it has been established that the body consists of seven constituents—three paternal and four maternal—the body is presented as the effect of its causes. If this were so, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti, for it says: "From the Self, space was produced; from space, air. Since these [elements] exist [prior to the body], they nourish the constituents (dhātus) situated within it. Therefore, because that previous explanation is untenable, he says "where" (yatra), out of a sense of dissatisfaction:
"Wherever the essences (rasas) reside, those born from their respective elements are the nourishers of the constituents."

Wherever they reside, the excellence of their respective defining qualities (guṇa) shines forth; thus, the rasas, being delimited by those respective defining qualities, become the generators of those specific bodily constituents (dhātu), and as such, those rasas are nourishers of the constituents.

Now, therefore, concerning the primary cause: who is the agent, and likewise the extent of his action; that very thing is the remedy. The body, covered by the mind, desire, the heart, phlegm, semen, and so forth, consists of ten [components].
Thus ends the commentary on the first question of Āyurveda composed by Yogānandanātha; it is well-known, esteemed by great men, an exposition upon every sūtra, and beneficial to the world.
The first question in Āyurveda is completed; now begins the second question.
Through the compassionate glance of their teacher, these [sages] [beheld] her who dwells within the cave of the heart...

We perpetually offer salutations here to Mahātripurasundarī, who speaks the eightfold speech, who dwells within the six lotuses as their companions in succession, and who exists as the physician for the cave of the heart.

The state of being a disease has been established. It is appropriate to state that the nourishment of the *dhātus* occurs through the cessation of disease. This being the case, since it is well-known in the world that there is no substance capable of removing [disease] without the *rasas* (tastes) such as *rasa* and the rest—which are the very things that counteract the provocation of the *doṣas*—the author, expressing dissatisfaction with this [view], says: "Possessing two tastes," and so forth.
[A substance] possessing two tastes, a taste deficient in its purpose, or a taste entirely devoid of its purpose, is a warder-off of *vāyu*.

The sweet taste (*svādurasa*) pacifies and prevents the provocation of *rasa* (the nutrient fluid). Even the provocation of *pitta* should be countered by the sweet taste. It is possible to state that a single substance may counteract two opposing defects (*doṣa*). A substance deficient in two tastes or excessive in one taste counteracts the provocation of both *pavana* (vāyu) and *pitta*. A substance with an excess of sweet taste counteracts the provocation of *pitta*. Therefore, it is established in the aphorism (*sūtra*) that a substance with an excess of taste removes *pavana*: "Astringent, bitter, and sweet [tastes] provoke *pitta," so say others.

Now, one might object: "The body consists of seven constituents (dhātus), and that which is produced from it must also consist of seven constituents. How many vessels (sirās) are there in the body? What are the receptacles (āśayas), vital points (marmas), and joints (sandhis)? Why is it that, setting all those aside, only three paternal and four maternal constituents are mentioned? Bearing this intention in mind, the author explains the vessels, vital points, bones, joints, receptacles, internal fires, and so forth existing therein, beginning with the word "six" (ṣaḍ).
There are sixty thousand thirty channels, thirty arrows, two hundred and ten joints, and eighty-nine carriers of sinews and muscles. || 2 ||

The entire body is everywhere enveloped by vessels (sirās). Likewise, the bones, the joints, and the internal receptacles (āśayas)—the whole body is covered by all these. All of this is composed of the elements (bhūtamaya); the meaning is that they arise from the mother alone. The humors (doṣas) are enveloped by vessels, located in the vital points (marmans), and situated within the receptacles. These, being the pathways of the humors in a healthy person, enter the other constituent elements (dhātus) when [diseased]. For the purpose of discerning the humors in both the healthy and the unhealthy states, one must analyze the entire body; having gained knowledge of each part, it is indeed possible to remove the provocation of the humors. Thus, he analyzes the vessels and other structures situated within the body.

Now, an objection may be raised: it is improper to say that the sweet taste (*svādurasa*), having entered within and become [the essence], removes the provocation of the wind (*anilaprakopa*), because its function is otherwise established by its role as an auxiliary to the nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). [For] the skin, the internal essences, blood, and so forth are made to circulate through their respective channels according to rule; how then could the sweet taste possess the quality of warding off the provocation of the wind? To address this doubt, he says: "Seven... [The text continues: ...Indeed, the sevenfold nature of the earth—which supports the seven constituents—and the sevenfold nature of the wind are dependent [on this]. Since the sweet taste, having entered within, becomes [the essence] and removes the provocation of the wind, [this is not improper]. Because it acts as an auxiliary to the task of nourishing the constituents, it is established in another way. The skin, the internal essences, blood, and so forth are set into circulation in their proper paths. How could the sweet taste have the power to prevent the provocation of the wind? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Seven..."

The seven elements are the support, and there are seven intentions; born from the digestive faculty (*grahaṇī*) situated in their midst, the sweet-tasting [substance] removes the provocation of *vāyu*. || 3 ||

The meaning of this is as follows: the seven layers of skin sustain the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*s), such as lymph-chyle (*rasa*), blood, and so forth. Furthermore, it is *anila* (the wind element) alone that maintains the state of stability by ensuring that the movement of lymph-chyle and other substances does not deviate from their proper channels. Since its quality consists solely in providing such assistance, it is logical that a sweet taste (*svādurasa*) removes the provocation of *anila*. It is *anila* alone that performs the service of facilitating the coming and going [of these substances]. Therefore, the meaning is that it is appropriate to consume substances with a sweet taste for the purpose of pacifying the provocation of *anila*. Regarding this, there is a statement in the Sūtra:
Wind, which consists of five aspects through its divisions such as prāṇa and the rest, is here [designated as] prāṇa when it moves to the head.
Moving through the chest and throat, it sustains the intellect, the heart, the senses, and the mind;
it effects the acts of spitting, coughing, belching, breathing out, and the swallowing of food.
The region of the chest is the seat of udāna, which moves through the nose, the navel, and the throat.
It counteracts the activity of speech, effort, vitality, strength, complexion, and their respective functions.
Thus, according to this statement, wind pervades the entire body; therefore, the meaning is that a sweet taste pacifies the provocation of wind.

Now, since it is universally known that such *āśayas* (receptacles) reside within all bodies and are observed to produce their respective effects as prescribed by rule, there are seven *āśayas* containing the seven *dhātus* (tissues), owing to their being common to all. This being the case, it would be impossible to determine among these *āśayas* the specific site for the generation of offspring. Furthermore, may the sweet taste born of the five digestive fires (*pācakapitta*) and wind (*anila*), which increases the seven skins, vessels, tissues, and *āśayas*, remove the provocation of wind.

Keeping in mind the well-known fact that this [element] is the sole cause of both disease and health for all bodies, he explains the location that serves as the cause for the generation of offspring: "The eighth," etc.
The eighth is the womb (*garbhāśaya*) of women. (4)
The meaning is that the intention (āśaya) which has procreation as its cause is possible only for women. In this regard, there is a statement from the *Śārīra*:
"The uterus (*garbhāśaya*) is the eighth [organ] of women, located between the bile-tract (*pitta-pakvāśaya*)."

The bile (*pitta*) is not conceived as being located in any other part of the digestive tract besides the stomach (*āśaya*); rather, because it is only in women that the causality for conception (*garbhādhāna*) is possible, the name of the woman is uttered first, followed by the name of the man in all the scriptures—this is declared to be the order of precedence. At the outset, the very constituent element (*dhātu*) of both the woman and the man enters the womb and produces [the embryo]. If that were so, the resulting mass would be merely a confluence of the constituent elements.

According to the principle that "as long as there is a cause, so long is there an effect," the absence of a cause for the observed production of the limbs is now seen. To address the objection—"How can an effect arise without a cause?"—he says, "Its own [heat]" (svam), out of a sense of unease.
Its own [heat]: the *ojas* whose essence is the flowing fluid by means of its own heat. Each [limb] has its own self as its very cause. (5)

One’s own limbs are produced from within oneself alone; otherwise, how could pleasure and pain be established through their positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)? Since the experience of pleasure and pain exists when there is the production of another [limb] through that positive and negative concomitance, it follows that in the production of another [being], one’s own body alone is the cause. Regarding this, there is a verse from the *Kāvya*:
"You know yourself by yourself; you create yourself by yourself;
and by yourself, as the agent, you dissolve yourself by yourself."
The scriptural statement:
"You arise from limb after limb; you are born from the heart.
You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns."

By the heat located in the womb, the mother’s essence of *pitta* flows forth; the essence produced from that becomes the generator of the head. That which consists of this essence becomes the *ojas*. By the heat located in the womb, the mother’s essence of the hands flows forth; the essence produced from that becomes the generator of the hands. By the heat located in the womb, the mother’s essence of the feet flows forth; the essence produced from that becomes the generator of the feet. The same applies to the sides.

The back, abdomen, shanks, penis, genitals, anus, limbs, and so forth—these parts of the mother's body flow [into the fetus] while it resides in the womb through her internal heat (*ūṣman*). Those [parts] that are produced from the essence (*sāra*) of that [heat] become the primary constituents (*sāra*) of those [corresponding] parts of the fetus. The nutritional essences (*rasa*) derived from the mother’s food nourish the other limbs distinct from those. Those limbs consist of the blood-element (*rakta-bhūta*). In each respective limb, the wind (*vāyu*) becomes provoked. To pacify that provocation of the wind, one should consume substances possessing sweet taste (*svādu-rasa*), which serve as medicine by means of neutralizing that [provocation].
Now, for the sake of making this known, he states the constituent parts that produce it: "The head," and so forth.
The head, hands, feet, sides, back, thighs, belly, shanks, penis, anus, and limbs constitute the body. || 6 ||

These flow into the mother’s womb; the meaning is that the various limbs manifest from them. Those fluids nourish the opening of the womb. By means of the heat residing in the womb, essences flow from the mother’s feet, sides, back, belly, calves, penis, and genitals. The essences produced by those [original] essences are the generators of the limbs such as the sides. And from that, the *ojas* (vital essence) consisting of those fluids comes into being, because the essence of the pregnant woman’s head, flesh, and internal organs has been drawn into the fetus.

Because the provocation of the wind (*pavana*) is appropriate within the womb, for that reason one should consume substances that are sweet and flavorful. Since the emergence of the limbs occurs after [the body has formed], and because the ears, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are extremely delicate, they are incapable of leaving their respective locations to enter the womb; therefore, how could the manifestation of the ears and other senses occur? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The ears... and so forth.
Likewise, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose. || 7 ||

All the sense organs and even the subtle bodies [enter], because the five elements residing in the mother’s own body are perceived within the womb; since the sense organs and so forth possess the specific qualities of those respective elements, and it is impossible to maintain that qualities exist without their possessor, the meaning is that they enter the womb together with their respective sense organs due to the entry of those respective elements.

Since the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth, by virtue of being substantial entities, flow through their respective internal heat (*svoṣman*), they serve as the cause for effects in those specific forms; thus, the constituent parts of the mother’s elements, having flowed [into the womb], become like a space for the *rasa* (nutritive essence) that causes the growth of the fetal parts within the uterus. Therefore, it can be said that between these two there exists a relationship of cause and effect. However, in this case, how could a substance devoid of form (*nirākṛti*) yet possessing apertures enter elsewhere? Because it lacks the state of being a composite substance with parts—such as the head, hands, and so forth—there is no opportunity for entry into a space that requires such parts.
However, it is impossible to say that this partless substance flows into the womb as the essence of the parts residing in its own mother; because of this incongruity, he says: "With apertures.
There are three vessels with apertures within each of the three [sections]; in the two feet, there are thirty-four vessels with apertures within.

The meaning of this is as follows: some internal channels are porous, each surrounded by three sirās (veins). Because space is all-pervasive and the body consists of the five elements, the element of space also enters it; since that [space] is a substance enveloped by three sets of three sirās, it is logical that [the embryo] should be discharged into the womb. Here, the meaning is that there are seven hundred such porous internal channels, each surrounded by three sirās, which are situated from the feet to the head.

It has been stated that the limbs flow right there into the mother’s womb. He explains this very point with the words beginning "pāda" (the feet). Because the lotus situated at the pair of feet was caused to flow into the womb, that pair of feet was produced. The two vowels *a* and *ā* were also produced right there. Immediately thereafter, [the body] becomes enveloped by the three channels (*sirā*) located at the mother’s knees within the mother’s womb. To the question of how the very essence of the mother’s limbs manifests there in the form of a mass of a corpse, he says: "pāda... etc. The lotus situated at the feet generates the vowel *a* and is enveloped by thirty-four channels. (9)

The meaning is that from the feet, which had become the limbs of the Mother, there arose a pair of feet consisting of the vowels *a* and *avaṇa* situated on those feet; specifically, on the left foot, it consisted of the vowel *a* together with the *svarita* and *pluta* accents. Regarding the upper parts of those [feet], namely the pair of knees, he says "the knees," explaining that they arose, each with its own heat, as consisting of flowing essence, surrounded by thirty-four veins, and producing the vowel *i* residing in the lotus of the knee.

The meaning is that the pair of knees was produced from the two syllables *i* and *va*, accompanied by the *svarita* and *pluta* accents, which were discharged into the womb and enveloped by thirty-four vessels within the porous interior; these [knees] arose through the consumption of substances that serve as the substratum for the humors of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*), which are impelled by the syllables that facilitate the functions of going and coming. He states that the knee-lotus—located in the region of the shanks that facilitate the functions of going and coming, and enveloped by twenty vessels within the porous interior—was produced: "the syllable *u*" (*uvarṇa*). The lotus in the region of the thighs, whose essence is the syllable *u*, is enveloped by twenty vessels.

The meaning is that the lotus of the thigh, which produces the vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* along with the circumflex (*svarita*) and protracted (*pluta*) sounds, flows with its own respective essence through its own heat and manifests within the womb.

He states—beginning with "the vowel *ṛ*"—that the lotus of the hip region, which makes known the vowels and is situated within the hollows of the pelvic area, is seen flowing with its own essence through its own heat;
this lotus is enveloped by twenty vessels. (12)

The lotus of the thigh region caused by the vowel *ṛ* is covered by twenty vessels and serves as the support for the vowels accompanied by the *svarita* and *pluta* accents; the lotus of the left and right thighs, covered by twenty vessels and assisted by the heat of the digestive bile (*pācaka-pitta*), produces much weight through the action of going and coming, and it manifests in the womb from the very body of the mother—this is the meaning.
He says "the vowel *lṛ*" [in verse 13] to state that the lotus of the pelvic region, which makes known the vowel *lṛ*, was likewise born;
the lotus of the pelvic region that generates the vowel *lṛ* is covered by thirty-four vessels.
The meaning is that the lotus of the pelvic region (*śroṇipradeśapadma*), which supports the weight of the upper body and is enveloped by internal vessels possessing apertures, becomes manifest.

Regarding the statement "the *e*-vowel," he explains that the very limbs of the practitioner become the support for the *e*-vowel—the support for the *e*-vowel, the circumflex (*svarita*), and the protracted (*pluta*) vowels—which is situated at the waist (*kaṭi*), the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and attached to the groin and its sides. Thus he says: "the *e*-vowel.
The lotus located in the pelvic region, which generates the *e*-vowel, is enveloped by thirty-four vessels. (14)
The lotus situated at the side within the seed-syllable, which produces the various colors, is enveloped by thirty-four veins. || 15 ||
The lotus situated in the groin region, which produces the menstrual flow, is surrounded by twelve vessels. || 16 ||
The lotus situated in the region of the seed-syllable, which generates the upper face, is encircled by two veins. || 17 ||

The meaning is that the vowels *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, and so forth, which serve for the functions of the couple, manifest within the womb as the lotus of the pelvic region and the lotus of the groin region—each surrounded by thirty-four channels—and as the mother's limbs, each flowing with its own essence of rasa through its respective heat.

These are the supports for the phonemes *e*, *ai*, *o*, and *au*, which consist of long, circumflex, and protracted vowels. Among the group of consonants that serve as the cause for the secondary suffixes (*anubandha*), [the text] explains the lotus that is the cause of the act of union—which serves as the cause for the generation of progeny and is situated at the side of the lotus supporting the *e*-vowels—by the words "ka-kha.
That lotus at its side, which generates the phonemes *ka* and *kha*, is enveloped by sixteen channels (*sirā*).

The meaning is as follows: the operation of the palate and the lips, which is the collection of causes for making the vowel *au* known—consisting of the wind enclosed within the thirty-four hollow channels that indicate the vowels *a*, *va*, and *r*—together with the marrow (*majjan*) accompanied by the long, circumflex, and protracted [vowels], being situated at its side, brings forth the space of the auditory cavity (*śrotrākāśa*).

He explains the lotus of the male organ (*meḍhrapadma*), which assists in the act of union, which is covered internally by sixty-three channels (*sirā*) with openings, which serves as the support for the deity of the syllable *ga*, which is the support for the semen produced from the seven bodily fluids (*dhātu-rasa*), and which consists of all the channels and elements—the lotus that is the abode of the god of love:
"The region of the male organ, which generates the syllable *ga*, is covered by sixty-three channels. (19)

Just as a mass (piṇḍa) comes to be in the womb, so too the substance produced from the essence of the mother’s food flows through its own respective heat; this should be stated to arise from the "penis-lotus" (*meḍhrapadma*), for it appears as a male-like mass. This is because, since it lacks the limbs of the mother, the [mother's] penis-lotus is unsuitable [as its source]. Nor should it be said that this description of its manifestation is improper, according to the principle that "one becomes a son due to the predominance of semen," and also because of the definition stating that the "conjunction of semen and blood is the womb" (*yoni*).

The union of these two is the *yoni*. The description of that [union] is the account of the manifestation of the respective limbs; because the lotus of the penis (*meḍhrapadma*) is the cause wherever there is a predominance of the semen residing in the male due to the transformation of the mother’s food, there is the account of the manifestation resulting from the conjunction of semen and blood, as well as their subsequent growth.

The meaning is as follows: each [organ] flows with its own heat (*uṣman*) in the form of fluid; thus, the manifestation of the male organ (*puṃliṅga*) is the increase of that which is produced by their conjunction (*sānnipātika*). Furthermore, because the female organ (*strīliṅga*) is also a "lotus of the vulva" (*meḍhrapadma*), it is logical to speak of its origin and the growth of its parts. Since both—the lotus of the male organ residing in the male and the lotus of the female organ residing in the female—are the abodes of the God of Love (*manmatha*), and due to the influence of the specific condition arising from the predominance of semen (*retaḥ*), it is appropriate that the growth of the parts of the lotus which is the cause of the long penis (*dīrghameḍhra*) occurs through its residence in the male; this is the intended sense.

Having distinguished the lotus located in the back region, which serves as the support for the lotus of the penis (*meḍhra*) and is surrounded by female-oriented channels, he shows it: "The word *ṅa*.
The lotus situated in the back region, which is the cause for the utterance of the sound *ṅ*, is surrounded by thirty-four channels. (20)

The meaning is as follows: one should worship the lotus in the region of the back, which is surrounded by thirty-four channels within the hollow *sarandhraka* and serves as the support for the deity of the letter *ṅa*; it bears the weight of the upper limbs and the entire body; it performs the action characterized by movement in the form of coming and going through the feet, knees, calves, thighs, waist, and hips; it experiences only the fruit that assists in the act of sexual union; and it serves as the support for the downward-moving wind (*apāna-vāyu*) and the locus for the region of the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*), being the cause for the expulsion of the waste produced therein.

Now, it has been stated that in the lotus of the generative organ (*meḍhra-padma*), which is common to both women and men, the very vocal tones produced by each respective caste (*jāti*) are the indicators of the body of that particular caste; furthermore, the castes born therein indicate even the differentiation of the body through those very tones.

Since the anal aperture situated in each respective location is also possessed of openings, and since the apertures located in the vulva, the penis, and the *meḍhra*-lotus vary in their deficiency or excess apart from the anal region, [the author], keeping in mind the intention that— apart from the path of the anal aperture which indicates the sound produced by a particular caste— the [wind] exiting through the channels of the veins supporting the apertures of the penis and *meḍhra* becomes the indicator of the knowledge of the distinctions between the letters (*varṇa*) through the scent, explains the deity of the letters supported by the gateway of the anus, beginning with "Ṅa."
The lotus in the region of the back, which is the cause of articulation, is surrounded by thirty-four channels. || 21 ||

The lotus at the back region, which serves as the support for the deity associated with the letter *ṅa* and is enveloped by thirty-four vessels (*sirā*), fulfills its purpose merely by being the opening of the back-region lotus through the passage of feces; thus, it indicates the non-difference between the vowels and their corresponding consonants—this is the meaning.

He explains that the lotus at the anus, which is the support for all internal organs (*āśaya*) and is surrounded by a circular ring, and the lotus at the penis which supports the colors of the vessels surrounding the source of creation (*yoni*), consists of the deities of the *ca* and *cha* letters; he reveals this in the words "ca cha. The side-lotus that produces the letters *ca* and *cha* is enveloped by fourteen vessels. || 22 ||

The meaning is that within the lotus encircled by the curved shape of the *guda*-lotus, the side-lotus—which consists of the deity of the letter *cha* and serves as the cause for the exit of the vital air (*pavana*)—manifests in the womb.
He states that the abdominal wind-lotus, which serves as the support for the digestive bile (*pācaka-pitta*) in the form of the stomach fire, manifests: "jajha" etc.
The abdominal wind-lotus, which is the cause for the utterance of the letter *ja*, is surrounded by fourteen channels (*sirā*). (23)

Because it serves as the support for the six lotuses which are the forms of the deities of the winds located in the *kuṇḍalinī* and the *ādhāra*, the navel-lotus—which is the support for the wind in the form of inhalation and exhalation and is nourished by the essence produced from the mother’s food—reveals its nature as the interior of the lotus-stalk situated within the *ālavāla*. He explains this with the syllable *ña*:
"The lotus in the region of the navel, which produces the letter *ña*, is surrounded by twenty channels (*sirā*). (24)

The meaning is as follows: the lotus at the region of the navel—which serves as the support for the wind located in the *kuṇḍalinī* and its sides, which possesses internal channels and is surrounded by twenty veins—is of the nature of the deity of the syllable *ña*; it generates the digestive fire (*pācaka-pitta-agni*), and through the heat of the breath-wind born from the fire-wheel (*agnicakra*), it produces the nectar situated in the thousand-petaled lotus of the head.

He explains the wind-cakra enveloped by the kuṇḍalinī in the form of the vessels surrounding the navel-aperture, and the wind-cakra enveloped by the navel-lotus which is surrounded internally within the apertures by thirty vessels—[expressing this] as "ṭaṭha.
The lotus in the region of the navel, which produces the phonemes ṭa and ṭha, is surrounded by thirty vessels. (25)

The meaning is that the wind-wheel (pavana-cakra) situated at the navel, which consists of the deity of the letters *ṭa* and *ṭha*, is enveloped by thirty channels; originating from the wind that serves as the support for Kuṇḍalī and is composed of the essence of the mother’s food, it nourishes the womb and manifests.

He says "ḍa-ḍha" to explain that the channel-wheel (ālavāla-cakra) located at the sides of the navel, which produces the line of body hair (romarājī), consists of the deity of the letters *ḍa* and *ḍha* and is enveloped by twenty-two channels; it arises from the flow of the essence produced by the mother’s food and grows as the branch of the line of hair in the womb.
It is caused by firm coloration, situated at the side of the line of body hair, and enveloped by twenty-two veins. || 26 ||

The meaning is that by means of the wind enveloped by the twenty-two channels within the hollow interior of the *sarandhraka*, the lotus of the two sides is produced, caused by the hair-line (*romarājī*) which brings the deity of the syllable *ḍa* to the cavity of the ear.
He explains the heart-lotus, which is the fruit of that hair-line, with the words "the syllable *ṇa*":
the heart-lotus, which is the support for the syllable *ṇa*, is enveloped by thirty channels.
The meaning is that the heart-lotus arises enveloped by thirty channels.
He states that the lotus of the two breasts, which manifests all the vowels and is enveloped by fifty channels, is likewise: "In the same way.
Thus, the lotus of the two breasts, which produces the phonemes, is enveloped by fifty channels.

The two lotus-like breasts are superior, being the cause for manifesting beautiful sounds; like the two lotus-like breasts, they indicate the vocal organ (*ghoṣadhātu*) of men. Having the form of a fleshy knot, they serve as the substratum for vowels including the long, circumflex, and protracted ones. Such a pair of breasts, consisting of flowing essence through their respective internal heat (*uṣman*), is produced from the transformation of the mother’s food; the meaning is that this pair of breasts arises within the womb.
He says that the lotus located in the region of the throat within the hollow part is produced as the cause for the manifestation of the letter *da*. Regarding the phrase "it is produced" (*jāyate*):
the lotus in the region of the throat which produces the letter *da* is enveloped by fifty channels (*sirā*).

The meaning is that the lotus in the region of the throat—which serves as the support for all letters, manifests all the channels, and is caused by the transformation of the mother’s food-essence (*rasa*) in the womb—is produced.
He says that [the lotus] arises covered by internal vessels with apertures, having the nature of the deities of the nine syllables including the *anusvāra*—thus he says "not" (*na*).
The lotus of the neck, which produces the nine syllables, is covered by sixteen vessels. (30)

The meaning is that the lotus of the neck (*grīvā-padma*) is produced within the womb, consisting of the nine phonemes (*navārṇa*), surrounded by sixteen vessels (*sirā*). The meaning is that the lotus, which serves as the support for the limbs of the neck and consists of the deities of the nine phonemes and the *anusvāra* residing in the station of the head, enters the mother’s womb and the limb of the neck is produced.

He says that the region of the arms is the locus of the phonemes *pa* and *pha*, a lotus enveloped by sixteen vessels, which is the mother’s limb, flowing with its own essence of rasa through its own heat, and whose nature is the deity of the phonemes *pa* and *pha*. Thus he says: "pa-pha.
The lotus of the arms, which produces the phonemes *pa* and *pha*, is enveloped by sixteen vessels.

The meaning is that the lotus which produces the *pa* and *pha* phonemes, enveloped by sixteen vessels in the two arms and situated within the hollow interior of the lower arm region, manifests in the womb.

He says that the lotus located in the inner region of the tongue, which has as its cause the binding of taste and so forth by means of the saliva situated on the tip of the tongue, which consists of the deity of the letter *ba*, and which is surrounded by two vessels, enters the womb containing the essence flowing from the mother’s body and becomes the lotus of taste-binding—thus he says, "babha.
The lotus in the region of the forearm, which generates the letter *ba* and is surrounded by fifty vessels, [is described]. 32.

The meaning is that the *prakoṣṭha*-lotus (the lotus of the forearm) emerges within the womb; it is the indicator of the letter *ba*, the lotus for the binding of the *rasa* (taste/flavor), possessing internal cavities and covered by fifty channels (*sirā*), having the deity of the letter *ba* as its essence, produced from the essence of the consumption of flavorful substances, and having flowed forth from the mother’s body.

He says "ma" to indicate that the hand-lotus is born, which takes the form of a dot accompanied by an *anusvāra*, has the deity of the letter *ma* as its essence, and makes known the placement of the hands that conveys the understanding of all meanings arising from the utterance of words concerning the objects of the mind.
It is the cause for the utterance of the letter *ma*, it makes known all words and their meanings, it holds a lotus in its hand, and it is enveloped by fifty channels (*sirā*). || 33 ||

The meaning is that the lotus-like hand appears, pervading all the veins of the same class which convey knowledge regarding the objects of sound and meaning dependent upon the activity of the palate and the lips.

He says that the lotus located at the tip of the tongue—which makes known the taste and other qualities of the saliva situated there, which consists of the deity of the letter *ya*, and which is encircled by two vessels—is the lotus that binds the rasa flowing from the mother’s limb; this [lotus] is born in the womb. He states: "The letter *ya*," etc.
The lotus that binds the *rasa*, which makes known the letter *ya*, is encircled by two vessels. (34)

The meaning is that the lotus situated at the tip of the tongue arises within the womb as the cause that makes all phonemes known, manifested in the form of saliva and consisting of the essence of the letter *ya*.

He explains that, by the power of the transformation of the mother’s food-essence, the lotus at the side and tip of the tongue arises in the womb as the essence of the deity of the letter *ra*, which resides within the cavity at the side of the lotus located at the tip of the tongue—thus he says "the letter *ra*.
The lotus of the lips, which produces the letter *ra*, is surrounded by sixteen vessels (*sirā*).
It produces the letter *la*, is situated in the region of Vācaspati, and is encircled by two channels.

The meaning is that the lotus-like lips, situated in the region of Vācaspati which produces all the phonemes, are seen within the womb as each [lip] flows with its own essence of rasa through its own internal heat (ūṣman).

He says "va" to explain that the lotus situated at the tip of the nose arises as the indicator of the phoneme *va*, which consists of twenty-four channels (*sirā*), is presided over by its respective deity, and consists of flowing essence through its own heat.
The lotus situated at the tip of the nose, which produces the phoneme *va*, is enveloped by thirty-four channels. (37)
The meaning is that the fragrant earth, possessing the ultimate fragrance inherent in all substances and enveloped by thirty-four veins, enters the womb and manifests while emitting its scent.

He says that the lotus situated in the two palates, covered by individual channels and serving as the cause for the utterance of the letter *śa*, reaches the region of the mouth and becomes the lotus of the ear-region—thus he says "śa":
"The lotus of the scent-bearer (*gandhavaha*), which makes known the letter *śa*, is covered by two channels. (38)

He explains that the two lotuses of the palate, which consist of the deities corresponding to the phoneme *ṣa* and are enveloped by two vessels (*sirā*), produce the water in the form of saliva located in the sense organ of taste—stating: "the syllable *ṣa*.
The two lotuses of the palate that generate the phoneme *ṣa* are each enveloped by a single vessel.

The meaning is that the letter *ṣa* arises when the air, having reached the auditory organ (*śrotrendriya*) via the two channels supported by the region of the palate, comes into proximity with the causal complex consisting of the activity of the palate and the lips.
He says that the lotus of the eye, which serves as the support for the color [of the iris], is born surrounded by fifty veins—referring to "it" (sā).
The lotus located in the region of the eye, which makes the color known, is surrounded by fifty-four veins. || 40 ||
The meaning is that the lotus of the eye-pupil of each respective person, which indicates its own phoneme, manifests within the womb.
He states that the lotus of the region of the wings, covered by two veins and possessing internal apertures, manifests— namely, "ha"—
meaning the lotus of the wing-region that produces the sound *ha* is covered by two veins.
The meaning is that from the mother’s food and drink, that which consists of the deity of the syllable *la* is born.

He states that the lotus in the region of the outer corner of the eye (*apāṅga*) manifests as consisting of the deity of the syllable *la*, covered by two channels within the *sarandhrakā*: "la" [iti].
The lotus in the region of the outer corner of the eye, which produces the syllable *la*, is enveloped by two channels.
The meaning is that the lotus of the mother’s side-glance, born from the essence of the mother’s food, manifests within the womb.

He states that the lotus of the row of thirty-two teeth, encircled by individual channels and consisting of the deity of the letter *kṣa*, is born—thus he says "kṣa. The lotus in the region of the rows of teeth, which indicates the letter *kṣa*, is encircled by thirty channels. (43)
The meaning is that the lotus of the row of teeth, born from the essence of the mother’s food, manifests within the womb.
He states that the lotus of the cheeks, enveloped by fifteen vessels and consisting of the deity of the letter *ra*, appears in the womb—thus he says "the letter *repha*.
The lotus of the cheeks, which produces the letter *repha*, consists of the deity of the letter *ra*.

The meaning is that the lotus of the cheek (*kapolapadma*), which consists of the deities of the letter *repha*, manifests within the womb (*garbhāśaya*). The lotus of the limbs, which is the support for the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa*, is presided over by the limbs beginning with the feet; for it possesses the knowledge of the phonemes that indicate the limbs, which are impelled by the effort of the wind arising from the activity of the palate, lips, and so forth—the activity directed toward the experience of the phonemes produced by the exertion of articulating those phonemes. Whatever is not thus is not thus, like a jar.

The cognition regarding the object that is the *svarita* accent has as its object the experience of phonemes produced by impressions dependent upon the operations of the palate and lips, because it has as its object the cognition of the experience of phonemes produced by desire, effort, and exertion; for what is not thus, is not thus. This activity directed toward the object of sound has as its object desire and cognition, because it generates a successful activity, just like a jar. These four inferences establish that all phonemes have as their objects the respective locations presided over by those [deities].

The seven hundred veins located within the hollow interior of the mouth, covering that region, are the cause for the production of phonemes through the distinct operations of the palate, lips, and lips' coverings; apart from the activity of knowing those [operations] and so forth, phonemes do not arise.

Otherwise, just as in the case of the sound of a lute (*vīṇā*), until the strings are struck by the wind produced by the action of the fingernails, they become the causes for generating their respective phonemes; thus, having established within the body of the lute-instrument that which produces those respective phonemes as the basis for generating those phonemes located in their respective places, and having grasped the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the causal actions that produce them and the sounds generated by them—namely, that "this [action] is the cause of such a phoneme" through the striking of the thumb-pads that generate those phonemes.

Because one performs actions that produce various specific castes (*varṇa*), only effects corresponding to those respective causes arise. Within the hollow interior of the earth, the thirty channels (*sirā*) are covered; when impelled by the striking of the thumb of the hand, they become distinct and differentiated through the resonance of the seven notes (*svara*) and other variations. These circles of musical intervals (*śrutimaṇḍala*), having attained a progressive gradation of clarity in sound, are heard as low, middle, or high pitches, with sounds resonating according to the particular action performed.

In the same way, having understood the bodily mechanism and grasped the pervasion of the respective phonemes, he states that sounds consisting of those respective phonemes—produced through the operation of the effort that delimits sound and acting as the instrument—are heard by means of the channels (*sirā*) that serve as their causes, being composed of phonemes presided over by their respective tones: "The sound born from the movement of the humors within the channels reaches the ears. (Sirā) etc.
