[Objection: Is it not the case that, according to the principle "space has sound as its quality," space alone is the generator of sound? Sound manifests only in the space delimited by the ear-canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) and nowhere else; the movement of the palate, lips, and so forth, serves merely as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). The vessels (*sirā*) cannot possess the status of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), for they only produce the form of the body's limbs; they do not bring about the cognition of sound. It is a delusion to think that because fire nourishes the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), it is therefore wholesome. Therefore, the explanation of the Sūtra according to the aforementioned method is not tenable.

To this it is replied: because space is unitary, there is an absence of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) that could produce the differentiation of multiple colors. The air circulated by the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) situated within the body is not intended here; rather, it can be stated that the air which is the cause of the effect of sound—arising from the contact of the parts of the body with the operation of the palate and lips—is the producer of sound. Thus, it becomes suitable [as a cause] due to the air produced from the conjunction of the parts of the body with the operation of the palate and lips.

As long as another sound is produced—conditioned by time, space, and limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—by means of the wind arising [from the original sound], either according to the analogy of the *kadamba* bud or according to the analogy of waves and ripples; therefore, it can be asserted that the wind produced by the conjunction with substances serves as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

Wherever the movement of the palate and the lips is observed, there alone is the sound caused by the term "wind" (vāta) heard through the sacred tradition (nigama). Therefore, it is indicated that the conjunction between those two is the inherent cause (samavāya-kāraṇa). It is made known that this oral conjunction, which is the effect caused by the movement of the palate and lips, serves as the instrumental cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) for the differentiation of phonemes (varṇa-bheda), such as the various letters produced from the channels (sirā) and so forth.

Due to the differentiation of phonemes, the effect consisting of the differentiation of cognition regarding the object of sound is produced by a causal complex (sāmagrī) that establishes diverse causes; thus, it is experienced that the capacity to indicate diverse phonemes arises from the mere distinction in the specific action of the cause.

That experience arises from a difference in causal complexes (*sāmagrī*); thus, through differences in place, time, and the specific form of the effect such as the jar, and due to the conjunction with a multiplicity of channels (*sirā*) and so forth, there arises the knowledge of distinctions among phonemes (*varṇa*) such as sounds uttered in low, lower, or higher degrees. This occurs because of the difference in those causal complexes, based on the accepted principle that "wherever a phoneme is related [to a particular state], that alone is its specific quality. Consequently, through the distinction of distance and proximity in space, and by means of the difference in the high, higher, or highest degrees of articulation, the distinction between various sounds consisting of those respective phonemes is perceived.

Two propositions have been accepted: first, that a sentence conveys a distinction between sounds; and second, that the effect is the cognition of a distinction between phonemes arising from a distinction between vessels (sirās). The probandum [of the inference] is that [the cognition of sound-distinction] is preceded by a cognition regarding the distinction between phonemes which serves as the cause for its utterance, because it consists of a cognition regarding phonemes produced by the distinction between vessels and so forth, like the sound of a kettledrum (*bherī*).
On this point, there is a statement from the *Śārīra* [section]: "Heat (*ūṣman*) belongs to the humors (*doṣas*), tissues (*dhātus*), wastes (*malas*), and so forth"—this is the teaching of Ātreya.
The *grahaṇī* is considered so because it seizes food by means of that [fire] as its presiding basis.
According to the system of Dhanvantari, that very [channel] is called *pittadhara* (the bile-sustainer);
it serves to nourish the lifespan, health, vigor, vitality, the elements, the bodily tissues (*dhātus*), and the digestive fire.

In accordance with this statement, the *grahaṇī-kalā* (the digestive faculty) is that which indicates the specific colors produced in various regions [of the body]; it is the knowledge of the distinctions in color and so forth arising from the consumption of various tastes; it has as its object the nourishment resulting from the digestion of those various tasted substances; it indicates the presence or absence of defects arising from the consumption of wholesome or unwholesome tastes; and it functions as the generator of the range of knowledge regarding the distinctions between high and higher-pitched sounds.

The meaning is as follows: because the effect produced by the fruit born of rasa from the consumption of various rasas is preceded by the cause of the utterance of specific phonemes (*varṇa*), and because that effect consists solely in the result of the sixteen *kalās* of the *grahaṇī* which apprehend those respective phonemes; therefore, by means of establishing a connection with the channels situated within the ear, the *grahaṇī*-kalā is designated as having the causal function of making sound known.

It is taught that the procedure (*vidhi*) consists in the non-piercing of those letters situated from the lotus-feet up to the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), which are connected to the veins located at the ends of the fields (*kṣetra*); specifically, the seven hundred veins are not to be pierced. Furthermore, the eighty-eight veins that sustain the body are not to be pierced, nor are those situated in the knots where veins are entangled, or in small and crooked knots; the meaning is that these are unfit for the purpose of letting blood.

The meaning is as follows: the *grahaṇīkalā* possesses the causal nature for the absence of disease through the consumption of non-contradictory tastes according to one's birth-rites (*jātakarma*). Known as the "digestive bile" (*pācakapitta*), when the *grahaṇīkalā* is attended by wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*), it becomes capable of making known—both to oneself and to others—the vowels (*anusvāra*) and consonants (*savarṇa*) from the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', which are well-balanced and strong.

If, due to the consumption of incompatible tastes, wind (*anila*) becomes undigested because of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), then the contradictory movements of the humors (*doṣa*), being truly causative of disorders, afflict the body. That which awakens [the disorder]—namely, the state of perceiving the incompatible according to the consumption of tastes, the manifestation of discoloration, weakness, and loss of voice—is perceived in those respective colors. Having recognized that the specific location presided over by those respective colors has become a site of disorder, the prescribed action (*vidhi*) consists in performing the remedy for each of them.
By this, one’s health is restored; whatever [remedy] there may be for whomsoever, such is its power.
That very thing becomes medicine and happiness by that very means at that time.

Because it has been stated thus: the meaning is that one should cause its removal by whatever means possible. Sound, which consists of phonemes perceived by the ear, is produced by the action of the movement of humors other than *sirā* (channels), provided it lacks any other cause; for it is produced by those [specific] causes, just like a jar. By this inference, it appears that all sounds consisting of phonemes are produced by the action of the movement of humors other than *sirā*. It has been established that the causality of these three resides in their collective power (*saṅgha*), and not in each one individually.

Surely, we maintain that the function of the channels (*sirā*) is caused by their role as the support for the body’s mechanical apparatus. This is because their being the cause of the production of sound is established through other means; for diseases arise from the movement and provocation of the humors (*doṣa*). Thus, when indigestion occurs due to the consumption of incompatible tastes, whatever causes arise from an excess of those factors become the causes of various diseases, which are themselves caused by factors other than those perceived as sounds.

For it is observed that by releasing the blood located in the specific vessels of those respective regions for the sake of curing various diseases, one brings about the cessation of the diseases that have those [regions] as their cause. Thus, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the disease residing elsewhere in the vessels and the effect of its removal through the release of the blood situated therein is indicated; this is because the instrument [of treatment] merely demonstrates a distinction from the specific action [of the disease]. Regarding this, there is the statement:
"The procedure for venesection (*sirāvidhi*), the procedure for surgery (*śalyavidhi*), and the application of instruments, alkali (*kṣāra*), and fire (*agnikarma*)."

Thus, because the statement of the Sūtra serves to establish the practical task of releasing blood from the veins, those [signs] do not have as their cause a task produced by verbal testimony. To this it is replied: having recognized the signs—consisting of discordant voices, sounds, and complexions—which arise from the awakening of specific channels (sirā) due to symptoms that constitute the primary causes of diseases born from the consumption of incompatible tastes, one acts solely for the purpose of curing those respective diseases by releasing the vitiated blood located in those specific channels;
therefore, the meaning is that there is no "establishment otherwise" (anyathāsiddhi).

Now, it might be argued that there are seven hundred vessels (*sirā*) that awaken the bodily constituents (*varṇa*); it has been stated that these very vessels, being situated at vital points (*marman*), are to be pierced. It has also been stated that whenever a disorder arises in a particular location, one must perform bloodletting from the vessel situated in that specific region. There are many such statements, for example: "In disorders of the head and eyes, one should release the vessel on the forehead," and so forth. According to those respective statements, the vessels situated in those specific regions should be pierced. Anticipating the objection that the *Sirāvyasūtra* (the section on unsuitable vessels) would then be rendered useless—since it would be teaching that vessels fit for piercing are not to be pierced—the author says: "Riktā" (empty). [The full verse is: *rītā nāḍī na vedyā syāt saṃvṛtā ca tathaiva ca | pūrṇā nāḍī na vedyā syāt saṃvṛtā ca tathaiva ca ||* "A vessel that is empty should not be pierced, nor one that is constricted; likewise, a vessel that is full should not be pierced, nor one that is constricted. This means: a vessel that is empty (*rikta*) should not be pierced because it contains no blood. Similarly, a vessel that is constricted (*saṃvṛta*) should not be pierced because its opening is blocked. Likewise, a vessel that is full (*pūrṇa*) should not be pierced because it is already filled with blood. Similarly, a vessel that is constricted should not be pierced because its opening is obstructed. Thus, the *Sirāvyasūtra* is not useless; rather, it serves to indicate that even if a vessel is located in a site suitable for bloodletting, it must still be examined to ensure it is fit for piercing. Otherwise, if one were to pierce a vessel without first ascertaining its condition, it would lead to complications such as excessive bleeding or hemorrhage. Therefore, the *Sirāvyasūtra* is indeed meaningful. Thus it is said: "A vessel that is empty should not be pierced, nor one that is constricted; likewise, a vessel that is full should not be pierced, nor one that is constricted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the term "empty" (*rikta*) refers to a vessel that is devoid of blood due to prior bloodletting or natural depletion. A vessel that is "constricted" (*saṃvṛta*) is one whose opening is blocked by swelling (*śopha*) or other factors. A vessel that is "full" (*pūrṇa*) is one that is overflowing with blood. A vessel that is "constricted" (*saṃvṛta*) is one whose opening is obstructed by a mass of phlegm (*śleṣman*) or similar substances. Thus, the *Sirāvyasūtra* is not redundant. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, the term "empty" (*rikta*) refers to a vessel that is depleted of blood due to previous bloodletting or natural loss. A vessel that is "constricted" (*saṃvṛta*) is one whose opening is blocked by swelling or other conditions. A vessel that is "full" (*pūrṇa*) is one that is replete with blood. A vessel that is "constricted" (*saṃvṛta*) is one whose opening is obstructed by phlegm or similar matter. Thus, the *Sirāvyasūtra* is not superfluous. This is the sense. Moreover, the term "empty" (*rikta*) denotes a vessel that is void of blood owing to prior venesection or natural deficiency. A vessel that is "constricted" (*saṃvṛta*) is one whose aperture is occluded by edema (*śopha*) or the like. A vessel that is "full" (*pūrṇa*) is one that is saturated with blood. A vessel that is "constricted" (*saṃvṛta*) is one whose opening is blocked by phlegm (*śleṣman*) or other substances. Therefore, the *Sirāvyasūtra* is not meaningless. This is the purport. Veins that are empty, over-expanded, or excessively full should not be pierced. || 46 ||

Empty vessels are the cause for the utterance of short syllables; excessive vessels are the cause for the utterance of long syllables; and excessively full tones are the cause for the utterance of svarita and protracted (pluta) syllables.

Now, one might object: "Among the seven hundred vessels (sirās), there are eighty-eight vessels that are the cause for the production of short vowels; they are the causes for the utterance of vowel-conjunctions, and they serve as the grounds for the application of the term 'valid cognition' (*pramā*) regarding the experience of objects of knowledge concerning the specific piercings (*vedha*). Because they are the cause for the activity directed toward words produced by those eighty-eight vessels, they possess beautiful tones. Therefore, we say that those [specific vessels] are not to be pierced. As for the downward-facing vessels that are the causes for generating short vowels, those vessels are to be emptied."

The *atirikta* (excessive) veins are those that produce variegated colors, follow crooked paths, and are excessively full; they possess excellent sounds conducive to the functions of the vital airs (*pavana*) that stimulate and direct the movement of inhalation and exhalation, and they are *pluta* (floating). Their status as instruments (*karaṇa*) has been established, because an instrument is that which serves as the cause of an effect that manifests the specific distinction of an action. Among the seven hundred veins, ninety-eight veins are internal and supported by the *sarandhraka* [membrane]; these very veins—whether *rikta*, *atirikta*, or *atipūrṇa*—are not to be pierced.

For some individuals, due to a difference in body, there are ninety-eight channels (*sirā*). Some of these are hollow within and serve as supports. This is because it is observed that for all sentences—which are produced by groups of phonemes (*varṇa*) of a single type that generate color (or sound)—they are perceived as being delimited by their respective bodies. Furthermore, it is impossible to state or to exclude that among the seven hundred channels, only certain ones are such producers [of cognition].

The Self, which has as its objects the knowledge of the various sounds and words corresponding to the forms of those respective bodies, is distinct in each body because it is perceived through differences such as the variety of pleasure and pain, and because it serves as the substratum for the diversity of sounds, accents, colors, limbs, substances, and qualities. Therefore, since they cause the awakening of others and consist of the bestowal of all phonemes (*varṇa*), they bring about the perception of that variety. To state that the seven hundred channels (*sirā*) do not pierce [the Self], they are to be enjoined as the awakeners of the distinctions among all phonemes.
Thus, the meaning is that the downward orientation of the seven hundred channels has been established.
"Dhanvantari, however, says there are three [additional] and two hundred joints. Starting from this statement, it is not according to the opinion of Dhanvantari:
"The *grahaṇī* is considered so because it seizes (*grahaṇāt*) food; it is the seat of that [digestive fire]."
"That very [vein], according to the system of Dhanvantari, is called Pittadhara.

This much has been explained: in order to make it known that those seven hundred vessels—which are the channels for awakening the effects of cognition regarding the objects of activity involving words composed of excellent phonemes—must not be pierced, it was stated in the *Śārīra* (Anatomy) section, "That very [vein], according to the system of Dhanvantari."

Having analyzed and shown that this very thing is the subject matter expounded in Āyurveda, it is said "that same [kalā]. Having digested the raw bile (*āmapitta*), when the digestive faculty (*pācakakalā*) becomes perfectly clear, it is designated as the *grahaṇī* because it makes known the colors of its substratum. When this faculty, produced from the consumption of substances with non-contradictory tastes, becomes powerful, it brings about the understanding of good complexion, a beautiful voice, graceful gait, and eloquent speech. By means of this, the space delimited by the ear-cavity [is purified], and thus it serves to establish longevity, health, and the element of luster (*tejas*).
On this point, there is a statement in the Sūtra:
"That which has gone astray [is corrected] by the pressure of instruments..."
One should partake of wholesome food and conduct until the vitiated humors (doṣas), having entered the blood, return once more to their own locations.
When the blood has been removed, food and drink that are neither too hot nor too cold, light, and digestive-stimulating are beneficial;
for at that time the body’s blood is unstable, and the digestive fire must be protected with particular care.

Having understood that the disease arises from the cause of its etiology through the utterance of words, and having acquired the knowledge of the procedure for that disease, one should administer treatment; this is the intended meaning—that having recognized the internal disorder merely by the utterance of words and having discerned the method of cure, one should act accordingly. The meaning is that the causal role of the vein (*sirā*) has been established by way of releasing corrupted blood, which is the function of the veins that indicate the causes of digestion, whether in their natural or unnatural state.

The purpose [of this section] is such that it can be stated once the nature of those veins—whether empty, excessive, or full—is known, as this indicates their non-puncturability. Therefore, because it is impossible to prohibit [puncturing] without knowing the location of the *marmas*, the author says "tāḥ" (those) out of this underlying intention:
"Those veins located in the *marma*-sites are empty. (47)

Because the movement of the vital air (*pavana*) is supported by the channels (*randhra*), the provocation of the humors (*doṣa-prakopa*) occurs through the incision of veins (*sirā*) that possess such channels; therefore, those [veins] are not to be pierced. Those veins which exist as internal sense organs (*antarindriya*), being porous due to their nature of providing no space for the movement of excessive internal humors, are not to be pierced, because they constitute the cause of the qualities associated with the vital points (*marmasthāna*). Their function depends upon the articulation of phonemes (*varṇa*) as far as they extend.

Those veins are not to be pierced; they are always excessively full, their channels being filled with wind (vāyu), serving as the cause for the movement of the humors (doṣas), and providing benefit to the auditory space by preventing its own impairment; furthermore, the meaning is that they reside in vital points (marma) and internal cavities (āśaya).

Now, among the ninety-eight channels (sirās), in whichever specific location a defect of color (varṇadoṣa) dependent on a particular channel is observed, and furthermore, when weakness of the digestive faculty (grahaṇīkalā) arises from the consumption of unwholesome tastes, a defect of color situated therein is seen; and due to the obstruction of the pathways for the movement [of the humors], disorders such as those of the wind (pavana) are also observed. In those locations where the channels that produce those respective colors reside, diseases born from the unwholesome tastes that serve as their causes manifest.

When there are disorders of the bones of the head, they are designated as "diseases of the head. When there are disorders of the vessels in the region of the eyes, one is designated as "suffering from an eye disease" therein. When there are disorders of the vessels situated in the region of the ears, one is designated as "suffering from an ear disease."

The humors (*doṣa*) and other factors situated in their respective vessels (*sirā*)—when the digestive capacity (*grahaṇīkalā*) has become weak due to the consumption of unwholesome tastes—give rise to diseases resulting from the failure of those factors to move through the pathways of the vessels located in those specific sites. By virtue of the agitation caused by this movement and non-movement, they undergo pathological changes in the vessels situated in those respective locations. It is the vessels themselves that first manifest these various disorders.

Because they are presided over by their respective locations, the vessels themselves—conditioned by those specific regions—are the indicators of diseases of the head, eyes, ears, mouth, nose, tongue, throat, arms, heart, and abdomen; diseases such as indigestion and weak digestion; diseases of the spleen (*gulma*), urinary disorders (*meha*), malabsorption (*grahaṇī*), diarrhea, and hemorrhoids; diseases of the respiratory system; jaundice arising from the line of hair (*romarājī*); diseases of the scrotum, calves, and knees; and diseases originating in the hips and waist. It is these very vessels that manifest [the ailments] in their respective locations.

Having emitted the diseases, the vessels situated at their respective locations communicate those very diseases by means of the movement of the *vāyu*; thus, the vessels themselves manifest the specific symptoms of each disease. Keeping in mind the underlying principle that—due to the consumption of unwholesome tastes (*virasa*) which cause those respective diseases, and due to the weakness of the bodily constituents (*kalā*), when *āma* is provoked—the very tastes that increase those specific [unwholesome] tastes are what bring about those respective diseases, he says: "Those vessels go to the vital spots (*marman*) and the internal organs (*āśaya*)."

[Objection: But was it not already established that the ninety-eight vessels, the seven hundred vessels, and those vessels that are depleted, excessive, or over-filled are not to be pierced? [Response: Now, since the discharge of blood from the vessels as directed by the specific rules for each disease is indeed the causal complex that eliminates disease, it is appropriate to explain which vessels are fit for piercing, as they are required for that purpose. What are those vessels like? Since it is necessary to know them immediately after [the previous discussion], and because there is a desire to understand the very thing that explains them, he says—starting with "sirā"—"Having known the procedure for the classification of vessels and blood, one should perform the discharge. (48)

This is the procedure solely for the release of blood located in the vessels (*sirā*). Some [vessels] are not to be pierced. Therefore, since the task at hand is to demonstrate which [vessels] are to be pierced and which are not, the meaning is that one should perform the release of blood from the vessels for the purpose of removing the specific effects residing in the blood of those respective vessels—that is, the diseases residing in the blood of those respective vessels.

Nor should it be argued that for the purpose of curing those respective diseases, the incision of veins caused by them is not appropriate because it is impossible to acquire knowledge regarding the specific veins to be incised—distinct from those located at vital points (*marmasthāna*)—without such an occasion. For in cases where diseases arising from indigestion due to the consumption of incompatible tastes become the very course of the humoral disorders (*doṣavikāra*), fasting must be practiced until the humors are fully digested.

Where a pathological disorder arises from the consumption of incompatible tastes (viruddha-rasa), resulting in an illness born of indigestion (ajīrṇa) and originating from discordant bodily constituents (dhātu), one should identify the vessels (sirā) by the specific sounds emitted therein. Having recognized that "this color is contrary to the color present in this location," and having understood the presence of the vessel that generates that particular color, one should ascertain the seat of the afflicted humor (duṣṭāśaya) where the morbid alteration of the blood (asṛgvikāra) is observed through the movement of the humors and constituents. Furthermore, one should identify the network of vessels caused by those factors and the specific site where the disease is localized by those causes.

The meaning is that the disease produced by those causes is to be removed by the act of venesection; thus the aphorism, "Having understood the procedure for the division of the blood in the veins, one should effect its release," has been stated. All of this has been explained in the second chapter of Āyurveda, so enough of this digression.

But surely, it is only the *vārḍhika* substance that serves as the cause for the production of offspring; this has indeed been established in the first aphorism. It was further established that whenever a disorder (*vikāra*) is observed, it is at that very moment countered by its remedy. How then is it established that even when a disorder exists, it is removed by fasting alone? And how is it that this must be accomplished by the release of blood from the veins? Due to such a sense of incongruity, he says: "Free from disease" (*nīruja*). Such are the parents, possessing limbs free from disease. (49)

Since all the limbs of both [parents] must be nourished to produce offspring, any disorder of the blood-element (*rakta-dhātu*) in those limbs acts as an obstacle. Therefore, this procedure is prescribed for the purpose of ensuring that disorder does not occur; thus the Sūtra declares that the limbs of the mother and father yield their fruit when they are free from disorder. They say that a man whose complexion and sense organs are clear, who desires the objects of the senses, whose flow of blood is well-maintained, and who is endowed with happiness, nourishment, strength, and luster, possesses pure blood.

In accordance with this statement, the term *puruṣa* (person) refers to women as well, because it denotes a term applicable to a couple; for in the procreation of offspring, the union of both is the cause. Now, it was stated previously that the purpose of the act of releasing blood from the veins is simply the bestowing of the fruit produced by the work of health. By this, the relationship of cause and effect between those two has been established.

The fruit of the karma arising from the parents' knowledge of the scriptures concerning the body is the attainment of the causal complex that effects the firmness of the bodily limbs, resulting in the relationship of part and whole among the members of the body. The semen (*śukla*) and the menstrual blood (*ārtava*) of those two, man and woman, having become thus, are established as a mass within the womb. From these very two, which are of the nature of seed, unmodified, and the cause for the production of progeny, the *sattva* (the conscious principle) manifests. Regarding this, there is a statement in the *Śārīra*:
"When the semen and the menstrual blood are pure, the *sattva*, impelled by its own karma and afflictions [takes up residence]."
The embryo is produced by the power of causal connection, like fire in the fire-drill.

Now, it might be argued that it has been stated that semen (*śukla*) and menstrual blood (*ārtava*) become pure merely by the removal of the blood located in the vessels (*sirā*) that cause disease. However, this is not sufficient for one whose internal substratum (*āśaya*) is not corrupted. These—namely, the non-contradictory *doṣas*, the purified sense organs, and the purified digestive fire (*analā*)—are to be brought about by the consumption of substances suitable for old age, arising solely from the removal of the vitiated blood located in the vessels mentioned in this sūtra. Now, since semen and menstrual blood serve as the causes for the production of the seed (*bīja*), how could they come to be without the consumption of earthy substances? Anticipating this objection, the author says: "Purified... (*śuddha-*).
Beings are born from earthly substances whose causes are pure intention, purity from defects, the fire of purification, and the quality of the senses. || 50 ||

By consuming rejuvenating substances (*vārdhika-dravya*), all the internal receptacles (*āśaya*) become completely purified, and the sense organs become free from the defects of degeneration. Likewise, the five vital airs (*pañcānila*) and the five digestive fires (*pācapitta*) remain undisturbed through the consumption of rejuvenating substances that produce lightness (*laghu-guṇa*). Furthermore, the consumption of *sāttvika* substances is the cause of *sāttvika* qualities; the consumption of *rājasa* substances produces *rājasa* qualities; and the consumption of *tāmasa* substances produces *tāmasa* qualities.
The meaning is that without the internal receptacles and so forth produced by the consumption of rejuvenating substances, the generation of seed does not occur.

Now, for the purpose of producing the body, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that brings it about must be assembled; that [complex] is necessary. Since the *āśayas*, the *doṣas*, the digestive fires (*analas*), and the sense organs (*indriyas*) nourish the body only when they are purified through the consumption of substances that promote longevity, they are not the actual producers of the body. Therefore, how can the connection between the production of the body and the *āśayas* and so forth be established at the outset without first assembling the causal complex that produces it? Due to this incongruity, he says: "Semen," etc. The union of semen and blood is the womb (*yoni*). (51)

Semen is produced from the male; blood is produced from the female. The womb (*yoni*) is the cause of these two. That which consists of their conjunction and serves as the cause for their union is designated as *sānnipātya*. It cannot be said that semen always possesses the capacity to produce offspring; rather, it becomes the cause of procreation only when the internal receptacles (*āśaya*) are purified. The same applies to the blood produced from the female.

Because of the extremely firm contact with a divine source (*divyayoni*), which serves as the cause for the activity of union between a fit man and woman, the region where the seed is deposited is called the *garbhāśaya* (womb); and since its status as the producer [of the embryo] is well-established, the meaning is that the living being (*sattva*), while still an embryo, enters the *garbhāśaya* immediately after [conception] and grows therein. Now, one might object: let the *āśayas* (receptacles/organs) be pure for this purpose; through them, the semen and blood (*śukra-śoṇita*) would also be pure, since these two alone constitute the nature of the seed.
How does it increase? How does it grow? And how can it be said to be the support of movement, termed "motion"? Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the womb... [Verse 52]:
"The unborn one, impelled by destiny, manifested in the womb."

The unborn living self (jīvātman), having entered the womb, became manifest—that is, it was seen—because of the existence of the Vedic scripture: "It leaves behind the mere seed; the sense-organ enters the womb, covered by the placenta; it casts off the membrane at birth; by means of the cosmic order (ṛta), the sense-organ [realizes] the truth."

Now, one might object: when the union of semen and blood occurs, the *sattva* enters the embryo and remains therein; that alone is the body. The definition, however, is that "the body consists of the five elements. By what cause, then, must the manifestation of these elemental masses be brought about? Likewise, space (*gagana*) is an eternal substance, while the quartet beginning with earth is non-eternal. Among these, fire (*tejas*) is the grasper of material objects possessing form (*rūpa*). That fire, residing within the eyeball, perceives all objects.

The eye is the cause of the cognition having that [color] as its object; and the substance possessing the salty taste, which produces that [cognition], is also a cause. Since the definition "the body consists of the five elements" would not be consistent without demonstrating the causal relationship between the effect—the cognition of that object—and its causes, he says: "as long as...
[it] possesses a form corresponding to the food [ingested]. (53)

The substance of fire and so forth is commensurate with the consumption of substances and conducive to the production of effects; it possesses the qualities of substances produced from the sweet taste generated by the consumption of substances possessing a sweet taste. That which is the object of the gustatory sense-organ resides at the tip of the tongue and perceives, having distinguished them, all the various types of tastes and so forth. This [organ] possesses the knowledge of objects possessing a sweet taste, being characterized by the capacity to produce an effect that increases even small amounts of substances resulting from the consumption of substances possessing a sweet taste.

As long as there is the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya*) located at the tip of the nose, which increases the pleasant taste produced by the consumption of substances up to that point and perceives both odor and taste, this [person] possesses the knowledge whose object is a specific odor belonging to an earthy substance that manifests all odors, such that [he knows]: "This [substance] possesses odor. As long as there is the visual organ (*cakṣurindriya*), which increases the digestive fire produced by the consumption of substances possessing a salty taste and resides within the eyeball, this [person] possesses the knowledge that has as its range the knowledge whose objects are the various distinctions of form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

"This person possesses a cognition whose object is a cognition regarding an object possessing the touch of the elemental substance [wind], which is conducive to the effect that increases the wind-element produced by the consumption of substances with a bitter taste. In this manner, according to the stated method, it has been demonstrated that a substance conducive to the effects that increase the fourfold [elements] beginning with the earth is caused by a cognition whose object is a cognition regarding an object of a particular tongue-faculty, and that such a substance—which is produced by the consumption of any substance possessing taste—is caused by a cognition whose object is a cognition regarding an object of that particular faculty.

Because negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) has been observed. Therefore, the meaning is that the causal relationship is apprehended through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). For that purpose, everything is analyzed and made known by means of the instrument of inference (*anumānapramāṇa*).

A substance qualified by earthness (*pṛthivītva*) is the object of a cognition possessing a sweet taste not produced by conjunction with earth, because, while being perceptible by the gustatory organ (*rasanendriya*) which does not reside in what is not co-locus with itself, it is caused by a cognition whose object is that [taste]; for whatever is not thus, is not so, like time (*kāla*) and so forth.

Earth-substance qualified by the absence of fire is the object of a cognition whose object is a substance possessing sour taste; because, while being graspable by the gustatory organ—which does not have as its locus that which is co-locus with it—it is caused by a cognition that is the effect of a cognition having as its object a substance possessing sour taste. Whatever is not thus is not so, like time and so forth.

A substance qualified by water (i.e., a watery substance) possessing the nature of fire is the object of the cognition of the taste of salt; because, while being graspable by the gustatory organ which does not reside in what is not co-locus with it, it is caused by a cognition that is the object of a cognition whose content is a substance possessing the taste of salt; for whatever is not thus, is not thus, as, for example, time and so forth.

A substance possessing a taste like that of bitter [substance] is the object of a cognition whose subject is a substance possessing a fire-ness distinguished from the sky, because it is the cause of a cognition which is the object of a cognition whose subject is a substance possessing a taste like that of bitter [substance], provided that it is graspable by the gustatory organ which does not have as its locus anything other than what is co-locus with itself; for whatever is not thus is not so, as, for example, time and the like.

The substance of fire qualified by the state of being non-fire has as its object a substance possessing a pungent taste, because it is caused by a cognition that is the object of a cognition whose object is a substance possessing a pungent taste—provided that [the former cognition] is graspable by the gustatory organ which does not have as its locus that which is co-locus with itself; for whatever is not so is not so, like time and the like.

A substance characterized by earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and possessing fire as its constituent matter has for its object a cognition [of something] possessing an astringent taste (*kaṣāyarasa*); because, while being graspable by the gustatory organ (*rasanendriya*) which does not reside in what is co-located with itself, it is the cause of an effect that is the objective domain of a cognition having an object possessing an astringent taste; for whatever is not thus, is not so, like time (*kāla*) and so forth.
On this point, there is the statement of the Sūtra: "Earth, water, fire, earth-water, earth-water-fire, ether, wind, fire-wind, and fire-wind-ether..."
From the elements being successively predominant in pairs, there arises the production of the sweet and other tastes.

Now, it must be stated that for this inference (*anumāna*) to be apprehended as an inference, it must be preceded by the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Here, the nature of inference is defined as: "the state of being an object of a cognition which has as its object a substance possessing a sweet taste produced by a substance characterized by earthiness and a predominance of *saṃsarga* (conjunction), and which is the object of a gustatory sense-organ (*rasanendriya*) that does not reside in what is co-located with itself. The sweet taste produced by that conjunction is the effect of a cognition whose object is the gustatory sense-organ; for when there is the apprehension of the pervasion between those two, the inference arises.

[Objection: Surely, once a causal relationship has been apprehended—as in the case of smoke and fire—it is possible to state that a sweet taste removes the defects of digestion. [Response: In that regard, if one were to state that every sweet taste alone removes disease based on an apprehension of the causal relationship as delimited by "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*), there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For this reason, with a sense of dissatisfaction, he says: "As long as... (verse 54). "As long as they bestow health, tastes are remedial. (54)

The sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes—which convey the meaning of the word *yāvat* (as much as)—are themselves the eliminators [of disease]; that is to say, they are the bestowers of health. Now, one might object: their status as eliminators should be stated only when diseases actually arise in all embodied beings; for an instrument is distinguished solely by its specific action, and there is a rule that its result must be immediate. [Therefore: "One should not consume unwholesome food in vain, nor should one take medicine in vain."
Because it is impossible to state the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) according to this statement, he says—out of dissatisfaction—"As long as... [and so on]:
"As long as it protects that which is born of the mother from the tastes already consumed. (55)

As long as the flavors have been ingested, as long as the flavors have been consumed, [the mother] shall protect and guard the maternal body and the seven constituents (*dhātu*). The meaning is that she should cause the preservation of the constituents born from those flavors to be maintained.

Now, it was stated that one should ensure the protection of the seven *dhātus* from the six tastes beginning with sweet (*svādu*). It is necessary to understand this very point. While it must be said that the consumption of non-contradictory astringent (*kaṣāya*) tastes is required, because there exists a causal relationship between the consumption of substances possessing an astringent taste and the human purpose of increasing the *rasa* and *rakta* *dhātus*, the relationship of cause and effect belongs only to those two and not to others. Since it can be asserted that the capacity to produce the seven *dhātus* belongs to the respective tastes and so forth that generate them, he says:
"Semen..."—from an excess of paternal seed, a son is born. (56)

From the moment the vital heat (*tejas*) situated in the person manifests within the womb, the *rasas* and other elements provide the capacity whose sole fruit is the production of the effects of the person’s transformations. The mother, by consuming food consisting of substances with sweet taste, should eat while promoting the increase of the white constituent (*śukladhātu*) caused by that sweet taste; therefore, a son resembling his father is obtained. This is because of the existence of the Vedic scripture: "The self, indeed, is the one named son. This is the meaning.

The embryo (*piṇḍa*) is produced from the blood of the mother, which arises from her consumption of substances possessing a sweet taste (*svādurasavat*), and it serves to increase the body. Because its nature is to bestow the fruit of the effect produced by that sweet taste, as long as the wife is pregnant, the *rasas* and other elements provide the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) for women just as they do for men; thus he says: "From [an excess of] blood... From an excess of blood in the mother, a daughter is born. (57)

The intended meaning is that because even that blood (*śoṇita*) is produced from a sweet taste (*svādurasa*), it becomes the cause for the effect of increasing the physical mass (*piṇḍa*), which is the body. Due to the excessive entry of blood, the fetus appears similar to the mother; due to the excessive entry of blood, it is seen [as such] in the formed mass (*piṇḍa*).
Here, "soft" refers to the mother-derived blood, flesh, marrow, vital fluid (*sṛk*), and so forth;
whereas the father-derived is "firm," consisting of semen, vessels (*dhamani*), bones, hair, and so forth.

Even that which is called "paternal" consists of semen, flesh, marrow, reproductive fluid, and so forth, produced from the mother’s consumption of substances with sweet flavors; these constituents (dhātus), being born from the mother’s nutritional intake, increase right there within her. Likewise, those produced from the father’s consumption of substances with sweet flavors [also increase there]. At the time of union, the father's veins, bones, hair, and so forth do not arise [in the embryo]; rather, at that moment, there is merely the conjunction of the mother’s own semen and blood, which serves as the cause for such production.

Immediately thereafter, nothing other than the mother’s nourishment of rasa and so forth serves as the means of growth. Until the completion of the body's formation, this [nourishment] is the sole cause for the presence or absence of diseases arising in the beginning, middle, and end. Therefore, it is indicated here that the rule is to cease the consumption of substances that are the sole cause of illness every single month. Regarding the doubt as to what would happen if, at the time of the union of the couple, both the semen and the blood were equal—even in the case of the consumption of substances intended for producing a son or a daughter—he says: "dvisama" (equal in two ways).
Where the *ṣaṇḍa* consists of two equal [parts]. || 58 ||
The unborn is born manifold. || 59 ||

The meaning is that, according to the manner previously stated, the consumption of the mother’s essence (*mātṛrasa*) is the cause therein. "Unborn" (*aja*) means he is not born; being of manifold forms and possessing many forms, that *jīva* is born—this is the meaning of the aphorism. Now, one might object: this too is untenable. If this produced body is established as being "unborn," then the entire collection of causes that establishes the single cause for disease and health would be rendered useless. Both its state of being unborn and its indestructibility are already established by its very nature. Furthermore, the scripture that teaches the causes which serve as the basis for the effect of health would also be useless. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Month by month... (*māsi māsi*).
Women have their menses month by month. || 60 ||

Every month women become *rajasvalā* (menstruating). The meaning is that for a period of four days, they are not fit to be touched. When all the causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) for the production of the *piṇḍa* (the physical body) are present, the *aja* (the unborn soul), impelled by destiny, enters the body of the menstruating woman. Once the *aja* has manifested, the causal conditions that have been present for that duration become fruitful.

By virtue of contact with that [reflection], there appears within the individual self (jīvātman) the conditioned impermanence, the conditioned form, the state of ignorance, and the possession of reflected knowledge of the living being (jīva). It is in this very way that it is designated in worldly usage—as "this one is old," "this one is dark-complexioned," or "this one is a Brahmin."

Now, since such notions as "I am happy" or "I am miserable" are untenable [in their own right], how is it that the individual self (*jīvātman*) receives the assignment of the fruits of action due to the defect of contact with the menstruating woman? It is that it undergoes the experience of happiness and misery through limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), but not by its own nature; because it is of the nature of the Self and is eternal, it obtains happiness, misery, and so forth through limiting adjuncts, but not by its own nature. This is the meaning. The expression used for this is "the defect of contact with the menstruating woman. Therefore, like a *caṇḍālī*, one should not touch her, nor should one speak to her. Regarding this, there is a scriptural passage (*śruti*):

"Therefore, one should not converse with a woman in her courses, nor sit with her, nor eat her food; for she remains wearing the color of the murder of a Brahmin. Furthermore, they say: 'Anointing oil is indeed the food of a woman; one must not accept anointing oil, but anything else may be accepted at will. Starting from that point, [it continues]: 'For her, a man of small stature should observe the vow for three nights; he should drink from his cupped hands or from a vessel that is not small, for the protection of progeny.'"
The meaning established here is that [this state] arose through the power of the fault of contact with a woman in her menses. Regarding this, there is a statement from the *Śārīra*:

"A woman observing celibacy (*brahmacāriṇī*) should eat a small amount of milk-rice (*kṣaireya*) or barley-gruel (*yāvaka*), which cleanses and emaciates the digestive tract, using a leaf, a clay bowl, or her hand."
Then, on the fourth day, having bathed and being pure, wearing white garlands and garments,
she who desires a son resembling her husband should look upon her husband before her.

Thus, according to the scripture, the meaning is that the aphorism, "The unborn one, assuming manifold forms, moves in many shapes," is meaningful, as it is supported by numerous scriptural passages (*śruti*).

When the full capacity of all the causal factors for producing offspring has been present for a long time, that living being (*jīva*), having entered a woman in her fertile period, experiences an excess of pleasure and pain due to the power of past karma (*pāpa*). To avoid this, bathing and other rites are prescribed; he states that through these, its avoidance will occur—namely, "on the fourth day.
One should bathe on the fourth day. (61)

The meaning is that on the fourth day, she should perform a ritual bath for the sake of removing that sin. Following that, she should perform the worship of her chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), the worship of the Guru and the deities, the honoring of gods and Brahmins, and a prayer to the deities for the welfare of her offspring. She says, "I am desirous of a son; for the sake of obtaining that prosperity, I shall approach my husband," and being thus purified, she should engage in union with her husband—this is what is meant by the word "pure" (śuddhā). "Purified, she should approach her husband. (62)
The meaning is: "May there be the attainment of a virtuous son."

Now, it may be objected that just as a woman who has become *rajasvalā* or *ṛtumatī* (menstruating), having formed the resolve, "May conception not occur for me," performs a ritual bath on the fourth day and approaches her husband according to the injunction—since conception is not observed to occur at times other than those days—it follows that the duties to be performed on the preceding days are not established as being subsidiary (*aṅga*) to the act [of approaching]. Thus, there is no lack of occasion [for such duties].

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is an injunction stating, "One should bathe on the fourth day"? Since the observance of the vow is enjoined for the three days preceding that, and because it is observed that an effect arises without delay when all causal factors such as the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) are present, and since the act of waiting until the fourth day serves as the efficient cause, and because the absence of that duration [of waiting] is seen to be the cause for the absence of the effect in the form of [sexual] union, the injunction regarding the effect—namely, the act of union with the husband after bathing on the fourth day—is more powerful; therefore, out of this unease, he says: "progeny" (*prajā*).
As long as there is a desire for progeny, so long is the effort caused by the union of the couple.

In response to the inquiry as to the reason for observing for a period of fourteen days by a man who has engaged in sexual intercourse with the desire, "May the fruit of procreation necessarily accrue to me," we state the reason: from the first day of menstruation, the seven bodily constituents (dhātus) flow out in the form of blood.

The meaning is that when the emission of the seventh constituent (*dhātu*) occurs in women, and if at that same time the emission of the final constituent occurs in men and there is a union in the womb, then the production of the effect will take place without delay. It is appropriate for a man to observe this period for up to fourteen days; during that time, the seven constituents exist in the form of blood, making it suitable for that duration. For instance, on the fourth day, there is the suitability for the emission of the final constituent.

Day and night constitute a single period; the time during which the emission of each individual element is observed is the "suitable time. On the fourth night, the final element of the woman flows out in the form of blood.

Conception occurs at that very time, for as long as the rule of the emission of the male constituent (*puruṣadhātu*) is observed; during that period, up to thirteen days, it is suitable because the womb-lotus remains in a state of blossoming so as to reach the uterus for a mere fortnight. The meaning is that it remains blossomed until the moment of their union (*sānnipātya*); at the moment of union, it closes like a bud. It remains open for only a fortnight.

For one fortnight it remains closed; two fortnights constitute a month, as in the saying, "Women have menses every month. Here, the meaning is that when there is a discharge of blood for women for only a single fortnight, it results in a disorder (*doṣa*). Regarding this, the statement from the *Śārīra-sūtra* is:
"The fertile period (*ṛtu*) consists of twelve nights, while the first three are censured;
on the eleventh night [of the cycle], a son is conceived, and on the others, a daughter."
"Then the preceptor should perform the ritual for producing a daughter according to the prescribed rule.

According to this statement from the *Śārīra-sūtra*, it is understood that in even-numbered days, when the causal conditions for producing a son are present, a son is born; whereas on other days, when the causal conditions for producing a daughter are present, a daughter is born. Her final constituent element (*dhātu*) alone becomes the blood (*rakta*). That specific time at which the union with the respective semen occurs is the time that bestows either a son or a daughter. Furthermore, the menstrual flow (*ārtava*) of a pregnant woman has the luster of ghee, honey, or oil.

That which is washed and becomes free from stain, resembling the juice of lac or the moon, is pure semen and menstrual blood (*śukrārtava*); it is clear, fluid, and the union of the couple with one another. Furthermore, the production of the embryo must be stated to depend on a specific state of the blood; however, that specific state is indeed a modification of the semen (*śuklavikāra*), because the body consists of the seven constituents (*saptadhātu*) and all the channels (*sirā*) are enveloped by these seven constituents. The meaning is that in women, the pure constituent takes the form of such blood. As for the cause of the birth of a male, it is time alone. To the question, "Is it the same for the birth of a female as well?", he says: "Two" (*dvīti*).
Sons are born on the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth days; daughters are born on the other days. || 64 ||

Now, it must be stated that [the husband] is the nourisher of the formed embryo; therefore, he must be provided with nourishing substances. In that regard, a specific time must also be mentioned. Let that time be the one when he acts as the nourisher. But surely, when the union of semen and blood has occurred, the embryo is already present; and in that very month, signs of pregnancy are observed in a woman who has reached her season. For the sake of protecting it, one should have her drink nourishing substances during the first period—hence he says: "In the first... [The nourishing substance is the preventer during the first period. 65.

When the signs of pregnancy have appeared and she is seen to be in her fertile season (*ṛtumatī*), medical treatment there consists of the consumption of nourishing substances; this is the prescribed regimen. In the second month, the consumption of nourishing substances serves as the remedy. Thus, until the end of the tenth month, the treatment involving nourishing and drying agents is ordained. By means of that, having protected the fetus, she gives birth to a son with ease—so he says: "That" (*tat*).
After that, during the fertile season, there are drying agents, and even thereafter, drying tastes (*rasa*) that promote fetal growth, to be used for as long as is appropriate. || 66 ||

Having analyzed according to the rules those things which are suitable for use, fit for consumption, blameless, causes for the maintenance of health, factors that prevent future diseases, and which do not produce defects to the extent of one's capacity—these are explained: "First," etc.
In the first, second, and third months, sweet tastes (madhurarasas) remove and ward off wind (pavana). (67)

A substance possessing a sweet taste (*svādurasa*), distinguished from two substances characterized by sour and salty tastes, is recommended for a pregnant woman during the first, second, and third months. This substance, whose flavor arises from the mutual combination [of those elements], is a food that counteracts the wind (*pavana*) provoked by the consumption of substances that give rise to discordant flavors—the very seeds of disease—and is thus suitable for the entire body and common to all living beings. The meaning is that one should consume items prescribed according to each specific category.

It has been stated that for that duration, [the fetus] is turned away by the consumption of those specific tastes which act as preventives. Since the effects of consuming contrary tastes are possible even at other times, and since the consumption of substances that promote fetal growth is necessary even then, those blameless substances—which serve as causes for the respective required actions, are suitable for use throughout the period, and produce the effect of preventing future diseases—are now analyzed and revealed: "Four," etc.
In the fourth, fifth, and sixth months, sour tastes (*amlarasa*) are the preventives that remove *pitta*. (68)

A substance possessing sour taste, qualified by the absence of substances that provide the perception of sweet and salty tastes, should be administered to a pregnant woman during the fourth, fifth, or sixth month. This substance—being the absence of the counter-positive of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) with respect to the substance possessing sour taste—is free from the absence of substances that cause the provocation of *pitta* through the consumption of incompatible tastes; therefore, the consumption of this other substance pacifies all *pitta* provocation, brings about health for the entire body, and serves as a cause for the benefit of all people.

The meaning is that one should have the pregnant woman drink substances possessing the sour taste (*amlarasa*) prescribed for each respective stage of gestation; by that very means, the fetus grows and becomes the cause for the proper development of its various limbs. Thus far, regarding the health of the woman carrying the child, it has been established that substances containing the sour taste are to be excluded. Fearing that other substances containing different tastes might be used by default simply because they are not prohibited, the author states with the word "sixth" (*ṣaṣṭha*):
"In the sixth, eighth, and ninth months, substances with a hot taste (*uṣṇarasa*) are to be administered, as they dry up the phlegm (*kapha*). (69)

Regarding the pregnant woman afflicted by disease during the sixth, eighth, and ninth months, the consumption of substances possessing a hot taste (*uṣṇa-rasa*), qualified by the absence of substances that provide sweet or sour tastes, is prescribed. A substance possessing a hot taste is a substance characterized by the absence of those very substances whose mutual non-existence constitutes its opposite.

Therefore, one should have the pregnant woman drink substances that are contrary to those [kapha-inducing factors], which are produced from food containing tastes opposed to kapha; which function to eliminate the presence of unwholesome substances and the consumption of such substances; which pacify the provocation of all diseases born of the kapha-doṣa; which bring about health for the entire body; and which serve as the cause of benefit for all living beings—namely, substances of various kinds prescribed by rule that possess a heating taste. Enough said.

[Objection: But has it not been established that the removal of the humors (doṣas)—wind, bile, and phlegm—belongs to the six tastes alone? According to the reasoning stated, substances possessing sweet, sour, and salty tastes are incapable of removing the disorders residing in the three humors; thus, following the statement "In that regard, the first [group] destroys wind," the capacity to remove the disorders as explained has been attributed to substances possessing sweet, sour, and salty tastes, and not to substances possessing bitter and pungent tastes. [Response: This is not so.

Because it is established that only these three [tastes] are the instigators (*prayojaka*) in the transformation of taste (*rasapāka*), and because bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes are included within those very [three]; furthermore, because a substance that acts as a preventer (*nivartaka*) cannot be an instigator in the absence of a cause. Nor can it be said that the preservation of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) constitutes the preventer, for if that were the case everywhere, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For this reason, he says—starting with "the thing to be removed" (*nivartya*): "The thing to be removed is the morbid alteration (*vikāra*). (70)

That which is fit to be turned back is the "removable" (*nivartya*), and that is the modification (*vikāra*). It must be investigated how the remover effects the removal of the modification; for since the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of all diseases is always present, it is impossible to determine its status as the remover of this or that specific disease by means of individual delimitations such as "this [medicine] is for this [disease]. Therefore, the meaning is that once a modification has arisen, because it is impossible to determine its status as the remover of this or that [specific cause], the modification is what is "removable," as established in the Sūtra.

[Objection: But was it not already established that when a disorder exists, sweet, sour, and salty tastes act as its remedies? [Response: That is questionable. With the underlying sense that in the statement "the disorder is to be removed," tastes and the like do not serve as the actual removers, he says: "Āma. The disorder of increased *āma* is the cause of all diseases. (71)

For this very reason, that fire which is produced by the *pācaka-pitta* digests only the matter located in the *pakvāśaya* (receptacle of digested food), because the disease arising from tastes contrary to it resides in the *malāśaya* (receptacle of waste).

That substance which possesses a preponderance of the quality of fragrance capable of perceiving tastes conditioned by the parts of earthly substances; which is a substance possessing a palatable taste suitable for digestion conditioned by the process of cooking; which is a substance distinct from those possessing salty and hot tastes with an excess of fiery particles, as well as from substances characterized by alkaline qualities born of the parts of light cotton and from substances possessing other tastes; which is a substance possessing oiliness due to an excess of non-substantial (spiritual) particles; and which, during digestion characterized by an abundance of the quality of sweetness, provides the digestive fire and is the object of the cognition of bitterness—that is an earthly substance.

Regarding substances classified as leaf-derivatives (*patravedha*), there is a threefold beneficial action; regarding substances classified as flower-derivatives (*puṣpavedha*) and fruit-derivatives (*phalavedha*), there is a threefold action that remedies defects; and regarding substances classified specifically as fruit-derivatives, there is a threefold beneficial action. It must be specified that substances prescribed by the rules for each respective class serve as remedies for their corresponding transformations, and are thus suitable for bodies possessing those specific characteristics. In that regard, they do not possess the power to eliminate disorders of other locations or of different classes.

Where it is observed that [a substance] is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and association (*sahacara*), there this rule applies; for that purpose, it is said "that specific substance. Where, throughout various times, the capacity to counteract substances possessing flavors appropriate to those respective times is invariably observed, there this rule applies; for that purpose, it is said "at those respective times."

"However many diseases there are, however many objects of action for their removers there are"—this is the rule regarding the relationship of cause and effect where it is observed that "when this exists, that exists; when this is absent, that is absent. Where such a grasp of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs according to this rule, there this principle applies. For that reason, it is said: "having that as its object. The meaning of the aphorism is that [remedies] are the removers of the specific modifications ordained by each respective genus (*jāti*). It has been stated that diseases residing in various genera are not removable [by a single means]. This can be asserted only when there is knowledge of all the removers.

Because it is impossible to know the true nature of all things, he says: "That which is to be removed" (*nivartya*). "That which is to be removed" refers to transformation (*vikāra*). Having understood that the means of knowledge is the cognition whose object is the knowledge delimited by the category of substance (*dravyatva*) regarding things that cause drying, nourishing, aging, and so forth, one realizes that because it pertains to all objects, substances such as the essence of flowers and fruits are useless for those [specific purposes].

The meaning is that since [the details] have been stated accordingly regarding the substances prescribed by their respective rules for the formulations of decoctions, powders, oils, ghees, electuaries, and rejuvenatives (rasāyana), we shall hereafter set forth the sequence of suitable foods and the method for consuming substances based on the knowledge of discerning what is wholesome and unwholesome.

Now, is it not the case that the activity directed toward leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth—which possess fruit—is of one kind, while that directed toward substances for drinking and eating, such as decoctions, oils, powders, clarified butter, electuaries, and elixirs (*rasāyana*), is of a different kind? Thus, the dual mode of assistance provided by all substances must be considered. One must state that there exists a single, inherent mode of operation which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) across all species, at all times, in all substances, and against all diseases.

Since it is not appropriate [to say that the relationship] holds only where the causal relation has been grasped through the means of valid cognition consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he says "that and that" (*tattat*) out of this sense of unease:
"That and that substance, at that and that time, regarding that and that object, is the remover among those things to be removed. (72)

The meaning is: in as many substances, in as many times, and in as many types of diseases, there exist [remedies] by way of being eliminators or by way of being causes, across all such classes; these are the substances prescribed for those respective classes.
He explains that very point with the words "the eliminator": the "eliminator" refers to the medicine. (73)

Now, it was stated that the modification (vikāra), which has as its object the specific quality to be removed, acts as the remover by causing upward and downward evacuation. Immediately thereafter, one might object that if there is an aggravation of the defects (doṣa) caused by that [modification], then the action of evacuation would become unsuitable; anticipating this objection, he says "doṣa... [in verse 74].
It is caused by the three doṣas. 74.
The meaning is that because the action of purgation is the effect of the three *doṣas*, it is impossible to establish [the remedy] as something that brings about their cessation.

Due to the underlying dissatisfaction that the fact of *āmavṛddhi* being produced by the *doṣas* would only be established by such a demonstration, he says: "Of all..."—namely, "the protection against *āma* is the remover for all living beings. (75)

The human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is the protection of all beings from *āma* (undigested toxins). When a disorder occurs, the first remedy to be applied is the elimination of *āma*. For instance, when *āma* is provoked, the means of its removal constitutes the human goal of protecting beings from *āma*. Now, one might object: "The protection from *āma* does not arise solely from earthly substances; rather, eating little food would nourish the bodily tissues (*dhātu*) and be beneficial to the humors (*doṣa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Fire" (*vahni*). This refers to substances that increase the digestive fire (*vahni*), specifically those substances that, as long as they are consumed, nourish the body and stimulate the gastric fire (*jaṭharānala*). || 76 ||

It nourishes the *dhātus* because it increases the digestive fire (*vahni*). Since that by which even the maintenance of the *anāma* (the subtle body) is increased, by that very same means it is both nourishing and depleting; it performs the functions of equalizing depletion and providing nourishment. This can be stated when there is a distinction between substances, for it is not sufficient merely to consume a substance that increases the digestive fire, as that alone does not fulfill the purpose. Rather, it must be said that it is a "substance possessing unctuousness" (*snehavat*), because such a substance is the cause of the action of depletion [in certain contexts]. Thus he says: "Those respective objects..."—those things suitable for unctuousness are the augmenters. (77)

The meaning is that although there is a single mode (*ekaprakāraka*) by virtue of being the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the property of being a substance possessing oiliness—which is a category that increases fire—there is still a difference between the objects (*padārthabheda*) due to their connection with the act of eating.

There are many substances that act as eliminators (*nivartaka*). It must be stated that all of them possess the capacity to induce [the elimination], because such consumption of all the substances is appropriate. He says "pure" (*viśuddha*) to indicate that pure substance, having been cooked together with oil, performs the function of the drying earth-element upon that cooking oil: "The eliminator consists of pure oil. (78)

There are many substances unfit for consumption that cause the onset of diseases, and there are many edible substances that bring about the cessation of diseases. Certain substances, having undergone a change in taste during digestion, effect the pacification of various diseases. When substances are combined with other substances, they yield the specific results produced by those combinations; when many substances are combined, they yield manifold results.

When there is a combination of incompatible substances, they yield the results of those incompatible substances. Having considered all of this, the preparation of a compound consisting of many substances of that same class becomes pure. For example, through the combination of alkali (yavakṣāra) and green substances, [the substance] abandons its own nature and appears red in form. When a substance comes into contact with another substance, it imparts the specific qualities prescribed by that other substance; it imparts whatever is produced by the combination of the substances involved.

A substance that possesses a taste produced by its conjunction with various ingredients is called "pure" (śuddha). When cooked together with such pure substances, a fat (sneha) that has been well-cooked through the process of drinking and heating imparts the qualities of fat. Due to being processed through cooking with as many substances as are characterized by sweet, sour, and salty tastes—which serve as the primary counteracting agents against the power that causes the vitiation of Vāyu—that pure fat bestows the qualities of all those respective substances.

"Over-cooked" (*atipācita*) refers to that which has been cooked to the point of being perfectly done. It is said that "over-cooked fat" (*atipācitasneha*) is a "reversing agent" (*nivartaka*). A reversing agent is that which serves as a remedy for diseases caused by the provocation of *vāta* and for wasting disorders (*śoṣa*). That, however, is pure fat (*śuddhasneha*). Regarding the case where fasting (*apatarpaṇa*) serves as a reversing agent, this statement is made:

"One should administer medicine when the food is digested, in the case of a stiff and heavy abdomen, for the purpose of digesting the remainder of the humors (*doṣa*) and for the kindling of the digestive fire."
The pacification of morbid humors occurs through fasting.

In accordance with this statement, the action [of purification] is caused by drying substances. By this, the causative role of drying substances is established. Now, the drying agent is described: that which, being caused by the combination of as many substances as are characterized by bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes, acts as the primary manifestor of qualities endowed with the power to counteract diseases of *kapha*, and which imparts all its qualities through those actions—that is pure oil (*śuddhasneha*).

"Over-cooked" means excessively cooked, reaching the limit of perfect ripening; that oily substance (sneha-dravya) is a remover of the multitude of diseases dominated by phlegm (kapha). Regarding diseases born of wind (vāta), the meaning is that in some cases they are removers [of vāta] while being desiccants (śoṣaka), and in others they are removers while being nourishers (poṣaka). He states the purpose of that oil: "limb... etc. Through the anointing of the limbs, the separation of limb from limb shines forth. (79)

For diseases localized in the limbs, the disease is destroyed through contact with the respective sites; due to the absence of extreme pain, it is removed by mere application of ointment to the limbs. For the restoration of life in the bones, ears, nose, and other joints—where there is no movement of the *doṣas*—friction and massage of the feet should be properly performed. By that means, the disorder is correctly eliminated from the contracted limb. The function that produces all the limbs within the embryo situated in the womb is caused by the mother’s body; for, while it is not caused by anything else, it is caused by that [the mother’s body].

It has been established that the bodily part [of the embryo] is produced from the body of the mother. This is because it is observed that the cause of the function of the digestive fire (jaṭharānala) residing within the embryo is the consumption of the essence of the mother's food; furthermore, that [essence] itself is produced from the nutritional juices (rasa) of the mother’s food. From the consumption of substances in which the earth element predominates, an earthly bodily part arises. The cause of the function of a bodily part consisting of water is the consumption of substances in which the water element predominates. The function of the digestive fire residing within the embryo is produced by the predominance of the fiery element (taijasa). Therefore, he says "the pregnant woman" [should drink ghee], implying that the fire produced within the pregnant woman is generated by her consumption of ghee. || 80 ||

The meaning is that the fire within the womb (*jātavedas*) itself becomes the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*). The fact that the limbs of winged creatures (*pratatriṇām*) are caused by their respective limbs, and that eggs are the producers of those limbs, implies that for the digestive fire as well, the ghee situated within the egg is the very cause. He states "of the sky-goers" (*khecarāṇām*) to demonstrate that such a relationship of cause and effect exists even for substances of those specific types among those born from wombs or eggs. Regarding the sky-goers, [the process occurs] while producing [them] together with ghee within the bird's body.

Because they rely on a predominance of fiery substances (*taijasadravya*) and because they follow an upward path of movement—just like the blazing of fire—those living beings grow while still remaining within the egg (*aṇḍastha*), due to their very bodies consisting of a preponderance of fiery elements. Those two parents themselves consist of bodies made of substances in which air and fire predominate, serving as the cause for the production of the egg. The meaning is that the physical forms (*piṇḍa*) born from them grow by themselves.

For what reason do birds attain the ascent to the path of the sky? Since the definition of a body as being composed of the five elements is common to all, and since movement consisting of coming, going, and shifting is a general characteristic of bodies, he says: "ascent"—meaning the ascent of those traveling upon the paths of the sky. (82)

The action of birds in ascending [the sky] results from their bodies possessing qualities of substances composed of fire and air; by this, movement in the sky, the capacity to perceive subtle objects, and endurance of cold, heat, and pleasure are obtained—this is the meaning.

Because the bodies of those who move on earth consist of a predominance of earthly elements, they possess the capacity to traverse the ground; furthermore, they maintain life-force (*āyu*), fire (*tejas*), and semen (*retaḥ*) born from the consumption of oily substances. Thus he says: "Ghee," etc.
By consuming food soaked in ghee, one maintains the life-force, fire, and semen.

The bodies of the *khecaras* possess a natural firmness of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). This firmness of the constituents is not pleasing to the bodies of those who move on the earth (*bhūcaras*).
