The meaning is that the firmness of their constituents arises from the consumption of various substances possessing specific tastes as a limiting condition (*upādhi*), and is not attained through their own inherent nature.

[Objection: But was it not stated that eating food soaked in ghee increases longevity and so forth? [Response: That is to be reconsidered, because eating food excessively soaked in ghee is a cause of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), and it is a cause for the depletion of life-force (*āyus*), vital energy (*tejas*), and semen (*retas*); furthermore, its heaviness (*gurutva*) is well-known. Those substances which cause indigestion are indeed causes of depletion. Since this is established through the means of valid cognition consisting of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he says: "By the use of suitable substances... [Verse 84]: "It increases through the use of suitable substances."

The "combination" (*yoga*) refers to the application of suitable substances that cause the cessation of disease. The "nature of being a substance possessing a taste that causes such cessation" is the causality for the effect, which is the absence of disease. That which is called "the cessation resulting from the use of a particular substance" is precisely the causality for the effect, which is the absence of disease. The meaning is: "May the bodily constituents (*avayava*) increase."

Is this not also untenable? For the performance of actions involving the use of suitable or unsuitable substances merely results in the demonstration that such substances are the cause of the effect consisting in the absence of all diseases; it does not establish their causality with respect to the mere preservation of the embryo. To clarify this point—that only the action which increases the physical mass (*piṇḍa*) has been demonstrated—the author, sensing a lack of clarity, says: "They grow" (*edhante*).
The seasons prosper for him. || 85 ||

In this context, by the mention of "seasons" (*ṛtu*), the state of being a cause for the growth of the fetus is established. However, this is not a section intended solely to define the seasons; rather, it is a stage intended to establish the causality of the process that increases the embryo situated within the womb. Herein, this [causality] is not explicitly illuminated, because the text merely establishes the process of increasing the embryo. To explain: a "season" (*ṛtu*) is that which indicates a specific time characterized by the functions of the season, the absence of such functions, and the factors that promote growth, all of which are directed toward the purpose of the seasonal activity.

The meaning is that such a specific time, characterized by the presence of the season and the consumption of substances that increase the parts of the embryo situated in the womb, causes the effects to grow.

[Objection: But how can there be an increase in the parts of the physical body (*piṇḍa*) by means of the growth of time characterized by the absence of the seasonal period (*ṛtu*), given that such a time of absence suitable for that [growth] is not observed? Because of this unease, he says: "From food... — "From food, beings are born" (86).

The intended meaning here is that the consumption of food substances for as long as they last—which is the cause for the manifestation of the sprout of the physical body—is the cause for the effect known as the absence of seasons (i.e., the maintenance of life). This is because the consumption of all types of flavorful substances is possible for everyone, yet the specific effect [of seasonal change] is not observed everywhere. Due to this lack of logical consistency, he says: "Once born..."—namely, "those who are born grow by means of food" (87).
The meaning is that it has been established that the womb-mass (jātapiṇḍa) has as its cause the consumption of the substances of the tastes mentioned previously.

The fact that eating food causes the firmness of the body is established by the means of valid cognition known as *anvaya-vyatireka* (positive and negative concomitance). This is because it is established by the principles of logic (*nyāyanaya*) according to the maxim: "When X exists, Y exists; when X is absent, Y is absent. Thus, when there is the eating of food, there is the firmness of the body, and in its absence, there is its absence.

And because [the reason] is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*): for Devadatta, who does not eat during the day, his existence is not possible without eating at night; thus, even for him, existence is not tenable without eating at night, as it would not be something that increases the parts of the body distinct from its own [already existing] parts, since one means cannot be the cause of the parts of another. Due to this lack of cogency, he says: "It eats and it is eaten" (Gītā 3.8). It eats and it is eaten by beings. (88)

The elements are of three kinds. Because the consumption of substances characterized as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* causes the growth of bodies preponderant in those respective qualities (*guṇas*), the body consists of the three *guṇas*. The meaning is that the elements arise from those specific substances which cause their growth. He concludes the stated point with the words "therefore": "Therefore, food is so called. (89)

Food bestows the elements, provides nourishment, and causes the growth of the limbs; it grants such qualities as these. By the word "iti," the reason is stated: food containing *rasa* (nutritive essence) brings about the growth of the limbs. Therefore, that which consists of the essence of food—which summarizes the aforementioned meaning—is pure food containing *rasa*; the meaning is that it is called "consisting of breath" (*prāṇamaya*) because it increases the limbs of the physical body.

Food, however, provides [nourishment] residing in itself along with its qualities, because it lacks the capacity to effect the growth of limbs. Eating dry food yields a contrary result. To the question, "How can it be said that food is the sustainer of life? he says: "Ghee... (v. 90). One should cause a pregnant woman to be given food soaked in ghee. Dry food gives a contrary result; only food soaked in ghee is effective for the purpose. Therefore, the meaning is that one should cause a pregnant woman to be given food soaked in ghee.
He concludes the point already stated once more: "Therefore... (v. 91).
Therefore, living beings are born, increasing the elements and causing the expansion of their own constituent parts. || 91 ||

It has been stated that eating food soaked in ghee promotes the growth of the body's constituent parts. When any disorder arises, it must be remedied by something that counteracts it. It cannot be said that food soaked in ghee alone is the remedy, because of its heavy nature. Therefore, [the previous view] is inconsistent; with this sense of dissatisfaction, he says—"That"—meaning: "In that case, the substance that dries up or nourishes is the medicine. (92)

When a disorder occurs, the depleting (*śoṣaka*) and nourishing (*poṣaka*) substances become the agents of action. In the case of a newborn infant during the first menstrual period, for a disease born of a depleting substance, the depleting substance is the remedy; for a disease born of a nourishing substance, the nourishing substance is the counteragent. Thus, until the end of the tenth month, they serve as mutual counteragents. The meaning is that for a fetus in the womb, whatever substance acts as a promoter, that same substance alone serves as the remedy.

[Objection: Is it not the case that even a newborn infant, like one still in the womb, is nourished by medicinal substances? For the knowledge of consuming substances does not develop in an infant who has just been born; this is because the act of consuming medicinal substances for treatment—which arises from the mother’s intake of food and its essence—is itself a nourishing substance. Since it is impossible to say that in this case too, only nourishing substances are the cause, [the author], due to this underlying dissatisfaction, says: "In this way," etc. Thus, there is progressive growth month after month. (93)
Taking the consumption of suitable tastes as the subject, one should increase [the dose] little by little.

With reference to these factors—namely the constituent parts (of the body), time, and place—the meaning is that the respective suitable substance, when increased, becomes beneficial and curative. This rule has been established regarding substances that are desiccating or nourishing. Thus, it is not appropriate to perform medical treatment on a monthly basis. Because it is unsuitable [to treat] merely by saying "one should eat substances that cause growth" for a body that is already growing, he says "yāvat" (as much as): "In that regard, the medicines are according to the age. (94)

Only substances that promote growth are recommended; otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle. By the power of the word *yāvat* (as much as), the intended meaning is the consumption of whatever substance possesses a suitable nutritive essence. It is not only every substance that promotes growth that acts as a nourisher, for by the force of time, they may possess a nature characterized by the quality of causing desiccation. Therefore, he says: "By ghee, those who are to be nourished are nourished" (95).

The meaning is that a substance produced by the cooking of ghee through its conjunction with fire—which possesses a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) and a cooked flavor (*pākarasa*)—is the cause of the effect [of rejuvenation], because it is a substance that imparts the quality of rejuvenation (*vārdhika-guṇa*) resulting from its conjunction with a substance possessing unctuousness (*sneha*).

When the *doṣas* have been diminished by means such as fasting (*laṅghana*) and when there is a depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), a nourishing substance performs its function [in that state], [thinking] "this is what provides nourishment. In that context, it is improper to employ a depleting substance as a counteracting agent; therefore, he says:
"No"—meaning, depleting substances are not to be used at the time of nourishing. (96)

The meaning is that performing the function of a nourishing substance at a time when it ought to perform the function of a depleting substance is improper. Now, one might object: "In common worldly usage, only the six tastes (ṣaḍrasa) are fit for such transactions; it follows that each substance possessing a single taste is the cause for nourishing a single constituent element (dhātu), since the capacity to nourish is established by its very nature and because there exists no substance apart from those possessing taste. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The six tastes [nourish] the seven constituents" (verse 97). The six tastes are the nourishers of the seven constituents.

Is it because [rasa] nourishes blood (*asṛj*) one by one, like the astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*), that it is the progenitor? Therefore, keeping in mind the intention that it is easy to state that the six tastes nourish the seven constituents (*dhātu*) because each is dominated by a single taste, [the author] says "rasa" to address the objection that this [previous argument] is inconsistent, since the fact that those [tastes] nourish the seven constituents is established by its very nature.
For *rasa* is indeed blood. (98)
He is indeed the essence. 99.

The nutrient essence (*rasa-dhātu*) becomes blood because it is produced from that single essence; while remaining within, it is designated as "blood," and when it goes outside, it flows in the form of sweat. That same essence, having gone outside through heat, becomes the sense organ of taste (*rasana-indriya*). Taste, in the form of saliva, is itself the ray (*raśmi*); the knower of that is the Self (*ātman*). Knowledge regarding that object is the cause of bliss (*ānanda*). The meaning is that bliss belongs only to one who possesses the knowledge that takes as its object the knowledge apprehending the sense organ of taste.

The two calves are for the sake of the two rasas; the nose is for the purification of the internal organ (āśaya); every month there is growth for all living beings, and in the first period of menstruation, there is the ninefold union of the appropriate yoga.
Thus ends the commentary on the second inquiry of Āyurveda, composed by Yogānandanātha;
this renowned commentary on the sūtras of Āyurveda, approved by great scholars, which provides an explanation for each aphorism and benefits the world, is now complete.
In the *Āyurveda*, this is the third question.

Now, it has been stated that having attained the knowledge of taste, one becomes joyful (*ānandī*). This is to be considered: the possession of the experience of bliss by individual souls (*jīvātman*) is such that the sensory cognition of external objects through the external senses is not itself the cause of bliss. The experience of cognition regarding those objects is caused by bliss only for the duration of the contact between the sense organ and the object; once that [contact] perishes, that [experience] perishes as well. Since the experience of external sensory objects perishes when that contact ceases, [the author], due to this lack of logical consistency, says—"Now" (*atha*).
Now begins the instruction on yoga. || 1 ||

By the word *atha* (now/thereupon), immediate succession is indicated. It has been established that the consumption of substances possessing the six tastes is the cause for the effect of bodily firmness. Therefore, keeping in mind that the elements, having become more firmly established, serve as the cause for achieving the conjunction of the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*), and that the experience of bliss regarding that object arises from the conjunction of the internal organ and the self, he says: "The contemplation of the Supreme Self by the individual self (*jīvātman*) is the cause of bliss."

[Objection: But surely the instruction on yoga (*yogānuśāsana*) may also be a cause for achieving the absence of indigestion; since that being the case, because the cessation of illness alone would be the result, one would obtain only the avoidance of an undesirable state as the fruit. To this, he says: "Therefore...
[and] "Therefore, yoga bestows its fruit" (2).

The experience of objects has the bliss of objects as its cause; likewise, the experience of the self has the bliss of the self as its cause, because the effect produced by that which has bliss as its cause is the same in both cases. Anticipating the question of what further fruit is obtained through the instruction on yoga, [it is said]: the effect produced by a cognition whose object is a cognition directed toward impermanent objects is itself impermanent. Since the self is an eternal substance, only a cognition whose object is a cognition directed toward an eternal substance constitutes bliss.

The meaning is that because the internal organ, the mind, has the nature of having the self as its object, the experience of bliss is obtained at all times; thus, since the conjunction of the self and the mind alone constitutes yoga, yoga bestows the eternal fruit.

[Objection: Since the Supreme Self is an eternal substance and is all-pervasive, the mind would always be in contact with the Self; consequently, there would always be an experience of bliss, because it is a rule that a sense organ, having come into contact with its object, reveals what is reached. Thus, the cognition whose object is that [bliss] would become an object of the Self. To this, he says: "prakṛti... (Yoga-sūtra 3). Yoga is the transformation of *prakṛti* consisting of the cognitive states (*pratyaya*) which have as their object the internal knowledge of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

Having taken as its object the Puruṣa as distinguished from Prakṛti by means of the internal organ, the mind, when the Supreme Self as distinguished by its attributes is made the object, there occurs a cessation of knowledge regarding the objects of the external senses; because the experience of such a Supreme Self as qualified by those attributes is the cause of supreme bliss, the yoga of knowledge concerning that [Self] is called *pariṇāmayoga*. The meaning is that whenever the substance qualified by both Prakṛti and Puruṣa becomes the object, then there is the experience of bliss.

If that were so, then since knowledge whose object is the Self as qualified by primordial nature (prakṛti) has the highest bliss as its cause, this [knowledge] should always take the experience of bliss as its domain; what then would be the use of knowledge directed toward the objects of the external senses, given that it is caused by the experience of only limited bliss? To this he says: "Rajas...
"Due to the predominance of rajas, it is unstable and, being extroverted, is the cause of pleasure and pain. (4)

The Supreme Self (paramātmā) remains characterized by the quality of passion (rājasa-guṇa) for some time, characterized by the quality of goodness (sāttvika-guṇa) for some time, and characterized by the quality of darkness (tāmasa-guṇa) for some time. When the qualities of passion and so forth become the very nature of the individual self (jīvātman), the Self becomes associated with those qualities; it then joins with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with its object, because the rule that the senses function by reaching their objects has been observed.

The meaning is that, due to the influence of defects touched by the quality of *rajas*, one conceals the experience of the Self (*ātman*) and experiences the pleasure of external objects. When the living being (*jīva*), characterized by the quality of *sattva*, becomes distinguished by the quality of *tamas*, then, being so distinguished, he experiences pleasure accompanied by suffering; thus he says: "Tamas" (verse 5).
Due to the predominance of *tamas*, through ignorance of what ought and ought not to be done, and being constrained by anger and other passions, he is deluded.

Due to the predominance of the quality of *tamas*, one whose mind is deluded by the absence of discriminative knowledge regarding duty experiences cognition directed toward that [object] through anger, hatred, and so forth; the meaning is that the pleasure directed toward that object, characterized by the three types of desire, is experienced. When there is the manifestation of the quality of *sattva* within *sattva*, then one becomes attached to the Vedānta scriptures which expound dharma, and through the performance of actions prescribed in the scriptures of one's own dharma, the pleasure born of good deeds is experienced—thus he says:
"From the arising of *sattva*, happiness" (verse 6).

The *sāttvika* [nature] is that which impels one toward sound and other objects that accomplish the absence of suffering. The meaning is that when the *sāttvika* quality manifests in the individual soul (*jīva*), it experiences the pleasure pertaining to heaven by performing actions that establish those qualities.

Now, it has been explained that the experience of the *rājasa* quality is seen in the individual self at some times, the experience of the *tāmasa* quality at others, and the experience of the *sāttvika* quality at yet others. In response to the inquiry as to what is the cause for this regular experience of the three qualities, he says: "By eating food of sweet taste... [verse 7], meaning that the cause of the *sāttvika* quality follows from the consumption of food with a sweet flavor.
He who eats food distinguished by a sweet taste becomes possessed of the quality of *sattva*. That individual soul (*jīva*) experiences the qualities arising from its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

He states that the three qualities have the consumption of sweet, sour, and pungent tastes as their cause—namely, "sour" (*amlī*): eating food that has become sour is the cause of the quality of *rajas*. (8)
Bitter [tastes] have tamas as their cause. || 9 ||

He who has a love for sweet flavor becomes one desirous of liberation. He abandons the eating of other flavors and consumes substances possessing sweetness; thus [the author] says, "The sweetness of the seeker of liberation" (mumukṣoḥ). || 10 ||

A substance possessing a sweet taste (*madhurarasavat*) is the cause of liberation (*mokṣahetu*), because, while being devoid of tastes that produce *rājasa* and *tāmasa* qualities, it is a substance possessing a taste that causes the *sāttvika* quality. Whatever taste does not bestow the *sāttvika* quality does not bestow liberation either, like a bitter taste (*kaṭurasa*). Sweetness is always fit to be drunk by those seeking liberation, because, by being the giver of the fruit of liberation—which is caused by the *sāttvika* quality—it acts as a producer of the *sāttvika* quality; and because the *sāttvika* quality itself is the cause of liberation.

Now, it may be argued that when there is an experience of pleasure through the *rājasa* quality, and when there is knowledge of the reality of the object which serves as the cause of that pleasure, an experience of the gradations of the objects of pleasure occurs. The experience of eternal bliss (*nityānanda*), which is the happiness that causes liberation, is produced by sweet taste (*madhurarasajanya*). In contrast, the happiness pertaining to the *rājasa* quality is experienced as being produced by sour taste (*amlarasajanya*). Therefore, because one cannot know the happiness produced by the knowledge that causes liberation—specifically the discriminative knowledge of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted—without the experience of the happiness produced by the *rājasa* quality, [the author], due to this underlying dissatisfaction, says: "Sour" (*āmletyādi*).
From the consumption of sour taste, a single kind of happiness is experienced. (11)

The meaning is that the pleasure produced by sour taste is a direct perception, whereas the pleasure pertaining to liberation—which occurs at a different time, place, body, and state—is experienced through past observation. Therefore, it is indicated by the word "alone" (*eka*) that this [sour taste] is the primary [source of pleasure].
Since the fact that something causes pleasure or the absence of pain cannot be known without experiencing its corresponding pain, he says: "hot," etc.
Hot taste produces pleasure because it is accompanied by pain. || 12 ||

The meaning is that the experience of pleasure is so called because it is the absence of the experience of pain. Now, an objection is raised: pain, which arises from the collection of causes and effects of suffering, is destroyed solely by its experience; however, the cognition of pleasure is preceded by the experience of pain, since the experience of pleasure is preceded by the cognition of the experience of the absence of pain—which is the counter-positive of the effect [of pain]. Furthermore, pleasure, like the persistence of pain, is also caused by pain. With the intention that the preservation of the causal complex for both pleasure and pain—being the cause of their respective effects—is itself the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) and the fruit, he says: "At that time... (*tadā*).
Then there is the establishment of the seer in his own true nature. 13.

The Lord, who is the Seer, exists in the state of his own essential nature (*svarūpāvasthāna*), yet he remains having become the very form of the world (*jagatsvarūpa*). This is because the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*) consists precisely in the experience of pleasure and the experience of the absence of pain—which is the counter-positive of the effect [of pain]. The meaning is that the Seer’s abiding in his own essential nature conforms to pleasure and pain. His body, which is the form of the world, is the locus of experience; "experience" (*bhoga*) means the experience of pleasure and pain.

Now, one might object: since the Supreme Self, the Lord, is untainted (*nirlepa*), devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), and possesses the experience of eternal bliss, how can there be in Him the variety of pleasure, pain, and so forth? For the state of presiding over a body is common to both the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the Supreme Self. To this, he says: "Pleasure..."—the three [qualities] consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion first manifest. (14)

"I am happy," "I am suffering"—such states consist of forms conditioned by karma because the self is essentially of the nature of *prakṛti*. The meaning is that when the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is veiled, all those attributes are perceived due to the self being mixed with *māyā*. For this very reason, the individual soul is observed to possess eligibility for action (*karmādhikāritva*). Since the self alone possesses eligibility for liberation (*mokṣādhikāritva*), the tasting of the essence [of the Self] is obtained only by it; the *sāttvika* quality produced thereby becomes an aid to liberation.

When the consumption of sour-tasting food is perceived, then the quality of *rajas* manifests; by that, one experiences pleasure alone. When the consumption of pungent-tasting substances occurs, then pleasure accompanied by suffering is experienced; therefore, he says "that"—that *rajas*, which is the collection of qualities born from its cause. 15.

Regarding the phrase "that [is] rajas" (*tadrajaḥ*), by the word "that" (*tat*), the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are intended. Among these, the effect of the first quality, *rajas*, is indeed a substance possessing an acidic taste (*amlarasa*). The meaning is that a substance with an acidic taste becomes the cause for that which consists of the *rajas* quality. Furthermore, the fact that it is produced from the sweet and salty tastes—which are the effects of the *sattva* quality—is because both *tamas* and *sattva* serve as causes;
this is because the plural number in the word "causes" (*hetavaḥ*) in the aphorism necessitates the inclusion of both *tamas* and *sattva*.

Now, an objection may be raised: according to the aforementioned method, it has been established that the unifier of the sweet, sour, and salty tastes is merely that which generates the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Since substances possessing tastes that alleviate diseases caused by *vāta*, *pitta*, and *kapha* are [already] established as effective through other means, one might ask: how can diseases produced by those [qualities] be alleviated by substances inferior to those that alleviate them? To this, he says: "Just as..."—namely, "those which alleviate diseases are desiccating and nourishing. (16)

Substances possessing a sweet taste are caused by the *sattva* quality; substances possessing a sour taste are caused by the *rajas* quality; and substances possessing salty or pungent tastes are caused by the *tamas* quality. These [single-taste substances] do not eliminate disease. Rather, it must be stated that a substance possessing many tastes—due to the combination of numerous ingredients—arising from the consumption of substances that either deplete or nourish, becomes the eliminator of disease. For when a disease manifests, it is followed by various complications (*āmaya*);
therefore, in that case, there must be an abundance of substances possessing multiple tastes to serve as the means for eliminating that disease.

Now, is it a substance possessing *sattva* and a specific *rasa* that removes disease, or is it just any substance possessing a *rasa*? It cannot be the first, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If you say it is the consumption of any substance whatsoever, then one would have to expect the same result from consuming a substance possessing only a single *rasa*. Since this would render [the specific prescription] otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*), he says—out of this unease—"suitable" (*yogya*). "Yoga" is the union with what is suitable. || 17 ||

The knowledge of the causes that follow diseases is preceded by the knowledge of the causes consisting of substances possessing various tastes, because a disease that has entered into many [types] arises from the causal complex of the combination of substances with many tastes.
Indeed, only a seer (ṛṣi) knows the result born from the combination of substances;
as for the statement in the *Bheṣajakalpa*:
It was compiled according to the rules, in accordance with the requirements of place and time.
Medicine prepared with various formulations acts as nectar.
The meaning is that, just as a predominance of tastes prescribed by specific rules according to the particular disease becomes the remover of that disease.

Now, one might object: according to the maxim that "an excess is not at all a fault," a substance possessing many sweet flavors acts as a remedy for wind (*vāta*); a combination of substances possessing many sour flavors acts as a remedy for bile disorders (*pitta*); and a substance possessing many salty and hot flavors acts as a remedy for phlegm (*kapha*). One might argue that the formulation of such combinations would constitute a "suitable application" (*yogyayoga*). Anticipating this objection, the author says "citta..."—for mental delusion (*cittavibhrama*) is a misconception (*viparyaya*). (18)

To the extent that the preparation of a compound occurs through the mixing of substances possessing incompatible properties—such as a disease-inducing substance and a substance with a bilious (pitta) taste—it constitutes a "contrary combination" (*viruddhayoga*). That, however, results in a mental delusion (*cittavibhrama*). Here, *citta* refers to the mind (*manas*). The meaning is that when, due to the identity of these two, silver appears in a mother-of-pearl shell where there is an absence of silver-ness, a mental delusion occurs.

[Objection: Surely, when the cognitive complex that apprehends a cognition having "silverness" as its qualifier takes the object in front of one as its object, it manifests that very object as qualified by silverness—just as is observed in the case of marketplaces and cities. Since this is so observed, how could there be a mental delusion in the absence of the entire set of conditions that constitute the scope of such a cognition? Anticipating this objection, he says: *atad* (not-that). [It is] the cognition of "that" in what is "not-that. (Verse 19)

In that case where silverness appears in a mother-of-pearl shell which lacks silverness, an error arises in the form "that [silver] in this [shell]," which is actually something else. In that situation, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—the causal complex that apprehends the cognition having that [silver] as its object—takes as its domain only the object qualified by that [silverness], because the causal complex that apprehends the object present before one exists. To this, he says: "Due to bile," etc.
Because of a single dominant type of bile, there is the [error]: "The conch is yellow. (20)

The arising of bile-related diseases occurs through the consumption of substances that aggravate the *pitta*. In that state, due to diseases such as *kāca* (cataract) or *kāmalā* (jaundice), there arises—by virtue of those respective defects—the cognition "this [object] in front of me, which is qualified by the quality of whiteness, is qualified by the quality of yellowness. And that [cognition] arises from food that is contrary to those defects. At that time, the cognition "the conch is yellow" arises.

Now, it may be objected: "Are not all diseases produced by the three *doṣas*? And are they not all produced by the consumption of specific tastes? Therefore, that which is stated in the aphorism—that mental confusion (*cittavibhrama*) arises from the consumption of substances antagonistic to *pitta*—is questionable. The cognition "this [conch] is yellow" appears with respect to a conch characterized by the quality of whiteness. This is incorrect; because of this dissatisfaction, he says: "That [cognition].
That cognition is produced by food that is antagonistic to *pitta*. (21)

And the cognition having delusion as its object is produced by bile (*pitta*). Furthermore, the cognition "the conch is yellow" is produced by food incompatible with pure bile; for, while being produced by an incompatible taste that generates diseases of wind (*pavana*) and bile, it is produced by food incompatible with that [bile], whereas that which is not so [produced] is not so, like a jar or other such things.

Is it not the case that a cognition having an error as its object arises regarding mother-of-pearl, such as "this is silver," and the same is perceived in the case of "the conch is yellow"? Both of these [erroneous cognitions] are preceded by the consumption of a substance possessing a flavor contrary to that which causes the non-existence of the effect (disease) to be removed by the consumption of a substance possessing the [correct] flavor; this is because they are substances that cause the absence of disease produced by flavors that are either too strong or deficient. Whatever is not so is not thus, like a jar.

Now, one might object: even when some substance has been made an object of perception and was previously experienced as a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), doubt still arises regarding that very same thing. In that case, the consumption of flavorful food is not the cause; therefore, he says "excessive" (*ati*).
Upon excessive scrutiny, doubt arises when there is a cognition of a defect (*doṣa-pramā*). || 22 ||

When there is contact between a sense organ and its object, knowledge regarding that object arises. However, with respect to that very object, at that very time, an error occurs due to the defect of excessive scrutiny. In that case as well, the previously arisen knowledge whose object was a valid cognition of silver—being produced by the defect of excessive scrutiny—does not become the remover of the doubtful cognition; such is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the consumption of a substance possessing a flavor contrary [to the cause] is what cures a disease caused by the consumption of a contrary substance? If that were so, then for diseases produced by a sweet (*madhura*) taste, only a sweet taste would be the cure. For example, it would be impossible to say that the consumption of the sweet-tasting substance of the plantain fruit (*kadalīphala*) is the cure for indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) caused by the unwholesome taste of the plantain fruit. The intended meaning is rather that sour tastes (*amlarasa*) and others would be the curatives.

The meaning is that as long as there is knowledge of eating substances—specifically, that at a given time, eating lighter food than the previous day's meal, exactly as it was perceived for that time, is beneficial—it follows that the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) consists in the preservation of the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the disease produced on the first day by means of substances appropriate for that time, which results in the absence of the disease suitable for that time.

Now, one might object: "In a case where a valid cognition has arisen from eating food that is delicious yet lacks flavor, how could there subsequently arise a doubt regarding the object of that very cognition—due to a defect in the eye caused by excessive staring—even after the knowledge of the jar has already been established? Anticipating this unease, he says: "Excessive... (atyanta-).
A defect of the visual organ can occur through excessively unblinking vision. || 23 ||

The meaning is this: due to the influence of those defects, that cognition is erroneous (*tatpramā*) with respect to the object not actually perceived; for, in a situation where the cognition produced by sense organs afflicted by defects is a valid cognition (*pramā*), it does not act as an obstacle to a state of doubt, and thus doubt arises therein.
One should not oppress the senses, nor should one over-indulge them.

According to this statement, there is no doubt that the excessive pampering of the senses is indeed "unblinking vision" (*animiṣadṛṣṭi*). It does not arise from the consumption of incompatible tastes (*viruddharasa*), because the causal complex for the perception of specific qualities (*viśeṣadarśana*) acts as an obstacle to doubt; thus, the causal complex for consuming tastes that remove that [doubt] lacks the capacity to produce it. When someone experiences an error (*bhrama*), it is because the causal complex that establishes the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* qualities is distinct [from the former]. Due to this underlying implication, he says "rajaḥ" (passion). Error arises from bile (*pitta*), which is the transformation of substances caused by the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*. || 24 ||

The consumption of substances possessing a sour taste that is devoid of its proper potency is the cause of the delusion that such qualities are being produced as primary; likewise, the consumption of substances possessing salty or pungent tastes that are devoid of their proper potency is the cause of the delusion that such qualities are being produced as primary. Therefore, delusion (*bhrama*) is produced by a taste that lacks its proper potency, whereas doubt (*saṃśaya*) is not of such a nature. This is the meaning.

Now, one might object: according to the principles of the Nyāya-śāstra, just as the certainty of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the cause of inference, so too the certainty of that [object] which prevents the occurrence of doubt or the ascertainment of its absence is the cause of that [cognition]; thus, erroneous cognition (*bhrama-jñāna*) can arise solely through the defect of unblinking vision. To this, he says:
"In that regard..."—that is, regarding those objects of visual perception which have been previously experienced. (25)
When an error occurs regarding an object that has been experienced by others as a valid cognition (*pramā*), that error must be removed by its sublater.

Now, one might object: once the cognition "this is a jar" has arisen following the contact between the sense organ and the object, a mental error may arise such that "the cognition produced in me is not valid. [The author] says "as long as" (*yāvat*) because of the underlying dissatisfaction with the argument that this is merely due to the absence of the object being within the range of sensory cognition when the senses are afflicted by a disease caused by eating substances with a particular taste.
As long as the embryo remains within the womb, so long is there the protection of the physical substance.

The meaning is that [the mind] remains within the womb. When this mind is directed toward an object such as a jar within the range of visual sensory cognition, another cognition that has arisen is not directed toward that [same] object; it is incapable of engaging with that object because it lacks the capacity to produce engagement, just like a valid cognition whose object is an error.

The erroneous cognition whose object is the sensory faculty afflicted by a disease produced by the consumption of substances lacking essence (virasa-dravya) has the mind as its subject, because it is characterized by a causal complex that falls within the scope of an experience of mental error. The "lump" (piṇḍa) which is the object of that cognition is the maintenance of the consumption of substances possessing the essence that counteracts that error. The meaning is that the cognition whose object is the error must be protected from those substances that possess the essence which counteracts it.

Now, it may be argued that when one consumes wholesome food—which serves as the causal factor for the absence of the consumption of unwholesome substances that produce delusion—and when there occurs a contact between the respective sense organs and their objects, no error arises because of the experience that the cognition possesses the qualifier in that which bears it (*tadvati tatprakārakatva*). This is because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that generates doubt is absent; for through the experience of a cognition whose object is the knowledge of the object that serves as the locus of the erroneous cognition, that [experience] has as its object the absence of error and the like.

He states that because a physical mass (piṇḍa) which is the object of that knowledge might be the object of erroneous or doubtful cognition, the effect of consuming some substance [as food] would be impossible; thus he says: "adoṣa... etc.
One might, in some cases, avoid a physical mass that has arisen from no defect. (27)

Those whose internal dispositions (*āśaya*) are corrupted, when there is contact between the sense organs and their objects, perceive only that which is the object of error; the meaning is that this pertains to the object of a cognition common to both [the erroneous and the non-erroneous], because it falls within the scope of a cognition regarding the sense organ that is not afflicted by defects.
For medicine is beneficial only when applied to the specific cause. || 28 ||

[Objection: Surely, when a cause exists, a disease arises; in that case, wholesome treatment (*pathya*) should be administered. In that context, eating light food is wholesome. Furthermore, when the *āśayas* (receptacles/organs) become vitiated by the *doṣas*, it must be said that there is an emptiness of the *āśayas* due to insufficient eating. According to the meaning of the aphorism, "When [the *āśaya*] is empty, the *vāyu* becomes provoked," because of the predominance of *vāyu* there and the absence of the state of proper movement within the *āśayas*, the sense organs (*indriyas*) become afflicted with disorders. In this situation, the aphorism stating that "wholesome medicine" is the remedy is not consistent; therefore, with this underlying dissatisfaction, he says: "As long as... (*yāvad*).
Up to those defiled [states] produced from the transformation of food. || 29 ||

The meaning is that even eating as much as one can in a day causes affliction for those with craving, while even eating a meager meal causes excessive affliction for those with craving; since neither of these two is wholesome, he is thereby refuting the very Sūtra [that permits such eating].
Defiled states are the afflictions; non-defiled states are not afflictions. || 30 ||
The meaning is that those which are afflicted are afflictions, while those which are non-afflicted are not afflictions.

[Objection: Surely, for one who has developed a disease from insufficient food, even excessive eating is not wholesome; and for one who has developed a disease from excessive eating, even insufficient food is not wholesome. Since it is impossible to state a remedy that applies to both cases, [the author], out of this sense of unease, says: "As long as..."—meaning, "as long as the medicine prescribed for each day is being administered. (33)

The meaning is as follows: where the state of having eaten [properly] is manifested through the absence of indigestion in those who eat day after day, and where the internal organs (āśayas) being free from defects bring about the health of the sense organs—that very knowledge of the object-domain is what can be said to possess the property of having that [object] as its qualificandum and that [form] as its qualifier.

Now, it was previously established that when the *āśayas* (receptacles) are empty, there occurs an aggravation of *vāta*. Even now, as long as diseases remain under discussion, it must be stated that the *āmāśaya* functions as the seat of digestion (*bhuktakaraṇa*). If that were the case, its state of being empty every day would be untenable; therefore, with this underlying concern, he says: "As long as...
"As long as pains arise from the collection of drying qualities (*śoṣaka-guṇa*), the medicine for those [pains] is the respective nourishing substance (*poṣaka-dravya*) that has arisen therein. (32)

The meaning is that as long as there exists a nourishing substance (*niṣṭhapoṣakadravya*) which serves as the counteragent to the diseases produced by drying substances manifested from a flavorful substance (*rasavaddravya*) that has become the cause of those diseases, for that long it remains the medicine that eliminates those diseases.
Dispelling the lack of propriety in the preceding sūtra, he says: "Ām. The function of the emission of *ām* must be performed. || 33 ||

It should be understood that the act of eliminating undigested matter (*āma*) must be performed daily. This is to indicate that once one has the knowledge, "Undigested matter has increased in me," the act of eliminating *āma* is the prescribed rule. The meaning is that this medicine is intended for one who possesses the knowledge, "Undigested matter arises in me every day," and for whom the mere removal of *āma* constitutes the performance of the rite.

Now, it might be argued that it cannot be said that nourishing substances are the remedy for diseases arising from the consumption of depleting substances. For "consumption of depleting substances" means the consumption of dry substances; when indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arises from that, fasting (*laṅghana*) alone must be performed to bring it to an end.

In that context, since a nourishing substance becomes a medicine (*bheṣaja*) by acting as a restorative, one might argue that after the manifestation of pain, once the provocation of the *doṣas* has been removed through fasting (*laṅghana*), a nourishing substance should serve as the medicine there for the purpose of increasing the bodily tissues (*dhātu*). However, this is not the case; for if a nourishing substance were administered at the very first moment the pain appears, the *doṣas* would become further provoked. Anticipating this objection, the author says: "As long as... (verse 34).

As long as diseases arise from the absence of substances that promote the sprouts of the *dhātus*, then unctuous substances (*sneha*) and the like, when processed with those specific nourishing agents, act as their restorers.

Since diseases manifest due to the consumption of certain incompatible tastes and substances, it is quite easy to prevent them by means of their antidotes even before they appear. They can be averted simply by abstaining from the consumption of those substances. Otherwise, once the sprout of disease has arisen, they would have to be countered by the remedy only after the manifestation of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) that serve as the causal basis for the disease's growth. In such cases, where pain has already arisen because the process of producing the sprouts of disease within the *dhātus* has occurred, the remedies consist of unctuous substances (*sneha*) and others combined with nourishing agents (*bṛṃhaṇa*).

Otherwise, the meaning is that unctuous substances (sneha) and the like, which nourish those [vitiated elements], when combined with their respective substances, eliminate diseases through drinking, massage, and external application.

[Objection: Since it has been introduced that all [beings] consume all substances, the consumption of every substance becomes a cause of disease. This could only be stated once the causal relationship between diseases and substances is known—that is, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between them is grasped such that "this substance is the cause of this disease" and "this substance is the remedy for this disease. However, because such an experience does not occur everywhere, the pervasion between those two does not exist; anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the mother," etc. The tastes residing in the constituent parts produced by the assimilation of the mother’s dietary essence (*āhārarasa*) are the initiators [of the embryo]. (35)

In this regard, by means of the drinking of breast milk and food, infants prevent the manifestation of the effect—the emergence of the sprouts of disease—within the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). For those who have already contracted diseases, there are treatments such as depletives (*śoṣakas*) and nourishers (*poṣakas*) that serve to remove them. Through the transformation of the mother’s nutritional essence (*rasa-āhāra-pariṇāma*), there is the preservation of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of all diseases. Since they remain free from disease through the drinking of breast milk, and because the statement "A man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties" indicates the presence of a factor that obstructs the effects of disease, one is able to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the inference of the sublated by the sublater (*nivartaka-nivartya*). This is the meaning.

Now, it might be argued that the nutritional essences (*rasa*) residing in the bodily constituents produced by the mother’s food and drink are what cure disease. However, when a disorder arises in the mother due to the consumption of unwholesome tastes (*virasa*), the essences residing in her milk become incapable of curing it and instead lead to further complications such as [the child's] improper activity. Anticipating this objection, the author says: "Without disorder.
"Having observed her to be free from disorder, one should have her give the breast-milk born of her own body (*mātṛja*). (36)

When the drinking of breast milk by an infant neither causes disease nor promotes it, then, by ensuring that this mother remains free from any disorder through substances that ward off disease, one should cause her children to drink the breast milk produced by her so that they become fit for consumption.
Even substances that nourish or deplete the child can be provocative; since the mere drinking of breast milk alone is not necessarily provocative, he says "fit" (yogyā).
One should nourish them with suitable substances. || 37 ||

One should nourish them with appropriate substances alone. When indigestion occurs due to the drinking of the mother’s milk and so forth, oily substances are not to be employed there; rather, ghee and oil prepared with formulations suitable for the specific diseases involved serve as the remedy—this is the meaning. The intended sense is that those very same appropriate substances are to be used. The meaning is that one should nourish those infants every day.

Now, it was previously stated that for those whose bodies are produced from a mother’s breast milk and are afflicted by disease, that milk acts as a remedy. Prior to this, the remedial nature of substances possessing the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*) had been established. Now, however, it is stated that the mother’s breast milk alone is the remedy for all diseases. If that were so, the remedial nature of substances possessing the six tastes would not exist; anticipating this objection, he says: "As long as...
As long as they drink breast milk, for that long the children [subsist on] the drinking of breast milk.

The drinking of breast milk nourishes the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) of infants; for while it is not caused by the consumption of solid food, it is caused by substances possessing nutritive essence (*rasa*). Conversely, the consumption of solid food does not nourish the constituents [of an infant], because it nourishes constituents that are unfit for such food and because it is produced from substances that are themselves nourishing. By means of this method of inference, the fact that the mother’s milk nourishes the infant's constituents is established through the evidence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus, the infant’s body is dependent upon the drinking of breast milk for as long as it lasts.

The meaning is that the mere fact of being a mother’s child does not always indicate childhood [in the sense of vulnerability]. When a mother suffers from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), diseases similar to her own arise in her child due to the force of that indigestion. By what means, then, should their remedy be provided? Because powders, ghee, oil, and so forth are unavailable and unsuitable for those infants, and because the diseases produced by such respective indigestions cannot be cured by the specific prescriptions intended for them—due to this underlying difficulty, he says "bāla" (infant):
one should provide a remedy suitable for an infant. || 39 ||

We shall describe the remedy for the diseases of children characterized by functions dependent on the nourishment of breast milk. That remedy is to be accomplished through purgation (*recaka*). Since the disease born from the mother’s intake of food and the drinking of breast milk arises from both bodies—the mother’s and the child’s—it generally increases due to the accumulation of undigested matter (*āma*). Therefore, the meaning is that the respective purgatives serve as the remedy for those various diseases by performing actions appropriate for delicate substances.

Now, one might object: doubt and error regarding a substance possessing salty or hot taste—which act as obstacles to valid cognition produced by visual perception—are themselves produced by defects in the sense organ of sight. How, then, are they removed by those [means] that remove them? To this he says: "By the ear," etc.
Auditory cognition arises from the sense organ of hearing. (40)

The consumption of a substance possessing a bitter taste acts as an obstacle to the auditory valid cognition (*śābdapramā*) produced by the sense of hearing; this is because the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [taste] are such that it obstructs the validity of the cognition. Since it must be stated that when the astringent, bitter, and sweet tastes are pure, they become eliminators [of such obstacles], one might ask: "By what cause are the doubt and error—which obstruct the realization produced by the knowledge of taste as an object of the gustatory faculty—eliminated? To this, he says: "By the gustatory... (*rasaneti*).
From the delusion produced by the sense of taste, and from defects such as the bitterness of undigested food (āma), doubt and error arise regarding what is of a single flavor. || 41 ||

The meaning is as follows: the consumption of substances that are contrary to those [substances] which cause the doubt and the certainty of absence—which respectively obstruct the knowledge of pure taste produced by the gustatory faculty and are caused by the error of consuming substances possessing a sweet taste—are the causes for obstructing the perception of valid cognition regarding the objects of sensory knowledge.
To the question, "By what means are the doubt and the error that obstruct the valid cognition produced by the knowledge of smell, which has the olfactory faculty as its object, removed? he says:
"From the olfactory faculty, the perception of smell is likewise [attained]. (42)

The consumption of a substance possessing a sour taste, which obstructs the valid cognition (*pramā*) of a pure odor produced by the olfactory faculty, is the cause of error and doubt; the meaning is that the ascertainment of that [sour taste] is the cause of that [error and doubt].

To address how doubt and error—which obstruct the verbal valid cognition (*śābdapramā*) produced by the knowledge of sound as the object of the auditory faculty—are to be removed, he says: "By the auditory faculty," etc.
Thus, from the auditory faculty arises the knowledge of sound. (43)

The meaning is that the consumption of substances with a pungent taste (*kaṣāya*), which obstructs the cognition of verbal valid knowledge (*śābdapramā*) produced by the auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*), becomes a cause for doubt and error regarding grammar (*śābdika*). Likewise, the consumption of substances possessing a bitter taste (*tiktarasa*), which obstructs the cognition of valid knowledge produced by the tactile perception of objects of the skin-faculty (*tvagindriya*), generates doubt and error regarding that [tactile object]. The meaning is established by the very principle that "that whose doubt and negative certainty (*vyatirekaniścaya*) are obstacles, the certainty of that [substance] is the cause of that [knowledge]."

For the purpose of removing the defects that obstruct the valid cognition (*pramā*) of knowledge regarding the object of the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*), let there be a suitable cause consisting of nourishing substances and depleting agents that serves as their remover. Since the remedial nature of nourishing substances consists in the application of a formulation joined with palatable substances, and that very medicine becomes the remover, it is said: "depleting" (*śoṣaka*). The erroneous cognition (*viparyaya-jñāna*) concerning the defects arising from the movement of wind and fire—which obstructs the blood produced by an excess of depleting substances—is caused by that which obstructs valid cognition. (44)

[Objection: Let it be that the knowledge concerning the objects of the five senses removes the obstructing pain. But how can there be the application of nourishing substances or the application of drying substances? Anticipating this objection, he says: "moist" (sārdra). In that context, the medicine is a moist substance. (45)

"Moist substance" (sārdradravya) refers to water, urine, honey, oil, and ghee; this constitutes a moist substance. The meaning is that the preparation of these [substances] is specifically enjoined. Now, one might object: "It is understood that a medicinal formulation consisting of nourishing substances combined with a small amount of drying substances would be curative. To address the doubt as to what result would follow from employing only a combination of moist substances at this stage, he says: "With unctuousness" (sasneha). It should be prepared moist and unctuous. || 46 ||

Just as it is said that a substance combined with an oleaginous agent (*snehayukta-dravya*) is a remover (*nivartaka*), so too, a terrestrial substance produced from an excess of nourishing substances (*poṣaka-dravya*) should be ground into powder and infused. By cooking it until it becomes free of liquid (*nirdrava*), one should boil it in fire. Then, through its drinking, application as an ointment, massage, or immersion bath, that very same medicine serves to remove the obstacles to valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding the objects of the five senses that were produced by those [obstructive factors]; thus, it need not be stated [separately].

In this regard, keeping in mind the intention that doubt and error can be eliminated by means of the valid cognition of perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), the nature of the valid cognition of perception is analyzed: "Visual," etc. Valid cognition is the knowledge whose object is distinct from that produced by visual perception and other [sensory perceptions]. (47)

The meaning is as follows: when there is the experience of a cognition having the visual faculty as its object, the fact that this cognition possesses a particular qualifier (tad-prakārakatva) in respect to what lacks that qualifier constitutes its object; likewise, "being other than that which is produced by a visual perception" is a cognition whose object is distinct from it. Since, once error has been removed by such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that very means of valid cognition can be known without requiring a separate medicine to eliminate the error.

[Objection: Surely, when a cognition of yellowness arises with respect to this conch for one whose eyes are afflicted by the disease *kāmalā*, the error of yellowness is not removed by the means of valid inference, "The conch is white, because it possesses the nature of being a conch," since the experience of yellowness in the object present before one is more powerful than that which removes it. Thus, the absence of specific defects would itself be the obstacle to error and doubt. To this, he says: "nirdoṣa" (faultless). "A faultless eye is the producer [of the correct cognition] therein. (48)
The meaning is that the state of having a particular qualifier (tatprakārakatva) in respect to a possessor of that qualifier (tadvati) is apprehended by an eye free from defects.

Now, one might object: when the pervasion (vyāpti) between smoke and fire has been grasped through repeated observation, and a delusion (*bhrama*) arises upon seeing a mass of dust where there is no fire, that delusion occurs precisely because the previously experienced grasp of pervasion lacks a defect as its object, and because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for a cognition whose object is a cognition of an external thing is absent; therefore, one need not say that such a delusion is produced by a defect. Anticipating this objection, he says: "the eye.
Cognition derived from a mark (*laiṅgika-jñāna*) apprehended by the eye is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). || 49 ||

Having repeatedly seen smoke with a defect-free eye, one perceives fire, [thinking], "Where there is smoke, there is fire. In that case, the consumption of substances possessing qualities that produce defects is not the cause, because delusion is observed even in its absence. Delusion arises precisely from the deficiency of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) regarding objects of knowledge within the domain of the external sense organs; for in those instances, no causal complex capable of producing disease is perceived. Both delusion and doubt are produced by a causal complex capable of generating disease, because they are produced by a causal complex that generates delusion.

In that regard, because the causal complex (sāmagrī) that produces diseases such as virasa is invariably observed [to lead to them], and because delusion is also removed by the authority of scripture (āgama), he states "delusion" [in the verse] to show that delusion is to be removed. Scripture (āgama) is the word of a reliable person (āpta) which generates the absence of delusion. || 50 ||

Valid cognition (*pramā*) produced by the words of a reliable person (*āpta*) does not act as an inhibitor of valid cognition produced by one's own defects, because the words of a reliable person generate the realization of the absence of error. Therefore, erroneous cognition regarding objects within the range of the senses—caused by defects arising from tastes or lack of taste—is sublated by perception, inference, or the authority of scripture; for it is the defects themselves that are established as the cause in those cases. This is the meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that where a delusion of smoke arises upon seeing a mass of dust, the cause is indeed the defect (*doṣa*) itself, and not the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that produces valid cognition? If that were so, since the causal complex of the defect would exist at the time the defect arises, there would be nothing but delusion everywhere. To this, he says: "The error (*viparyaya*) has as its object the cognition produced by a defect. (51)

The meaning is that because erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*) arises solely from a defect, in a case of delusion such as "the conch is yellow," the inference of whiteness serves to remove that delusion. Now, an objection: after the contact between the sense organ and the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), when a cognition having the mother-of-pearl as its object has arisen, there occurs the realization, "I possess a cognition having the mother-of-pearl as its object. Immediately thereafter, another person's delusion arises regarding that very same object.

When another person utters the sentence, "A cognition has arisen in him that this is that [though it is not]," Devadatta—due to his experience of the knowledge of the word's power (*śaktijñāna*)—subsequently experiences a doubt regarding his own cognition of mother-of-pearl: "Is this cognition of mother-of-pearl that arose in me valid or not? Thus, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises in Devadatta’s cognition concerning the object of his own prior experience of mother-of-pearl. Because there is a lack of consensus that such a delusive cognition is not caused by a disease produced by the imbalance of bodily humors (*rasavirasaja-roga*), the author says: "By the word" (*śabda*). The conceptual construction is the object of the cognition produced by the application of the word.

The substance present before one, which is fit to be within the range of the senses, ought to be the object of a cognition whose content is the knowledge of "shell-ness," because it possesses the capacity to motivate purposeful action. In this context, the cognition produced regarding this object has silver as its content, because it is generated by a causal complex distinct from the complex that apprehends a doubtful cognition; furthermore, this cognition having silver as its content is invalid, because it generates unsuccessful activity. Since doubt can thus be removed through the method of inference, [the aforementioned conclusion follows].

In this context, since the consumption of substances that are tasteless due to the presence of doubt or delusion is not observed [to produce a result], the meaning is that knowledge produced by a statement uttered by another has as its object a valid cognition (*pramā*).

Now, one might object: "This [cognition] has as its object the sense-organ directed toward the thing present before one, because it is produced by the causal complex that grasps both the cognition whose object is a valid cognition and the cognition whose object is not a valid cognition, just like the causal complex that produces a cognition having both nacre and silver as its objects. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The real" (*sat*).
This means it has as its object a cognition that lacks the discernment (*viveka*) regarding the distinction between the real and the unreal.

In this matter, Devadatta’s cognition has the mother-of-pearl as its object, while Yajñadatta’s cognition has silver as its object. Since it is impossible to determine in this case that "this is a cognition whose scope consists of both the existent and the non-existent," this cognition is not produced by disease; rather, it is produced by the words of another. Because other cognitions are produced by disease, the very fact that the cognition arisen in me is not produced by disease means that it is precisely that which constitutes doubt, having as its object a cognition devoid of the determination of either existence or non-existence. This is the meaning.

Regarding this, he explains what has been interpreted by some as follows: the word "sat" (real) refers to the object before one's eyes, which is the shell fragment that is the sensory object. With reference to that object (*tatpadārtha*), the cognition "this is silver" arises regarding the shell—which is the object of the knowledge of the thing present before one, produced by a collection of conditions such as the glittering resembling silver found in marketplaces and towns. This [cognition] is either the object of that ignorance (*ajñāna*) or has the unreal (*asat*) as its object; it is called the "knowledge of the discrimination of their relation."
The meaning is that whatever object becomes the content (*viṣaya*) of a cognition devoid of other [objects], that very object is what is intended by "the object of a cognition.

Now, one might object: "It should be stated that validity (*pramātva*) consists in being the object of a cognition devoid of cognitions of other objects. If that were so, at the time of this cognition whose object is a cognition, since the totality of all objects is absent, how could the cognition of the thing-in-front be known as valid? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Abhāva... Sleep is a mental modification (*vṛtti*) supported by the notion of non-existence (*abhāva*). || 54 ||

The meaning is that when there exists a cognition of another object at the time of the causal complex that apprehends the cognition whose object is the thing standing directly before one, it is indeed possible to know that [the former cognition] possesses validity with respect to what is other than that [other object].
That cognition arises from the consumption of a substance possessing bitter and pungent tastes.

Now, it might be argued that when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the sensory contact with all objects is present, each respective object can be apprehended by its corresponding causal complex. Therefore, since every causal complex that apprehends knowledge of all objects—up to and including the causal complex that apprehends knowledge of the mother-of-pearl—is impossible at that time, some other causal complex must be stated.
That causal complex is the one possessed by the consumption of substances with bitter and pungent tastes; the meaning is that such a causal complex becomes the apprehender of all objects.

[Objection: But how is it possible for the mother-of-pearl to be "other than all objects," given that all objects are not present? Since it cannot be grasped as being in front [of one] according to the method stated above, [the author], due to this dissatisfaction, says: "By means of valid cognition...
Memory is the non-loss of an object experienced through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 56 ||

The meaning is that at the time of apprehending a cognition whose object is something present before one, those previously experienced objects—being presented under the universal of "objecthood" (*padārthatva*)—do not become objects of doubt. The sense is that by recollecting those many objects in the mind, it is indeed possible to ensure the absence of forgetfulness (*pramoṣa*). The causal complex for the arising of the *sattva* quality is the consumption of substances possessing a sweet taste.
For that reason, he says "sweet," etc., meaning that by means of the mind, it is indeed possible to grasp all objects under the universal of "objecthood" and thus remember them.
Due to the emergence of the sattvic state arising from the transformation of the sweet flavor, there occurs the designation "this is that very one. || 57 ||

The meaning is this: for one who consumes substances possessing a sweet taste, the quality of *sattva* arises by virtue of that quantity. By the power of that *sāttvika* quality, it is indeed possible to grasp the presence of all objects through the mind. Therefore, it is understood that the designation "this is that" occurs.

Now, since the quality of *sattva* arises through the transformation of pure rasa, when there is contact between the sense organ and its object, it is possible to apprehend the validity residing in that [object] by way of having that [object] as its locus and that [quality] as its qualifier.

By eating tasteless food, one becomes ill and perceives validity (*prāmāṇya*) in that which lacks it; this is because the collection of defects (*doṣa-sāmagrī*) is powerful therein. Thus, it has been stated that the consumption of substances with or without taste constitutes the causal complex for grasping validity or invalidity. Anticipating the objection that "in that case, it would be possible to grasp validity now through the power of yoga practice," he says: "the other" (*itara*). "The other" refers to the internalized practice consisting of the cessation of contact with the other sense organs.

When there is contact between one's own sense organ and its object, those other things which obstruct the cognition of validity residing in the cognition of that [object]—namely, the objects that constitute the causal complex for the superimposition of other entities—are expressed by the word "other" (*itara*). When the causal complex for apprehending the cognition of one's own sensory object is present, there arises both the cognition of that object and the absence of cognition of that [same] object. Likewise, there is the cessation of connection with other sense organs.

The cessation of that [mental activity] is regulated within the inner self by the internal organ, the mind, through the power of practice; the meaning is that its validity is indeed apprehended by means of that cognition through such regulation with respect to the object present before one.

An object known as "this-ness" (idaṃtva) appears as distinct from others. When validity (*prāmāṇya*) is apprehended through the method of inference—namely, "the knowledge arisen in me has for its object something other than doubt or error, because it generates successful activity"—then, due to the strength of a disease caused by internal defects from consuming unwholesome substances, how could doubt regarding the object before one be removed? Anticipating this objection, he says: "viṣaya... etc.
Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the repeated application of effort toward the stream [of practice] arising from detachment from sense objects. (59)

The meaning of this is as follows: silver is not the object of the knowledge whose scope is the domain of one's own visual faculty; in this regard, freedom from delusion is dispassion (*virāgatva*). Within the internal flow of the mind, there is a continuous stream of cognition (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*) such as "this is mother-of-pearl. The enthusiasm for the knowledge produced by meditating upon that is joy (*prīti*). Repeated application (*paunaḥpunya*)—meaning either recurrence or intensity—is the state of non-attachment (*vairāgya*) associated with dispassion, characterized by the absence of doubt, action, and so forth, such as "this is mother-of-pearl, this is not silver."

The object present before one must be mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), because while it is not the object of a cognition whose content is silver, it is nonetheless a cognition possessing an object. The meaning is that the absence of invalidity (*aprāmāṇyābhāvatva*) is established for the cognition of mother-of-pearl produced in the mind. Now, an objection: even for successions of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-jñāna*) which grasp what has already been grasped, and for a cognition of a word that produces an invalid cognition—such as "this is silver" regarding something present before one—the cognition of doubt or error regarding that [silver] in the mother-of-pearl occurs spontaneously (*svataḥ*). Anticipating this lack of satisfaction, he says: "dṛṣṭa... (perceived...).
Thus, there are the designations of mastery over thirst for perceived and scriptural objects.

The meaning is that even for one who has lost all desire (*vigatatṛṣṇā*)—that is, one for whom the craving for the nacre lying before them has vanished—that very object becomes the focus of what is called "mastery" (*vaśīkaraṇa*).

Now, an objection may be raised: when all the causal conditions for sense-object contact are present regarding the nacre lying before one, and there occurs an experience (*anubhava*) characterized by the object as possessing that specific quality (*tadvati tatprakāraka*), why is that experience not an obstacle to erroneous or doubtful cognition? For the causal conditions for error, which have as their object the very thing that generates error, are still present.

For instance: the cognition produced in you does not have the mother-of-pearl as its object, but rather has silver as its object, because the possession of qualities such as glittering—which resides in the silver found in the marketplace—is a common property [between the two]. Therefore, even by means of the instrument of inference—namely, the inference that "the cognition produced in me is one whose object is an error"—it is impossible to know that [the cognition] possesses that qualifier in that locus (*tadvati tatprakārakatva*).

Because knowledge produced by direct perception (pratyakṣa) acts as an obstacle to valid knowledge produced by inference (anumiti), [the author], finding this unsatisfactory on the grounds that validity is not grasped in either case, says: "By those two"—meaning, by those two, there is the cessation of mental fluctuations (cittavṛtti). || 61 ||

That which exists in the mind (citta) or the internal organ (manas) is a mental modification (cittavṛtti). By those two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), there is no apprehension of the object as possessing that specific qualifier; the meaning is that this is because it is caused by diseases arising from [the consumption of] delicious and tasteless food.

But surely, this person possesses the consumption of substances containing pure *rasa*, and he possesses the knowledge of the absence of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). When the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between these two is grasped in this manner, it is impossible to speak of the knowledge of invalidity. To explain: it cannot be said that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) which produces valid cognition is the same as the causal complex of consuming substances containing pure *rasa*. For, immediately after a cognition arises regarding a present object as possessing a certain qualifier when it does indeed possess it, another error may arise regarding that same object due to the influence of some defect (*doṣa*).

For that reason, the employment of speech has arisen. Immediately upon hearing the statement, "This produced cognition has invalidity as its object," a doubt arises regarding the cognition whose object is validity. Bearing in mind the intention that even the consumption of unpalatable food constitutes a causal complex for the apprehension of invalidity, he sets forth another causal complex for the production of error, beginning with "yāvat": "The suppression of the vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—as they circulate through the channels and vessels of the bodily constituents (dhātus), is a cause of error. (62)

Where the cessation of the five vital breaths (prāṇa), etc., is observed, there the arising of disease occurs. By the obstruction of those winds, the internal receptacles (āśayas) become vitiated; the bodily constituents (dhātus) also become vitiated. Consequently, due to conditions such as cataracts (kāca) and jaundice (kāmalā), doubt and delusion arise—this is the meaning. Now, one might object that if this were so, the knowledge of validity (prāmāṇya-jñāna) would be destroyed everywhere whenever the causal complex (sāmagrī) for generating doubt and error is present. Anticipating this objection, he says: "proximate," etc. (āsanna-).

One whose internal self is caused by knowledge of proximate objects, who is free from disease through the practice of yoga and the restraint of the vital breath (*pavana*), becomes long-lived. || 63 ||

Now, one might object: "Surely, immediately after the contact of a jar with the sense organ, when the causal complex for apprehending that cognition is present, there would be the experience of an erroneous cognition; let its validity (*prāmāṇya*) residing therein indeed be grasped. But how can the validity regarding the objects of the other [four] sense organs be grasped in a cognition whose object is that [first] cognition? Furthermore, 'detachment' (*virāga*) from the cognitions of the objects of the five senses means specifically intense attachment (*viśeṣeṇa rāga*); therefore, the meaning is that there is specifically intense attachment toward the cognitions of the objects of the five senses."

Immediately following the contact between the sense organ and its object, when the entire causal complex—including the conjunction of the self (*ātman*) and the mind (*manas*)—is present, a cognition arises regarding its respective object. Its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is caused by that [complex], because it is produced by a causal complex distinct from the complex that apprehends invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*), just like the validity of the cognition of a jar produced by me.
