Here, "self" (*ātman*) refers to the living being (*jīva*). "Internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*) refers to the mind (*citta*). The "conjunction" (*yoga*) is its union with the living self (*jīvātman*).

By virtue of that—that is, by virtue of its cause—the material cause of error, which obstructs the validity residing in the cognition that has that [object] as its domain, is the prevention of wind; this is the cause of health, because it is produced by the causal complex for the absence of invalidity (aprāmāṇya). This is the meaning.

Now, is it not the case that detachment (*virāga*) among the five objects of the senses means specifically *not* having passion (*vi-rāga*)? [If so,] one obtains as the mere fruit of the scripture the experience of those objects; by that, there arises a contradiction with liberation. On the contrary, it becomes a cause for disease. How, then, is long life attained through this? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Therefore," etc. Therefore, the effect is that which results from the pentad beginning with the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (64)

The meaning of this is as follows: The body consists of the *doṣas*, *dhātus*, *malas*, and the *āśayas*, because it is the substratum of *prakṛti* which supports the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*, etc. upon which [the body] subsists. That which is not so [composed] is not so [a body], just like a jar. "The body is the locus of activity" (*ceṣṭāśraya*); thus, being the locus of activity is the defining characteristic of the body. Activity (*ceṣṭā*), however, is that form of vibration (*spandana*) which aims at the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. Therefore, the body is the result of the five vital breaths. And that *prakṛti* is the locus of such activity.

All of this has been established by the Śruti. That Śruti states: "The vital breaths—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—are of the nature of the white color; she [the Gāyatrī] is three-footed and consists of the three vyāhṛtis. In this regard, the scriptural statement is the authority: "Bhūḥ is indeed prāṇa; bhuvaḥ is apāna; suvaḥ is vyāna. By these, the great head is formed. Mahaḥ is food."

"Indeed, by means of food alone do all the vital breaths (prāṇas) flourish. Therefore, the pentad beginning with *prāṇa* must be protected; being the cause for the effect of freedom from disease, how could it not be a cause for liberation? He who has the pentad of *prāṇa* and the rest under his own control also attains long life. Thus, it is said that the pentad of *prāṇa* and the rest is the effect that bears fruit. Consequently, the final meaning is this: the consumption of substances possessing pure *rasa* (taste/essence) effects the preservation of the body, whereas the consumption of substances possessing vitiated *rasa* effects the destruction of the vital breaths.

Now, the result of the pentad beginning with *prāṇa* is as follows: the *prāṇa* wind performs the action of moving the body. That wind, remaining unmodified, performs the action of going and returning by means of the two feet, as well as actions from the feet to the head such as the closing and opening of the eyes, thus performing its characteristic action of movement. Furthermore, there is a purpose for the *apāna* wind: residing in the regions of the genitals and the anus, it undergoes modification while itself remaining unmodified.

And the function of the *vyāna* wind is as follows: having itself become fivefold through the digestive bile (*pācaka-pitta*), and causing the digestive bile to also become fivefold, it seizes the food, digests it, and distributes it. Having divided the consumed food into its essential essence (*sāra*) and waste (*kiṭṭa*), it releases them. It causes entry into the receptacles (*āśaya*). Pervading the entire body, it remains there. And the purpose of the *udāna* wind is: moving as far as the nose and other openings, it initiates speech; and it brings about the increase of strength and complexion.

And the function of the *samāna* wind—remaining near the abdominal air (*jaṭharānila*), it releases the essence of the food consumed and the digested food into the body. Such is the result of the five winds. Because it is not necessary for them to bestow the fruit of liberation, [the author], expressing dissatisfaction with that view, says: "By means of the unseen [force] (*adṛṣṭa*)...
[The soul] is conjoined with the mind by means of the sense-organ through the unseen force. (65)

The Lord is unseen; being impelled by Him, the mind—having perceived through the sense organ directed toward the contact with an object the resulting cognition of that object, and having perceived the result of the injunction regarding what is to be rejected or accepted based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—abandons the cognition of other objects and ordains for the individual soul (*jīvātman*) the fruit of knowledge whose scope is the knowledge of the Self, as well as the fruit pertaining to the hereafter. Thus, the meaning is that the mind bestows upon the living being a superior fruit produced by its conjunction with the Self.

[Objection: Surely the self (ātman) is conjoined with the mind (manas), the mind with the sense organ (indriya), and the sense organ with the object (artha), because of the rule that sense organs function by reaching their objects. Consequently, the self experiences the fruit which is the object of the cognition regarding the sense-object. That fruit is not for the sake of the next world (āmuṣmika), because the fruit of the cognition produced by the contact with the object is more powerful; [anticipating this] objection, he says—"all," etc.: "All elements (dhātavaḥ) have come under the sway of sattva. (66)

By means of the cessation of the mind, the cessation of inhalation and exhalation, the cessation of external air through the mouth, and by performing the action of filling one's own belly, there is also the removal of external air through the path of the back. After that air has performed its function even in the region of the navel, it follows the course of the vessels situated within the abdomen; the meaning is that, following the obstruction of the region of the throat for inhalation and exhalation, it circulates from the feet to the head.

Now, it may be argued that since dispassion (*vairāgya*) regarding objects of knowledge perceived by the external senses has the mind as its object and is caused by the knowledge of the Self, one must say that in this case, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that grasps the experience of the absence of error—which resides in the knowledge of external sensory objects—is indeed a causal complex distinct from the causal complex that produces error. For instance, the effect of the absence of disease arises through the power of the vital air (*pavana*) resulting from the practice of yoga, which itself is produced by the restraint of the five senses.

If that were so, would the elements not become even more solid? Anticipating the objection that the fruit taught in the scriptures is obtained by virtue of the causal relationship regarding the absence of disease, the author says, "At which time," etc., out of dissatisfaction with that view:
"At which time, through which conjunction, and according to which rule, progeny are born as bestowers of fruit. (67)
The elements produced from that conjunction are the movers. || 68 ||
Whichever daughter one might desire, thinking, "May she be dear," one should give her away after performing the *niṣṭhā* rite; she indeed becomes dear,
and she does not return again.

In this context, however, by virtue of the accomplishment of health, a person attains a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties. Now, one might object: "The birth of a daughter's son brings liberation for the parents; since it is necessary to strengthen their bodily constituents (*dhātu*), the attainment of liberation occurs through the performance of the effect that is the absence of disease. Anticipating the objection that the daughter’s child is thus the direct causal aggregate (*sāmagrī*)—since it arises from the female-produced excess of blood—the author states: "The woman and the man... "The woman and the man are two portions of the Self, [arising] from the desire to create the body of the one whose form is divided. (69)

Between a woman and a man, the predominance of the semen—which is the cause for producing a son—is the cause for the birth of a son; the predominance of the blood—which is the cause for producing a daughter—is the cause for the birth of a daughter. According to the Smṛti, sons and the like are of a form distinct from oneself. For one seeking liberation, the engagement [in worldly life] is preceded by the preparation of the causal complex for the birth of a daughter, because that very causal complex for the birth of a maiden fit for giving is the cause [of such engagement]. That which is not thus is not thus, just like a jar.

The "collection of conditions for the birth of a daughter" (*putrikā-janana-sāmagrī*) refers to the collection of conditions for the birth of a daughter that possesses the capacity to produce a son, because it serves as both the cause and the effect of the experience of union motivated by one's own pleasure. One might ask: "How can the collection of conditions for the birth of offspring be obtained without the accomplishment of worldly conditions? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Prakṛti... [and so on]. It is recorded in the *Smṛti* that "Prakṛti and Puruṣa are the parents. (70)

This being the case, since [the Lord] would be a person characterized by qualities (*guṇa*), the Lord as mixed with *māyā* would have to be the one who bestows the fruit of the next world; because this is unsatisfactory, he says: "The practice of yoga (*vṛtti*)," etc. The practice of yoga is the repeated application [of the mind], due to a lack of enthusiasm for the essential nature (*svarūpa*) which remains veiled by mental modifications (*vṛtti*). || 71 ||

The Puruṣa is separated by its own functioning (vṛtti) because it has arisen from an association with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), being the cause of the connection that produces progeny. By its very nature, its state of being separated by functioning arises precisely from its being a substance woven together with the guṇas; that alone is its true form. Upon that [form] the mind is placed. The enthusiasm of that mind is joy (prīti). From joy alone comes attachment in the heart.

One who, possessing detachment from other objects, meditates upon the Self, delivers that meditator who is submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra. That alone is the supreme fruit; for that very purpose is the motive for the commencement of Āyurveda. The meaning is that this [meditation] alone becomes the cause for bestowing many human goals (puruṣārtha). For one in whose mind enthusiasm arises, the repeated application of that mind brings about satisfaction.
Through the power of constant proficiency in practice, spiritual steadfastness regarding all objects, having clarified the mind, becomes the bestower of liberation.
The stage [of *bhūmi*] consists in the practice of repeated observation arising from an excess of reverence. (72)

There, through further contemplation, one realizes its true nature. Because it is the cause of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) and because it bestows the highest happiness in this world, the "ground" (*bhūmi*) in the context of the yoga of further contemplation means the ground (*bhūḥ*) of immeasurable bliss.

Now, [the author] says "that" (*tām*)—addressing the objection that [bliss might vanish] when all objects are destroyed within the sphere of the Self, since that [Self] would then be destroyed; thus he says:
"Having reached that state, one should give [it]. (73)

He who gives a daughter, distinguished by her ornaments, beauty, and other qualities, to a learned man (śrotriya) born of a noble family—such a person who engages in the giving of a daughter obtains the fruit of happiness and liberation; the meaning is that he also enjoys worldly happiness in this life.
He states the fruit of giving a daughter with the word "priyā":
she becomes truly beloved. || 74 ||

The meaning is that the Lord becomes the guarantor for the granting of the fruit of giving a daughter in marriage. The sense is that for one who performs the giving of a daughter in marriage for the sake of pleasing the Lord, both the fruit pertaining to this world and the fruit pertaining to the next world are bestowed.

Now, it might be argued that one who desires the very birth of a daughter, impelled by the affliction of his own karma, performs a gift for the sake of pleasing the Lord; and thus it has been said that the Lord, becoming well-pleased, himself acting as a guarantor, bestows the fruit. In that case, the only fruit of the act of giving a daughter would be the pleasure of the Lord. To address the unease as to what fruit he himself obtained from that, [the text] says: "Not here, not here does he return again" (75).

Whatever pleasure, pain, and so forth he experiences in this world, the Lord does not take that away; however, the Lord does take away his isolation (*kaivalya*). He does not return to this world, nor does he experience the suffering of the womb and the like. Therefore, by the power of the practice of yoga, the body consists of the seven constituents (*dhātu*); thus, the fruit of the body is both worldly and liberation. Detachment (*vairāgya*) alone ordains the fruit of both; thus he says: "worldly... Detachment is the knowledge that [the body] is to be destroyed solely by the enjoyment of objects experienced in this world and the next. || 76 ||
Dispassion is caused by the bliss of uninterrupted knowledge, which consists of the bliss of the Self that is beyond the reach of sense objects. || 77 ||

Aiming for fruits other than those arising from results pertaining to this world or the next, the Self—because it is produced by the mind having experience as its object—causes the abandonment of the experience of sensory pleasure, which is produced by knowledge and constant dispassion toward those [sensory objects], and realizes that the experience of the knowledge of the Self is the supreme human goal; thus, it rejects the experiential knowledge of other objects. Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the knowledge that worldly and otherworldly fruits are perishable.

The fruit pertaining to this world and the next, which consists of the experience of sense objects, is trivial; for once that experience has been attained through great effort, it perishes. Therefore, the meaning is that dispassion alone yields a superior fruit, as it is the cause of the fruit of liberation.

Now, since the Supreme Self is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), there is an absence of contact between the senses and their objects; consequently, there is no knowledge regarding the self, and thus the experience of bliss consisting of that knowledge is all the more unestablished. However, if the perception of an object resulting from sense-object contact is itself the perception of the experience of knowledge regarding happiness, then that very knowledge is the cause of the experience of bliss. That effect—the knowledge produced by consuming pure, flavorful food which brings about the firmness of the bodily elements and the senses—is caused by bliss; this is the perception established by the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this, he says: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, the elements are the supports for the ground of those diseases. || 78 ||

It has been stated that knowledge produced by the contact of the sense organs with their objects is the cause of bliss. Therefore—meaning, by virtue of that cause—the *dhātus* (elements) are the five sense organs, which act as the agents producing their respective diseases. Now, it is well known that the body is the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*). This being so, since it is the effect whose purpose is directed solely toward the fruit of the objects, and is destroyed only by the destruction of its object, it would be impossible to deny this. Keeping in mind the intention that the time of experience lasts only as long as the duration of the perception of the objects, he says: "Experience," etc. The body is the locus of experience. (79)

It is the locus (*āyatana*) of those substances (*dravya*) that are fit to be objects of enjoyment regarding all purposes. Enjoyment (*bhoga*) is the experience of pleasure and pain; for even in the case of pain, it consists in the apprehension of substances characterized by desires directed toward objects fit for enjoyment. Therefore, the body is the locus of enjoyment, because it can be stated that "being a body" is the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of being the locus of enjoyment.

Now, one might object: the bliss born from the experience of that object is indeed the object of my desire, because it aims at an activity directed toward a mental state which desires an activity regarding an object of pleasure, which in turn is the object of a cognition of the experience of pleasure; whereas the cognition of an object of pain lacks the quality of being an object of my desire. For that very reason, the collection of means for producing those things that assist in enjoyment is itself the fulfillment of the purpose.

[Objection: But since pleasure is also accompanied by suffering, pleasure too is indeed suffering. Furthermore, the experience of suffering arising from sense objects must be accomplished by karma distinct from that which produces [ordinary] suffering. Therefore, according to the reasoning stated, the effect consisting of the experience of knowledge through the perception of external sensory objects cannot have bliss as its cause. Anticipating this objection, he says: "That [is... "That is dispassion toward the gunas resulting from the discernment of the Supreme Puruṣa. (YS 1.16)

That alone is the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*) which is a cognition having as its object a cognition produced by an eternal substance, and which has bliss as its cause; that is the manifestation (*khyāti*) whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*). He who possesses the cognition of bliss is called "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*); he is one who always experiences bliss. My own activity, however, is distinct from suffering because it is prompted by desire; and desire, being of the nature of happiness, is the means to the supreme human goal.

The meaning is that what is intended by the term "dispassion toward the gunas" (*guṇavaitṛṣṇya*) is a cognition produced by a cognition regarding a person who has consumed sweet flavors, which is caused by bliss (*ānanda*). "Discernment of the Puruṣa" (*puruṣakhyāti*) is discernment having as its object the knowledge of the Supreme Puruṣa.

Dispassion caused by the bliss of objective knowledge is not a cognition directed toward the external objects of the senses, because of the absence of contact between the sense organs and their objects; rather, it is a cognition having as its object the cognition within the internal organ, which would be caused by the experience of all objects. Because of this underlying intention, he says "as far as" (*yāvat*).
Vitarka is that cultivation which consists of the mental representation of the objects of the senses and their corresponding cognitions. || 81 ||

"Reasoning" (*tarka*) means "investigation" (*vicāra*). The investigation consists in determining that for all cognitions of sensory objects, the experience of their respective objects is caused by bliss; this is the meaning of "the action which is the effect of knowledge assisted by reasoning. When the sequence of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that reflects upon the object is to be cultivated through the knowledge of reasoning, then, through that cultivation, the experience of the respective objects of all cognitions of sensory objects becomes caused by bliss; such is the meaning.

Now, is it not the case that as long as there is cognition through the experience of objects, so long is there a cause for [limited] bliss; whereas the cognition through the experience of the Supreme Self (paramātman) is the cause of supreme bliss, since the body is the locus for both? In this regard, considering that the experience of objects is destroyed solely by the destruction of the objects themselves, while the experience of the Supreme Self—having the Supreme Self as its object—is an experience of eternal bliss, the author states "the former" (*pūrva*), keeping this intention in mind:

"The former" refers to the non-conceptual state (*nirvikalpa*) which consists of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the verbal meanings and the mental recollection (*ullekha*) of the sequence of what precedes and what follows. (82)

One who possesses the experience of knowledge through the external senses is "with deliberation" (*savitarka*). "With deliberation" means being with conceptual construction (*savikalpa*). The continuous pursuit of conceptual knowledge is itself the pursuit of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). That [pursuit] has as its object a knowledge that is inexpressible (*anirvācya*). It is the state of being devoid of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that involves the recollection of words and their meanings. That alone is the activity of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*). Devadatta ought to become liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) due to the experience of knowledge concerning the Supreme Self. Through the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) duties, the knowledge of the experience of the Supreme Self is indicated.

Since that [observance] also serves as the cause for strengthening the body, it is necessary for performing the function of maintaining health. Therefore, the meaning is that the body truly becomes the "abode of experience" (*bhogāyatana*). In this regard, there is a statement from the *Smṛti*: "The obligatory and occasional rites bring about the destruction of evil;
moreover, the knower of the Veda, by means of practice, purifies his knowledge."
A person whose consciousness has been ripened by practice attains isolation (kaivalya).
Regarding this, the statement in the Sūtrasthāna is:
"One should protect food and drink from poison, especially that of a sovereign."
Security and well-being depend upon him, as do dharma and the other goals, which are bound to him.
Thus, the meaning is that it serves as the cause for strengthening the body.

Now, one might object: "The Supreme Self is not an object of the mind, because it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), because it is a partless substance (*niravayavadravyatva*), and because it is bodiless (*niṣkāyakatva*), like time; thus, it is impossible to say that the mind has the Self as its sphere. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Internal" (*antar*). "Savicāra" (contemplative meditation) is the conjunction with the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of space and time, which takes as its object a thing delimited by the attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). || 83 ||

The Supreme Self (paramātman) is to be investigated; for this very reason, He is to be known through valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) assisted by reasoning (savitarka). To illustrate: [the existence of a creator] is to be known through inference assisted by reasoning, as follows: "The sprout and so forth have an agent, because they are effects, like a pot. The state of being supported by objects delimited by the attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the property of having the mind as its object; this is because the Self is always experienced [by it]. Its delimiting factor (avacchedaka), the body, becomes fit for the experience of objects when it exists.

The meaning is that for him as well, the strengthening of the body is necessary. The mind takes the Self as its object; its essential nature is of the form of bliss. Having thus taken the Supreme Self, distinguished by such qualities, as its object, it rests upon Him. Thus, the fruit of the effort toward the purpose—which is the production of the effect known as the absence of disease—is the reasoning (*tarka*) consisting of inquiry. Therefore, it is said that the inquiry of yoga consists of place, time, and mental disposition (*bhāvanā*). Place, moreover, becomes threefold through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of substance.

In some cases, the consumption of substances produced in a particular region causes an excess of *vāta* for the inhabitants of that region; in some cases, the consumption of substances born in a particular region causes an aggravation of *pitta*; and in some cases, the consumption of substances produced in a particular region causes an aggravation of *kapha*. The meaning is that one should consider how the substances available in those respective regions, which alleviate those specific diseases, bring about the strengthening of the bodies of the people living in those regions.

The meaning is that one should bring about the consumption of various substances at their respective times—which also serves to alleviate bile-related diseases—by accomplishing those specific purposes through careful consideration, and thus reach the [proper] time.

Now, since the mind requires knowledge of all objects distinct from the Self for the sake of illuminating the Self, knowledge aided by reasoning (*tarka*) becomes necessary; that reasoning serves as an indirect cause for the knowledge of the Self. Thus it is said, "with reflection" (*savicāra*). If it is then asked how "without reflection" (*nirvicāra*) can also be a means to liberation—since "without reflection" implies an absence of reflection—the author says "in this" (*asmin*) to address this unease: "In this [state], the manifestation of the mere attribute delimited by space, time, and nature is 'without reflection' (*nirvicāra*). (84)

In this Brahman, there is an absence of limitation by way of space, time, and substance; that which appears here is merely the superimposition of attributes upon it. Since the absence of knowledge regarding other objects is present therein, the lack of inquiry into other objects is what is meant by "nirvicāra" (without inquiry).

[Objection: Surely, when knowledge of all objects has arisen, bliss (*ānanda*) occurs; the absence of this is "beyond reflection" (*nirvicāra*). [Reply: If that is so, how could there be the experience and perception of bliss? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Bliss" (*sukha*).
That bliss is directed toward the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) due to the overflowing of the manifestation of happiness.

Even for the purpose of experiencing bliss and joy, that which is manifested when one is asleep is itself that very bliss. It becomes the cause for the intensification of the mind as it is cultivated through the state beyond discursive thought (*nirvicāra*). Therefore, the meaning is that bliss pertains to the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) and pertains to the cognitive power of the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa-jñānaśakti*). Now, an objection may be raised: although the Supreme Brahman is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*), it nevertheless possesses attributes. To be "devoid of attributes" means the state of being partless (*niravayavatva*) serves as its defining characteristic. Since the Self (*ātman*) is also devoid of attributes, it cannot be said that the mind has the capacity to perceive it.

Because [the Self] is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) since it is a partless substance (*niravayavadravya*), and because the mind (*manas*) is also devoid of qualities, it is impossible to assert that [the mind], by virtue of being a sense organ (*indriyatva*), can grasp knowledge whose object is the Self. Thus, since the Self is not an object [of perception], it is impossible for the senses to reach it, and consequently, the mind also becomes ineffective. To this, he says: "In this...
"In this [Self], samādhi is traditionally defined as having as its object only the reality of the existence of that which is to be grasped. (86)

In this Brahman, the individual soul (jīva) is capable of grasping it; because its object is the Supreme Self (paramātman), the existence of Brahman is revealed as the very cause of the world’s manifestation. Thus, Brahman as Truth (satya) becomes beyond even the reach of the mind, for it is impossible to assert that the qualityless Brahman can be apprehended by the mind. What is perceived is knowledge whose object is pure existence (sattā-mātra). That state in which the mind is absorbed together with the self is known as *samādhi*.

If it is argued that it is improper to say that the attributeless Brahman (nirguṇa-brahman) is the creator of the world, we say no. Because the attributeless Brahman lacks limbs such as hands and feet, it cannot be said to have the nature of the world. Nevertheless, its true nature is set forth in the Śruti:
"He passes over into this self consisting of mind;
he passes over into this self consisting of consciousness."

According to this scriptural passage, the world is established as being non-different from the nature of Brahman, and the supreme Brahman is established as being devoid of attributes (*nirguṇa*). It should not be suspected that, under the view of a purely attributeless (*śuddha-nirguṇa*) Brahman, there could be no meditative absorption (*samādhi*) at all because it would be beyond the reach of even yogis, nor that the mind’s engagement with the Self would be impossible; for such perceptions occur because the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is conditioned by *māyā*. Furthermore, it should not be feared that the world, being impermanent, would lead to the conclusion that the Self is also impermanent, since [the Self] is perceived as such only through its association with *māyā*.

Therefore, however, there is a distinction between entities until the cessation of *māyā*. For as long as *māyā* is not removed by one’s meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is no such distinction between entities, because that absorption brings about the cessation of *māyā*. The meaning is that when there is the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*) by the mind, then it is possible to say that the Self is the object of the mind. When the cessation of *māyā* is perceived within the individual soul (*jīvātman*), that [soul] becomes the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*) manifesting in the form of the world.

Just as in the cognition "this is a jar," there is the state of having the jar as its object, so too the attributeless Brahman becomes an object of the mind; that alone constitutes valid knowledge (*pramā*). For this very reason it is said, "That is remembered" (*sā smṛtā*); the meaning is that *prakṛti* itself is what is remembered. Samādhi is the cause of liberation for all, yet it is unattainable for everyone because of the absence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that results in such valid knowledge.

Because the consumption of substances possessing a sweet taste bestows the quality of *sattva*, the quality of *sattva* is the cause of *samādhi*. This is because it is produced by a sweet taste that serves as the cause of the *sāttvika* quality, being distinct from the sour and pungent tastes which generate the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*. Therefore, the sweet taste alone is the cause of *samādhi*; hence he says: "The sweet taste...
"The sweet taste, arising through the flow of honey-like [substance] unaltered by the wind (*pavana*) residing in the plasma and blood, fills [the body] and takes refuge in the thumb. (87)

The sweet flavor (madhurarasas), moving through the blood constituent (rasāsṛgdhātu) while maintaining the equilibrium of the vital wind (pavana), resides in the *kuṇḍalinī*. By means of inhalation and exhalation, it draws up the nectar situated in the head-lotus and satisfies [the body] from the feet to the crown of the head. Having performed the retention (*kumbhaka*) by means of the wind moving through the path of the *iḍā*, one should circulate it as far as the big toe and sprinkle each respective limb; such is the meaning.

One might object: "Since the *kalā* is powerful, it should be said that she draws the nectar situated in the head by means of the inhalation and exhalation breaths of the wind born from the sweet essence (*madhurasaja*), thereby effecting the nourishment of the head. But how does the *kalā*, being weak, effect the nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) through that nourishment extending from the feet to the head? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therein. There, the *kalā* situated therein moves about, causing the ten-petaled lotus to blossom. (88)

The meaning is that [Kuṇḍalinī], causing the ten-petaled lotus—the support for the *pittakalā* arising from the *kuṇḍalī*—to blossom, emits nectar (*amṛta*). Now, it was previously stated that the vital air (*pavana*), having brought forth the nectar situated in the head-lotus, effects the nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). However, this present section concerns the accomplishment of the equipment for *samādhi*. The fruit of *samādhi*, moreover, consists in the experience of the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*). The equipment for that [fruit] accomplishes the effect of the absence of bodily modifications; through that, the direct realization of the Self is obtained. Indicating a lack of satisfaction with this [explanation], he introduces another introductory passage beginning with "the thumb" (*aṅguṣṭha*).
The Puruṣa is the size of a thumb and is seated within the thumb. || 89 ||
The Lord bears the body of the entire world.

The nourishment from nectar (amṛta) extending from the feet to the head—which results in bodily firmness produced by the collection of factors that accomplish the absence of disease—is caused by the effect of meditative absorption (samādhi). That which is not so [caused] is not so, like a jar; thus, through the practice of yoga brought about by bodily firmness, the attainment of liberation occurs. Regarding the statement, "The Person is the size of a thumb," the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) is the measure of a foot. On this point, the Śruti says: "One foot of Him is all beings; His three feet are the immortal in heaven. The Person rose up, three-footed, above."

Thus, this scripture remains having established that [the Self] is the size of a thumb. He indeed becomes the Lord (Īśvara). That Lord, too, having brought down the nectar situated in heaven by means of his three feet and having satisfied his own body, sustains even the world-body. The meaning is that, rather than depending on the collection of means for knowledge whose object is the internal organ and the self—which are within the scope of the Lord in the form of Virāj—there may arise the direct realization of the Self through the collection of means for grasping knowledge whose object is the knowledge regarding the self whose world is the body of the universe.

Now, one might object: even for yogins, the *mūlādhāra* is the primary source which, by drawing up the nectar situated in the head through inhalation and exhalation, effects the nourishment of the body, since it sustains everything. Even without yoga, that function can certainly be performed; therefore, he states another natural consequence: "The *mūlādhāra* is the primary source, the nourisher of all the bodily constituents. (91)

The meaning is as follows: through the inhalation and exhalation centered upon the *mūlādhāra*—which is in the form of *kuṇḍalinī* and consists of the wheels (*cakras*) of air and fire—the consumption of the nectar of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) occurs. By means of the vital wind (*pavana*) produced through the practice of yoga, one attains the strengthening of the constituents starting from the *mūlādhāra*, the provision of digestive fire (*jaṭharānila*), the attainment of long life, and the making meaningful the experience of knowledge regarding the objects of the senses for as long as that state persists.

[Objection: Is not the tree of the body nourished by the water of nectar (*amṛta*), since the *vyāna* wind—which is exceedingly abundant in nectar—is that which delimits its pervasion throughout the body? [Reply: It may be said that the root-supporting lotus (*mūlādhāra-padma*) possesses the quality of nourishing [the body] when there is contact with the wind that pervades the entire body and nourishes all the constituent elements (*dhātu*); however, because that [lotus] serves merely as the support for the *kuṇḍalinī*, and lacks pervasion over the whole body, even its capacity to nourish is not acceptable. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The wind moving through the channels (*sira*) brings the nectar situated in the head-lotus and sprinkles it. (92)

The meaning is that the *vyāna* wind, which is always the medium of circulation within the pathways of the vessels (*sirāmārga*), being situated in the *mūlādhāra*, draws up the nectar located there; thus, the wind becomes powerful as it moves through the previously mentioned elements of *rasa* and blood at the root of the lotus of the feet, which is the seed for the production of the tree-like body.

Now, one might object: "Since the very heat of the breath-wind, obtained during the first departure [of the vital energy], arises from Kuṇḍalinī—who is composed of the entire circle of fire and wind and consists of nectar—and since, having brought forth the produced nectar, it gathers all of that with the exhalation-wind to nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), that alone serves to strengthen the body; what, then, would be the fruit of the Vyāna-vāyu filling the lotus of the feet? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The body... [Verse 93]:
"In that same way, it is the primary cause of the sprouts and branches of the body."

"The body has five branches" means that the body itself is the sprout, endowed with five branches, which is supported by the lotus that serves as the foundation of the root. The meaning is that its branches are the limbs. Now, it might be argued: "It was stated that the root-supporting lotus is the basin for the sprout of the body; therefore, it is not logical that it should assist in the karma consisting of the movement of the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) which nourishes the nectar of the phonemes residing in its parts and their respective presiding deities. To this, he says: "Of those respective... [tattad-].
The nectar moving through the channels of the veins (*sirāmārga*) is the nourisher of the phonemes and deities residing in those respective locations. (94)

Consisting of the essence of each respective deity, [the body] extends from the letter *a* to the letter *kṣa*, and is presided over by the respective presiding deities of the limbs (*aṅga-adhiṣṭhāna*). The nectar (*amṛta*) moving through the channels (*sirā*) of those [limbs] becomes its nourisher. Furthermore, the *vyāna* wind, which circulates from the feet to the head, also becomes its nourisher. The foot-lotus that produces the vowel *a* takes the form of the branches and joints. Up to that extent, the nectar residing in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-padma*) becomes its protector; thus he says "that" (*tat*). That river flows upon the support of that foot-lotus. (95)

The meaning is that a flow of nectar occurs by following the network of channels (sirāsandhāna) as far as the lotus-feet. Now, one might object: since it is appropriate for the nectar arrived through the power of the inhalation and exhalation residing in Kuṇḍalinī to be made to flow only as far as the basin of the foundation-lotus (ādhārapadma), how is it that making it flow as far as the foundation-lotus itself is not tenable? To this he says: "By the flesh," etc. Filling the digits (kalās) with the wind moving through the path of the channels following the flesh, one should sprinkle the nectar. (96)

The meaning is that, following that path, one should sprinkle [the body] down to the lotus of the feet by means of the *iḍā* wind. By that, having gratified the deities of the phonemes (varṇa-devatā) residing in their respective locations, one should protect them; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "It must be said that the nourishment of the nectar (*amṛta*) by the wind occurs only for those specific constituents (dhātu), namely plasma and blood; since the other constituent, blood, lacks the nourishment of nectar, life would not be possible. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Flesh," etc. There exist channels (*sirā*) that follow the flesh. || 97 ||

The meaning is that the vital air (pavana), having entered the path of the *iḍā*, brings forth nectar situated in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-kamala*) and, by satiating the flesh-element (*māṃsa-dhātu*), becomes the nourisher of the body. [Objection]: Since the vital air of the lymph-chyle and blood-elements establishes the fixed order of the functions that effect the division of the limbs of the body, how can it be consistent for the vital air to nourish the blood-element when the vessels belonging to the flesh-element are not its primary agents? It would be more appropriate for the vital air to merely nourish those [blood-elements] while moving through the vessels and providing only the blood-element itself; thus, it does not become the nourisher of the blood-element. Anticipating this objection, he says: "dvīti" (twofold).
The root of the lotus-feet is like a tree with two thousand branch-like channels. || 98 ||

The meaning is that the basin for the lotus-feet, which has two thousand veins as its branches, brings forth nectar—the very sprouts that grow from the lotus-feet—and serves as the support for the nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). To address the doubt as to how these sprouts arising from the two thousand veins could serve as the support of the body by nourishing the seven constituents, he says: "Seven.
The body consists of the seven constituents. (99)

Regarding the phrase "six tastes," these are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent; for it is well known that they exist by depending on substances numbered as six and possess the quality of nourishing. As for "constituent" (*dhātu*), it is said: "Chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents. Therefore, it is stated that the body consists of the constituents.

Now follows the Yogaśāstra as the answer to the question just presented. Within it, the teaching that the body consists of seven constituents (*dhātu*) is set forth in order to demonstrate that the very fruit of practicing yoga is the nourishment of these constituents; thus, the meaning is that "longevity arises. This is because the constituents are nourished by the *rasa* (nutrient essence) and other factors, since they subsist upon pure *rasa* substances. Therefore, the point is that it is well-established that the constituents are nourished by the *rasa* and so forth.

Thus ends the commentary on the third chapter of Āyurveda composed by Yogānandanātha; this renowned work, esteemed by great scholars, provides an explanation for each sūtra and serves as a commentary on Āyurveda that benefits the world.
Complete. Regarding the fourth question in Āyurveda:

Now, it might be argued that it is impossible to state that the *rasa* (taste) and other factors nourish the bodily tissues (*dhātu*), because it has been established that only the wind of inhalation and exhalation situated within the *kuṇḍalinī* provides the nectar (*amṛta*). To address the doubt as to how the *rasa* and others could nourish the tissues, he says: "Gata... [and so forth].
Through the practice of the meditative absorption attained by means of the seasonal cycles of coming and going, there is the presence of yoga. || 1 ||

The meaning is that because Kuṇḍalinī consists of the circles of wind (anila) and fire (anala), the breath-wind—which itself consists of the circle of wind—attains the nature of heat upon its first movement; it is precisely because of this state of heat that it is possible to extract the nectar situated in the lotus of the head. Therefore, since the nourishment of the bodily constituents (dhātus) results from the power of that nectar and is caused by meditative absorption (samādhi), the presence of the Yogas occurs through that activity. Thus, the sense is that the nourishment of the constituents by Yoga has been established through a traditional sequence.

Since rasa and the other [tastes] are the causes for the nourishment of the *dhātus*, the demonstration of their causality implies that one must consume substances possessing rasa; for the causality of consuming such food toward the nourishment of the *dhātus* is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). To address the doubt as to how it is understood that "the *samādhis* nourish the *dhātus*," he says—starting with "intense" (*tīvra*)—that the *samādhi* called "intense conjunction" (*tīvrasaṃyoga*) is the proximate [cause]. (2)

The "intense application" (*tīvrasaṃyoga*) of mental self-contemplation (*ātmanididhyāsana*) consists in its being inherent in the self while being incapable of being produced by any causal complex that brings about knowledge of other objects. The meaning is that for those [practitioners], meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is itself the cause of knowledge regarding objects other than the self, which has the self as its object. Now, one might object: since the Supreme Self is all-pervasive (*vibhu*), a very firm latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the mind’s union with the self is established by its own nature; therefore, the author states "impulse" (*saṃvega*) to address this unease. Impulse is a very firm latent impression that serves as the cause of action. (3)

"Vigour" (saṃvega) is the cause. Its characteristic is that which distinguishes it from mere specific action; it is the delimiting factor [of that action]. The meaning is that this very thing becomes the cause of action and also becomes a more firm latent impression (saṃskāra). By the word "more" (tara), the sense is that it is an even stronger cause.
Now, one might object: this resolution is untenable, for thus says the Śruti:

Because of the existence of the Śruti passage: "From food beings are born; once born, they grow by food. It is eaten and it eats beings; therefore it is called 'food' (anna). Food is nectar; they call it the life-force," [the author] states "gone" (*gata*) out of dissatisfaction with the idea that the samādhi established by this authority has not been perceived. For those who possess the distinction of means consisting of going and returning, the fruit of samādhi is near at hand.

In this context, mere knowledge concerning the process of inhalation and exhalation (*gatāgata*) is not intended. Rather, what is intended here is that state in which bodily nourishment—which sustains the *dhātus*—is maintained even in the absence of eating food. Such individuals are indeed supreme yogins. The defining characteristic of them is the possession of knowledge regarding the distinctions in the methods of inhalation and exhalation. The "method for strengthening the body" consists of inhalation and exhalation in the form of *gatāgata*; "distinction" (*bheda*) means that which is differentiated, namely, the distinction produced by yoga born from the [practice] following the consumption of food.

The fruit of *samādhi* is the strengthening of the body. Through the body, one becomes entitled to perform all actions; the meaning is that the body becomes the cause for virtuous deeds and so forth, leading to liberation. Now, an objection may be raised: since the coming and going of the winds of inhalation and exhalation is established by itself for embodied beings, how can an action that is self-evident—without a specific injunction—act as a strengthener of the body, or how can it be conducive to liberation? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Gentle" (*mṛdu*), etc.
Therein lies the distinction due to its being gentle, moderate, or intense (*atimātra*). (5)

The breath-wind (śvāsānila), having entered the path of the *iḍā* and moving very slowly, makes the body free from disease; that very [wind] becomes the cause of liberation (*mokṣa*). Thereafter, having gone to the middle path and moving very slowly as far as the region of the navel, it causes firmness of the body and becomes the cause of liberation.

If, by means of excessive practice, one enters the path of the *suṣumṇā* and completely fills the abdomen, then that [prāṇa], having entered the *piṅgalā* path of the body, becomes the cause of unsurpassed liberation for the body. Due to the distinction of these [methods] and through the power of practice, he who performs *kumbhaka* at all times even without effort becomes free from disease; by accomplishing the path of *Rājayoga*, he becomes one who has renounced all karma. By that alone, he enjoys the fruit of liberation. Regarding this, there is a Śruti:

"By the yoga of renunciation, the striving ones of purified being, at the time of their final end in the world of Brahman, all are completely liberated through the supreme immortality"—by this scriptural authority, having become one whose sphere is knowledge free from doubt, and having experienced the enjoyments of all objects through the performance of actions that sustain the body's firmness, and having realized that the things which are the objects of those enjoyments are perishable, one’s knowledge regarding the Self always becomes the cause for the experience of supreme bliss even in this world. This alone is the distinction [of the yogi] over [the householder]; such is the meaning.
The *rājayoga* also occurs. Regarding the distinction among those possessing the means (*upāya*)—which are divided into categories such as weak (*mṛdu*) and so forth—he says "weak," etc.
The distinctions of the means are weak, middling, and excessive. (6)

In the manner previously described, proceeding through the mild, moderate, and intense stages is for the purpose of curing diseases that have not yet been cured by medicinal substances. The meaning is that this very method, by way of performing actions that strengthen the body, becomes the means for attaining the fruit of liberation. Now, one might object: "If it has been stated that the method for the three paths extends even to the point of performing actions that strengthen the body, then does not proceeding further than those paths also constitute a method? To this he says: *mṛdu* (mild), etc. Mild conjunction (*saṃyoga*), moderate conjunction, and intense conjunction. (7)

Even the gentle breeze of moving through the *iḍā* channel becomes a means for awakening the *kuṇḍalinī*. Likewise, the wind moving through the path of the *suṣumnā*, and the action of awakening the *kuṇḍalinī* produced by its contact with the *kuṇḍalinī*, become means for liberation. The meaning is that the collection of factors for achieving firmness of that body constitutes the means.

Since the mere strengthening of the body by means of the winds caused by the three *guṇas* is not the ultimate purpose, [the author] says "in three ways" (*tridhā*) to explain that, by performing actions distinct from the means of those *guṇas*—namely, by kindling the fire of yoga—one reduces the mass of sins accumulated over many births to ashes and thus becomes a cause for liberation.
By piercing in three ways, there arise nine types of yogins. (8)

The fruit of the threefold modification of the vital air (pavana) is now described: the conjunction of the gentle air is the conjunction with the gentle Kuṇḍalinī; the conjunction of the air of medium velocity with the Kuṇḍalinī is [the conjunction with] the medium [Kuṇḍalinī]; and the conjunction of the air moving on the path of intense speed with the Kuṇḍalinī is the intense conjunction.

The conjunction of the middle breath (*madhyamānila*) consists in its reaching from the region above the navel up to the heart-lotus, and then, following the internal pathway of the restrained wind situated there, coming to rest within the Self (*ātman*). That itself is *samādhi*. It is attained through the arising of self-knowledge. That indeed is the middle conjunction. The intense conjunction (*tīvrasaṃyoga*) extends further upward to the lotus of the head.

Above that, the filling of the channels (sirāmārga) caused by the movement of the vital air (pavana) arriving through the path of the Suṣumṇā is the sustainer of life for all bodies, because that action is beneficial to the entire body. The meaning is that it protects the body by becoming ninefold for the purpose of maintaining bodily health.

[Objection: Is it not the case that *samādhi* which fills the abdomen by obstructing the external wind within the channels of the *iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā* serves only to benefit the health of the body, since such movement does not assist the primary limbs? Furthermore, since the movement of the wind merely serves the purpose of filling the vessels (*sirā*), how can it be said that "these are the moving ones"? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Five," etc. [Verse 9]: The group of fifteen lotuses located in the region of the shanks supports a thousand vessels and contains fifty vital points (*marman*).

Samādhi is the conjunction with the wind that assists the formations of going and coming. It can be said that the lotus of fifteen [petals], which serves as the support for Kuṇḍalinī, located in the region of the shanks and covered by a thousand channels, effects the connection with the vital points (marmans) and provides the assistance for movement through the two shanks; therefore, these are shown to be "mobile" (jaṅgama).

The limb of the body located in the region of the calf-lotus is like a fifteen-petaled lotus, serving as an aid for the action of locomotion, because it is a limb of a moving body; for that which is not so is not so, like a pillar. That [limb] consisting of fifteen lotuses is covered by a thousand veins supporting a thousand feet, because it is a single limb covered by two hundred and fifty-five veins; for that which is not so is not so, like a limb of a stationary body such as a pillar.

It consists of fifty phonemes located within the fifty vital points (*marmans*), because it serves as the substratum for the bodily movements and gestures that signify those respective phonemes; for whatever is not thus is not thus, just like a jar.
Samādhi is the conjunction with the vital air (pavana) that assists the formative forces (saṃskāra) of going and coming.

Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*): concentration is an action characterized by the activity of movement, because it is dependent upon a substance that makes known the causes produced by the desire for knowledge and effort based on the vital air (*pavana*), just like a jar.

He speaks of the sounds produced by the operation of the palate and lips: "by the hands," etc. [This refers to] that which makes known a command following the placement of the hands, because it is dependent upon a cognition whose object is characterized by the act of gestural expression (*abhinaya*) that makes known those sounds. Thus, the explanation of the meaning of the aphorisms of Āyurveda has been performed by means of the instrument of inference (*anumāna*).

Is it not the case that the body presided over by consciousness is the locus of movement, because it consists of the experience of pleasure resulting from the action produced by that locus of movement? For that which is not so is not so, like a body devoid of consciousness. A living body possesses a self (sātmaka), because it possesses breath and other such signs. That which is not a living body does not possess breath and the like, like a corpse. Since movement is dependent on the will of God and is contingent upon the effects impelled by God, he says: "By God," etc.
The body is that which is the substratum of activity impelled by God, and the substratum of activity directed toward objects aimed at beneficial or harmful results. (11)

What kind of consciousness is that which serves as the basis for activity impelled by God? It is such that it lacks the capacity to grasp form like the eye, and lacks the capacity to grasp sound like the sense of hearing. Therefore, bearing in mind the intention that the nature of consciousness cannot be grasped [by these means], he says: "By God... Knowledge of produced sound is the proof for the existence of consciousness. To explain: the phonemes presided over by their respective organs—sounds consisting of syllables produced through the movement of the palate, lips, and so forth—are sounds impelled by God, because, while not being produced by the body and its like, they are caused by a produced operation, just like a sprout and similar effects.

"The sprout and so forth have an agent because they are effects, like a pot"—thus, it is claimed that inference is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of God, and by that reason He is perceived. However, since the effect arises when the causal complex consisting of the seed, soil, water, and vitality is present, the existence of God is not established by that either; for, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the visible causal complex that produces the sprout and so forth exists, just as in the case of a pot. The existence of the example, such as the sprout, is itself the proof. Furthermore, that which is delimited by a body is the locus of purposeful action (*ceṣṭā*).

There are many limbs capable of being the substratum of movement; since the contingency of constant motion would always arise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) of the definition. Anticipating this objection, he says: "By the Lord," etc.

The nature of volitional activity (*ceṣṭā*) is the vibration for the purpose of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful, but not mere vibration in general. All such activity rests upon the impulsion of the Lord (*īśvara*); this being so, there is no over-extension of the definition. The meaning is that the Lord acts as the guarantor (*pratibhū*) to bring about everything that is fit for experience—whatever karma corresponds to one’s fortune and whatever depends upon its specific locus. Because He is the prompter (*prayojaka*), the meaning is that the existence of the Lord is established by way of His impelling [the world] through the form of volitional activity.

Now, it was stated that the body is the locus of volitional activity (*ceṣṭā*). If that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the Lord] always performing such activity, since He is established as pervading all bodies and limbs; thus, because His very performance of activity would become the sole motivator, the author says "beneficial and harmful... with a sense of dissatisfaction.

The initiation of movement for the sake of attaining the beneficial and for the sake of avoiding the harmful is impelled by the Lord (Īśvara). The self (ātman) is conjoined with the mind (manas), the mind with the sense organ (indriya), and the sense organ with the object (artha), because of the rule that the sense organs function by reaching their objects. The meaning is that the Lord becomes an experiencer of bliss through the knowledge of experiencing those objects to whatever extent He desires to perform actions for that purpose.

[Objection: Surely, for one who has the consumption of pure *rasa*, the sense organs and so forth become very clear. Furthermore, the consumption of *rasa*-rich substances is caused by the support of desire (*iṣṭāśrayahetuka*), because the limbs of the body are nourished by the consumption of *rasa*. Therefore, since it is possible to speak only of the relationship of cause and effect between the consumption of pure *rasa*-rich substances and the body whose nature is movement, [the author], due to this unsatisfactory point, says: "Pure," etc. [The body] is of the nature of movement by virtue of the wind (*pavana*) that has entered the channels (*sirā*) and is impelled by the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) produced from the food of pure *rasa*. 12.
Regarding this, the statement is as follows:
"The fire digests the food; devoid of food, it digests the humors (doṣas);
upon the depletion of the humors, it digests the constituent elements (dhātus); and upon the depletion of the elements, it digests even the vital breaths."
The meaning is that, according to these words, the strengthening of the body and the movement of the limbs occur solely from the consumption of *rasa*.

[Objection: Surely, the consumption of pure *rasa* merely nourishes the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Consequently, due to the absence of disease, the five sense organs also acquire the knowledge of their respective objects through the consumption of substances containing pure *rasa*; thus, they even grasp the "possessing that [object] as its qualifier" (*tadvati tatprakārakatva*). Therefore, it would follow that there could be no assistance toward action characterized by movement. Anticipating this objection, he says: "the shanks" (*jaṅghā*). By virtue of the application of the transformation of the flow of nectar (*amṛta*) that nourishes the lotus of the shanks, one moves. || 13 ||

The meaning is that the fifteen-petaled lotus situated at the entrance of the shanks nourishes that lotus by means of the stream of nectar brought [there] under its influence, thereby becoming an auxiliary to the activity consisting of its movement.

Now, what is the proof for the existence of God? It is the engagement in action consisting of movement toward objects that procure one's own beneficial results, and the engagement in action consisting of movement toward the cessation of harmful results. Both of these are produced by the consumption of pure *rasa* (nutritive essence) and serve the purpose of strengthening the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). All such actions involving movement regarding every object of karma proceed by means of the vital air (*pavana*) through the impelling of the flow of nectar within the channels (*sirās*). Since, according to the reasoning stated previously, the performance of action is sufficient to accomplish the movement of the limbs of the body even without a God— [The argument continues: ...therefore, the existence of God is not established by this. However, [the opponent] might say: "Even if the movement of limbs occurs through the power of karma alone, the initial impulse (*preraka*) for that karma must necessarily be attributed to someone other than the body itself; otherwise, there would be no distinction between a living body and a corpse. Furthermore, since the body is composed of insentient matter (*jaḍa*), it cannot possess the capacity to initiate action on its own. Therefore, the existence of a conscious being distinct from the body, who acts as the impeller of the body, is established. To this we reply: No, because the impelling cause of the body’s activity is the *sattva* residing within the body itself. Just as the movement of a stone occurs due to the contact with a magnet, so too the activity of the body proceeds from the contact of the body with its own internal *sattva*. Thus, the existence of God is not proven by this either. Moreover, the movement of the body is observed even in the absence of a conscious agent, as in the case of a tree swaying in the wind. Therefore, the existence of God is not established by this proof. Furthermore, if the existence of God were established by the mere fact of the body’s movement, then the existence of God would also have to be admitted in the case of trees and the like. Consequently, the existence of God is not proven by the movement of the body. Rather, the existence of God is established by the fact that the body is a composite whole (*saṃghāta*) and possesses a specific arrangement (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*). For a composite whole that possesses a specific arrangement must necessarily be presided over by an intelligent being (*buddhimat*), just as a palace or a chariot is. Since the body is such a composite whole, its existence proves the existence of God. This is the correct view. As for the argument that "the existence of God is not proven because the body’s movement is accomplished by karma alone," that is incorrect. For the body’s movement is not accomplished by karma alone; rather, it is accomplished by karma in conjunction with the Lord. Just as a potter requires both clay and a wheel to produce a jar, so too the Lord requires both karma and the body to bring about the body’s movement. Therefore, the existence of God is established. Furthermore, the body’s movement is not possible without the Lord, because the body is a composite whole and possesses a specific arrangement. Hence, the existence of God is proven by the body’s movement. "For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone. Therefore, because it would otherwise be untenable [to claim that God is not established], he says: "Lavaṇa... etc.

God is a particular Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, and latent dispositions, which set in motion the flow of the qualities (*guṇa*) produced by the wind of the flavor of salt. 14.

A single Lord, characterized by the quality of *tamas* and produced from the salty taste, resides within the body. Although that Lord is eternal, he is said to be "produced" because the quality of *tamas* is non-eternal; being characterized by that quality, he is designated as such. A Lord characterized by the quality of *sattva*, produced from the consumption of substances possessing a sweet taste that generates wind, resides in a body characterized by that same quality; he is unborn (*aja*). He is unborn with respect to afflictions (*kleśa*), qualities (*guṇa*), fruitions (*vipāka*), and latent dispositions (*āśaya*). Therefore, untouched by these, free from disease, the Lord is a specific kind of *puruṣa*.

Both of them reside within the body. Of these two, one is ageless, entirely independent, and pervades the entire body, serving as the facilitator of all actions. Through the knowledge of objects that serves as the cause for the experience of its own bliss, desire arises; that action consisting of movement is *pravṛtti*. Because it makes known its own sovereignty, the other is the Lord (*Īśvara*), who is distinct from *māyā*, stainless, devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), partless, and whose nature is eternal bliss, beyond the reach even of yogis.

The meaning is that both of those birds have remained after abandoning the tree of the body. The *jīva* consists of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, its maturation (*vipāka*), and latent dispositions (*āśaya*). "Afflictions" (*kleśa*) refers to ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, because they cause one to suffer. "Karma" refers to the impermanent actions consisting of substances that are neither prescribed nor prohibited, as will be described hereafter. "Maturation" (*vipāka*) refers to the fruits of karma—namely, birth, lifespan, and the experience of pleasure and pain—as will be described; these arise from the consumption of salty and pungent substances caused by the quality of *tamas*.

Their intention (*āśaya*), consisting of the locus of the causal ground (*nidāna-sthāna*), is the individual soul (*jīva*) variegated by illusion (*māyā*). Through the thousand channels situated in the lotus of the calves located within that intention, by means of the knowledge of effort arising from the self-will, and through the power of the vital air (*pavana*) that impels coming and going, I am Dharma in the calves and in the feet. I am established in the earth; I am established in the kingdom; I am established in the horses; I am established in the cattle; I am established in the limbs, in the self; I am established in the vital breaths, in the back; I am established in heaven and earth, in the sacrifice.
The meaning is that I enter into the bodies established by the Veda and perform action.

But surely, the movements and other functions residing in the limbs of the body are dependent upon the self; by this, the Supreme Self (paramātman) is established. The effect of the knowledge regarding the object of the Supreme Self’s will is preceded by the knowledge regarding the object of the individual self’s will, because it is the cause of the effects of action impelled by pure consciousness (śuddhacaitanya). That which is not so is not thus, like a jar. By means of this method of inference, the Supreme Self is established.

The proof of the Self (ātman) is established by the following inference: "The movement of the tongue, lips, and other organs, which serves as the locus for making known all phonemes impelled by the channels and veins situated along the path of the currents, must have an agent, because it is an effect, like a pot. To that end, he explains the movement of the limbs of the body, beginning with the word "srota" (channel).
The eighteen-petaled lotus, which is the support for the movement of perception and the coming and going [of breath] within the three hundred vessels of the channel-path, exists [as such]. || 15 ||

Those three hundred veins, which move through the channels of the vital points (*marman*), serve as the boundary for the flow within the channels of this body, which is the locus of such activities, because it is presided over by the Self (*ātman*). The eight-petaled lotus situated in the region of the throat is the impeller of the wind that causes the utterance of all phonemes and is the support of its presiding deity, Prāṇa. When there is knowledge—which is the cause of that very activity—then, by performing actions characterized by movement, the Self can indeed be known; this is the meaning.

Now, action, which is of the nature of motion, is produced by the impulsion of God. By the inference, "This action has an agent because it is an effect," the Supreme Self, remaining within, performs the action. Here, the state of being an action consisting of motion is a state produced by the effort of God. This being so, since the causal relationship between those two is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the meaning is that God is established by this inference.

The provocation of the *pavana* (vāyu) is averted by consuming foods that produce the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) and possess sweet, sour, and salty tastes. By eating such food, the body—remaining free from disorder—performs its natural activity characterized by movement. When specific disorders arise, it performs corresponding actions; for the three qualities are the instigators of action. Due to the consumption of food that is unpalatable or lacks the supporting sweet and sour tastes, one is unable to perform actions properly. In that case, the external air [is drawn] through the path of *iḍā*, which serves as the remedy, because it is the means of curing even curable diseases.

From the consumption of food that is tasteless or possesses an excess of sweet, sour, and salty tastes, a disease of the stomach arises; for that too, this very [remedy] serves as the medicine. When the wind-humor (*pavana-doṣa*) is not provoked, the performance of bodily functions is indicated; when it is provoked, the absence of bodily activities is observed. Eating food that becomes the cause of disorders in the body and so forth is the cause of those respective actions. Therefore, the meaning is that the resulting effect is precisely the preservation of the prior non-existence of disease. The Lord, moreover, having assumed limbs such as hands and feet, performs the action that produces the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). And thus says the Śruti:

"The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth; the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) was made from his arms; that which is the Vaiśya was his thighs; from his feet the Śūdra was born. The moon was born from his mind; from his eye the sun was born; from his mouth Indra and Agni [were born]. This is the proof for the existence of the Lord as distinct from the body and the internal self.

Remaining within, one performs actions; therefore, one must daily consume wholesome food. Otherwise, diseases arise. Consequently, due to the embodied soul's lack of capacity regarding the instruments [of action], abdominal disease becomes incurable. Filling the channels of the vessels with external air is the remedy for abdominal disease, because when that which is contrary to its application has ceased, the instrument—the practice of filling with air—becomes effective. Yoga is the conjunction of the self and the mind, because it brings about the state of yoga.

He alone becomes the provider of the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*). Regarding abdominal diseases, substances that ignite the fire are the remedy, because they serve as medicine in that context due to their capacity to produce the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) for the yoga-fire. He explains the etiology of abdominal disease arising from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) with the verse beginning "sweet" (*svādu*):
"Generated by the wind (*anila*) produced from sweet, sour, and salty tastes, filling the channels (*sirā*), it moves toward the region of the hip-lotus (*jaghanapadma*). (16)

From the consumption of substances that are either sweet-tasting or tasteless, and from indigestion, an increase of undigested matter (āma) and water occurs, resulting in the development of abdominal enlargement (udara). || 17 ||

The consumption of substances that are either sweet-tasting or tasteless is a cause of abdominal diseases (*udarāmaya*). When indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) occurs due to that digestive fire, it arises from the excessive increase of the watery element (*ambubhūta*); by this, the digestive fire becomes weak. Furthermore, an excess of the fire-related *doṣas* occurs. Regarding this, the statement of the *Nidāna* says: "All diseases indeed arise when the digestive fire is weak, but abdominal diseases especially do so; they are produced from the accumulation of impurities through indigestion and unwholesome foods."
Obstructing the upward and downward channels that carry water,
and having vitiated the prāṇa, agni, and apāna, [the humors] located in the skin, flesh, and joints cause disease.

Having reached the stomach, that *āma* is divided eightfold. Through indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arising from the consumption of unwholesome tastes, disease is produced; by the absence of the totality of factors that would counteract it, it generates an increase of *āma* and other humors. Because of this, even the wind (*anila*) becomes sluggish. Since the body is composed of the five elements, the provocation of the wind is averted by the consumption of sweet tastes; conversely, the provocation of the wind is observed to result from the consumption of substances with unwholesome tastes.

Therefore, due to their arising and increasing, even the internal vessels located within the hollow organs become compressed; because of this lack of air circulation, the fluids overflow until the belly is completely filled. These vessels are seen within the tissues of plasma, blood, and flesh. Consequently, that water in the belly does not undergo digestion like the bodily tissues (dhātus); that becomes the disease of the abdomen (udarāmaya). This very disease is divided into eight types—this is the meaning.

[Objection: Surely a substance that possesses manifest unpleasant taste (*virasa*) is a cause for the provocation of wind (*pavana*), because it is a substance possessing manifest unpleasant taste despite having a manifest [quality of] being grasped as sweet. How then is it that a substance possessing sweet taste is not a counteragent that prevents the disease produced by a substance with manifest unpleasant fruit-taste? [It is not so] because it is a substance that initiates the provocation of wind; for whatever is not thus is not thus, like a jar. Furthermore, through the cessation of acidity (*āma*), even abdominal disease (*udarāmaya*) does not arise, because its utility consists in the maintenance of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that [disease]. Thus he says: "Sweet... (*svādu*).
In that case, the medicine is a purgative substance possessing a sweet taste. || 18 ||

This means the medicinal substances that eliminate abdominal diseases (udarāmaya), namely those used as decoctions, pastes, electuaries, and drugs. In this context, regarding abdominal disease caused by Vāta, all these aforementioned items are applicable because they are all potentially suitable. Thus, he prescribes that treatment should be administered after determining the appropriate time for each specific substance, since the remedy consists of substances fit for purgation; he indicates this with the word "gradually" (śanaiḥ): one should cause purgation to occur only very slowly. || 19 ||

Thinking that the abdomen of all living beings is a reservoir for water, while fire, strength, and vitality are reservoirs for fire, one should exhale very slowly. One should perform the task of purging the water residing within the network of channels (sirās) located inside the body, which causes abdominal disease; for the purpose of curing that, one should effect the evacuation of the water situated within. Regarding this, the statement from the *Nidāna* is as follows: "In all [such cases], there is drowsiness, exhaustion, a sense of being encased in a hut, weak digestion, burning sensations, swelling, flatulence, and finally the emergence of water."
"But all [these] are reddish from this [cause], without swelling, and not excessively heavy;
they are covered with networks of veins and always produce a rumbling sound.
Having suppressed the urge at the navel and having made an effort, the pain vanishes."

In accordance with this statement, that which effects the removal of the water produced by the disorder of the *sirās* (channels) is the action of purgation (*virecana*); by that, the abdominal disease (*udarāmaya*) is removed, because [the disease] consists of the watery substance caused by the disorder of the *sirās*. The meaning is that the object suitable for that purgation is the remover.

Is it not the case that abdominal diseases manifest frequently even in elephants, horses, and other animals? Since substances possessing sweet flavors serve as medicine in those cases, are those items not applicable there? No, because it is intended to include only those substances suitable for humans. This is because the etiology of flatulence—the primary cause of those abdominal diseases—is common to all people. Thus, the substances fit for enjoyment that are employed for the treatment of the disease are those which alleviate the provocation of the bodily wind (*pavana*).

The quality of being a substance possessing a sweet taste manifests in all substances prescribed for their respective classes. Regarding this, there is a rule: since the quality of being a substance possessing a sweet taste is possible for all [substances], and since the causes of intake and so forth involve similar substances for all living beings, "a substance possessing a sweet taste is the medicine therein"—this is the meaning propounded by Āyurveda.

The meaning is that it was proclaimed with a resonant voice like the ringing of a bell that his [the physician's] role is to nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) of all living beings, and that for humans, both substances of delicious taste and those of unpalatable taste are established as being conducive to health when they are measured correctly.
