According to the statement, "The root-support (*mūlādhāra*) is the strength of men, for that which is semen is indeed life," the regulator is also known. The meaning is that this is correctly established by the aphorism: "Exhaling very gradually for all living beings."

Now, a question arises: should the act of purgation be performed using each substance individually, or should they be administered in very small quantities, or should there be a combination of all of them, or should there be a partial application of each to bring about the cessation of the *āmadoṣa*? It is not the first [option]: if one were to claim that the purgation must be performed with each individual substance, then the injunction regarding the quantity to be used for the aforementioned purgative substances would become purposeless. Nor is it the second: because by administering them in very small quantities, there would simply be an absence of the cessation of the *āmadoṣa* itself.

[The first view is] that it effects the cessation of pure *āmadoṣa* and the cessation of abdominal diseases (*udarāmayana*), because its purpose is fulfilled by bringing about the cessation of the action that causes abdominal disease. It is not the third [view]—if it is argued that "it consists in performing a yoga that equalizes all bodily constituents (*dhātu*s)," then there would be excessive purgation; the *dhātu*s would be drained away. By that draining, there would be an aggravation of the *doṣa*s due to their being depleted. Therefore, [the opponent argues] that this much [of the treatment] would be useless. Because of this dissatisfaction, he says: "By means of *pavana*," etc. "The sequence of treatment nourishes the strength of the digestive fire (*agni*) without causing the aggravation of *pavana* and the other [wind-related factors]. (20)

Regarding the phrase "due to the non-aggravation of wind and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the humors of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) are indicated. The prevention of their aggravation would be the resultant purpose. Since that [aggravation] is a destroyer of digestive power (agnibala), and since the resultant purpose consists of the effect of the collection of factors that increase the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni) by whatever means possible, the therapeutic procedure for all abdominal diseases consists in increasing the digestive fire.

Since the absence of the effects of the provocation of *vāta* and the other humors is a result produced by [the consumption of] pure substances, one grasps the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that the knowledge of defects such as impurities arises from the consumption of pure tastes. Through repeated observation, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) can thus be grasped. Likewise, the causal relationship that "the consumption of substances with contrary tastes is the cause of abdominal diseases" is to be grasped. Therefore, it is intended here to explain the sequence of therapeutic actions for the purpose of producing the effect of non-provocation of *vāta* and the others.

For instance—the substance that effects the cessation of desire caused by abdominal disease is not merely the motivator [of the action]; rather, a conjunction with substances that do not provoke the wind (vāta) must be employed. That alone constitutes the sequence of treatment. Therefore, this "non-disaster" (*avipatti*) indicates that the effect of the non-disaster is brought about through the three humors (*doṣas*). This administration of purgation increases the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*), because, while it removes the diseases arising from substances that cause weak digestion (*mandānala*), it is itself a substance that promotes the digestive fire. This very point has been established in the context of treating abdominal disease, which involves the removal of the humors.
Vyāghrī, aśvagandhā, punarnavā, oil-cake, śigru, garlic, and pīlu,
along with vajravallī, karikarṇa, kuṇḍala, sūraṇa, and bitter leaves, remove disease.

In this *yoga*, purely purgative substances and purgative substances possessing sweet tastes (*svādurasa*) have been set forth. Substances that possess the functional property of being purgatives without causing the provocation of *vāta* and other *doṣas* have also been set forth. It was stated in the previous aphorism that the mere act of purging does not necessarily cause the provocation of *vāta*; however, that [statement] is to be reconsidered, for by it, the provocation of *pitta* occurs. The symptoms that constitute its etiology—such as giddiness (*bhrama*), fainting (*mūrchā*), burning sensations (*vidāha*), distaste for food (*arati*), and anorexia (*aruci*)—are to be recognized.

This means the symptoms of abdominal disease (*udara-roga*) arising from an excess of *pitta*. Due to the consumption of substances with astringent, bitter, and sweet tastes, the wind (*pavana*), provoked by such causes, obstructs the movement of the wind situated within the channels of the vessels (*sirā-mārga*) and causes the essence of the *rasa* and *rakta* tissues to flow out. That very essence should be understood as *pitta*. It should be stated that this is the indicator of the abdominal disease of *pitta*. By means of the internal hollow organs, the obstructed *pitta* fills the intervening passages.

Due to the filling of the interior of the abdomen by the essence of the *rasa* and *rakta* tissues through the movement of the wind (*anila*), it is like the digestion of the tissues. Because the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) has undigested matter as its object, that very [fire] increases due to being obstructed in the belly; this is what he calls the disease of *pittodara*. He says "devoid of *rasa*" (*virasa*):

from the movement of the wind situated in the channels of the veins, produced by indigestion resulting from the consumption of unpalatable substances, there is an excessive flow of *rasa* through the vessels; thus, from indigestion, the increase of the water of *āma* gives rise to the abdominal enlargement (*udara*). || 21 ||

The causes of *pittodara* (bilious abdominal enlargement) arising from the consumption of tasteless (*virasa*) substances must be stated. Pitta becomes aggravated by the consumption of tasteless substances that possess an astringent (*kaṣāya*) taste, or by the consumption of tasteless substances that possess a bitter (*tikta*) taste, because these substances are undigestible due to their fiery nature. Its alleviation should be achieved through fasting (*laṅghana*) alone. Where the consumption of tasteless substances with astringent, bitter, or sweet tastes is observed, there arises the disease of *pittodara*. Regarding this, the statement of the Sūtra is: "Astringent, bitter, and sweet [tastes] [aggravate pitta], while others [aggravate it] in other [conditions]."

Regarding the phrase "in others": substances possessing bitter (*tikta*) or sweet (*svādu*) tastes, which are contrary to [the taste of] *kaṣāya*, alleviate the provocation of *pitta*. Substances with tastes other than those [three] provoke *pitta*. Among these three [categories], the consumption of substances with tastes other than that which caused the provocation of *pitta* arising from the consumption of a single-taste substance is what alleviates it. Pure tastes distinct from those [three] are not the cause of abdominal diseases; rather, they are tastes contrary to the one that provoked *pitta*. This is the intended meaning of the statement: "In others, *pitta* becomes provoked."

The meaning is as follows: the consumption of substances that are neither astringent nor bitter, yet possess a taste distinct from a sweet taste and are devoid of flavor, is caused by abdominal disease (*udarāmaya*), because it consists of the consumption of substances not digested by the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*). That which is not so [i.e., not caused by undigested food] is not so, like a jar (*ghaṭa*). Conversely, the consumption of substances that are of a single taste or devoid of flavor is not caused by abdominal disease, because it consists of the consumption of substances digested by the digestive fire. By means of this inferential proof (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), it is well-established that the combination of the consumption of astringent, bitter, and sweet-tasting substances that lack flavor is the cause of abdominal disease.

Now, an objection: since the causal substances for the eight types of abdominal diseases (*udarāmaya*) are substances possessing the six tastes or those that have lost their natural taste, and because there is an absence in the world of substances other than these—meaning an absence of substances that could cause other diseases—it would follow that everyone would suffer from abdominal disease. Anticipating this incongruity, he says: "To that extent" (*tāvat*).
"To that extent, [the swelling] indicates edema (*śvayathu*) due to the specific locations within the vessels. (22)

When there is a disorder of the vessels (sirā) supported by the region of Vāta, the disease of Vātodara arises according to the aforementioned method. Likewise, when there is a disorder of the vessels supported by the region of Pitta, Pittodara arises. When there is a disorder of the vessels supported by the region of Kapha, Kaphodara arises. The very function of the vessels caused by those respective Doshas constitutes the dual Dosha (Dvandva-dosha); thus, there are three types arising from two Doshas: one disease of Udara caused by the Doshas of Pavana (Vāta) and Pitta; and one disease of Udara caused by the Doshas of Kapha and Vāta.

There is one abdominal disease (udarāmaya) caused by bile and phlegm (pitta-kapha), and one abdominal disease caused by the three humors (tridoṣa). Altogether, eight types of diseases have arisen. Regarding the phrase "situated in the vessels" (sirāgata): when the digestive fire (anala) becomes weak due to the obstruction of the movement of the vital air (pavana) within the channels of the vessels produced by various incompatible or unwholesome tastes (rasa), indigestion (ajīrṇatva) results; that [obstruction] is its defining condition (avacchedaka). The meaning is that the very cause of abdominal disease—based on the specific locations and the three humors—is what constitutes the respective defining condition for each case.

Keeping in mind the intention that the disorder of the vessels located in the region of *pitta* can be known once the disease of *pittodara* is recognized, and that it can then be cured by its specific remedy, he says: "By wind...

The symptoms caused by the provocation of *pitta*—namely, dryness, extreme coldness, lightness, excessive pain, loss of appetite, discoloration, a bad taste in the mouth, drowsiness, fainting, burning sensations, vertigo, thirst, fever, diarrhea, and yellowness of the limbs—are caused by the provocation of *pitta* and the resulting abdominal disease (*udarāmaya*). (23)

Regarding the quality of dryness (*rūkṣaguṇatva*): due to the excessive movement of the wind (*pavana*) within the channels and apertures of the vessels (*sirāmārgarandhra*), a sensation of heat arises in those respective limbs. In that case, the dryness of that wind-disorder (*pavanavikāra*) is the defining characteristic. Where the movement of the wind is slight and an obstruction of the wind-flow is observed within the channels and apertures of the vessels, there extreme pain (*ativedanā*) arises. In the same way, a bad taste in the mouth (*virasāsyatva*) and discoloration (*vivarṇatva*) are the symptoms; this is because the wind pervading the entire body has been seized by disorder.

In response to the inquiry, "Since there is no sensation in all parts of the body, how can there be sensation in only one part?", the following rule is established: as long as the *sara* (vital essence) produced by the consumption of unwholesome food is perceived in specific locations of the channels (*sirā*), this is the law. Furthermore, the doubt and its resolution are provided as follows: regarding the disorder of the wind (*pavana*) that circulates through the entire body, the knowledge that there is no sensation throughout the whole body arises precisely because of the circulation [of the disorder] within those specific channel-locations; thus, the health of each respective limb is perceived [only] through that circulation.

The purpose of medical treatment is precisely for those respective parts [of the body], because by consuming substances that counteract them, the defects (doṣa) produced by the consumption of incompatible tastes are removed; thus, the meaning is that happiness shall prevail once the provocation of the defects has been averted.

Some [authorities] maintain that because the interior channels of the vessels (sirā) are filled with water produced by incompatible tastes, a change of color and an alteration of taste are manifested. By this, it can indeed be understood that the disease of the abdomen (udarāmaya) is caused by the consumption of substances whose tastes are discordant with those that pacify the provocation of Vāta. Now, the symptoms arising from the causal factors of Pitta-type abdominal disease are described:

Fainting, burning sensations, vertigo, thirst, loss of appetite, fever, and yellowness of the limbs are caused by the provocation of *pitta* and abdominal diseases. The consumption of substances that are astringent, bitter, sweet, or tasteless—which counteract such provocation—causes a disturbance in the movement of the *vāyu* (wind) within the channels and vessels pervading the regions of *pitta*, leading to the drying up of the *māṃsa-dhātu* (muscle tissue). This is because it is produced by the consumption of tasteless substances that provoke the *vāyu-doṣa* and excessively dry up the *māṃsa-dhātu*. Whatever is not thus [produced] is not thus, like a jar.

Thus, by way of inference: the essence of the flesh (*māṃsasāra*), produced by the drying up of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), is caused by the disease of the bile-gall bladder (*pittodara*); for it is a substance that is the essence of the bodily constituents resulting from the indigestion of the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*). From that, fainting (*mūrchā*) also arises. Due to the depletion of those constituents, a burning sensation (*dāha*) occurs. From contact with other substances, the essence of the constituents produces vertigo (*bhrama*). Because of that, the digestive fire is expelled from its place; due to this outward flaming, fever (*jvara*) arises. And from the excessive manifestation of that essence, passion (*rāga*) is produced.

Because the essence has departed from the element of flesh (*māṃsadhatu*), a bilious condition (*paittya*) is perceived. It is explained that this is the disease of bilious abdominal enlargement (*pittodara*), characterized by such symptoms.

Hereafter follows the enumeration of the eight types of abdominal diseases: Kapha, having its essence produced from the channels of the bodily constituents—semen, marrow, fat, skin, hair, and blood—and accompanied by dyspnea, cough, giddiness, burning sensation, darkness of vision, and [excessive] phlegm, produces further kapha. (24)

Because the fat element (*medas*) is produced from the flesh element (*māṃsa*), when there is a disorder of that [flesh], one produces phlegm (*kapha*) characterized by dyspnea, wheezing, vertigo, burning sensations, thinness of the skin, and the accumulation of essence-phlegm (*sārakapha*) arising from the vessels of that [skin]. The remedy for the provocation of the phlegm humor (*kapha-doṣa*) is the consumption of substances that are bitter, pungent, and astringent in taste, and which are devoid of [agreeable] flavor.

It is caused by the disease of *kapha*-type abdominal enlargement (*kaphodara*), because it dries up the *medas* (fat) tissue through a disorder in the movement of the *pavana* (vata) wind as it travels through the channels of the vessels pervading the regions where *kapha* resides; this is due to its being produced by the consumption of substances that are unpalatable in taste and which generate a drying quality that produces an excess of *medas* tissue, thereby provoking both *pavana* and *pitta*. Whatever is not thus [produced] is not thus, like a pot.

Now, it may be asked: are not the astringent, bitter, and sweet tastes the removers of the provocation of *pitta*, while their contrary tastes are the causes of the provocation of *pitta*? Likewise, the sweet, sour, and salty tastes are the removers of the provocation of *vāta*, while their contrary tastes are the causes of the provocation of *vāta*. Thus, a substance that is sweet in taste but contrary to it [in its post-digestive effect] is a cause of the provocation of both *vāta* and *pitta*. When there is a provocation of *vāta* caused by such a contrary taste, a dual provocation (*dvandva-prakopa*) occurs in the disease pertaining to those [two] factors.

Because the aggravation of *vāta* and *pitta* is caused by the consumption of sweet-tasting or tasteless substances, it is stated that where the occurrence of diseases produced by two or three types of tastes is observed, the intake of sweet-tasting or tasteless substances generates a dual-natured (*dvandva*) condition—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "pavana" (wind).

One should understand that this abdominal disease (*udarāmaya*) of *vāta* and *pitta* follows the characteristics of both previously mentioned [tastes] and is produced from two or three tastes that cause the aggravation of wind and bile.
25. The meaning of this is as follows:

A substance that causes the provocation of wind (pavana) and bile (pitta) is produced by the consumption of substances that are unpalatable (virasa) to those respective tastes; for while it is not produced by tastes other than those, it is produced by those specific tastes—just as a jar is not so produced. Furthermore, a wind-related disease is produced by substances unpalatable to the sweet and sour tastes, because, while it lacks the causal factors of diseases produced by other [tastes], it possesses the quality of being a substance that generates the effects of that specific disease. This can be determined through negative inference (vyatirekānumāna). Sweet, sour, and salty tastes are the alleviators of wind-provocation, whereas abdominal disease (udarāmaya) is produced by substances unpalatable to those [sweet, sour, and salty] tastes.

That which possesses astringent, bitter, and sweet tastes is a pacifier of pitta; that which is devoid of those tastes is a provocateur of pitta. Therefore, because it consists of the consumption of substances whose sweet taste has become vitiated—thereby generating a provocation of both doṣas—it becomes a provocateur of two doṣas. The two types of diseases arising from the three kinds of tastes are abdominal ailments (udarāmaya) produced by the provocation of vāyu and pitta. The meaning is that their diagnosis should be understood from the specific symptoms characteristic of each.

But surely, the state of being "virasa" (unpalatable or discordant) is understood for sweet, sour, salty, and other tastes in the Sūtra; it is stated that such a *virasa* provokes *pavana* (vāta) and *pitta*. This being the case, the state of being *virasa* would also apply to astringent (*kaṣāya*), bitter (*tikta*), and sweet (*svādu*) tastes according to this Sūtra, and it would be stated that such a *virasa* becomes a provocateur of *pitta*. This is not tenable. For what is called *virasatva* is a substance possessing a taste that is contrary to the provocation of the *doṣas*.

How can the consumption of substances possessing those [specific] tastes be beneficial to the three *doṣas*, given that it is observed only in the case of substances that are complete, possessing qualities exceeding the qualities of the tastes produced at a particular time? Regarding this, there is the statement of the Sūtra: "Sweet [food] generally increases *śleṣman*, except for aged *śāli* rice and barley, mung beans, wheat, honey, sugar, and the meat of wild animals."
Generally, sour substances generate pitta, with the exception of pomegranate and āmalaka;
salt is generally unwholesome for the eyes, with the exception of rock salt (saindhava).
"Bitter and pungent substances are for the most part non-aphrodisiacs and provokers of Vāta,
with the exception of Abhaya, Paṭolī, Śuṇṭhī, Kṛṣṇā, and Rasona.
Astringent substances are generally cooling and astringent (stambhana), with the exception of Abhayā."

In this manner, it has been established that the six tastes are causes for the provocation of diseases; however, it should not be said that they are not the removers of disease, because if that were the case, it would be possible to claim that substances with those same disagreeable qualities (*virasa*) produce disease. Furthermore, since a sweet taste consists of substances possessing many qualities, it can be said that it is "sweet and increases *śleṣman* (phlegm). Thus, the statement "the sweet is generally phlegm-increasing" is not to be doubted.

The meaning is that such a substance possessing a bitter taste (*virasa*) causes all the [humoral] defects (*doṣa*), since it can be said of the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*) as well. In this way, the meaning of the aphorism concerning the disease of wind-phlegm abdominal enlargement (*pavanakaphodarāmaya*) should be applied according to the previously stated method. Likewise, this much of the meaning should also be applied to the disease of bile-phlegm abdominal enlargement (*pittakaphodarāmaya*). In this manner, seven types of abdominal diseases arise. Following that, he explains three aphorisms beginning with "kapha" (*kapha*...).

The abdominal disease (udarāmaya) caused by the provocation of kapha and pitta should be understood as being characterized by the respective symptoms following from two or three tastes. One should know that the abdominal disease of kapha and pitta is the affliction of kapha and pitta produced by the knowledge of the symptoms of both, following from two or three tastes. The abdominal diseases of vāta, pitta, and kapha, which fall within the scope of knowledge regarding their respective symptoms following from two or three tastes that produce disorders of rasa, blood, muscle, and fat, are difficult to cure. || 26 ||

Now, one might ask: what is the proof for the existence of abdominal disease (*udarāmaya*) caused by the consumption of food whose taste has become vitiated, which in turn generates the three *doṣas*, given that the very cause for generating them is absent? In this regard, there are three types produced by a single *doṣa*, three born from two [combined] *doṣas*, and one produced by all three *doṣas*. Thus, abdominal disease is of seven kinds.

Anticipating the objection that—since this point forward, for the sake of completing the number eight, there is no distinct elemental humor (*bhūtadoṣa*) in the case of abdominal disease (*udarāmaya*), and since the causality of *vāta* and the others has already been established as being sevenfold by virtue of their specific limiting conditions (*upādhi*), and because another type of abdominal disease cannot be known due to the absence of a cause (as an effect does not arise in the absence of its cause)—he provides the following resolution: "Likewise, there is the abdominal disease of *plīhodara*, which is produced by parasites (*krimi*). (27)

The meaning of this is as follows: *klima* refers to diseases born from a state of distaste (*virasa*). From those, diseases such as splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*) arise, because *klima* takes the form of a fleshy knot produced by the essence of the humors (*sāra*). Since it acts as the instigator of the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*), it is likewise driven by the same [disorders of the] *doṣas*. Therefore, the meaning is that the eightfold classification of abdominal diseases (*udarāmaya*) is thus logically consistent.

Since this is the occasion for the exposition of the diseases of *pāṇḍu*, swelling (*śopha*), and spreading eruptions (*visarpa*), and because these conditions share the same origin—being produced by the three *dhātu*-disturbances as a result of the action of the wind moving through the channels of the vessels that generate abdominal disease (*udarāmaya*)—and since their description follows immediately after the definition of abdominal disease, he says: "Pungent," etc.

The consumption of substances possessing pungent, sour, and salty tastes produces impurities that obstruct the channels; this provokes the upward-moving wind which fills the heart and the openings of those vessels, thereby causing *pāṇḍu*, swelling, spreading eruptions, and pain. (28)

Bitter, sour, and salty tastes, as well as substances with those corresponding potencies (*virasa*), provoke *pitta*. Those same substances, when consumed in their improper potency, cause *pāṇḍu*, edema (*śopha*), and erysipelas (*visarpa*). The disorder of *āma* produced by the consumption of such substances causes the diseases of *pāṇḍu*, edema, and erysipelas. That morbid condition, having reached the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and ascended through the openings of the vessels (*sirārandhra*) into the heart, assumes the form of *pāṇḍu* because it disturbs the movement of the wind (*pavana*), because it vitiates the vessels pervaded by it, and because it corrupts the blood located therein while remaining pervasive within them.

When there is a disorder of the blood (*rakta*), inflammation (*śotha*) occurs. Because it causes a disorder of the flesh (*māṃsa*), erysipelas (*visarpa*) arises. The bile (*pitta*) therein remains in an undigested state (*āmam*). Due to its location within that diseased site, it becomes a producer of morbid transformation (*vikāra*). Because it has the nature of poison (*viṣa*), the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) become corrupted. The symptoms produced by that [corruption] manifest here and there.

Then, because it is of an amorphous nature, the *pitta* fills the portion of the vessel-cavities within the heart with the essence of the *āmāpitta*; having been discharged into the *pakvāśaya*, that very essence of the digested matter becomes urine. Having entered the heart-lotus and remaining right there, it causes throbbing in the heart. Due to the entry of the *pitta* into the tongue through the support of the lotus enveloped by two vessels, and its entry into the cavities of those vessels, a loss of appetite is observed in the tongue.

Having filled the portion of the vessel-cavities with the essence of the bile located in the heart, it flows into the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*); because that very essence of the digested food becomes urine, the absence of the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*) appears. Its entry into that constituent element (*dhātu*) also appears yellow, having abandoned its previous color by virtue of being of that same nature. Having completely filled the fifty vessel-cavities and channels, it enters the lotus of the eye; there, yellowness is perceived.

Due to the entry of the essence of bile (*pitta-sāra*) into the channels, apertures, and vessels of the hundred veins, the branches and fingers thereof—having abandoned their previous colors through the appearance of black, reddish-brown, golden, and yellow teeth—shine with a yellow hue. The blood situated therein appears multicolored. Regarding how the essence of bile, residing in the heart-lotus within the blue-natured navel-whorl that serves as the support for the Kuṇḍalinī and the foundation of the navel-whorl, enters the paths within the thirty channels supporting the navel-whorl and generates various disorders, he says: "Whirling," and so forth.

Dizziness, fever, thirst, vomiting, craving, fainting, internal burning, trembling of the limbs, loss of appetite, and pallor are the characteristics of *pitta*-dominant *pāṇḍu*. Excessive pain in the feet, knees, calves, thighs, hips, back, sides, and waist, diarrhea, dryness, extreme coldness, and trembling of the entire body are the characteristics of *vāta*-dominant *pāṇḍu*. (29)

The symptoms of *vāta-pāṇḍu* (wind-induced anemia) are now described—beginning with "pāda" (the feet). The lotus-feet, which are the foundation of the body's complexion and other qualities, possess a basin-like structure surrounded by thirty-four vessels. Due to the obstruction of the nectar (*amṛta*) descending from the lotus-head, there occurs an excess of undigested matter and bile (*āma-pitta-atisāra*). This serves as an indicator for the signs of diseases such as *śobha*, *pāṇḍu*, and *visarpa*. When the wind (*pavana*), which knows the disorders arising from the consumption of unwholesome tastes, enters the *rasa* and blood tissues (*dhātu*), it brings about the disorder of the pale-yellow form (*pāṇḍu-rūpa*). That same wind, if it enters the muscle tissue (*māṃsa-dhātu*), results in swelling (*śvayathu*). If that same wind enters the [subsequent] tissues, the disease of *visarpa* (erysipelas) arises.

If a deformity arises in someone's foot, the pronunciation of the letters located in that region will be indistinct and difficult to hear, as if they were being pronounced unclearly. Alternatively, one should recognize the presence of swelling in that region, or diseases such as jaundice, leprosy, or erysipelas.

The lotus of the knee, situated at its proper location, is supported by the thighs and encircled by thirty-four vessels; it serves as the channel for bringing nectar from the head-lotus through inhalation and exhalation, and it effects the refinement of the essence of the *āma* and *pitta* produced from wholesome and unwholesome tastes. Through the agitation of the wind (*vāyu*) moving within those channels, there arise, as before, the diseases of jaundice (*pāṇḍu*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), and so forth. The meaning is that from the corruption of the *rasa* and blood tissues (*dhātu*) comes jaundice; from the corruption of the flesh tissue comes the appearance of swelling; and from the corruption of the fat tissue, the diseases of erysipelas manifest.

Those spreading diseases (visarpa) characterized by a pale luster—which produce the effect of the absence of the movement of wind within the channels of vessels surrounded by lotuses located in various regions that serve as the substrata for those respective colors—and which, as before, vitiate the bodily constituents (dhātus), resulting in the inaudibility of all the phonemes (varṇas) despite the presence of the entire apparatus for their utterance; these should be known as arising from the provocation of wind (pavana). Furthermore, due to the flow of nectar situated in the head-lotus, which is the seat of the lotuses in the region of bile (pitta), there occurs in the vessels themselves the effect of the conjunction of the essence of undigested matter (āma) and bile, produced by tastes contrary to that [nectar].

This is because it makes known the knowledge of the characteristics of those diseases. For as long as there is contact with the vessels, it indicates the absence of the respective diseases characterized by their specific symptoms and reveals their respective causes. Starting from the region of the back, and from the lotus below the seed-vessel (bīja) and the penis, there are fifteen lotuses presided over by the winds that generate the respective seed-syllables (bījas)—namely the *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa* groups—which serve as the bases for bile (*pitta*) and produce the effects of the disorders arising from the provocation of bile.

When the causal complex for the provocation of *pitta* is present, the symptoms that indicate those various color-transformations serve as indicators of their respective causes. The meaning is that the *pitta* residing in the fifteen foundational lotus-seats, extending up to the region of the lips, manifests those very symptoms right there. Hereafter, the signs of the diseases of *kapha*, anemia (*pāṇḍu*), leucoderma (*śobha*), and erysipelas (*visarpa*) are revealed—beginning with "dyspnea" (*śvāsa*). Dyspnea, cough, nasal catarrh, [affliction of] the eyes, eyelids, ears, cheeks, teeth, excessive rhinitis, and a piercing pain in the head are the symptoms of the diseases of anemia, leucoderma, and erysipelas. (30)

In the region of *kapha*, namely the heart, due to the presence of *āmapitta* and diarrhea, the heart is enveloped by thirty vessels; because the vital air (*pavana*) residing in these vessels is obstructed, dyspnea (*śvāsa*) and asthma (*khāsa*) arise. Furthermore, there is an excess of impurity (*mala*) in the eyelids, eyes, ears, cheeks, and teeth, as well as intense pain that is clearly perceived. These symptoms—characterized by the diseases born of the provocation of *kapha*, such as anemia (*pāṇḍu*), urticaria (*śobhi*), and erysipelas (*visarpa*)—are made known through their respective etiological factors (*nidāna*).

Now, it might be argued that diseases of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) are established as such through the provocation of wind, bile, and phlegm; however, this is questionable. It must be stated that the cause of disease is either the consumption of food with unwholesome tastes, or the consumption of an excess of substances possessing pure tastes, or the obstruction of the force of the wind residing in its respective seat. This being the case, the provocations of the wind that circulates throughout the entire body arise from the defect of contact with unwholesome tastes and poisons, because that wind possesses the quality of moving pervasively through the body.

Let there be an aggravation of the wind (*pavana*) due to contact with that bitter poison; however, because phlegm (*kapha*) and bile (*pitta*) are inherently immobile (*paṅgu*), it is impossible to speak of their contact with a bitter poison. In response to the doubt—namely, how one knows "this is a disease of phlegm" and "this is a disease of bile"—the author says, "like one seized by an external poison":
"Like those seized by an external poison, they [the humors] corrupt the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). (31)

This is because it is observed that one who has been bitten by a snake or the like becomes afflicted by poison. Even in the absence of direct contact with that poison, due to their own lameness, bile (*pitta*) and phlegm (*kapha*)—which, like the wind pervading the entire body, are contained within the body—will undergo an aggravation of the three humors (*doṣatraya-prakopa*) through contact with the wind already permeated by the poison. Similarly, in this case as well, since the conjunction of the wind pervading [the body] with the wind bitten by the poisonous fluid exists within those two, it can be said: "this is the disorder of bile" and "this is the disorder of phlegm."

In that case, since every disease arises from the provocation of *pavana* (vāta) and all diseases are dependent upon the provocation of *pavana*, it would follow that all diseases are produced by *pavana* alone. Therefore, because *kapha* and *pitta* can serve as distinct limiting factors (*avacchedaka*), it has been stated in the Sūtrasthāna: "On account of its pervasiveness (*vibhutva*), its rapid action (*āśukāritva*), its strength (*balitva*), and its provocation of others, one should indicate the predominance of a disease through its independence (*svātantrya*) or dependence (*pāratantrya*)."

If it is argued that, according to this statement, wind (*pavana*) alone is understood to be the primary cause of all diseases, we say no. Although it pervades the entire body, it does not nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). This is because it possesses the quality of being a substance that kindles the dull wind; for a substance possessing the quality of kindling—which removes the dullness of the fire—lacks the capacity to nourish the *dhātus*. Since the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*) is itself a portion of bile (*pitta*), when bile is provoked, the fire becomes dull. Consequently, there would only be a provocation of phlegm (*kapha*).

The provocation of *pitta* and *kapha* leads to the destruction of the body because they are substances that obstruct the pathways of the wind (*vāyu*) which nourishes the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) situated within the channels of the vessels (*sirā*). The capacity to destroy the body is what defines a disease, since there is no destruction of the body apart from *pitta* and *kapha*. As for *vāyu*, its causality regarding disease is established through its association with them. Therefore, the meaning is that *pitta* also possesses primacy by virtue of being the principal factor.

The purpose of establishing the primacy of the wind (*pavana*) disease is that it is simply impossible to state that the causality of morbid conditions exists without the wind that pervades the entire body.

Now, an objection is raised: the diseases of anemia (*pāṇḍu*), edema (*śopha*), and erysipelas (*visarpa*) are produced by causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) that have as their objects the specific cognitions of those respective [individual] entities. However, a causal complex that grasps the cognition of one object cannot be the grasper of many objects; a cognition having many objects as its domain is not produced by a causal complex that grasps the cognition of one object, precisely because it is produced by a causal complex that grasps the cognition of one object.

For instance, when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for a pot and its sense organ is present, knowledge regarding the object "pot" arises, while knowledge regarding the object "cloth" does not. It is exactly the same here as well. How could a causal complex that produces one disease be a causal complex that produces an effect which establishes the purchase of a disease? This is because it is never observed that a single causal complex can apprehend multiple effects. Otherwise, if such were the case, when the causal complex for apprehending a single object is present, there would necessarily arise knowledge regarding all objects. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Vāta... (wind, etc.).

Due to the obstruction of the movement of Vāta caused by the combination of substances that are devoid of the essence of Vāta and Pitta, and due to the vitiation of the tissues (dhātus) of Rasa and Rakta, the skin becomes white-haired (prematurely), which is the cause of the disease of paleness (pāṇḍuroga). || 32 ||

The meaning of this is as follows: diseases arising from the provocation of *vāta* and *pitta* are produced by the processing of substances that have lost their natural flavor (*rasavirasadravyasaṃskāra*). Consequently, by obstructing the movement of the vital air (*pavana*), they vitiate the *rasa* and *asṛk* tissues; where greying of the skin (*tvakpālitya*) is observed there, one should recognize the diagnostic cause (*nidāna*) of *pāṇḍuroga*. This is the meaning: that very condition is *pāṇḍuroga*. Now, an objection may be raised: "From the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the provocation of *vāta* and *pitta*, the provocation of *vāta* arises; from the causal complex for the provocation of *pitta*, the disease of *pitta* arises. How then can greying of the skin be an indicator of *pāṇḍuroga*? To address this dissatisfaction, he says: "In the heart" (*hṛd*).

When the essence of wind, bile, and poison resides in the heart, it withers the lotus-feet; due to the obstruction of the flow of nectar caused by the union of the thirty-four channels that awaken the [subtle] letters, diseases born of the wind (vāta) increase. || 33 ||

The meaning is as follows: due to the obstruction of the flow of nectar through the channels of the veins that nourish the lotus-feet [of the vital centers]—an obstruction caused by the movement of wind pervading the *āmāśaya* (stomach) arising from the consumption of substances with deficient or contrary tastes—the essence of *āma*, *pitta*, and poison obstructs the flow of nectar. This results in *pāṇḍuroga* (jaundice/anemia) produced by a disorder of *vāta*. The essence of *āma* and *pitta* situated in the heart becomes the indirect cause (*paraṃparāhetu*) of this condition. That very same factor also becomes the cause of *vātodara* (wind-belly/ascites), and it also serves as the indirect cause of *vātapittaja-pāṇḍuroga* (jaundice caused by *vāta* and *pitta*), as well as the cause of *vātāmaya* (wind-born diseases) produced by *anila* (wind).

For this very reason, it has been established that the occasion for the discussion of anemia (*pāṇḍu*), edema (*śopha*), and erysipelas (*visarpa*) follows immediately after the description of abdominal diseases (*udarāmaya*). This is because the impure blood, bile, chyle, and toxic substances that serve as the causes of these aforementioned diseases are one and the same. The perception of various effects arising from a single cause occurs due to differences in limiting conditions (*upādhi*). Even though gold is a single substance, the effects produced by it are perceived as manifold according to their respective forms, since a multiplicity of causal adjuncts is observed therein.

One might object: since such cognitions as "this is a wind-type anemia (vāta-pāṇḍuroga)," "this is a bile-type anemia (pitta-pāṇḍuroga)," and "this is a phlegm-type anemia (kapha-pāṇḍuroga)" exist, the underlying causes that produce those effects must indeed be the *doṣas* themselves; for since substances in the form of undigested bile (*āmapiṭṭa*) or poison produced by unwholesome tastes (*virasa*) generate those tastes, the *doṣas*—which are the respective producers of those conditions—are the very causes of the diseases of anemia, edema, and erysipelas (*visarpa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Amṛta... [and so forth].

It is the devourer of the essence of wind, bile, and poison, residing within the six vessels of the heart—the openings that awaken the unmanifest and sustain the sprout of the flowing stream of nectar; it is the cause of the provocation of the vital wind (pavana). || 34 ||

The meaning is as follows: the six hollow internal channels (sirās) serve as the cause for filling with nectar those very lotuses which produce effects that bring about the cognition of their respective letters, by means of the inhalation and exhalation winds capable of bringing down the nectar situated in the head-lotus; these channels act as the basins (ālavālas) for those lotuses.

[Objection: Surely, the cause of the disease produced by the obstruction of the flow of nectar moving through the channels must be the essence of undigested bile (āmapittaviṣasāra), because it has as its cause the disease born from the latent impression (saṃskāra) of contact with those channels; for whatever is not thus is not thus, like a jar. Since this would lead to the undesirable conclusion that the essence of undigested bile alone is the cause, [the author], expressing dissatisfaction, says: "In the channels" (sire).

When the wind moving through the channels of the vessels follows the flesh-element (māṃsa-dhātu) located in the knees, shanks, thighs, seeds (vīja), sides, and lotuses, and obstructs the movement of the wind within the internal hollow channels that awaken the phonemes *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *e*, *o*, and *ai*, an aggravation of the wind (*anila-prakopa*) occurs. || 35 ||

Through the contact with the channels that serve as the support for the lotuses situated at the sides of the knees, calves, thighs, and seeds—whose essence consists of undigested matter (*āma*), bile (*pitta*), and nutrient fluid (*rasa*)—and through the corruption of the flesh element, there arises the tactile perception of the *i*-vowel, which obstructs the movement of the vital wind (*pavana*) and is caused by the two lotuses of the knees. Through the non-contact with the channels that perceive the *u*-vowel, there occurs an obstruction of the movement of the vital wind, caused by the two lotuses of the calves and thighs. Likewise, through the non-contact with the channels that perceive the *ṛ*-vowel, knowledge arises from those channels, resulting in the obstruction of the movement of the vital wind.

It becomes the cause for awakening a discordance (*visvara*) produced by the movement of the vital air (*pavana*) that has entered the path of the channels (*sirāmārga*). To the extent that there is a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) producing a disease, it performs the function of awakening a discordance that serves as the etiological cause (*nidānahetu*) for each respective disease. Since the effects of abdominal enlargement, jaundice, edema, erysipelas, leprosy, blood-disorders, wind-disorders, and vital-air disorders are produced by a single causal complex, the meaning is that it generates the differentiation of those diseases precisely through the differentiation of the effects of the vital air situated in those channels.

The meaning is that the etiology of each respective disease consists in the utterance of words composed of specific phonemes (*varṇa*) and accents (*svara*) located in those [channels], which serves as the cause for the diagnosis of those respective afflictions.

Surely there are many disorders of the wind (*pavana-vikāra*). For instance, there is the wind of the eyes, the wind of the ears, the wind of the head, the wind of hemiplegia (*pakṣāghāta*), the wind of the bow-like curvature (*dhanurvāta*), the wind of facial paralysis (*ardita*), the wind of abdominal tumors (*gulma*), the wind of the spleen (*plīha*), and the wind of the waist. There are also many indicators characterized by their respective symptoms. These arise from the specific variations in the movement of the wind as it circulates through the channels (*sirā*), manifesting as various disorders located in their respective parts of the body.

Since it is illogical to think that the wind (*pavana*), being one and the same, becomes designated by various names, causes afflictions to specific limbs, and acts as a destroyer of life merely due to the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) residing in those respective parts, he says "that" (*tat*):

"The different types of wind disorders arise from the distinctions of the limiting adjuncts which serve as the bases for the different types of provocation of the wind moving through the channels of those [limbs]. The remedy is a substance that is antagonistic to undigested matter (*āma*), bile (*pitta*), poison (*viṣa*), and morbid humors (*rasa*). (36)

The meaning of the term *tat* refers to diseases arising from the loss of potency in undigested matter (*āma*), bile (*pitta*), and chyle (*rasa*). When a disorder of the vital air (*anila-vikāra*) occurs within the channels of the openings of those vessels, it causes a contact with the vessels that convey the letter *u*, due to the diversity of the movement of the wind following its various causes; this results in the obstruction of the flow of the wind and is the cause of swelling in the lotus-like region of the waist. Similarly, contact with the pathways of the vessels that convey the letter *e* results in the obstruction of the flow of the wind and is the cause of swelling in the lotus-like region of the generative organ (*bīja*).

The obstruction of the movement of the wind (vāyu) within the channels of the veins that manifest its specific color is the cause of swelling in its side; it has undigested matter (āma), bile (pitta), and the essence of the nutrient fluid (rasa) as its seed, which is the cause of the swelling in the side. This is because it produces the movement of the wind within the channels of the veins that manifest that specific color. That which is not so is not so, just like a jar.

Thus, by inference: the movement of the vital air (pavana) within the specific channels and cavities of the veins that serve as the substrata for those respective lotuses—which is the cause for the presiding of the vowels—is the indicator of the cognition of words consisting of phonemes distinguished by beautiful tones; because it is the cause for the awakening of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) brought about by the external air through the operation of the palate and lips via cognition, desire, and effort. For what is not thus is not thus, like a jar. Furthermore, the cognition of the causes of various diseases is caused by the cognition of words consisting of phonemes dependent on those respective veins; because it is produced by a causal complex that has no other cause than [the state of] non-deficiency. For what is not thus is not thus, like a jar.

The lotus that serves as the substratum for phonemes—which awakens the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the activity of the palate and lips arising from the drawing in of external air—is the cause of the awakening of sound through the provocation of air (*pavana*) resulting from the consumption of unwholesome substances. This is because it is a substance that makes known the cognition characterized by the provocation of air, and its essence consists of undigested matter (*āma*) and bile (*pitta*). From contact with whichever vessels (*sirā*), diseases are produced in those respective limbs. The totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) that generates all wind-related diseases is the essence of *āma* and *pitta*, because its nature consists in the contact with the vessels attached to those respective limbs.

Just as a single lump of clay is the cause of various forms of pots, so too, due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) produced by the bodily constituents, it is designated as "ear-wind disease," "eye-wind disease," or "head-wind disease," even though it is like space (*ākāśa*).

Now, it cannot be said that undigested matter (*āma*) and *pitta* are the sole cause of abdominal enlargement, jaundice, edema, erysipelas, leprosy, and diseases of the wind (*vāta*), because a difference in effects is observed through their respective distinct names. Therefore, it must necessarily be understood that there is a difference in the causes. One should not say that there is a difference [between them] merely because they are like "pot" (*ghaṭa*) and "jar" (*kalaśa*); for all of those can be known as possessing the nature of a pot (*ghaṭatva*)—namely, the state of having "pot-ness" as its qualifier—insofar as they possess the form of a broad-based, bulbous belly, such that one can recognize "this is a pot."

It should not be argued that the same will apply here as well—that one can know "this is jaundice" or "this is edema" by way of having a cognition qualified by the property of being a disease (*rogatva*) within the locus of being a disease; for while those individual modifications of grapes (*mṛdvikāra*) possess the utility of fetching water, and while there is a cognition of the difference between individual jars (*pṛthubudhnodara*) of that shape, the single uniformity of the shape *pṛthubudhnodara* is nonetheless observed. Thus, even by means of the example, it is not experienced as mere cognition of non-difference.

If it is argued that here too, just as in that case, the experience of knowing the distinctions in treatment based on the distinctions in the forms of the results is observed, we say: no. For even here, there is an absence of difference in the effect (*kārya*). To explain: in the aforementioned diseases, the essence of undigested matter (*āmapiṭtasāra*) is the sole cause.

How can the experience of various distinct names [for diseases] based on their respective different treatments be denied? To this we reply: the essence of undigested matter (*āma-pitta-rasa-sāra*) is the sole cause of abdominal enlargement, jaundice, edema, erysipelas, leprosy, gout, and disorders of wind (*vāta-vikāra*). It is that very same thing which produces these effects, because it is a substance that causes the obstruction of the movement of the vital air (*pavana*) within the channels of the vessels (*sirā-mārga*). This obstruction of the movement of that vital air is caused by this very disease.

In certain variations of its manifestation, that same disorder causes the whitening of the skin by vitiating the lymph-chyle and the blood; it is then perceived as having the mere difference of being designated by the term "pāṇḍuroga" (jaundice). When, however, due to a specific connection with those vessels, it obstructs the movement of the wind (vāyu) and dries up the muscle tissue (māṃsa-dhātu), while other muscle tissues become enlarged, it is designated by the term "śobharoga."

When that which obstructs its movement becomes a corrupter of the fat-element (*medas-dhātu*), there arises the knowledge that it is the disease of "wind-spreading" (*pavana-visarpa*) because of the swelling in the form of external eruptions; that essence of undigested matter (*āma-sāra*), having corrupted the fat-elements and enveloped the muscle-element (*māṃsa-dhātu*) situated outside them, enters the skin-element (*tvak-dhātu*) and spreads outward, whereby it becomes leprosy (*kuṣṭha*).

As long as the vessels supporting the feet (*pavanādhāraka-sirā*) are seized by the essence of undigested matter, bile, and chyle (*āma-pitta-rasa-sāra*), they produce the discoloration of those respective vessels that causes the functional transformation of the lotuses [of the feet]; thus they are called *kuṣṭha*, because they produce a vile distortion of the limbs. The vessels supporting the lotuses of the feet, having reached the heart and being joined with the refinement of the essence of the chyle, bile, and undigested matter, discharge their toxic essence. Having filled those lotuses, it flows out from the toes of the feet; the meaning is that the branches [the fingers and toes] become withered.

Now, one might object: "Since diseases are caused by indigestion (ajīrṇa) arising from the presence of flavors (rasa) or the absence of flavors (virasa), and specifically because they are caused by the toxic essence (sāra) of undigested bile (pitta) residing in the lotuses that support the vessels within the fat, bone, and marrow tissues—this being established by the means of valid cognition known as negative inference (vyatirekyanumāna)—therefore, the substances used for fasting and its associated applications must be the very agents that remove those diseases, as they possess the property of being substances that remove diseases through a causal complex distinct from the complex that produced the indigestion. To this, he explains the collection of aphorisms from the Āyurveda: [The text continues with the explanation of the sūtras.]

That which arises from the unwholesome taste caused by the provocation of *pavana* (vāyu) becomes localized in the regions where the accumulation of *rasa*, blood, and flesh occurs. Due to an excess of sweet, sour, and salty tastes, when indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) occurs, the provocation of *pavana* arises. By virtue of the connection with the vessels (*sirā*) that support the lotuses which serve as the substratum for these letters (*varṇa*), the diseases of *pavana* increase. When the desire that produces them is dried up, they cease.

When there is an increase of *āma* due to indigestion from the consumption of unpalatable food, a disorder of *pavana* (vāta) arises through the contact with the channels (*sirā*) located in the *rasa*, blood, and muscle tissues. This is the essence of *āma-pitta*. Having entered the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and then the heart-lotus, like the spreading of poison, it corrupts the elements (*dhātu*) by contacting the channels within them as far as the cause of the disease extends. Once the elements—*rasa*, blood, muscle, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—are corrupted, the diseases of jaundice (*pāṇḍu*), edema (*śopha*), and erysipelas (*visarpa*) gradually increase.

When there is a transformation of the fat element (*medodhātu*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*) certainly arises. The meaning is this: that essence of undigested matter and bile (*āmapittasāra*), having corrupted the elements of lymph, blood, and flesh, manifests externally due to its presence within the fat element; this very manifestation is the cause of the disease of leprosy.

[Objection: Surely, due to the excess of the three *sāras*, there are many diseases produced by *āmaja* (undigested matter), whereas diseases born of *ajīrṇa* (indigestion) are numerous. Since a difference in their effects is observed, a difference in their causes must be stated. [Response: This can be said in that case because the *sāra* of *āma* and *pitta* is of one form, and because the action of corrupting the *dhātus* is the same for swellings (*śopha*), anemia (*pāṇḍu*), and erysipelas (*visarpa*). However, keeping in mind that the effect of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*)—which is distinct from those effects—is different, he describes the cause for the onset of leprosy with the words "from the previous" (*pūrvasmāt*). It appears twice as broad as the previous one. (37)

A twofold increase in thickness is perceived compared to the preceding elements. Furthermore, because it consists of the nature of flowing fluids following the arrangement of the fibers (tattus), its breadth appears through the dilation of the vessels (sirā). As long as the essence of undigested matter (āma) and bile (pitta) comes into contact with the vessels, that specific contact with the vessels becomes the cause of those respective diseases. This being so, a diversity of effects is perceived due to the diversity of their causes.

The state of possessing variegated forms that follow the forms inherent in the threads, up to the variegation that conforms to the forms inherent in the threads, produces the variegation of the cloth generated therefrom; for the qualities of the cause indeed initiate the qualities of the effect. As long as there is contact with the veins (*sirā*), so long does it produce a disorder located in the lotuses supported by those veins, because—given that it has the causality of producing effects other than those [other] diseases—it has that [vein-contact] as its cause; for what is not thus, is not thus.

It is indicated that the veins, when characterized by a specific conjunction of *āma*, *pitta*, form, and poison, generate various types of effects, such as jaundice (*pāṇḍu*), *śobha*, erysipelas (*visarpa*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and blood-wind disorders (*raktavātāmaya*).

The meaning is that even though the essence of undigested bile (*āmapitta*) is one, the predominance of the substance that produces it serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for its causal capacity.

Now, when the wind (*pavana*) pervading the entire body becomes provoked, the drying up of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) suitable for its movement occurs; because it is a substance possessing the quality of dryness (*rūkṣa*) which performs the single function of drying, the state of being a performer of the action of drying the constituents—characterized by infinite delimiting factors—is established from the very beginning.
Regarding this, it is said: "Wind is dry, light, cold, rough, subtle, and mobile."

Therefore, keeping in mind the intention that the drying up of all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) cannot be accomplished merely by a disturbance of the wind (*pavana*), because the essence of the undigested matter (*āma*), bile (*pitta*), and nutrient-fluid (*rasa*) are situated in only one part [of the body], he explains the disturbance of the wind with the verse beginning "three thousand":
"Caused by three thousand channels, it becomes sweet and burns. (38)

If the collection of phonemes produced by the wind situated in the lotus of the bodily element-region (*dhātupradeśa*) were to express a discordant sound (*visvara*), then, because it would be the cause of the effect of a wind-disorder arising from the consumption of sweet substances that provoke the wind, the collection of phonemes produced by the wind situated in the lotus of the bodily element-region—possessing the tastes of sweet, sour, and salty—would, if it expressed a discordant sound, [result in] the consumption of sweet substances that provoke the wind.

Those vessels, numbering three thousand, which support the lotus-feet and function to preserve the prior absence of wind-disease (vāta), exist within the body; what need is there to mention that substance which obstructs the respective movements of those vessels that serve as the substratum for the flow of wind? That [substance] becomes a cause for the provocation of that wind. It does not, however, deplete the bodily constituents (dhātus); rather, the meaning is that it results in pain and the manifestation of disease.

Now, it may be objected that while the sweet taste (*madhurasa*) in all substances generally pacifies the provocation of *pavana* (wind), the sweet taste residing in the vegetable kingdom (*sthāvarajāti*) actually causes the provocation of *pavana*, whereas a substance possessing the sweet taste residing in the animal kingdom (*jaṅgamādi*) removes the provocation of *pavana*. Nevertheless, both are supreme nourishers of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Keeping in mind the intention that the sweet taste of vegetables causes disorders of the *rasa* and *asṛk* (blood) constituents, while the sweet taste of animals nourishes all the constituents, [the author] establishes the cause for the generation of progeny, beginning with the word "progeny" (*prajā*).
It becomes the cause for the production of wisdom. || 39 ||

The essence of the flesh of mobile beings becomes a modification of milk (*payovikāra*). Even though it lacks the essence of other [mobile] species of the same genus, it is indeed a nourishing, sweet-tasting nutrient for all bodies. That sweet-tasting essence causes the generation of progeny, because it is a substance that carries the transformation of the seminal element (*retodhātu*). For the sky-dwellers (*khecarāḥ*), the sweet-tasting essence of egg-born creatures removes the provocation of wind (*pavana*). The meaning is that those produced from modifications of milk originating in the bodies of land-dwellers remove wind and nourish the white element (*śukladhātu*).

Because it is impossible to state that the sweet tastes residing in immobile substances—such as those produced from sugarcane stalks and the like—nourish all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), since they consist of the essence of immobile matter, and because there is a sense of incongruity in saying that the sweet taste residing therein is heavy, he says: "In the case of sweet [tastes]...
From the consumption of sweet taste, the blood constituent (*rakta-dhātu*) arises. (40)

The consumption of sweet flavors residing in stationary beings (sthāvara) increases the tissues of plasma and blood (rasa and asṛk) in mobile bodies, because it is a substance produced from materials such as stalks of sugarcane that possess flavor. The meaning is that the sweet flavor residing in stationary beings is an increaser of the tissues of plasma and blood. He states the purpose of the sour flavor residing in stationary beings: "sour" (āmla).
The consumption of sour flavor provides the tissue of flesh (māṃsa-dhātu). || 41 ||
He states the purpose of the salty taste among the immobile [tastes]: "The salty taste," etc.
The salty taste bestows the fat constituent (medas-dhātu). || 42 ||

The meaning is that the salty taste (*lavaṇarasa*) of stationary beings (*sthāvara*) increases the fat tissue (*medodhātu*) in mobile bodies (*jaṅgamaśarīra*). Now, one might object: "It is impossible to state a distinction such as 'the sweet taste (*svādurasa*) of stationary beings aggravates the wind humor (*pavana*), whereas the sweet taste of mobile bodies alleviates the aggravation of the wind. For just as the bestowal of qualities (*guṇapradāna*) for the six tastes can only be stated with respect to distinct substances, the bestowal of qualities for the six tastes of stationary beings would necessarily result in a distinction based on their respective species. Anticipating this objection, he says: "First... (*ādyeti*).
The essence of the first element has its cause in the lotus of the shank. || 43 ||

The ten-petalled lotus situated within the fat-tissue (*medas-dhātu*) and located in the region of the throat is increased by bitter taste (*tikta-rasa*). The nectar (*amṛta*) arriving via the thousand channels is its nourisher. Regarding the term "first" (*ādya*): it refers to a substance possessing sweet taste (*svādu-rasa*). Regarding the term "two": how can it be known that the essence of the qualities of a substance produced from the union of earth and water—a substance possessing sweet taste—is itself the counteragent? The sweet taste that nourishes the white tissue (*śukla-dhātu*) becomes a corrupter of the blood-tissue (*asṛg-dhātu*) when it is of the first two types of taste.
The sweet taste residing in mobile substances nourishes all the tissues.

Likewise, cow’s milk and cow’s ghee—being modifications of the *rasa* and *asṛk* tissues, nourishing those very tissues and being non-contrary to them—serve as the support for the letters presiding over the *jaṅghā-padma* (ankle-lotus) which rests upon the *pāda-padma* (foot-lotus). Because that sweet-tasting substance (*svādurasadravya*) nourishes the entire body and possesses a sweet taste that subdues the *anila* (vāyu), it brings about a favorable state (*sugati*). Thus, having become the support for those respective lotuses and the letters presiding over them, it draws the nectar located in the *sahasrāra-padma* through the thousand channels (*sahasrasirā*) and [distributes it].

Having flooded the lotuses that serve as the supports for their respective phonemes (*varṇa*) by means of the knowledge that experiences those respective phonemes, the wind becomes the nourisher of the vowel *ai*. The meaning is as follows: the bitter taste (*tiktarasa*), having increased the Pitta humor, takes its own support—the ten-petaled lotus situated below the navel—and, having flooded the ten-petaled lotus of the Svādhiṣṭhāna which has been brought there by the wind with nectar (*amṛta*), it reaches the region of the ears of the consonants beginning with *ha*; thus, the bitter taste becomes the nourisher of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) of flesh and fat.

Now, it may be asked: since there are seven notes (*svara*), how is it that these notes are heard as they spread from the internal channels of the hollow organs to the region of the ear? Starting from the lotus of the feet up to the seed-vessel (*bīja*) at the side of the navel is the locus of the wind (*pavana*); for this very reason, it performs the action characterized by movement. Through the two shanks and the two feet, there occur the departure and arrival [of breath] with the thought "I am Dharma. Thus, it is the wind alone that effects the various movements of coming and going, which consist of the nature of motion.

He proceeds by means of that very [method]; for, beginning from the lotus at the side of the seed-syllable up to the hand-lotus, each of the five groups of consonants—ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and pa—is presided over by its respective lotus.

The air situated within the hollows of the channels, having entered the lotuses of one’s own ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), abides there for the purpose of pronouncing the conjunctions of various phonemes (*varṇa*), for the purpose of pronouncing well-formed words (*supada*), for the purpose of pronouncing sentences consisting of collections of such words, and for the purpose of making known the intended meaning. This is because it is impossible to make oneself known to another apart from the employment of words and sentences. Therefore, the consonants (*hal*) and others, together with the vowels (*aj*), are able to communicate their intended meaning to others.
For this very reason, it was established at the very outset by the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) in the science of grammar (*śabdaśāstra*): [text continues]

The entire meaning of these three sūtras—"vṛddhir ādaic," "adeṅ guṇaḥ," and "iko guṇavṛddhī"—is elaborated upon in the Mahābhāṣya. Therein, it is established that consonants and other [sounds] become the causes of grammatical operations (kāryakāraka) together with vowels (aj).

The wind, residing in the respective vessels (sirās) that carry the groups of five letters situated within the lotuses of the various regions of the body—such as the gall-bladder (pitta), the ego-sense (abhimāna), and the stomach (kukṣi)—reaches the ears in order to awaken the meanings of the phonemes as established by the scriptures, which are of the nature of their respective presiding deities and possess the color of clarified butter (ājya). Accompanied by its own resonance, it produces sounds arising from the movement of the humors (doṣas) located in the vessels, beginning with the consonants (hal). Thus, he states that the wind alone conveys the phonemes situated in the lotuses of the regions of bile (pitta): "Tikta... [and so forth].

The ten-petaled lotus situated in the region of the waist, located within the fat tissue (*medas-dhātu*), is nourished by the nectar (*amṛta*) that has arrived via a thousand channels (*sahasra-sirā*). That nectar, produced there from the site of *kapha* where bitter taste (*tikta-rasa*) predominates, is the sustainer of it. The obstruction of the wind (*pavana*) arriving through the path of *piṅgalā* is a good medicine and a perfect nourisher. || 44 ||

The qualities produced by the processing of consuming bitter-tasting substances lead, through the influence of diseases caused by consuming various opposing tastes, to the hearing of sentences composed of clusters of words consisting of phonemes articulated by healthy individuals; this [hearing] becomes the cause for the discernment of the specific diseases presiding over those respective words.

The meaning is as follows: having recognized the form of the phonemes produced by the utterance of deficient phonemes—which arises from a causal complex located in various lotuses that causes diseases dependent upon the operation of the palate and lips—one understands that for a phlegm disease caused by an excess of sweet and sour substances (which produce phlegm), the nectar that serves as its remedy is the excellent medicine produced by the obstruction of the wind coming through the *piṅgalā* channel.

He says "outside" (bahiḥ) to show that even in the absence of a substance that would counteract a disease caused by the utterance of low-sounding syllables, the expulsion of air from outside and its filling [into the body] serves as the remedy:
"One should expel the air from outside; one should fill that very same [air back in]. (45)
He states the fruit of this: "Therefore"—that is, from that [practice], one becomes long-lived. || 46 ||

But surely all this is not tenable when taken together. When the causal complex consisting of the movement of the palate, lips, and other organs is present, the desired object becomes the referent of the sentence through the hearing of the sentence produced by sounds reaching the region of the ear. It is not the case that it is made known solely by the channels of the phonemes residing in that lotus [of the heart], for that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Indeed, the scripture itself provides the authoritative proof here: "What one meditates upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech; that one performs with action."

Furthermore, since there exist Vārttika statements such as, "The throat is the place of articulation for *a*, *ku*, *ha*, and the *visarjanīya*; the palate for *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa*; the lips for *u*, *pu*, and the *upadhmānīya*; the head for *ṛ*, *ṭu*, *ra*, and *ṣa*; and the teeth for *lṛ*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa*," [one might object that] because those specific channels lack the necessary causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) to bring the phonemes residing in their respective lotuses to the region of the ear, [the author], expressing dissatisfaction with this, says: "By the moon... (verse 47). The lotus impelled by the wind belonging to a digit of the Moon closes; it blossoms due to the wind belonging to a digit of the Sun.

When the totality of the activity of the palate and lips is present, the *candrakalā* (the lunar digit) closes like a bud due to the wind arising from the sound of the moon. Keeping all this in mind—that the very closing of that lotus is the cause for entering the path of the lower vessels (*dharasirā*) within the porous [channels] by means of the wind produced by the totality of the activity of the palate and lips that generates those phonemes, in order to grasp the phonemes presiding over those respective lotuses—it follows that the various diseases have their origins in the alteration of the voice from its original state.

The proof for the statement that [the lotus] is the cause for the cognition of diseases presided over by that [lotus] is precisely the experience of the knowledge arising from hearing the pronunciation of letters. When asked what kind of knowledge that is, one would have to point to the experience itself; it cannot be explained [conceptually]. When a difficult pronunciation is made, because [the letter] *ka* resides in the location adjacent to the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the wind generated by its activity travels through the path of its channel, seizes the letter *ka*, and carries it to the region of the ear. At that time, the word "ka" is produced here.

Having entered the cavity of the ear, it becomes manifest. The primary place of origin for those phonemes (*varṇas*) is the throat itself. Phonemes such as *i*, *cu*, *ya*, and *śa* also become manifest by reaching the region of the palate. Phonemes such as *ḷ*, *tu*, *la*, and *sa* also become manifest by reaching the region of the teeth; thus, the meaning is that even those belonging to their respective classes [of sounds] become manifest through this sequential process. In this way, having taken the aid of the solar digit (*sūryakalā*), she causes the various lotuses to blossom and generates the phonemes.

In this way, the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*) and the digit of the sun (*sūryakalā*) effect the closing and opening of their respective lotuses. Having fixed in the mind that a word uttered as possessing a certain meaning becomes the object [of cognition] for exactly that much of an intended meaning—one knows it to such an extent and desires it to that extent—it performs the activity of the palate and lips. Consequently, the air, having arisen and reached the wind residing in the corresponding channels, aims at the collection of phonemes (*varṇasamūha*) which constitute the word (*pada*) expressing that desired meaning; thus, by means of the totality of the activity of the palate and lips, sound is indeed produced. This is the sense.

[Objection: But surely, when sound accompanied by air is heard due to the contact of a drum and a stick, that air becomes the conveyor of the sound even without the operation of veins (*sirā*) and so forth; could it not be the same in this case as well? [Reply: No. For even that [drum] has a body; being enveloped by a leather casing and existing within the space, it is designated as the "body of the drum. How then could the production of sound occur there without the operation of the air moving through the veins? It is exactly like that that the word consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) is heard.

In that case, as for how it is experienced that "the sound of a drum has arisen," only a sound consisting of such a resonance (dhvani) is heard. That [sound] is not composed of articulated phonemes (varṇa), because its occurrence would be impossible without the activity of the vocal organs and so forth presided over by consciousness. Since this causal complex consists of resonant sound (dhvanimat-śabda), there is no intentionality directed toward [articulated phonemes] therein.

If it is objected: "Since the auditory faculty is presided over by consciousness and the activity of the palate and lips is the same [in both cases], how could there be a sound consisting of phonemes [in animals]?"—[we reply: Just as with humans, because animals such as cattle lack a continuous throat, a sound consisting of phonemes is not heard, nor is there an understanding of meaning; yet this activity exists for their benefit. In this case, the very absence of a continuous throat is the determining factor. Therefore, grass and the like become their food.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the throat being unobstructed (*aviralakaṇṭhatva*) alone is the cause for the production of sound consisting of phonemes (*varṇātmaka-śabda*)? If so, since the state of having an unobstructed throat exists even for sky-dwellers (*khecarāḥ*), why is there no production of sound consisting of phonemes in their case? For the quality of having an unobstructed throat is common to sky-dwellers just as it is to humans. Why, then, is sound consisting of phonemes not perceived from them? Only some indistinct sounds are heard."

Even though humans lack knowledge of those [non-human] objects, members of those respective species possess knowledge regarding the sounds uttered by them; otherwise, they would not even engage in purposeful activity. Since such activity would otherwise be inexplicable, knowledge regarding the sounds is postulated.

Letters consist of sounds uttered by creatures belonging to various species with unimpeded throats, because the engagement [of creatures] based on the cognition of sounds uttered by them regarding their respective species is observed, just like the object of engagement following the cognition of a sound uttered by me. Therefore, since the engagement of creatures distinguished by various species—following the experience of cognition regarding objects prescribed by the rules for those respective species—is observed, keeping this intention in mind, he says: "Iḍā.
It flows through both the iḍā and piṅgalā [nāḍīs]. (48)

The sounds uttered by beings distinguished by their species, such as those of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* breaths, consist of phonemes (*varṇa*). This is because they possess the nature of sound produced from the sequence of the closing and opening [of the petals] of the respective lotuses presided over by the digits (*kalā*) of the Moon and the Sun. It is not so for animals and the like, because they consist of both vowels and consonants at once. For this very reason, an animal eats uncooked food such as grass, because it consists of both the two winds and the two fires. The same applies to the sky-dwellers (*khecarāḥ*).

Even for aquatic creatures, there is the consumption of uncooked food; through the winds moving within the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels, the digestive bile (*pācaka-pitta*) flows forth. For humans and other species, according to the distinction of the *yugas*, sounds uttered by birds, animals, and others become composed of phonemes (*varṇātmaka*) once they reach the presiding deities of those respective colors associated with the moon and sun, as it is explained in the Purāṇas and other texts. At the beginning of other *yugas*, because the five vital airs (*prāṇa*, etc. reside within the bones, at that time sounds become composed of phonemes.

This can be stated only because all bodies possess a self (*sātmakatva*). By means of the inferential proof (*anumāna*)—"A living body possesses a self because it has breath and so forth"—it follows that whatever bodies possess a self, all of them necessarily possess breath. The vital airs (*prāṇa*) and other winds present in bodies seized by the time of the Kali age reside within the constituents (*dhātu*) of lymph and blood (*rasa* and *asṛj*).
