Conversely, the vital airs and other winds residing in bodies seized by the times of other ages reside in the bones.
In the statement "Bodies seized by the time of this age are characterized by unrighteousness (*adharma*)," the property of being unrighteous (*adharmatva*) is the limiting condition (*upādhi*).

[Objection: But surely, since all bodies possess breath and so forth by virtue of being delimited as "body," and since the delimiting factor of "body-ness" exists even in stationary objects (plants), it would follow that they too have the capacity for vocal utterance; anticipating this objection, he says—"the six.
[This refers to] the Mūlādhāra, which is the primary source of the six lotuses. || 49 ||

Those whose bodies are presided over by the six lotuses possess the capacity even for the utterance of speech; such is not the case for stationary beings (*sthāvara*), because the capacity to nourish—possessing the essence of nectar located in the head-lotus—is the defining characteristic of mobile bodies. Since they possess a head that is presided over by the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-padma*), the state of possessing the nectar in the head-lotus serves to nourish the body. Therefore, those stationary bodies are trees.

Therefore, for them, the *mūlādhāra* lotus does not consist of six petals. Although the property of being delimited by a body is common to all, the meaning is that only those bodies whose *mūlādhāra* lotus consists of six petals possess the capacity for the utterance of speech.

But is it not the case that even for stationary beings (sthāvara), the root-support lotus (*mūlādhāra-padma*) consists of ten petals and is composed of bitter and pungent tastes; that very same [lotus], when situated in the head-lotus, consists of the elements of bone, flesh, and fat? Furthermore, the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-padma*) appears in the respective heads of humans, and for stationary beings as well, the tip of the branch is that very same [lotus], since the tips of the branches proceed from the nature of the head and the root of the crest.
Because the characteristic of being the root-support—the origin of the six lotuses—is present in stationary beings as well, [the author] states "bitter," etc., due to this lack of finality.
The ten-petaled lotus, which serves as the support for fat and marrow and receives the bitter and pungent tastes, is sprinkled there with nectar that has arrived via a thousand channels. || 50 ||

Branches, sprouts, and so forth arise with a predominance of bitter or pungent tastes. At the time of the manifestation of a sprout, either a bitter taste or a pungent taste appears as its appropriate essence (*sāra*), because that very sprout serves as the support for fat (*medas*) and marrow (*majjā*). Thus, the sprout and so on are themselves the ten-petaled lotus (*daśadala-padma*), and they also constitute the root-support (*mūlādhāra*), since both are observed at times to be the sowers of seeds; this is the meaning.

Now, one might object that because the *kuṇḍalinī* power is absent in trees as it is in humans, and because they lack inhalation and exhalation following the paths of *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, the sprinkling of nectar (*amṛta*) upon the body of a tree is impossible due to those very factors. Anticipating this dissatisfaction, he says: "The *iḍā*... [etc.
It sprinkles the nectar located in the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*. (51)

The very movement of their leaves constitutes the inhalation and exhalation of the trees. The tip of the branch consists of a ten-petalled lotus because it is beautiful, because it is composed of exquisite loveliness, and because its nature is the experience of the knowledge of pleasure derived from the objects of the sense of sight. That ten-petalled lotus situated at the tip of the branch has the objects of the sense of sight as its domain, because its essential form is the object of the experience of pleasure. The meaning is that for the trees, that lotus alone is the nourisher.

Now, as for what was said—that the tips of the branches are beautiful, lovely, and delicate because they serve as the cause for the experience of pleasure when they become objects of visual perception—that is to be reconsidered; for since all things are indeed objects of visual perception, it is impossible to say that all things are objects of the experience of pleasure. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of all objects" (sarvārthānām). [The verse continues:
"That which is the means of accomplishing all happiness for all objects that serve as causes. (52)

Regarding the phrase "of all objects": it has been stated that the section beginning with "He offers the *samidh* oblations; he thereby secures spring among the seasons. He offers the *tanūnapāt* oblation" possesses the quality of teaching the subject of *dharma*, because it serves as the cause for the performance of sacrifices that accomplish the attainment of heaven.

Because it establishes the meaning regarding the fruit in the form of the initial stage of the realized meaning (*phalitārtha*); because it is a substance that brings about the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) in the form of the meanings of words (*padārtha*); because it is the cause of flowers and fruits that result in the thought, "This is a human goal"; because it is the object of desire itself; and because it serves as the cause for the third human goal [pleasure], [this work is for] the best of Brahmins—a scholar who knows all the scriptures, knows the Dharma, possesses knowledge of manual skill and the like, is always inclined toward helping others, and [attains his goal] through the knowledge of the meaning of Āyurveda.

Since the physician is the cause for attaining liberation, medical treatment becomes a cause for liberation. Scripture alone is the authority that establishes this. For instance: "The horse-fig tree is your seat; the leaf is your dwelling made ready. You shall indeed be sharers of cattle, if you save the man."
When I, seeking strength, take these plants in my hand,
the self of the wasting disease perishes, as if before the seizer of life.
"He among whom the medicinal herbs have gathered like kings in assembly—
he the Brahmin is called a physician, the dispeller of Rakshasas and the remover of disease."

The meaning is that since the *Ṛgveda* 10.97 exists as scripture, and because it contains the purpose for attaining liberation specifically through the learned Brahmin (*vipra*) who has been treated [medically], it is possible to state that the tips of its branches (*tacchākhāgrāṇām*) bring about the fourfold aims of human life (*caturvidhapuruṣārtha*). [As it is said: "The head of the sacrifice was cut off."

The gods said to the two Aśvins, "You two are physicians; restore this head of the sacrifice. The purport of this section is that the wielding of weapons is unbecoming for Brāhmaṇas. This medical treatment involving weapons is prohibited as long as it is unsuitable for Brāhmaṇas, being forbidden within the specific category of medical treatments. Therefore, the medical treatment involving weapons must not be performed [by them]; it should be caused to be performed by Śūdras alone.

Even in that case, having understood the distinctions of the channels and so forth as propounded in those respective scriptures, the one who is the instructor of the rule that "it must be caused to be performed by Śūdras alone" is himself the performer. The very same Śruti is the authority for this as well, because of the existence of the injunction: "They distributed the medicine between those two in three parts: one third in the fire, one third in the waters, and one third in the Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, having placed a vessel of water nearby and having seated a Brāhmaṇa to the south, one should perform the healing.
Thus it is propounded in the Āgama scripture.

"May Śauri come to us with skill, like a physician for those with long-standing and acute ailments. The meaning is that medical treatment must be administered to protect those seized by calamity; for this very reason, it is said to be the accomplisher of all happiness.

[Objection: One might argue that whatever action is undertaken with the aim of pleasing the Lord serves as an aid and thus bestows all fruits. However, in this case, since these trees merely serve as medicinal substances for the purpose of medical treatment, how could they be said to bestow the fourfold goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*)? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Prakṛti... [Verse 53].
There is an identity between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.

At all times, Prakṛti and Puruṣa are the benefactors of the fruit; they become the givers of life to all beings. And so says the Śruti: "He understood that food is Brahman. For indeed, from food alone these beings are born; by food, once born, they live; into food they pass and merge. Having understood this—this very Śruti is the authority here.

Therefore, directed toward that end—namely, for the sake of pleasing the Lord, for the benefit of human goals, and for the protection of the world—those two became the bodies of the stationary (sthāvara). They cause the growth of the bodies of the moving (jaṅgama), and both of them increase. [The stationary beings consist of] those whose essence is the root, those whose essence is the pith, those whose essence is the bark, those whose essence is the bulb, those whose essence is the sap, those whose essence is the flower, those whose essence is the fruit, those whose essence is the exudation, those whose essence is milk, and those whose essence is bone or marrow; as well as those whose essence is the stalk.

All of these consist of fifteen essences (*sāra*) and possess stable bodies. The meaning is that the specific varieties of these respective essences serve as the remedies for their corresponding diseases. Now, an objection may be raised: all bodies are composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), because sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are qualities (*guṇa*) of shape and so forth, and it is impossible to establish their existence apart from those qualities; since qualities cannot exist without their possessor (*guṇin*), how can these essences function as removers of disease? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Earthen," etc. (*pārthiva*).
That in which an abundance of earthy components is perceived is the "sāraka" (essential) substance, possessing the qualities of earth. || 54 ||

Both sour taste (*āmlarasa*) and fragrance (*sugandha*) are qualities of the earth element (*pṛthivī*). Possessing fragrance (*gandhavattva*) is the defining characteristic (*avacchedakatva*) of earth. Sourness and fragrance are perceived simultaneously. That very specific part [of a plant] becomes the remedy for that specific disease. For instance, when an abundance of fragrance is perceived in flowers, it should be understood as the "essential substance" (*sāradravya*) of that flower. Now, one might object: since the *arka* tree has milk as its essential substance, that alone would not suffice for the purpose.

Its leaves ward off the wind; even the bark of its roots wards off the provocation of the humors of wind (vāta-doṣa); its flowers cure the disease of worms. Thus, three types of essence (sāra) are found in this tree. Among these, because the essence of the root and the essence of the leaf are perceived as being possessed of such potency, those two essences are to be known solely through experience.

As long as that milk is perceived by the sense organ, it is merely designated as "the essence of the leaf-juice" (patrasāra) or "the root-essence" (mūlasāra) because of its status as the substance milk used for that specific purpose; however, since it is impossible to describe it primarily as such [in its entirety], he says "one" (eka) out of this dissatisfaction:
"That which removes a single disorder is a 'single-essence' (ekasāra). (55)

Because this *arka* tree lacks distinct odors and lacks distinct tastes among its various parts, it is a remover of the provocation of wind (*pavana-prakopa*), since it is a substance possessing a bitter taste (*tikta-rasa*). This is the inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*) that must be stated. In the same way, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) must be stated. For instance: whatever substance possesses a bitter taste is a remover of the provocation of wind, because a substance possessing a sweet taste (*svādu-rasa*) which removes bile (*pitta*) is itself a substance that removes the provocation of wind. Such is the form of the pervasion.

Once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between these two has been grasped, one should not suspect that there is an asymmetrical pervasion (*viṣamavyāpti*). For whatever substance removes bile also removes the provocation of wind (*pavana*); that is, every substance that removes bile is a substance that removes the provocation of wind. This is because a substance possessing sweet taste (*svādurasa*), which removes bile, is itself a substance that removes the provocation of wind. In this manner, the pervasion can be grasped; however, it is not the case that every substance possessing bitter taste (*tiktarasa*) alone is a remover of bile.

For example, it is easy to state the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in this form: "The essence of the fruit of the poison-tree (*viṣataru*), while causing the provocation of bile (*pitta*), is a substance that counteracts the provocation of wind (*pavana*), because it is a substance possessing a bitter taste. In this case, "being a substance fit for consumption as food" is not a limiting condition (*upādhi*). A substance possessing a bitter taste that is fit for consumption as food and fit for enjoyment counteracts the provocation of bile, whereas mere bitterness alone does not.

Just as the substance that is the essence of the fruit of the poison-tree (*viṣataru*) is not a substance fit for enjoyment or consumption, so too a substance possessing a bitter taste (*tiktarasa*) is not a substance fit for enjoyment or consumption; thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in this regard. Whatever is not a substance fit for enjoyment or consumption is also not a remover of the provocation of bile (*pitta*), just like a jar (*ghaṭa*). A substance possessing a bitter taste is not a remover of the provocation of wind (*pavana*).

It should not be suspected that where the state of being a substance possessing a single taste (*ekarasa*) appears, even though there is multiplicity of essence (*aneka-sāratva*), this essence alone would be the remover of the provocation of a single humor (*doṣa*). This is because it is a substance possessing a bitter taste (*tikta-rasa*) that is distinct from substances possessing tastes other than those suitable for enjoyment (*bhoga-yogya*). Therefore, in whatever substance both the state of having a single odor (*gandha*) and the state of having a single taste appear, even if there is multiplicity of essence therein, all of that becomes the remover of the provocation of a single humor.

The meaning is that because that which appears in each respective limb possesses a single essence, that very essence pervades all limbs; therefore, it should be understood as a substance possessing that single essence.

[Objection: Is it not the case that where there is the perception of a substance exceeding the water-substance (*ab-dravya*), it is precisely in those regions of the parts where the sweet taste is tasted that the savory taste is perceived? Furthermore, in that case, an excess of the parts of the water-substance is also perceived; for there is an absence of the presence of specific parts belonging to a single essence (*sāra*). Keeping this intention in mind, he says: "The water-substance," etc.
Whatever there is that results in the perception of a savory taste produced by an excess of the parts of the water-substance, that is *sāraka* (essence-containing). (56)

It has been stated that wherever an excess of the constituent parts of the substance water (*ab-dravya*) is perceived, there alone is an excess of sweet taste (*svādu-rasa*) found; thus, the possession of sweet taste is said to be the defining characteristic (*avacchedaka*) of the substance water. This, however, is to be reconsidered. The body consists of the five elements (*pañca-bhūta-ātmaka*); among these, bodies such as trees and young girls possess an excess of the substance water. In those cases, the substance characterized by an excess of water is perceived. Its defining characteristic (*avacchedaka*) is the possession of bitter taste (*tikta-rasa*). Therefore, it causes the provocation of the wind (*pavana-prakopa*).

The essence of the fruit of the poisonous *viṣatara* tree, which possesses a bitter taste (*tiktarasa*), is a remover of the provocation of wind (*pavana*). In that case, the substance possessing an abundance of water-like properties is a remover of the provocation of wind and has a sweet taste (*svādurasa*). Bitter taste serves as its delimiting attribute (*avacchedaka*), because a substance possessing water-like properties lacks such a delimiting attribute. A sweet taste that is delimited by a substance possessing water-like properties becomes a producer of the provocation of wind; however, the sweet taste of a stalk of sugarcane, which consists of a substance possessing an abundance of water-like properties, also becomes a remover of the provocation of wind.

Thus, since there is an absence of [other] qualities in the intended meaning, it is rather a remover of the provocation of bile (*pitta*). Therefore, the intention is that the sweet taste residing in the substance water becomes a remover of the provocation of wind (*pavana*). He provides the resolution with the words "those which": "Those bodies which consist of the substance water—in each of those, there is a certain appropriate sweet taste. (57)

The intended meaning is that it acts as a pacifier of the provocation of *pavana* (wind). It should not be suspected: "Since the substance water possesses the quality of extreme coldness, it cannot be a substance that pacifies *pavana*; what then is the status of the scriptural teaching which establishes that sweet, sour, and salty tastes pacify *pavana*? [The answer is: The sweet taste inherent in ghee (*ghṛta*) pacifies the provocation of *pavana*, as do milks and likewise the qualities of oils, including the qualities of castor oil (*eraṇḍataila*).

The intended meaning is not that a naturally sweet taste produced in a body due to the absence of an excess of water-elements necessarily pacifies the provocation of *pavana* (wind). Rather, because the sweet taste residing in a stalk of sugarcane is enveloped by an excess of water-elements and constitutes an extremely cooling substance, that sweet taste is inherently *madhura* (sweet/sweetening) and therefore does not pacify the provocation of *pavana*. The intended meaning is that such a sweet taste [when not so conditioned] pacifies the provocation of *pitta* (bile).

Now, it might be argued that where there is an excess of water-substance parts, due to the extreme sweetness of the sweet taste residing in that body, the property of being water (*jalatva*)—which belongs to a substance possessing that excessive sweet taste—is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*); and consequently, the possession of cold touch (*śītasparśavattva*) must also be its delimiting factor, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) can be grasped such that "wherever there is the possession of cold touch, there is the property of being water."

How could the sweet taste residing in water characterized by cold touch be a remover of the provocation of wind (pavana)? This is because it contradicts empirical experience; for indeed, a substance possessing a sweet taste characterized by cold touch is a cause of the provocation of wind.

In order to prevent the provocation of the wind caused by that [coldness], water characterized by a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by contact with fire would be the remover of that wind-provocation. Thus, by virtue of its contact with fire, that water abandons the quality of coldness which generates wind; how then could that water become the remover of wind through its contact with fire? Therefore, wherever there is an abundance of aqueous constituents, there too the state of possessing an exceedingly cold touch is possible.

Therefore, because of the objection as to how that which possesses a sweet taste fixed in those [qualities] could possibly counteract the provocation of the wind (pavana), he says: "That" (tat). That is the excellent medicine which counteracts the wind. || 58 ||

The meaning of that term is precisely the sweet taste produced from a mobile body. That sweet taste produced therefrom is a counteragent to the provocation of the wind (*pavana*). All bodies are composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*). It is only where the perception of fragrance—an indicator of an abundance of earthy substance—is observed, that the sweet taste produced therein functions as a counteragent to the provocation of the wind. We do not speak of a sweet taste residing solely in water, because water is an insentient substance and lacks a body.

Now, it may be argued that in the injunction regarding the drinking of *uṣas* (dawn-water), the consumption of pure water is taught in the scriptures as a remover of all defects; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with those scriptural teachings. Furthermore, the entire world is incapable of living without water. By its very nature, it has been designated by the lexicographers (*naighaṇṭukas*) with the name "life" (*jīvana*).

If it is argued that what was stated—that the sweet taste residing in water pacifies the provocation of the wind (vāta)—is not acceptable, we say no; for it is appropriate that the substance of water serves as a support for the life of stationary beings (sthāvara), and thus the substance of water constitutes their very life. However, it is not so for mobile beings (jaṅgama). Even for them, it has been stated that the sweet taste residing in water—which arises from a refinement produced by contact with fire—acts to pacify the provocation of the wind.

In that regard, even in the rule concerning the drinking of morning water (*uṣaḥpāna*), it is stated that water characterized by the performance of the *haṃsodaka* rite is recommended for the practice of morning drinking. In the other case as well, regarding the quality of water characterized by the refinement produced by contact with fire (*analasaṃyoga*) as being a remover of wind, "contact with fire" is the limiting condition (*upādhi*). Wherever the state of being water characterized by the refinement produced by contact with fire appears, there the capacity to remove wind is also possible.

Because there is an invariable rule that water characterized by the quality of purity and coolness causes the provocation of wind (pavana). The sweet taste residing in water characterized by the quality of coldness is not a remover of the provocation of wind. In this regard, the scriptural statement is the authority: "Fire is the remedy for cold. The meaning is that in the injunction for its removal, contact with fire alone is the limiting condition (upādhi).

Now, is it not the case that salt-taste is produced from the substance water, because it is a substance that is a modification of water, since the salt-ocean itself is the sea? Salt is produced from that [ocean], being generated by its cooking; it is highly pleasing, characterized by a fragrant and sour taste, and it pacifies the provocation of the wind (vāta), whereas when uncooked, it does not possess those qualities.

Because it is a substance characterized by the absence of specific fragrant qualities, how can a substance that dries up the salty taste (lavaṇarasa) be a pacifier of wind (pavana), given that it is a substance that pacifies phlegm (kapha) like a pungent taste (kaṭurasa), since the salty taste is included within the category of pungent tastes? At that time, the salty taste characterized by its specific temporal state does not become a disorder of wind, because the pungent taste possesses the qualities of a fiery substance (analadravya).

Substances characterized by sweet, sour, and salty tastes are removers of the provocation of *pavana* (wind), because they are substances possessing qualities inherent in watery substances (*ab-dravya*), just like the *jambīra* fruit. Salty taste is a remover of the provocation of *pavana*, because it possesses the qualities of watery substances. However, not all water [is such], precisely because of its possession of sweet taste; for there is no production of salty substances from substances that possess sweet taste. This is because the salt ocean, like a physical body, consists of the seven constituent elements (*saptadhātu*).

But surely some trees possess multiple essences (*sāra*), since among trees of a single species there must be an abundance of various elemental constituents (*bhūtāvayava*). For example, among trees of the *śigru* species, there is the essence of the seed, the essence of the leaf, the essence of the flower, the essence of the bark of the root, and the essence of the root; these *śigru* trees possess such essences. To explain how a single tree appears to possess multiple essences in relation to the predominance of certain substances, he says: "not [merely] small" (*anala*).
That substance which, through the perception of a superior form produced by the addition of anala-substance components, possesses as much rasa as possible, is sāraṅka. || 59 ||

That substance in which the state of possessing an excess of fiery constituent parts is perceived—due to its being a substance with an excess of fiery parts—is a substance characterized by an excess of fire. Whatever substance, through the perception of an increased form, possesses as many qualities as it has and serves as a cause for the delight of the eyes, such a visually perceptible substance is *tatsāraka*.

Even though some [trees] may be unsuitable for humans, they are nonetheless beneficial for the many beings born from what is suitable for them; because they possess an abundance of fiery (analabhūta) components and an abundance of substances, it can be said that they contain manifold essence (*sāra*). Thus, their entire essence serves to pacify the provocation of the wind humor (*pavana*). Since the substance consisting of fire (*analadravyabhūta*) is more abundant than all other elements, such highly essential trees serve for the benefit of all living beings—this is the meaning.

[Objection: Surely, as many trees as there are, each is a remover of its respective disease because it possesses the nature of being a tree-substance, just like those [trees] already established [in medical tradition]. Furthermore, due to the difference in substances according to place, season, and soil, they destroy the specific defects of various living beings. Some trees are beneficial for the sustenance of the world’s life. Therefore, he ought to possess knowledge of all things at once; since it is impossible to determine [the truth] in the absence of such knowledge of all things, he says: "The sky... etc.
The proof is his perception of the quality of sound, which exists in addition to the substance of space (*ākāśa*).

In this context, "the state of being sound as a substance distinct from space" means that even in the absence of knowledge of the scriptures regarding the respective conjunctions of substances, place, body, time, and action, the word uttered by a reliable person (*āpta*) is authoritative in all cases. Having understood that a scripture is that which is effective in whatever place and for whatever purpose—such as knowing that a specific substance is the remedy for a particular disease—the knowledge of the effects produced by words such as "space" (*gagana*) and so forth serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is this: although the fact that any given object is a remedy for a particular ailment is established by the words uttered by an authoritative person agreed upon by many disputants, in such a case, the perception of the quality of the sky (ākāśa) and so forth is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Thus, having reflected upon and observed all this—that substance which possesses the essence arising from the five elements [is subject] to distinctions determined by specific locations, distinctions determined by specific bodies, and distinctions determined by specific times—one should prepare medicine after understanding that essential substance. The resultant meaning is that the knowledge of the true principles of the subjects expounded in Āyurveda alone has been established.

Is it not the case that the sweet juice found in stationary plants (*sthāvara*) cannot be a medicinal substance suitable for alleviating the provocation of *pavana* (wind), because it lacks being produced from a body composed of the seven constituent elements (*saptadhātu*), like the stalk of a sugarcane? Whatever sweet juice is not produced from a body composed of the seven constituent elements is not a medicinal substance suitable for alleviating the provocation of *pavana*, because it lacks being produced from a body composed of the seven constituent elements, like the stalk of a sugarcane.

That which does not produce a sweet taste from a body composed of the seven constituent elements (dhātus) cannot be a sweet taste that pacifies the provocation of wind (pavana), just like the sweet taste produced by the fruit of the palmyra palm (*tāla*). The sweet taste residing in a stalk of sugarcane causes the provocation of wind precisely because it is a sweet taste produced by ripening over time, and lacks the quality of being produced by fire-cooking; for whatever is not thus [i.e., does not cause the provocation of wind] is not thus, just like a jar. In the same way, a sour taste does not pacify the provocation of wind.

Because it lacks the quality of being a substance possessing a sweet taste produced by a body composed of the seven *dhātus*. Likewise, a substance possessing a salty taste does not alleviate the provocation of *pavana* (wind), because it lacks the quality of being produced by a body consisting of the seven *dhātus*, and because it is a substance possessing a sweet taste produced by the ripening of time; thus, it serves to provoke *pavana*—this is the meaning. A plant substance possessing a salty taste does not alleviate *anila* (wind), because it is a plant substance grown on saline soil (*ūṣara*), like any other such accepted instance.

Thus, even by means of the instrument of inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), one might argue that bodies composed of up to seven constituent elements (*dhatu*) have substances possessing their own sweet taste as the remedy for wind (*pavana*); because of this unsatisfactory implication, he says: "bitter" (*tikta*). The bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes provide nourishment to the tissues of plasma, blood, flesh, fat, and strength; and all trees consist of the four elements beginning with plasma (*rasa*). This is because they are substances in which the qualities of the bitter, pungent, and astringent tastes predominate and where strength is predominant. [Conversely,] they lack the tissues of semen, marrow, and bone, and thus consist of substances in which the qualities of the sweet, sour, and salty tastes—which nourish those [latter tissues]—predominate. This is the meaning.

But surely there are sweet, sour, and salty tastes residing in immobile beings; what then is the destiny of those whose primary taste resides in them? The meaning is that they are fit to be described as qualities of substances because they consist primarily of taste.

Now, one might object: "Are not the bodies of both the stationary (sthāvara) and the moving (jaṅgama) composed of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*? Therefore, since it is easy to say that 'the body is enveloped by the seven constituents (*dhātu*)', and that being enveloped by the seven constituents is the defining characteristic of a body, it would likewise be easy to say that 'the body consists of the six tastes (*rasa*)'. Consequently, there is no decisive reason (*vinigamaka*) to claim that stationary bodies consist of only four constituents, as the nature of being a body is equally applicable to all things defined by that characteristic. Keeping this intention in mind, he says: "From the exhaling, the inhaling, and the sustaining [breaths], it blossoms" (62).

Through the retention of the winds during exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*), by means of the closing and opening of the lotuses presided over by their respective phonemes (*varṇa*), the awakening of those respective phonemes arises. Therefore, this body is enveloped by the seven constituents (*dhātu*), because it consists of substances that serve as the cause for the utterance of phonemes; however, they [the plants] are not so, due to their lack of such capacity and because they possess only half a body consisting of four constituents. Furthermore, their buds, flowers, leaves, creepers, and so forth, perform the closing and opening [of petals] by virtue of contact with external air.

They designate [the body] merely as the sustainer of the *recaka* (exhalation). Therefore, it performs action characterized by movement. Now, one might object: "A mobile body produces another body, because it is a substance that serves as the cause for the production of stationary [bodies]. Likewise, a tree produces another tree, since both are identical in being substances that serve as the cause for the production of stationary [bodies]. For this very reason, how can the fact that even stationary bodies consist of the seven constituents (*saptadhātu*) be denied? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The *liṅga*..."
And from the union of the male organ and the female organ, procreation through offspring and livestock is produced. || 63 ||

Because the *liṅga* (genital organ) is the cause of procreation, and because at the time of procreation in stationary beings (*sthāvara*), the effect of union with another tree is not observed; and because, being stationary bodies, it is improper to speak of them [in the same way] as mobile bodies (*jaṅgama*). For this very reason it has been said: "The body is enveloped by the four elements, beginning with *rasa*. Now, one might object: "This is the speech of a woman, this is the speech of a man"—thus there is a perception of the difference between the two.

Due to the lack of activity in the palate and lips, the air produced there generates sound as it moves through the cavities of the smiling mouth; entering the vaginal opening of women, it produces speech that indicates the female gender.

Because the region of the lotus situated between the shanks and the private parts has a small aperture, the sound consisting of phonemes (varṇa) enters the lotus-opening located at the male organ. Since the differentiation of the air produced by the lack of activity in the palate and lips is common to all, yet the sounds uttered by women are distinguished by their specific causal apparatus (*sāmagrī*), those sounds are perceived as being characterized by an excess of vowels (*aja*).

In the same way, even though the factors such as being produced by a person and the activity of the palate and lips are identical, how is it perceived that a sound uttered by a woman is different from a sound uttered by a man? Keeping in mind the intention that this is because the causal complex for the cognition of the sound is identical, he says:
"From the difference in the regions of the back, thighs, penis, and genitals, the vowels and so forth arise."

Upon reaching the region of the calves, the penis, and the feet, sound comes into being. This is explained by analyzing it as follows: having reached the porous regions of the calves and the penis and emerging outward, the sound consisting of phonemes (varṇātmaka-śabda) is heard as it makes known the predominance of phonemes such as *ha* and others; thus, it can be recognized that "this is the word *puruṣa*."

In this way, from the totality of the activity of the palate and lips of women, a sound produced by the movement of the tongue and the opening of the mouth reaches the cavity of the ear region; having reached the openings of the channels of the veins located in the region of the back and the lotus of the generative organ, and emerging from the support of the vaginal cavity, the sound is heard with an abundance of phonemes such as vowels and so forth. That sound is perceived as distinct, being recognized as "the sound uttered by women. There exist many bodies characterized by their respective species.

The distinction between the phonemes arises from the difference in the delimiters of their respective bodies. It must be stated that only those porous regions located in the various lotus-seats (*pṛṣṭhayoni*) serve as the indicators for the distinctions between those respective phonemes. In this same way, the distinction among the people of the Puruṣa-world should also be understood.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the lotus located in the pelvic region—which serves as the support for Kuṇḍalinī, who consists of the winds of inhalation and exhalation—is the support of all vital breaths (*prāṇa*), because it has the form of a watering trench for the flow of nectar situated in the head, and because it is the cause for fulfilling the function of that nectar-flowing trench? Therefore, through the power of yogic concentration (*dhāraṇā*), there would be nourishment of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Anticipating this objection, the author says: "The pelvis" (*kaṭi*).
[It is] the support of the body located in the pelvic region. (65)

The lotus situated in the region of the waist is surrounded by four channels; because it is the cause of the activity of movement through the hands and feet—which are the elements that produce the phonemes of the *o* class—and because it possesses the essential nature of performing the function of going and coming as a means, it alone is the sustainer of the body. This is the meaning. It is not, however, like the lotus that supports all phonemes, which is supported merely by the wind that is the cause for the support of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Now, one might object: "Is not the knowledge of the meaning of Āyurveda caused by the performance of yoga—which accomplishes the four aims of human life—since it serves as the cause for the direct experience of the realization of the Lord? When the Lord is well-pleased, He bestows the very fruits desired by the mind. Therefore, what greater fruit is obtained by abandoning the practice of yoga and instead producing diseases through the consumption of various unwholesome substances, only to then apply the remedies that alleviate them? To this, he says: "Not from the navel... and so forth.
Situated below the navel, originating from Kuṇḍalī and surrounded by five thousand channels, the hundred-petaled lotus is produced. || 66 ||

Situated below the navel, the lotus of the digestive fire (jaṭharānala) lies between those two [the kidneys]. It is enveloped by five thousand channels. It is the primordial source of all the lotuses that support the various bodily constituents (varṇa). Its nature consists of the substratum of the seven dhātus and the five elements. That hundred-petaled lotus, remaining free from morbid transformation through the consumption of substances with non-contradictory tastes, exists constantly generating the nectar (amṛta) located in the cranial lotus by means of their respective essential substances.

By means of the movement of the vital air (pavana), which is free from morbid transformation (vikāra), and by nourishing that hundred-petaled lotus, the seven constituents (dhātu) are sustained. Whether through the consumption of elixirs (rasāyana), the warding off of diseases, or the eating of wholesome food, the body is kept free from transformation; the meaning is that long life is thereby obtained. Therefore, the preservation of the body alone is the means for accomplishing all human goals (puruṣārtha). A healthy body is the cause of all bliss and the cause of the knowledge of bliss.

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are indicators of the self as their objects, because they serve as the substrata for the sense organs; that which is not so is not thus, like a jar. This healthy body is a means for the practice of yoga, because it is a body presided over by a self whose object is the mind and whose nature is the knowledge of reality, just like a body presided over by consciousness. The knowledge of the reality of all categories is the cause of liberation, because it is caused by the knowledge of what is to be attained, which is distinct from the objects to be abandoned and their means.

This healthy body is preceded by the experience and knowledge of all objects, because it is preceded by the knowledge of the consumption of substances that eliminate disease. The subject matter set forth in the four questions of Āyurveda is dependent upon these four types of inference, because it is preceded by the knowledge of the meaning propounded in the aforementioned scripture.
Thus ends the commentary on the fourth chapter of Āyurveda, composed by Yogānandanātha;
this well-known commentary on the sūtras of Āyurveda is esteemed by great men and intended for the benefit of the world.
Complete. This is the fifth question in Āyurveda.
[I have composed this] by means of the rising glances of grace from my guru, who dwells within the cave of the heart.
Contemplating my companion within the six lotuses in succession,
and constantly causing the eight goddesses of speech to dance with laughter, I meditate here again and again upon Mahātripurasundarī.

Now, is it not the case that the hundred-petaled lotus situated below the navel is the support of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the substratum of all the sense organs? It has been stated that this lotus, enveloped by five thousand channels (*sirā*), increases longevity because it is filled with wind after drawing up the nectar residing in the cranial lotus. Therefore, if the three *doṣas* remain in their natural state, it can be said that this very lotus is the cause of all well-being. Consuming substances possessing pure essence brings about the proper movement of the *doṣas*.

The consumption of substances with incompatible tastes (*virasa-dravya*) causes morbid transformation (*vikāra*), because it is impossible to grasp knowledge regarding such objects without first having specific knowledge of the *doṣas* and other factors situated in their respective locations. The qualities of substances possessing pure tastes increase the pure *dhātus*, whereas the qualities of substances with incompatible tastes cause morbid transformations. For this very reason, he explains the location of the *doṣas* and their essential nature, beginning with the words "from the navel" (*nābheḥ*). The *doṣas*—wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*)—situated below the navel and above in the heart, whether combined or uncombined, complete or incomplete, mutually produce diseases. (Verse 1)

The vital air (pavana) resides below the navel; the region above that is the space situated above the navel, which serves as the source of the Pitta disorder. Above that, the region of the heart is the seat of the Kapha disorder. All of this, along with the knowledge of the qualities and defects of all substances, serves as the cause for understanding the nature of the disorders. Therefore, the knowledge of the disorders and so forth is essential, because without such specialized knowledge, it is impossible to diagnose those respective diseases.

To explain: what kind of wind is it? Having assumed the form of inhalation and exhalation residing within the *kuṇḍalinī*, it becomes twofold. That very same wind is designated as fivefold through the distinction of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), namely the divisions of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*.

That very vital breath (*prāṇa*), having entered within all the channels (*sirā*), gathers all the phonemes (*varṇa*) presided over by their respective lotuses; then, through the impact produced by the operation of the palate and the lips, and by virtue of the distinctions among its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it causes the power of the movement of those various winds to reach each respective lotus. Having brought the sound consisting of the collection of phonemes residing in those various lotuses to the region of the ear, it produces the cognition generated by the knowledge whose objects are the meanings of those specific sounds.

Wherever indigestion arises from the consumption of tasteless substances, it produces a state of abnormal movement in the wind (pavana) that has entered the pathways of the vessel-cavities, resulting in the flow of breath and exhalation characterized by the nature of *anila*. Where there is knowledge of this abnormal movement, there is the experience of intense pain associated with it.

When the wind, having entered its respective channels, moves in a contrary direction as far as the respective lotuses and grasps the phonemes (*varṇa*), and when that [wind] reaches the cavity of the ear such that it is perceivable by another, then the word consisting of those phonemes is heard. As long as the wind, having approached the phoneme-grasping [channels], proceeds along the path of the *doṣas*, then all the *doṣas* become incapable [of functioning]. That very same wind moves only very slightly when indigestion has arisen due to the consumption of unpalatable food.

"Thus, there is an incomplete movement": the meaning is that where a mixing movement (*saṃkara-gati*) of those winds or others is observed, that itself becomes the disease. Now, an objection is raised: in the description of the three *doṣas*, no scripture is perceived that establishes them as nourishers of the *dhātus*. When they are vitiated, they become corrupters of the *dhātus*; however, if they are not vitiated, they assist in maintaining stability without deviating from their natural state. Therefore, what fruit is obtained by the removal of the *doṣas*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Where...
Wherever the *rasas* reside, those [winds] produced from them act as nourishers of the respective *dhātus*.

In whatever case there is the consumption of substances produced from a predominance of a particular element to the extent that they exist, those substances depend upon that specific element and nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) that counteract [the imbalances] thereof. This is because the juices of plants, to the extent that they are manifest, contain rasas that dry up and nourish the bodily constituents of the various manifest elements, since these substances possess rasas of the same class as those which cure the diseases born from the consumption of the unwholesome (*virasa*) juices of plants.

The meaning is that as long as there is a medicine that removes the suffering caused by the depletion of the bodily constituents (dhātus) dependent on other parts of the body due to the sap produced by sprouting plants, such a construction of an inference—based on the apprehension of pervasion through the cause of the effect—is possible; for once the pervasion between the remover and the removed is apprehended, it can be stated in the same way in all subsequent cases as well.

Now, it must be stated that the nourishment of the tissues (*dhātu*) by the tastes (*rasa*) and other factors occurs through the pacification of the provoked humors (*doṣaprakopa*). It was established in the previous aphorism that tastes residing in the various elements (*bhūta*) are the removers of diseases produced by the components of those elements. This, however, requires further consideration. It can be said that some tastes are nourishers of the tissues, while some tastes are corrupters of the tissues. When indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arises from incompatible tastes, the various diseases prescribed [in the scriptures] manifest accordingly.

When those [humors] are accompanied by defects (*doṣa*) and have entered the constituent elements (*dhātu*), their respective morbid transformations manifest within them. When, through the consumption of non-antagonistic tastes, the humors remain undisturbed, they maintain the equilibrium of the *dhātus*; and when the humors are pure, they protect both the *dhātus* and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). However, if they become vitiated, they become destroyers of the *dhātus*, the *prāṇas*, and the sense organs (*indriya*). Keeping in mind the intention that it is appropriate to explain how the tastes such as *rasa* cause the provocation of the humors and how they bring about the alleviation of that provocation, he describes the specific qualities of the six tastes, beginning with "two" (*dvīti*).
Possessing the essence of the twice-born and the essence of wealth, yet devoid of the essence of those lacking wealth, he is one who wards off the wind.

The phrase "the substance possessing two tastes" means that a substance characterized by both sweet (*svādu*) and sour (*amla*) tastes is a remedy for the provocation of wind (*pavana*). A substance possessing only a sweet taste does not necessarily alleviate wind, as there are exceptions in the case of sugarcane juice, plantain fruit, coconut, and palm fruit. The meaning is that when the quality of being sweet and the quality of being sour are perceived together in a single substance, then that substance, characterized by those specific tastes, becomes a remedy for wind.

A substance possessing exclusively a salty taste does not counteract wind, because the salty taste produced from saline soil lacks the capacity to counteract wind; however, sea-salt is not like that. Sweetness is the defining characteristic of the substance water. This being so, sea-water salt is included within the very essence of the sweet taste inherent to water, since the sweet taste residing in water is filled out by the earth-substance characterized by a salty taste.

If that were the case, then it would be perceived if it existed; however, one should not say that it does not exist simply because it is not perceived. The meaning is that a substance characterized by saltiness is indeed recognized as being savory within substances such as condiments, and it is certainly possible to employ the conventional expression, "this is perceived as savory because it possesses a savory taste. Some regions of the earth are characterized by a salty taste, while others are characterized by a sweet taste, as this is observed in the waters of various lands, wells, and so forth.

Wherever there is the perception of a salty taste, the property of being produced from such a type of soil is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) therein; for it is observed that the quality of sweet taste belongs to water produced in a well characterized by sweet water, since in that case the presence of saltiness—which is produced from a soil lacking the quality of being a producer of salty taste—is found, and because the perception of sweet taste can be explained in that instance.

The meaning is as follows: since a substance characterized by the salty taste produced in the Saindhava region arises from pure earth, the possession of an acidic taste is the defining characteristic (avacchedaka) of that earth. Precisely because it is produced from such substances in various locations, it can indeed be said to counteract the wind (pavana). In that context, because it is characterized by the qualities of two substances whose purpose is the two tastes, its activity directed toward those two tastes serves to counteract the wind.

"Substance devoid of rasa" refers to a substance lacking rasa, such as mercury (pārada) and similar substances; for in those cases, the rasas of medicinal herbs and the like are never perceived at any time. In that regard, its capacity to arrest the vital breath (*pavana*) is established by all people and established by the consensus of all scriptures. The term "mercury" (*pārada*) is illustrative; since "rasa" is a great essence common to inferior metals and so forth, everything is included by the word "mercury. Within this substance of mercury, the *rasas* and other qualities become manifest.

However, many [scholars] maintain that it is well known for other substances to possess a low taste (hīnarasavattva) while acting as a purgative; for it is well established that this quality [of having a low taste] brings about the cessation of wind (pavana).

This is precisely the intended meaning of the statement in the *Sūtrasthāna* as well. For instance, non-deviation (*avyabhicaritatva*) is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Following the apprehension of pervasion in the form "wherever there is the presence of a sweet taste, there is the quality of counteracting wind," one proceeds to inference. The sweet juice contained within a stalk of sugarcane counteracts the provocation of wind because it is permeated by constituent parts consisting of water and earth, just like the juice of a cucumber fruit. By this inference as well, it is certainly possible to state that a single sweet taste possesses the quality of counteracting wind; such is the meaning.

[Objection: Is it not the case that when sweetness arises in a substance possessing an acidic taste due to the process of digestion over time, that very substance remains an acidic taste? Furthermore, the consumption of substances with discordant tastes causes disorder; likewise, it could be said that a substance possesses two tastes. [Reply: To address the doubt as to how such a substance could be a taste that pacifies *pavana* (wind), he says: "Sweet...
Sweet and extremely sweet [tastes] sequentially destroy wind and bile, respectively, and produce phlegm (*kapha*).

That which is called "sweetness" (*madhuratva*) is a substance possessing a sweet taste distinct from substances possessing other tastes, and it is that which counteracts wind (*pavana*). Due to the influence of time, it becomes sweet; that substance possessing its own sweet taste counteracts the provocation of bile (*pitta*) and does not become a substance possessing a discordant taste. Because it is a substance characterized by a specific genus of a single taste, it is indeed a substance of a single taste.

When it is perceived that a substance characterized by the genus of being a substance possessing an acidic taste becomes a substance possessing a sweet taste due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of digestion over time, at that time it is not a substance possessing a taste contrary to that [sweetness], because it is a substance whose state as a substance has passed beyond the time suitable for that [contrary taste]. In this case, the limiting condition is the state of having passed beyond the time [suitable] for a substance possessing a contrary taste; therefore, that very substance possessing a sweet taste becomes a substance possessing an exceedingly sweet taste which counteracts the provocation of *pitta*. This is the meaning.

Because its purpose is fulfilled merely by the capacity of a substance possessing a single taste, qualified by the genus of substances having a sour taste (*amlarasa*), to counteract wind (*pavana*), and because there is no other substance that counteracts defects other than wind, he says: "sour and very sour" (verse 5).
Sour (*āmla*) and very sour (*atyamla*) are likewise [to be understood]. (5)

When a substance characterized by the sour taste (*amlarasa*) acquires an excessively sour taste due to the influence of the digestive process (*pāka*), it cannot be said to alleviate other *doṣas*, because it remains a substance belonging to the same class of a single taste. Therefore, the intended meaning is that its well-established function is solely to alleviate wind (*pavana*).
Since the same would apply to substances possessing a salty taste (*lavaṇarasa*), he says: "salty... (*lavaṇa...*) [and so forth].
Salt destroys wind (vāta) and produces phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta).
The meaning is that because there is an absence of the perception of bitter, pungent, or astringent tastes, and because it is an alkaline substance (*kṣāradravya*), it acts as an exciter of *pitta*.

Now, one might object: "It is appropriate to say that the salty taste (*lavaṇarasa*) excites *pavana* (wind), but it is not suitable to say it excites *kapha*; furthermore, because it is an alkaline substance, it ought to alleviate *pavana*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Deficient or excessive... "Salt taste, when deficient or excessive, destroys *kapha* and *pavana*, and produces *pitta*. (7)

The saline taste produced from a substance possessing the quality of sweet flavor is a mild saline taste; the saline taste produced from a substance with an excess of sour flavor, such as that originating from the region of Sindh, is an intense saline taste. Because it is a substance produced from water through contact with the submarine fire (*baḍavānala*), we maintain that its saline taste acts as a remedy for phlegm (*kapha*).

In order to state that the bitter taste produced from the elements of space, sun, and earth counteracts the provocation of the *kapha* humor, [the author] explains how the bitter taste, precisely because it is produced from the substances of space and air (*nabho'niladravya*), provokes the wind (*pavana*) and yet counteracts diseases of *kapha* and *pitta*: "The bitter...
"The bitter [taste] destroys *kapha* and *pitta*, and produces wind. (8)

Regarding "bitter" (*tikta*): the bitter taste is produced from ether (*nabhas*) and air (*anila*). Because ether is a partless substance (*niravayava-dravya*) and air is also a partless substance, the body born from both of them possesses a bitter taste. Consuming substances with a bitter taste brings about the cessation of the provocation of phlegm (*kapha*). Everything that has been set forth is thus correctly established.

The meaning is as follows: because that which destroys *pitta* is produced by the conjunction of the wind element (*anila-bhūta*) in excess with the space element (*gagana-bhūta*), and because a bitter taste is born from the conjunction of the wind element and the space element that kindle the *rasa-grahaṇī-kalā*, it can indeed be stated that [this substance] counteracts the provocation of *pitta*, since both are substances that pervade all scriptures.

Now, it may be objected that it is impossible for that bitter taste (*tiktarasa*) to cause the provocation of the wind (*pavana*), because it is produced by itself. [This is not so,] for substances such as *nimba*, *kuṣṭha*, *bhūnimba*, *śṛṅgī*, *śārkara*, *karkāṭaka*, *kuṭaja*, *paṭola*, *kumāri*, *bhūtalatā*, *talapoṭu*, *karkandhū*, *devadāru*, *guggulu*, and others—which possess the quality of bitter taste—are substances that counteract the effects of the provoked wind; they are substances fit for enjoyment, and they are substances that serve as causes for the kindling of the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*).

One should not raise the objection: "Since it is known that all these [substances] are pacifiers of the provocation of *pavana* (wind), why is it said that they 'produce *māruta* (wind)'? The intended meaning is that the consumption of substances possessing a bitter or unpleasant taste (*virasa*) produces the provocation of *pavana*. "Consumption of unpleasant substances" means the consumption of substances with conflicting tastes; the sense is that such consumption becomes equivalent to consuming poisonous substances. He states—beginning with the word "bitter" (*kaṭu*)—that a pungent taste (*kaṭurasa*), arising from an excess of the constituent elements of fire (*anala*) and wind (*anila*), is a pacifier of the provocation of *kapha*. Pungent [taste] destroys *kapha*, [but] it is caused by *vāta* and *pitta*. (9)

The fact that pungent taste (*kaṭurasa*) alleviates phlegm (*kapha*) is well known; likewise, its capacity to provoke bile (*pitta*) is also well known. Pungent substances, being of pure taste, cause the cessation of phlegmatic diseases while simultaneously provoking bile. These two points are well established. By virtue of being a substance with a pungent taste produced by the elements of fire (*analā*), wind (*anila*), and earth (*bhūta*), it removes the provocation of phlegm, provokes bile, and also brings about the cessation of the provocation of wind (*pavana*).

Ginger, *rāsnā*, *karṇagranthi*, *cavya*, radish, *tamālapatra*, *ardhaka*, garlic, and asafoetida—these are pungent substances (*kaṭurasadravya*). Although it is established by the aphorism that they cause the provocation of *vāta*, the intended meaning is that even the consumption of these as a single taste (*virasa*) provokes *vāta*. For this very reason, he explains another aphorism: "Pungent" (*kaṭuka*), etc.
Pungent and extremely pungent [substances] destroy *kapha* and *vāta*, but produce *pitta*.
(10) The meaning is that pure pungent taste (*śuddhakaṭurasa*) causes the provocation of *pitta*.

Astringent (kaṣāya) destroys phlegm (kapha) and bile (pitta); it produces wind (māruta). An astringent that is deficient or excessive destroys phlegm and wind; it produces bile. The commentary on the aphorism "Astringent destroys phlegm and bile; it produces wind" should be applied in exactly the same manner.

Now, it has been established that among substances possessing the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*), a substance with a single taste possesses a specific action (*tattatkarma*) and a specific result (*tattatphala*) in the form of the alleviation of a particular disease. However, regarding substances with multiple tastes, where the observed result of their combination is likewise the alleviation of a particular disease, one considers that a collective group of substances with various tastes acts as the agent of that effect. With this in mind, a multiplicity of substances with various tastes is found in medical formulations for the purpose of curing a single disease; in such cases:

Since substances possessing many tastes are incapable of curing a single disease, and since it is impossible to state that multiple substances possess the capacity to cure specific diseases as a delimited property (avacchedaka) of their respective curative powers—because the delimiters of the qualities that cure each individual disease are distinct—if one were to claim, based on the maxim of the *Nyāya* scriptures that "that which has many parts and many qualities [performs the function]," that the combination of many substances produces the effect, this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Because the principle that "a single substance is the remover of a single disease" has been observed many times—since it is frequently seen that even for a disease produced by the cause of the obstruction of impurities (*mala*), the capacity of a single purgative substance (*recakadravya*) alone to remove it is observed repeatedly among many substances—and because even in those cases, the postulation of multiple substances involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), while the capacity of a single substance alone to remove a single disease is observed many times; due to this underlying dissatisfaction, he says: "In the case of *doṣa*... "In the case of *doṣa*, the remedy consists of one or more tastes (*rasa*) that are of a nature opposed to all the tastes [that produce] the disorders caused by the three *doṣas* or other causes. (12)

Regarding the phrase "caused by the three *doṣas* or caused by other factors": the result of consuming substances possessing non-contradictory tastes (*rasa*) for the purpose of maintaining the absence of or the prior state of the three *doṣas* is precisely the avoidance of what is undesirable. A substance that possesses a taste which acts according to the natural course of the *doṣas* is not a cause of the *doṣas*. Consuming substances with tastes that are discordant with the *doṣas* and which produce effects conducive to them is the cause of morbid transformation (*vikāra*). Consuming as many substances as possess tastes that serve as causes for effects contrary to those [discordant ones], and employing the appropriate combination of consuming multiple substances whose essence consists of those very same tastes, results in the cessation of a single disease.

The consumption of a substance possessing a rasa produced by a formulation suitable for decoctional drugs cures those respective diseases; the consumption of a substance possessing a rasa produced from powdered drugs formulated with many substances cures those respective diseases.

Through the consumption of substances possessing multiple tastes—substances produced by the application of various single ingredients such as oils, ghee, electuaries, and rejuvenatives (rasāyana)—which are endowed with specific refinements (*saṃskāra*), that which results in a state of a single taste becomes a substance of one flavor. That [substance] then yields the fruit of a single quality from those many substances. It has been established that in the Kali Yuga, power resides in a collective (*saṅgha*) and not in a single substance, for in the Kali Yuga, power resides in the collective because [individual substances] have been overcome [by the age].

It is like the benediction of Brahmins. Just as the power residing in the words uttered by the mouth of a single Brahmin becomes manifest in their assembly because that individual power has been surpassed [by the collective], so too, since trees do not possess a single, more firmly established power within each individual sap, power will arise in the assembly; thus, the blending of many substances results in an effect that counteracts those respective [ailments]. It is precisely the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by many yogas that bestows the fruit of that specific rite. In this Kali age, due to the abundance of unrighteousness (*adharma*), many diseases arise.

Therefore, because the physical bodies are limited in size, the factors that neutralize those afflictions yield their fruit in some cases, while in other cases they yield that respective fruit even when the complete collection of auxiliary conditions (*sāmagrī*) is absent. For this very reason it has been said:
"Their pacification occurs through medicines, gifts, recitation (*japa*), burnt offerings (*homa*), worship, and so forth.
The meaning is that in this age, one must necessarily rely on many such auxiliary conditions.

Now, when validity is established through the method of inference—namely, "this substance is the remover of the disease not produced from that other substance," and "this disease is curable by that specific substance because it possesses that specific substance which removes it"—then [the following] arises: that valid cognition (*pramā*) is the achiever of successful purposeful activity (*samartha-pravṛtti*). Having ascertained the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between those two, one engages in activity toward that object.

In that regard, when there is doubt concerning the substance that removes a disease, there is an absence of activity toward the effect of its removal; for it is all the more impossible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between those two. Activity occurs only when there is the certain knowledge that "this [substance] is the remover of the disease," because there is no doubt regarding a determined object, and such certainty is the cause of that activity. If, while doubting whether a single substance is the remover, one were to engage in collecting other substances, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "From rasa and so forth... "Those substances whose essence consists of rasa and the rest are the removers of all diseases. (13)

When a disorder of the bodily constituents (dhātus) such as lymph-chyle, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and semen has arisen, one determines that a specific substance is the remedy for it; once the knowledge arises that the procedure of purgation (virecana-vidhi) must be performed therein, the method of administering *harītakī* is carried out. By consuming such *harītakī*, the expulsion of the accumulated waste occurs. In this case, because the determination [of the causal relationship] is clear, it is easy to grasp the universal concomitance (vyāpti) swiftly. Here, *harītakī* is used as an illustration.

Only the mere class of substance characterized by those specific qualities of taste is intended here. Where it is understood that the doshas seized by morbid transformation (vikāra) circulate through all the dhātus, the rule (vidhi) is prescribed therein as the preparation of appropriate formulations using multiple substances for the purpose of curing diseases located in those various dhātus. By means of all such remedial substances, the consumption of substances possessing taste is what is intended.

The meaning is that the sense of the aphorism—that "all tastes born from the essence [of the medicinal substance] are removers of all diseases"—has been correctly established; for, immediately after grasping the pervasion (vyāpti) between the mere substance that removes a disease and the property of being a remover of that disease, the capacity for effective action is also ascertained.

Now, surely there exist many substances capable of acting as various eliminators; let these alone be the medicines. Since every substance consists of a collection of multiple substances possessing their respective inherent tastes, such a substance possessing those tastes becomes a "great-tasting" (*mahārasavat*) substance, because it is a composite of substances with manifold tastes, just like a collection of many uttered sounds. By this inference, just as a great resonance (*mahāghoṣa*) arises when many sounds are unified, so too [does a great medicinal effect arise].

In the process of combining substances of many kinds that belong to the same genus, it produces manifold benefits. In the preparation involving the synthesis and cooking of suitable substances—such as decoctions, powders, oils, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and elixirs (*rasāyana*)—the cessation of all diseases is preceded by this knowledge; that is, it is preceded by the knowledge of the specific substances possessing the tastes that alleviate those respective diseases, because [the preparation] consists of a collection of distinct substances possessing multiple tastes. Otherwise, the treatises that expound the individual qualities of each of those plants would be rendered useless.

If that were the case, it would be impossible for many substances to possess a single taste, since it is well-established that tastes themselves have primary and secondary relationships; furthermore, because they are of one kind, it would be impossible to determine that their delimiting factor is singular. Anticipating this objection, he says: "free from defects" (*adoṣa*), etc. [It is] that which nourishes the *dhātus* without causing defects and possesses multiple *sāras*. (14)

For the purpose of removing the defects inherent in various substances, through the power of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) enjoined by their respective injunctions, a substance free from defects arises—one that is highly substantial and possesses many tastes and qualities; it is precisely that which is called a "substance free from defects. Thus, the state of possessing taste (rasavattva) serves as the defining characteristic for every substance that nourishes the respective bodily constituents (dhātu). The meaning is that even though such a substance is a single entity, being endowed with multiple tastes, it bestows those many qualities.

Now, one might object: "When substances possessing the six tastes (ṣaḍrasa) are capable of nourishing the bodily constituents (dhātu), then it would be impossible to say that those tastes cause the provocation of wind (pavana) and the other humors, while simultaneously nourishing those very constituents; therefore, at such times, those tastes would not be provocative, since their role as nourishers of the constituents is easily established. Keeping this concern in mind, the author explains both points—that diseases arise from the tastes and are likewise cured by them—by stating "pakva... [and so forth].

The wind and the other [humors] located in the stomach and the colon increase through substances that are sweet, astringent, pungent, bitter, sour, and salty, which are suitable for digestion over time, and through various substances characterized by retention and evacuation; thus, the two types of diseases flourish. (15)

Regarding the statement "the wind and other [humors] go to the receptacles of digested and undigested food," this refers to the humors (doṣas) located in the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) and the receptacle of waste (malāśaya). Consuming substances that are exclusively sweet in taste becomes a cause for the provocation of phlegm (kapha), while the provocation of wind (pavana) arises from the consumption of sweet tastes. To alleviate that provocation of wind, one should consume substances with salty and sour tastes. Furthermore, consuming substances that are exclusively pungent in taste generates the provocation of bile (pitta).

The meaning is that one should consume substances with a sweet taste and substances with a bitter taste for the purpose of pacifying the provocation of *pitta*; the sense is that both serve to remove *pitta*. In this manner, the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the Supreme Brahman, the author of Āyurveda, has been described. For instance: from the consumption of substances with an excessively pungent taste, and from the consumption of substances characterized by the quality of dryness (*rūkṣa-guṇa*), which is a cause for the provocation of *vāyu*, the provocation of *vāyu* arises.

Because it is observed that the consumption of pungent-tasting substances causes the provocation of the *grahaṇīkalā* (the digestive organ), which arises from the qualities of dryness (*rūkṣa*), aggravation (*prakopa*), and heat (*taijasa*). Consequently, when there is a provocation of *pavana* (Vāyu), because the *grahaṇīkalā* possesses a nature that acts as a fueling agent, the *pavana* becomes the cause of excessive inflammation; or alternatively, it becomes the cause of extreme sluggishness. Therefore, the consumption of pungent-tasting substances causes the provocation of *pitta*, because such substances—possessing a pungent taste—are the cause for the provocation of *pavana* characterized by the quality of dryness.

Since the *grahaṇī-kalā* itself consists of the substance of bile (*pitta-dravya*), when it moves with the regular course of the wind (*anila*), the *grahaṇī-kalā*, being purified, becomes ignited. When it moves with an irregular course, it becomes disordered and weakens the digestive fire (*anala*). Consequently, diseases of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) manifest; this is the meaning of the description of the intention of the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*).

The substance that undergoes ripening over time is characterized by qualities superior to all purgatives; that [specific] potency is characterized by internal qualities that eliminate undigested matter (*āma*). The substance that produces *āma* is the cause of all diseases. From the consumption of substances characterized by these qualities, diseases increase. [Objection:

But it has been stated that when the causal complex for the production of those diseases exists, the respective diseases manifest solely through the humors (*doṣas*)—wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*). That should be considered, for instance:

The body consists of the five elements (*pañcabhūtātmaka*). The preservation of the body is necessary because the body alone is the abode of all diseases. Indeed, the body is the producer of qualities arising from the collection of beneficial effects produced by the predominance of constituent parts included within the various substances that constitute the manifested elements; this is because it is generated by the consumption of rasas and substances belonging to the same class as those that increase the parts of each respective element. Therefore, the diseases residing in each particular element are caused by the effects arising from the predominance of the parts of that specific element.

The qualities of earth are heaviness and dullness; those of water are oiliness and coldness; those of fire are smoothness and greater density; those of air are softness and mobility; and those of space are subtlety and clarity. These qualities act as remedies for their opposites. Through the appropriate application of place, body, time, substance, and action, they may destroy disease to whatever extent it exists.

The perception of the quality of heaviness in the body, which perceives an excess of earthy components, arises along with the quality of dullness; both of these are qualities of earth. Therefore, the body consists of the five elements as perceived through an excess of earthy components. Its nature consists of the experience of the cognition of odor—which is the delimiting factor for the earthly substance perceived through an excess of its components—and thus it consists of the five elements as perceived through an excess of such earthy components.
Consequently, the body consists of the five elements as characterized by an excess of substances possessing such tastes and their specific modifications.

Thus, the state of possessing fiery qualities—which serves as the delimiter for a substance possessing the nature of fire that perceives an excess of non-luminous material parts—is essentially the experience of a cognition that perceives the fiery form which makes known the excess of the fire-element and the excess of the fire-substance. This consists of the five elements characterized by an excess of those respective fiery parts. Consequently, due to this excess of a substance composed of the five elements qualified by such qualities, food is caused by the transformation of the parts of the fire-element.

In this manner, it should be applied to all substances. For instance: the consumption of a substance characterized by an excess of the qualities perceived as earthy and an abundance of taste causes a transformation of the constituent parts of the earthy substance. The consumption of a substance characterized by an excess of the qualities perceived as watery and an abundance of taste causes a transformation of the constituent parts of the watery substance. The consumption of a substance characterized by an excess of the qualities perceived as fiery and an abundance of taste acts as a cause for the transformation of the constituent parts of the fiery substance.

Thus, according to their respective applications, it has been established that substances possessing the six tastes—which consist of the destruction of diseases—serve to cure various ailments. This, however, is to be considered, for as follows:

The purpose of this [treatment] is both to provoke the three *doṣas* and to alleviate the provocation of the three *doṣas*. It has been established that it acts as a pacifier of specific *doṣas* according to the distinctions of place (*deśa*), body (*deha*), and time (*kāla*).
