Since that [previous explanation] is not able to withstand scrutiny, he says—starting with "of the healthy" (*svastha*)—to express his own view:
"The healthy and the unwell, those born of *sāma*, those without *āmaya*, those involving *doṣas*, and those not involving *doṣas*. (17)

As long as one consumes earthy substances (*pārthivadravya*), the *doṣas* remain in their natural state (*svastha*). As long as one consumes substances with discordant tastes (*virasadravya*), when indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) occurs, the *doṣas* become disordered (*asvastha*) because they occupy each other's locations. The capacity to produce effects other than those specifically prescribed is the defining characteristic (*avacchedaka*) of those very [substances]. The consumption of those respective substances brings about the natural state of the *doṣas*. Those [disorders] which arise from the consumption of substances that cause contradictory movements and effects are called *sāmajāmaya*. Through the consumption of substances that counteract them, health (*nīrogatva*) is restored.

Regarding the phrase "sadoṣā" (accompanied by defects): therein, those [humors] which are transformed (*vikṛta*) are seized by morbid change (*vikāra*). Because they move through the bodily channels that dehydrate the *dhātus*, they are called "doṣaga" (moving in the humors). By consuming substances that have the causal power to produce the absence of such morbid changes, they become free from defects; this is the meaning. It has been established that "this is the movement of the humors' morbid change" and "this is the movement of the absence of the humors' morbid change" are produced by the consumption of substances possessing contradictory or non-contradictory tastes. This remains established because it is caused by the knowledge of the mere consumption of substances possessing contradictory or non-contradictory tastes, as demonstrated through the following logical formulation (*anumāna*): [The states in question are produced by the consumption of substances possessing contradictory or non-contradictory tastes, because they are caused by the knowledge of the mere consumption of substances possessing contradictory or non-contradictory tastes].

Those powerful [elements] such as fire and the rest, which experience the delimitation of the meaning established by this [text], protect the body in that manner; the food consumed by it is digested by that fire, because the meaning established by this is possible. Due to this lack of finality, he says: "vihita... (Verse 18). "The tastes that are the cause of the prescribed digestion; the contrary tastes situated within the post-digestive state (vipāka); and the irregular humors (doṣas) moving through the channels of the irregular humors and bodily constituents (dhātus). || 18 ||

The knowledge of consuming substances with conflicting or non-conflicting tastes is preceded by the knowledge of consuming substances containing tastes that reside within the prescribed tastes and their post-digestive transformations (*vipāka*); for it is preceded by the knowledge of the remedial [knowledge] arising from the knowledge of consuming substances possessing those tastes which are the cause of the effects of such disorders. Those [substances] whose tastes are contrary to the tastes residing within are the causes of disorder; they are "those with discordant humors" (*viṣamadoṣāḥ*) because they afflict the humors, and they are called "those moving along the pathways of the tissues" (*dhātumārgagāḥ*) because they travel through the channels of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). This is the meaning of "those very ones being the discordant humors."

The very palm of one’s own hand, which makes known the knowledge of the transformation produced by eating substances possessing that particular taste, and which perceives the knowledge pertaining to the object of the olfactory sense—having recognized daily that this [knowledge] is the cause of health as long as the absence of [excessive] tastes is observed therein—one sees, through repeated observation, that the tastes which are the causes of the diseases residing within manifest upon the surface of the right palm.

The knowledge of health ought to be a cognition whose object is the cognition of the absence of unwholesome tastes, which are the causes of diseases produced by the consumption of unwholesome tastes. To explain: the knowledge of a taste present in the hand—which is an object of the olfactory sense—is a perceiver of the cause of the knowledge of disease produced by the consumption of unwholesome tastes; that cause is the consumption of substances possessing an excess of those [unwholesome] tastes, which brings about the manifestation of unwholesome tastes within the body as a result of digestion (*vipāka*), which are the causes of disease.

The cause of the modification of the parts of the substance *anila* (wind) is the consumption of substances possessing qualities contrary to those of *anila*, specifically the consumption of substances in which those [contrary] tastes predominate. This is likewise caused by the modification of the parts of the substance *ākāśa* (space), because that which possesses a contrary object serves as the cause by way of being its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

Is it not the case that every substance possessing a particular taste, in accordance with its specific qualities, acts as a destroyer of whatever disease corresponds to that taste? For instance, a substance characterized by an abundance of the astral (nābhasa) bitter taste—which is concordant with the astringent taste that indicates a predominance of the ether element—would counteract the excess of the astral bitter taste located within the cavity of the ear, which obstructs the perception of sound in the space of the auditory canal. Therefore, it should be understood that this [substance] possesses an abundance of the qualities of ether.

In the same way, a substance characterized by a predominance of the qualities of air (vāyu) is also to be understood. Knowledge of a substance that is soft, stable, heavy, and liquid serves as an indicator of a predominance of the constituent parts of the element air within a subject of contradictory properties; thus, it is a substance composed of the five elements (pāñcabhautika) whose subject matter concerns such contradictions. Likewise, a substance that increases the fiery qualities while possessing an abundance of qualities such as smoothness and density serves as an indicator of a predominance of the element fire (tejas) within a subject of contradictory properties; thus, it is a substance composed of the five elements.
Thus, the watery substance characterized by the quality of oiliness—which indicates an excess of the water element—is contradictory [to the expected state].

Likewise, heaviness and dullness indicate the nature of earth; because of the substance's sour taste, that which indicates an excess of earthen components and a sweet taste consists of all five elements and is therefore contradictory. Having understood all this, medical treatment should be administered.

Now, it may be argued that medical knowledge (*cikitsājñāna*) is preceded by knowledge whose object is contradictory. To have a contradictory object means to have as its object the knowledge of contradictory substances, because in that context, the knowledge of contradictory substances functions as a cause by way of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*). This being so, the definition of the body is that it consists of the five elements (*pañcabhūtātmakatva*). That definition is preceded by the knowledge thereof. Regarding this, there is the Śruti: "From space comes air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, earth; from earth, plants; from plants, food; from food, the body composed of the five elements."

At the time of medical treatment, knowledge of substances is essential for the wise. Without this entire body of knowledge—namely, knowledge of substances regarding the application of time, knowledge of substances regarding the application of place, and knowledge of substances regarding the application of the body—how could there be knowledge of substances possessing tastes that consist of the five elements? To this he says: "The body... [verse 19].
The appropriate application of the body, place, time, substance, and action continues until the disease is destroyed.

Having understood the variation of substances according to the difference of place, medical treatment should be administered. Having understood the variation of substances according to the difference of time, the performance of medical treatment is the prescribed rule. The application of these actions is as follows: the formulation of a compound (yoga) prescribes the specific qualities of various substances for those belonging to particular places; it prescribes the specific qualities of various substances for bodies characterized by particular times. Thus, the meaning is that the combination of flavorful substances, through the differences of body, place, and time, bestows manifold qualities.
According to the appropriate application of the actions of those respective substances, they destroy diseases to the full extent.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the action of substances possessing various specific qualities is performed through the knowledge of differences in place and time, by means of actions involving substances containing the tastes that counteract those [doṣas]? Furthermore, since even a disorder produced by the agitation of multiple dhātus may consist of only a single dhātu, how could there be the cognition 'this is a dual-doṣa' or 'this is a triple-doṣa' unless there were the presence of the resulting seasonal conditions (rasāmayas)? Addressing this underlying doubt, he says: *virasa...* "Those [disorders] which proceed through the path of a single type of dhātu due to dual doṣas arising from the digestion of unwholesome and irregular food are 'dual-doṣa' disorders. (20)

That which is called "the digestion of discordant tastes" (*virasaviṣamapacana*) refers to a substance produced by the combination of substances possessing conflicting tastes; having entered the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), it produces a transformation corresponding to those substances. The digestive fire (*pācakānala*) that processes it also undergoes a transformation and likewise performs an irregular digestion of tastes. The movement of the vital air (*pavana*) generated by that refinement causes the activity of the palate, lips, and other articulators that signals sounds of discordant syllables. It also causes the lotus that serves as the support for those words to close like a bud.

Even thereafter, by the administration of other substances possessing tastes that provoke *pitta*, it maintains a connection with the qualities produced by those respective impressions (*saṃskāra*). When it produces various morbid transformations (*vikāra*), it is then made known precisely through the movement of wind (*vāyu*) characterized by *pitta*. Being joined with the transformation of *pitta* born from impressions due to the disorder of the humor (*doṣa*) of taste, it reaches and traverses the pathways of the various tissues (*dhātu*), vitiates those respective tissues, and brings about the manifestation of their specific disorders.

The meaning is that at that time, it is indeed possible to know: "This is the fault of the provocation of *pitta*. In the same way, the consumption of another substance that causes the provocation of *kapha* is possible; then, it establishes the qualities that indicate the provocation of *kapha*. Thus, when it is known that "Devadatta is afflicted by a disease of *kapha* and *pitta*," the movement of the wind (*vāyu*) characterized by the qualities of those respective substances—which indicates the qualities of those respective *doṣas*—is made known even to others.

This wind disorder associated with phlegm produces a movement that indicates a dual disorder of wind and phlegm. At that time, the very defect of wind—arising from the specific qualities of the impressions produced by the consumption of irregular tastes—becomes capable of moving through the pathways of many *dhātus*. The meaning is that it also effects the nourishment of those respective *dhātus*.

Now, one might object: by consuming a substance whose taste (*rasa*) provokes *pitta*, one acquires the qualities that cause the provocation of *pitta*; this very process should be understood as the "movement toward the provocation of *pitta* and *vāta*. Similarly, by consuming a substance whose taste is contrary to (*virasa*) that which provokes *kapha*, one brings about the qualities that provoke *kapha*; at that time, it is designated as the "movement toward the provocation of *kapha* and the other two" (*dvandva*). Thus, it can be conventionally treated as "this is a disease of the three *doṣas*" (*tridoṣa-roga*) through such a mode of cognition.

To the question, "Since the specific constituent parts that produce those [individual *doṣas*] are not perceived, how can there be the cognition here that 'this is a disease of the three *doṣas*'? he says: "By the final... (*carama*).
The disease of the digestion of the final essence (caramarasapācana) resides in the three humors (tridoṣa). || 21 ||

The marrow element (*majjā-dhātu*) and the semen element (*śukla-dhātu*)—these two are perceived as the final elements (*carama-dhātu*). Diseases of wind (*pavana*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*) reach as far as the bone element (*asthi-dhātu*); at that time, they merely cause the drying up of those respective elements but do not destroy life. However, when a disease produced by the consumption of incompatible tastes (*viruddha-rasa*) enters the marrow element, one then departs from life and goes to *nirvāṇa*. At that time, it should be understood as the "course of the three humors" (*tridoṣa-gati*).

[Objection: Surely, by consuming various substances that are contrary [to the humors], those respective *doṣas* become provoked; all diseases are born from the provocation of the *doṣas*. Therefore, for the sake of curing those respective diseases, the digestion (*pacana*) of the *doṣas* must be performed. To this he says: "As long as... (yāvad). [The treatment] continues until the digestive remedy for the *doṣas* has ceased its action. || 22 ||

The meaning is that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this regard is the inference produced by the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which is based on the repeated observation of the fact that as many diseases as there are are all produced from the corruption of the *doṣas*. These *doṣas*, dominated by unwholesome tastes (*virasa*), undergo transformation in the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*) and circulate through the pathways of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). It has been stated that these raw tastes (*āmārasa*), such as those of fire and so forth, upon their manifestation, become objects of the sense of smell.

The effort toward the method of maturing those [humors], which acts as an obstacle to proceeding toward the defects contrary to that [health], is to be observed by means of fasting (*laṅghana*). He states that this is the realized meaning with the words "as long as" (*yāvat*): the time for the maturation of the humors depends upon the purification of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). || 23 ||

The disease of *kapha* arising from indigestion caused by the consumption of substances that possess immortality-like properties—which produce disorders of the *rasa* and *rakta* tissues born of incompatible tastes—is treated as follows: fasting (*laṅghana*) is the very medicine, which consists of abstaining from the consumption of substances with unwholesome tastes that cause disorders of *vāyu*, *pitta*, and others distinct from those [kapha-related disorders]. Fasting is the medicine until the point where it has ascended through all the tissues (*dhātu*). The meaning is that performing the action of eliminating the other *doṣas* is an excellent medicine. That same [condition] should be understood as a disorder localized in a single tissue (*ekadhātugata-āmaya*), whereas [the previous case] was a disorder pervading all tissues (*yāvaddhātugata-sāmaya*).

The purposeful effort toward the process of digesting the morbid humors (*doṣa*) and their transformations by means of the digestive fire, which is intensely thickened by the stomach (*pakvāśaya*), results precisely in the act of fasting (*laṅghana*).

Now, [one might object]: "The knowledge of the absence of the provocation of the *doṣas* has for its object a cognition produced by a cognition distinct from the cognition regarding the consumption of unwholesome tastes (*virasa*) which are the causes of the effects of various diseases, because it has for its object a cognition that generates a capable inclination"—by such a mode of formal inference (*anumāna-prayoga*), once there is the knowledge of the cessation of disease, the knowledge of the absence of disease arises.

Keeping in mind the underlying concern—how the knowledge of the absence of that [disease] can be obtained without the provocation of the humors (doṣas)—he states another underlying intention for the sūtra beginning with "viruddha":
"By ascending through all the bodily constituents (dhātus) born from mutually antagonistic tastes, one becomes possessed of a single constituent. (24)
He explains the meaning of this:

"The movement of the humors (doṣa) and tissues (dhātu) caused by a specific latent impression (saṃskāra) arising from indigestion produced by eating a substance with a single discordant taste—that movement arises from eating a substance with a single discordant taste. When it is observed that this movement results in the circulation of multiple tissues, how can the knowledge arise that 'this is a disease causing a disorder of a single tissue,' given that the state of having indigestion produced by eating a substance with a single taste lacks the quality of being produced by eating multiple substances with discordant tastes? Therefore, a disease born from eating substances with discordant tastes [is diagnosed] only after it has ascended into the various tissues."

It should not be argued that, because there is no means of reversal [for the disease], the absence of the cause [of the disease] indicates the absence of the disease itself—and since that absence is not caused by anything else—the effect, which is the absence of the disease produced by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), must necessarily be brought about by fasting (*laṅghana*), the counteragent to its cause; and thus, by the means of inference (*anumāna*) that "wherever there is an absence of indigestion, there is an absence of disease," once a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the two is established, the digestion of the humors (*doṣapacana*) would be the counteragent. [Reason: Because the absence of the cause of a disease serves as the indicator for the absence of that disease, and because that absence is not caused by anything other than [the removal of the cause]. [Example: This is a disease arising from a single element (*dhātu*) or destiny (*gati*); this is a disease arising from two humors (*doṣa*) or destinies. [Application: Therefore, the absence of the disease produced by indigestion must be brought about precisely by fasting, the counteragent to its cause. [Conclusion: Thus, when the pervasion exists—namely, that "wherever there is an absence of indigestion, there is an absence of disease"—then the digestion of the humors would be the counteragent. This is not to be said.

The *doṣas*, having become corrupted, become agitated; it is precisely this agitation of the constituent elements (*dhātu*) that causes the destruction of life. Therefore, it should be understood that the practice of fasting is necessary until one reaches the knowledge of the *doṣas* returning to their non-altered state. By means of this, the cessation of the provocation of the *doṣas* occurs—this is the meaning.

Now, it may be argued that when indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arises from consuming substances containing conflicting tastes (*viruddharasa*), the prescribed rule is to perform fasting (*laṅghana*) until that indigestion is digested; for this is appropriate up until the cessation of the provocation of the humors (*doṣaprakopa*). This is because it is observed that once the indigestion is removed by fasting, the provocation of the wind humor (*pavana*) is likewise removed. In that case, substances such as oil (*taila*) serve as a remedy. However, when indigestion arises from consuming substances whose tastes provoke the bile humor (*pitta-doṣa*), its provocation occurs.

Since fasting and similar measures eliminate pitta, its cessation occurs through decoctions or powders. Likewise, when indigestion arises from consuming substances that cause the transformation of food (pacana-vikāra), a disorder of kapha is produced; astringent extracts, pastes, powders, and so forth serve as their remedies. Thus, there are many means for the alleviation of various diseases. When the humors (doṣas) become aggravated by indigestion, they cause a disturbance of the bodily tissues (dhātu-kṣobha) for a certain period of time. In that regard, this is the procedure for performing fasting.

When a disorder characterized by the drying of the bodily constituents (*dhātu-śoṣa*) as its sole effect is observed, arising from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), a corresponding fever (*jvara*) arises; for in that case, the digestion of the *āma*-dosha acts as the regulating factor. That [dosha] produced by indigestion, remaining within, partakes of all other tastes (*rasa*) that have become vitiated (*virasa*). The dosha produced by those impressions partakes of the other doshas.

When that *doṣa* (humoral disorder) reaches the pathways of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and performs its function of agitating those constituents, the very first moment one perceives a distinct perception of an unpleasant odor on the surface of one's own palm—that alone serves as the determining factor for the etiology (*nidāna*) of such a fever. This is because it constitutes the cause of the subsequent effects arising from the provocation of the *doṣa*, extending up to the point where the knowledge of the prior absence of those specific effects and the absence of their manifestation are cut off.
The meaning is that until that point, the administration of fasting (*laṅghana*) serves as the appropriate medicine.

Now, one might object: "Let the procedure of fasting (*laṅghana*) be prescribed for as long as the knowledge of a specific fracture—caused by the vitiation of the bodily fluids (*rasa*) due to indigestion residing in the bones—has arisen. However, the effect of a future disorder arising from the movement of humors (*doṣa*), namely the effect of irregular fever (*viṣamajvara*), cannot be treated by gathering the knowledge of its concomitance through repeated observation once the knowledge of its symptoms has arisen; for how can there be a determination of inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*) regarding a future disease when there is no knowledge of its symptoms? To this, he says: "By taste," etc. (*rasa-iti*).

Fever born of undigested matter (āmaja) arises when it is overcome by the dominance of a single humor due to the excess of tastes that are indigestible, tasteless, or incompatible; having fallen from its own site, it manifests externally as a blazing heat. || 25 ||

Is it not the case that the analysis [of the compound] is *doṣāṇāṃ pācanam* (the ripening of the humors)? Here, it is a genitive *tatpuru�sa* compound. It appears that the very act of ripening those [humors] is the remedial action (*nivartaka-karma*). Since it is possible for the humors to have as their sole result the alteration of the movement of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), if it were stated that "the ripening of the humors must necessarily be performed by means of fasting (*laṅghana*)," there would be a logical contradiction.

In an action that nourishes the *dhātus* and assists the human purpose, there is the performance of the act of fasting (*laṅghana*) for the sake of digesting those *doṣas*; this is because such an action has as its sole nature the capacity to accomplish a task that is weaker than the [original] *doṣa*. This is because when an effect must be produced by a superior causal power, it is likewise [the case] when one performs an action whose causal power is weaker than that [original cause]. It is likewise so in the case of performing the act of fasting for the sake of digesting those *doṣas* during an action that nourishes the *dhātus* and assists the human purpose.

The effect of digestion free from the defects of the final stage of wind (*vāyu*) is indicated [by this]. Therefore, the procedure is to perform fasting (*laṅghana*) until there is cessation of indigestion arising from that discordant taste (*virasa*). Otherwise, due to the indigestion of tastes, the tastes themselves become discordant. Through the abundance of those discordant tastes, the humors (*doṣa*) also become weakened in strength. When the cause is deficient, the effect becomes deficient; where discordant tastes manifest, there the humors also become vitiated.

Due to the excessive increase of the humors (doṣa) and their transformations, when indigestion (ajīrṇa) born of a loss of relish occurs, even the act of kindling the digestive fire is not performed by the movement of the humors. The meaning is that the gastric fire (jaṭharānala), abandoning its own place and flaring up externally, manifests as a fever accompanied by phlegm (sāmajvara).

Now, it may be argued that mere worldly conditions alone are not the cause; rather, things such as the performance of good deeds and specialized knowledge are also possible [as factors], yet sin committed in a previous birth afflicts one in the form of disease.
Whichever karma, whether auspicious or inauspicious, has been performed must necessarily be experienced.

This is to be understood according to the statement of the Vārttika: when the consumption of substances that are either flavorful or flavorless occurs, diseases may arise in some individuals. Since it is impossible to state as a universal rule that this happens in all cases, one must follow the maxim "everything is wholesome for the strong. Accordingly, in the case of a strong person, even when a state of undigested rasa (rasājīrṇa), an excess of unpalatable rasa, or a clash of incompatible rasas occurs, disease is not observed there. Thus, in certain instances, mere worldly causal conditions alone are not the cause.

Since effects consisting of undigested food (*āma*) and the like are possible, and since the force of *prārabdha* karma is powerful, it would be futile to maintain that diseases born of the indigestion of *rasa* (*rasājīrṇa*) can occur everywhere. Therefore, where there is an increase in *āma* that produces disease, the corresponding effect of such a disease manifests. To illustrate: due to the variety of effects arising from the indigestion of *rasa*, from deficient or antagonistic *rasas*, and so forth, one can further state the variety of causes that generate those respective diseases.

As long as there is a disease produced by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), fasting alone is its remedy, because it is removable by a causal complex distinct from the complex that merely removes the disease, and because it cannot be removed without the causal complex consisting of fasting and the like. Therefore, whatever kind of causal complex for consuming unpalatable substances occurs, such a variety of the effects of that disease is possible. For instance—since all diseases arise due to the predominance of their respective causes, thirteen types of fever and disorders of the *sannipāta* (combined humors) come into being.

When a disorder arises due to the contact with unpalatable tastes and the vitiated humors (*doṣa*), having reached all the channels and regions of the head-lotus from the nectar situated there—this being produced from the state of sweet taste—then the undigested essence (*āmarasa*) ignites a fever characterized by the disease-form known as *tāndrika-doṣa*. This occurs because it is born from the indigestion of rasa, from unpalatable tastes, and from excessive or incompatible tastes that have not been digested. Indeed, that sweet taste is the disease of rasa-indigestion, which is the *tāndrika* humor.

That [rasa], having its flavor rendered tasteless by dependence on that [dosha], arises from the accumulation of diseases born of such retention, through the force of the movement of vāyu, and from the association with the accumulation of undigested (āma) and virasika substances; in that case, contact with nectar (amṛta) becomes nourishing.

It must be an object of knowledge concerning the cognition of the absence of similarity between the movement of words and the movement of the wind that has entered the channels of the vessels located within the porous interior of the *sarandhraka*—which produces indigestion and serves as the support for the movement of air—and which indicates a fever with undigested toxins (*sāmajvara*) caused by defects in the joints associated with odors; this cognition pertains to the fact that the collection of the five letters of the *ka*-group, situated in the regions of the feet, abdomen, genitals, and back, manifests the state of the other letters and their movements, because it possesses an excess of humors produced by tastes that are undigested, tasteless, excessive, or incompatible.

"That which is not thus is not thus. This is due to the contact with thirty-four and thirty-six vessels (sirās), which indicate the words consisting of the five groups of consonants beginning with *ka*—associated with the letter *a*—in their sequence through the regions of the joints, the groin, the fever, the feet, the seeds (*bīja*), the flanks, the penis, and the back, as impelled by the defects residing in the junctions (*sandhi*).

This is an internal-dosha-associated sāma fever, because it possesses an excess of doshas produced by undigested tastes, a lack of relish, and incompatible tastes; and because it indicates abdominal pain in the navel, pain in the feet, bodily luster, distress, and loss of strength; and because it is characterized by the manifestation of the five consonants of the *ca*-group located in the navel-lotus and the regions of the knees, heart, back, and abdomen—these being the specific indicators of kapha-originated heat and internal dosha-induced sāma fever, which are recognized through their similarity to other such phonemes.

Due to the contact of the thirty-four channels with the five consonants of the *ca*-group—located at the back of the knees, the navel-lotus, and the knee-lotus—a fever arises characterized by internal defects such as burning, intense heat, various forms of delusion, agony, excessive head-shaking, diarrhea, hiccups, and severe dyspnea. It inflames [the body] and, having circulated through all the pathways of the *dhātus* for ten days, it separates the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) from the *dhātus*. Therefore, this is designated as "internal defect" (*āntaradoṣa*).

This is the internal defect: when there is a collection of words consisting of a group of syllables that convey meaning—such as those situated on the back and sides near the knee-lotus, or those located in the region of the navel which convey the five *ca*-group consonants constituting the *upadha* (penultimate) syllable—the sentence causes a sound characterized by a resonance distinct from the other syllables appropriate to the *ca*-group to be heard. Having necessarily perceived that difference in the syllables, at that time, due to contact with the bile (*pitta*) produced by that disagreeable meaning, the nectar moving through the channels of the vessels causes the drying up of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) residing in that lotus.

It may also be remediable; however, this [condition] should be understood as an incurable disease. It is known through the following inference: the heart-lotus, which is surrounded by thirty-four vessels—[a state characterized by] the knowledge that the lotus of the calves (which indicates *sāmajvara* caused by the defect of incompatible food) possesses no similarity to other phonemes in manifesting words consisting of the five letters of the *ṭa*-group, and likewise the navel-lotus surrounded by a wheel of thirty vessels and the line of hair surrounded by four vessels—possesses an excess of humors produced by undigested tastes, an excess of unwholesome tastes, and an abundance of tastelessness due to indigestion (*rasājīrṇa*); for whatever is not thus [remediable] is not thus [incurable]. Thus, by means of such an inference.

The cognition produced by the collection of words consisting of the phonemes *o*, *va*, *dha*, and *ga*—which indicate the five consonants of the *ka*-group applied to the lotus of the shanks, [and which] are characterized by the lotus-line of hair surrounding the lotus of the shanks, the lotus of the feet, the lotus of the navel, the lotus of the sides, and the lotus of the heart; [this cognition arises] from a fever of a non-distinct, contradictory [mental state].

Due to the contact of all the channels (sirā), that which is capable of producing dryness along with pain is burned. This is because the lotus situated at the heart is supported by thirty-four channels that bring about the perception of color and are covered by two pairs of channels supporting the sides, which are themselves connected to the row of body hair; these, in turn, are connected to twenty channels hanging from the lotuses of the calves that awaken [sensations], and to thirty channels hanging from the lotus covering the navel that awaken [sensations]. Furthermore, because the wheel-like lotus covering the navel occupies a circular region, the fever burns there.

It likewise manifests in the abdomen; it inflames the heart-lotus, produces a burning sensation, and causes vertigo. Therefore, because he is characterized by these symptoms, that patient lives. This *sāmajvara* is born from the provocation of the *pitta* humor, as it is the effect of the provocation of the *pitta* humor. Due to contact with an excess of humors produced by the undigested essence (*rasājīrṇa*) of nectar moving through the channels of the veins supporting various lotuses, and by the influence of excessive and contradictory tastes, it inflames the region of the calf-lotus.

Likewise, the region of the navel lotus is burned; and in the same manner, it causes pain in the region of the heart lotus. Because it consists of substances that nourish the nectar of the syllables pervaded by the impressions of discordant tastes—which indicate the transformation of the colors within that lotus—it produces a burning sensation and induces fainting. That very fever of the humors (*doṣajvara*) is designated as the "confusion-defect" (*vibhramadoṣa*).

The lotus of the thighs, which generates the *ṛ*-vowels; the two lotuses of the breasts, enveloped by fifty vessels of the five *ta*-group consonants; the lotus of the throat region, enveloped by thirty vessels; and the lotus situated within the neck, enveloped by sixteen vessels—the channels and pathways of these vessels that sustain the movement of the vital air (*pavana*) become afflicted when they come into contact with vessels characterized by an excess of morbid humors (*doṣa*) arising from undigested food, a preponderance of unwholesome tastes, or incompatible tastes. Thus, the fever accompanied by undigested toxins (*sāmajvara*), joined with the defects of the vessels, circulates through the pathways of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) for a period of fifteen days.

Because it possesses the desire for the expansion of the lotus situated in that region, the fever that has spread through all the limbs via the afflicted channels is pacified. However, by virtue of contact with the undigested and flavorless state of the nutrient-fluid (*rasa-dhātu*), that *rasa* becomes a disorder of the tissues (*dhātu-vikāra*) and causes coldness of the body. The lotus in the pelvic region, which generates the letter *ṛ*, is surrounded by thirty vessels; the lotus that awakens the letters *pa* and *pha* is surrounded by sixteen vessels; and the lotus that supports the letters *ba* and *bha* and produces speech and chatter is surrounded by fifty vessels.

This *sāmajvara* is designated as the disorder characterized by delirium (*pralāpa-doṣa*). The fever recurs for a period of fourteen days, which is the duration of the provocation of the humors (*doṣa-prakopa-kālāvadhi*). Furthermore, the pelvic region (*kaṭi-pradeśa*), which produces the letter *e*, is surrounded by four vessels and serves as the substrate for the letters *ya*, *va*, *ra*, and *la*. Likewise, there is the lotus of the *rasa-bandhana* (vital essence-binding) presided over by the letter *ya*, which is surrounded by two vessels; the region of the *uṣṭha-padma* (camel-hump lotus) which indicates the letter *repha* (the letter *r*) and is surrounded by sixteen vessels; and the *gandhavāha-padma* (fragrance-carrying lotus) which conveys the letter *la* and is surrounded by two vessels.

Due to the excess of humors (doṣa) arising from undigested tastes, deficient tastes, excessive tastes, and incompatible tastes, fever born of the *āmāśaya* (undigested matter) manifests itself externally by causing a disturbance in the lotus of the tongue—which is encircled by two vessels and indicates the letter *ya* through the binding of tastes—and in the region of the lotus of the chest—which is encircled by sixteen vessels and indicates the letter *ra*. Thus, it takes the form of disorders such as deafness and crookedness, while burning outwardly.

The experience of the cognition of the distinction between the cognitions of individual letters arises from a preceding cognition regarding the distinctions among various fevers caused by specific humors (*doṣa*), because it is a cognition whose object is the contact with vessels (*sirā*) supported by the lotuses presiding over those respective letters—which are produced by a causal complex generated by a single cause—just as [the cognition] has as its object the contact with vessels produced by the complex of factors supporting the lotuses presiding over those respective letters. Whatever is not thus is not thus, like a jar; such is the inference (*anumāna*) that serves as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the experience of the cognition of the distinction between letters.
The meaning is: because of possessing the experience of a cognition whose object is the knowledge of a fever produced by the [three] humors (doṣa).

Now, the meaning is as follows: all diseases arise from undigested food (*āmāśaya*), from the transformation of tastes (*virasaja*), from disorders born of indigestion (*āmayājīrṇa*), and from the vitiation of tastes (*virasa-viṣama*). Although they appear in various forms due to temporal differences within a fever of balanced humors (*sāmajvara*) produced by a single set of causal conditions, nevertheless, even for an effect born of a single cause, there exists a diversity of causes when the continuity is interrupted by a powerful external factor. Therefore, since the effect is one and the same in its nature as a product, the cause of everything must also be one. Consequently, that which delimits the effect produced by indigestion is the very remedy that eliminates indigestion alone.

For this very reason, diseases produced by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), as well as diseases arising from the unwholesome and irregular tastes (*virasa-viṣama-rasa*) born of indigestion, become differentiated according to the specific variations of their respective causes. The meaning is that because diseases arising from the unwholesome and irregular consumption of food due to indigestion are distinct from those caused by mere indigestion, their respective remedies are also distinct. Nevertheless, for diseases produced solely by indigestion, fasting (*laṅghana*) alone is the exclusive remedy.

In that regard, it does not depend even on another set of conditions for its cessation, because it is produced by a minimal causal complex. He states, "by unbalanced tastes," etc., [meaning]: various diseases arise from the consumption of unbalanced tastes and corrupted tastes other than indigestion (ajīrṇa) produced by that same unbalanced taste-complex. The time for the digestion of the *doṣas* is dependent upon the refinement (*prasāda*) of all the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), beginning with those whose tastes have been processed by the digestion of unbalanced tastes. || 26 ||

The purpose of human effort (*puruṣārtha*) consists precisely in the performance of that which brings about the cessation of diseases produced by the consumption of unwholesome tastes (*viṣamarasa*), for such effort aims at the very result of counteracting the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from the defects of unwholesome tastes. Therefore, the remedy for those diseases is specifically that which destroys the particular latent impression produced by the effects arising from the consumption of substances possessing unwholesome tastes. Consequently, even diseases produced by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) are distinct [from other types], because they are produced by the humors (*doṣa*) resulting from the unwholesome and irregular tastes generated by indigestion.

Although indigestion is one and the same in both cases, the effect nevertheless differs due to the diversity of causes, namely the difference in the tastes that serve as its generators. This is the meaning.

Is it not the case that fever (*sāmajvara*) is differentiated by the diversity of its causal conditions (*samayabheda*), much like the manifoldness of its remedies? One set of causal conditions for the production of fever takes the form of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*). Another set of causal conditions consists of the factors that produce the irregular movement of the humors (*doṣaviṣamagati*), arising from contact with vessels (*sirā*) containing the unpleasant and discordant tastes born of indigestion. The remedy for that, however, is the causal condition consisting of the consumption of various substances possessing those unpleasant tastes.

It must be stated that one should perform the digestion (*pacana*) of each respective humor (*doṣa*) by means of its specific counteragent, until the absence of humoral disorders born of the *doṣas* is reached, and until the movement of the humors has ceased. If that were the case, as long as the movement of the *doṣas* residing in the bone, marrow, and semen (*śukla*) continues, it causes the loss of life; because there would be no application of those counteragents, the time for the digestion of the *doṣas* depends upon [the physician's] skill (*prasāda*). Thus, the digestion of the *doṣas* does not bring about health until that point. Due to this incongruity, he says: "In this way" (*evam*). "In this way, those located in a single *dhātu* are easily curable. (27)

In the manner described above, this rule applies where a disorder arising from the movement of a single *dhātu* (tissue element) is observed; there is no such fixed rule regarding disorders caused by two or three *doṣas*. Thus, the meaning is that diseases involving a single *dhātu* are easily curable.

Now, by what means is the movement of the *doṣas* and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) to be known? The movement of the *pavana-doṣa* (wind humor) is to be understood through its natural transformations. Since it is impossible to describe the movement of the "lame" *kapha* and the "lame" [wind], they are both termed "lame."

The region of wind (*pavana*) extends from the lotus of the feet up to the region of the navel, reaching as far as the seed-lotus (*bījapadma*). The region of bile (*pitta*) begins from the side-lotuses of the seed-lotus and extends up to the heart-lotus. The region above that, extending up to the region of the head, is the region of phlegm (*kapha*). Having thus understood the distinction between these regions and determined such a movement of the humors (*doṣas*), one is able to practice by discerning: "This disease is curable; this disease is incurable. The combination of one humor with another humor is called a dual disorder (*dvandva*).

In some cases, *tridoṣatva* (the state of being caused by three *doṣas*) refers to the combination of all three *doṣas*. To address the underlying doubt as to how everything is to be understood, he says: "arising from two tastes," etc.

Those arising from two tastes, those resulting from the movement of two *doṣas*, those following the flesh and fat, those where a single *doṣa* is predominant in its digestion, and those born from two *doṣas* are difficult to cure. (28)

Regarding the two tastes that serve as the causes for the provocation (*prakopa*) of *vāta* and *pitta*: a taste that is slightly sweet yet disagreeable (*virasa*) is the cause for the provocation of *vāta*; a taste that is excessively sweet yet disagreeable is the cause for the provocation of *pitta*. Those very same disagreeable tastes produce distinct effects. The disorder (*vikāra*) arising from these two is called "born of two tastes" (*dvirasaja*). The term "movement of two doṣas" (*dvidoṣapracāra*) is explained as follows: it moves, thus it is "moving" (*cara*); it moves intensely, thus it is "intense movement" (*pracara*). As for the statement, "those which are the constituents of rasa, blood, and muscle are followed by muscle and fat," it means they are associated with the muscle and fat tissues.

The head consists of six lotuses; the head is the support of flesh, while that which supports fat is distinct. The two *rasas* (fluids) that cause the drying up of those tissues are distinct. Among them, those two *rasas* which function toward their own corresponding effects are the primary agents of action (*karmakāraka*). Thus, this application of the aphorism occurs wherever the digestion of a single dominant *doṣa* by means of *rasa* is observed. Another method is also indicated.

Some explain that "pacana" (digestion/cooking) refers specifically to the removal of the provocation of humors caused by the vitiation of tastes through the administration of digestive, lightening, and medicinal therapies. What is intended here is that the processing of the primary tastes of the great minerals—such as mercury, its subordinates, and metals—which consists of the application of medicinal formulations, brings about the cessation of all diseases. The tastes inherent in those substances are designated as "fiery" (*taijasa*). Through contact with fire of a similar nature, the respective qualities manifest within those tastes.

All this fiery substance (*taijasadravya*) is a remedy for diseases produced by the provocation caused by undigested matter (*āma*), virasas, and poisons (*viṣa*). It is the cause of the manifestation of superior tastes within substances possessing the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*) through contact with fire, because it is a substance whose form consists primarily of the qualities of taste over a long period of time, like oil, ghee, or electuaries (*lehya*).

The quality of the six flavors (ṣaḍrasa) and so forth residing in a substance possessing great potency produced by contact with fire is characterized primarily by qualities distinguished by the taste-qualities—such as becoming sweet or bitter—arising from the causal conditions of time, processing, and application; this is because it is a substance whose temporal duration is increased and whose qualities are distinguished by the manifestation of qualities produced by contact with fire. "Whatever is not thus is not thus, like time and so forth"—this is intended to demonstrate that the knowledge arising from the means of valid cognition (anumāna) serves as the indicator of that substratum.

Thus, regarding dual diseases (*dvandvaroga*), among all substances, there is knowledge of the counteracting agent (*nivartaka*), knowledge of the non-counteracting agent (*anivartaka*), and knowledge concerning both; this knowledge is the cause for the effect that counteracts the disease. This is because it possesses the nature of a substance whose sole function is to counteract [the disease]. Furthermore, other tastes (*rasa*), secondary tastes (*uparasa*), and the great tastes (*mahārasa*) common to metals provide a quality (*guṇa*) through the application of a formulation (*yoga*) produced by the conjunction with other substances. This is because they possess the nature of substances due to the absence of the presence of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that would bring about a different, adverse taste.

Is it not the case that fevers produced by the indigestion (ajīrṇa) of unpalatable substances caused by the provocation of the respective *doṣas* are remedial to those specific *doṣas*, while fevers produced by the indigestion of sweet-tasting substances that cause the provocation of the *doṣas* are also remedial to those specific *doṣas*, because they are produced by the indigestion of sweet-tasting substances that cause the provocation of the *doṣas*? Furthermore, the unpalatable tastes produced by indigestion perform the function of being complications (*upadrava*) of fever, because they are substances that serve as the cause for a fever characterized by those complications.
To demonstrate the arising of the ten types of diseases that constitute complications which generate the knowledge of the provocation of fever, he explains [the verse] with the word "evam" (thus).
And thus they are born from mutual faults. || 29 ||

Ten complications arising from fever manifest as mutual causes: dyspnea, fainting, vertigo, vomiting, thirst, diarrhea, hiccup, cough, bodily pain, and delusion. These are the ten complications of fever.

The causal complex that brings about the manifestation of those afflictions is the cause of the effect known as the aggravation of fever (*jvara-prakopa*). This is because [the complex] consists of contact with unwholesome tastes, foul odors, poisons, and worms; up to and including contact with the channels (*sirā*) that support the lotuses which sustain the bodily constituents (*dhātu*); and the mutual interaction consisting of diseases produced by the derangement of the movement of the vital air (*pavana*) arising from such contact, and diseases produced by the movement of the vital air residing within the channels. Thus, the meaning is that diseases born of one another's humors (*doṣa*) have the aggravation of fever as their causal effect.

Now, one might object: if a fever born from the excess of three tastes has reached the tissues of flesh and fat (*māṃsa-medas*), and if a fever born from the excess of the three aforementioned tastes pursues the fever all the way to the tissues of bone and marrow (*asthi-majjā*), then—since a fever born from unpalatable tastes (*virasa*) which causes the provocation of the three *doṣas* ascends into the tissues of bone and marrow—it could be designated as a "fever of the three *doṣas*" (*tridoṣajvara*). To this, he says: "From two tastes" (*dvirasa*).
Diseases that correspond to the nature of the *rasa* of the three *doṣas* arising from the excess of two tastes are incurable. (30)

The two tastes that cause the provocation of *vāta* and *pitta* become the provocators of fever (*jvara*) arising from the state of undigested matter (*āma-rasa*). At that time, the state of possessing the taste of undigested matter (*āma-rasa-virasavat-tva*) produces a contradictory effect, because it is a substance whose causal factor is time (*kāla-hetuka-dravyatvāt*), which generates another discordant taste starting from the two tastes and ending with the discordant tastes. Thus, this fever, having pervaded the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*), becomes a destroyer of life. Such a disease is incurable. To illustrate:

As for the statement that "the effect of the collection of factors consisting of undigested matter (*āma*) and tasteless bodily fluids (*amarasa*), which produces various fevers, liberates the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) after drying up the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*)"—this requires reflection. *Āma* is the causal complex that produces fever alone; having generated the fever and itself established the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced at that very moment within those respective effects, it ceases to be perceived as a distinct entity. This is because, just like things produced by various other causal complexes, all fevers are produced from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*).

If it were the case that a fever produced merely by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that generates fever releases the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), then there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, with this reservation, he says: "In this way," etc.
Thus, those [fevers] located in a single *dhātu* are incurable. (31)

In the manner thus described, those afflictions and diseases are life-destroying, because they are substances that cause harm to life by being the causes of fevers following upon the defects produced by their acidity, just like diseases arising from the consumption of poison. Furthermore, the vessels supporting the lotuses that indicate the five groups of letters following the path of the *varṇa* (phonemes) nourish and dehydrate the bodily constituents (*dhātus*), because they are the support for the body which is dependent upon the fluids (*rasas*) contained therein.

Because it possesses the nature of a rasa-element (*rasa-dhātu*) that functions as the cause of the pathological transformation resulting from the movement of the *doṣas*—which has reached the channels (*sirā*) that activate the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) following that [initial] taste—and because, having reached the undigested element (*adhaudha-dhātu*), its movement causes disorders of the wind (*pavana-vikāra*) due to its capacity to produce other disorders, it brings about both dyspnea (*śvāsa*) and fainting (*mūrchā*). Since both of these are observed to be born from the rasa-element, that very fever (*jvara*), having dried up the rasa-element, manifests upon reaching that element in order to dry up the other elements.

Dizziness and vomiting occur; likewise, having reached the muscle tissue (*māṃsadhātu*), hiccup and grief arise. In this very same way, having reached other tissues, dizziness and the disease of hiccup are produced. That same fever, producing cough day after day, persists. Having reached the bone (*asthi*), it causes swelling. That same fever, following the course of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*), takes hold of the marrow tissue (*majjādhātu*) and expands. Then it assumes ten forms of disease. Thus has the explanation of the aphorism regarding those born from other humors been provided.

Now, it may be argued that defects such as those arising from tastes, the loss of taste, excessive tastes, and incompatible tastes are the causes of all diseases. Furthermore, the defects consisting in the knowledge of pure tastes—which indicate the absence of morbid transformations caused by the defects arising from the loss of taste due to the lack of knowledge regarding the manifestation of the qualities of *ajīrṇa* (indigestion)—are the agents that bring about the cessation of those morbid transformations. Thus, these defects are the causes of all diseases.

Thus, when the three *doṣas* are corrupted, they become the causes of transformation for the body and its inhabitant, who consist of the *doṣas* and the *dhātus*. However, by the power of the ripening of virtuous karma (*sukarma*), the *doṣas*, being uncorrupted, become preventers of transformation. As for the assertion that all diseases are born from a loss of taste (*virasa*), that is not tenable under scrutiny; with this in mind, he says—due to the underlying dissatisfaction—"they are not *doṣas*":
"Those who are free of *doṣas*, those with *doṣas*, and those with balanced *doṣas*—all these are subject to disease. (32)

The five vital airs—prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—are those that assist in the functioning of the body. How is it that the state of being "non-defect" (adoṣatva) of that which supports the body appears correctly? Because even pitta is indeed a *doṣa*, it encompasses the nature of the fivefold defects; it collects, digests, separates, and excretes. Since these five types of functions support the body, and because the *doṣa* of kapha also acts as a strengthener of the body, the triad of *doṣas* protects the body.
Therefore, one should not suspect how the state of being "non-defect" can be beneficial to the body.

The meaning of the term *adoṣa* (non-defect) is the absence of the *doṣas*' capacity to produce morbid transformations (*vikāra*). *Sadoṣas* refers to those *doṣas* characterized by a state or quality that brings about the effects of transformation; such *sadoṣas* cause the depletion of the seven bodily constituents (*dhātus*). Consequently, the body's state of being *sadoṣa* is acquired through the force of experiencing past unwholesome actions (*duṣkarma*). By this, the constituents are afflicted and suffering is experienced. *Samadoṣatva* (equilibrium of the *doṣas*) means the state of the *doṣas* being characterized by a course of action that avoids both [depletion and aggravation] and does not increase them. By this, the constituents are nourished, and they attain freedom from disease (*nīrogatva*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the body must be protected in such a way that the humors (doṣas) remain in equilibrium. At all times, some cause for the effect produced by the humors residing in the body—which has a single taste as its underlying cause—must be stated; this very effect, namely disease, which arises from the transformation of tastes into vitiated states, is to be understood in this manner.

Now, an objection may be raised: "It has been stated that disease is the disharmony (*vaiṣamya*) of that *doṣa* which is characterized by an irregular course (*viṣamagati*), whereas health is the designation for the balanced course (*samā gati*) of the *doṣa*. If that is so, then the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*) consist of the seven constituent tissues (*dhātu*). The consumption of the six discordant tastes (*virasa-ṣaṭka*) causes the wasting of the tissues (*dhātuśoṣaka*), because such substances possess the nature of tastes that are discordant with the *doṣas* and *dhātus*. By this inference, the causal relationship of tastes and other factors toward the effect of tissue-wasting is established. Therefore, the disharmony of the *doṣas* is disease, and the equilibrium of the *doṣas* is health. Since what has been propounded contradicts this [view], he says: "ta iti" (Regarding those...).
These three are the causes of the defects, namely the seven constituent elements (dhātus). || 33 ||

The designation "seven constituents" (*dhātavaḥ*) is merely conventional. It is certain that there are only six tastes (*rasas*). One need not ask how their number could be seven; for it is true that one may speak of "six tastes and seven constituents" with the intention of expressing the non-distinction between taste and blood (*asṛk*), since taste itself is blood. Thus:

A substance possessing the quality of having a sweet taste is experienced as a "tasteful substance," because there exists no substance that possesses a taste distinct from a manifested taste. Therefore, since qualities such as taste do not subsist without a substratum possessing those qualities, a substance is necessary; for it is said that "qualities have a substance as their locus. Because the body is a substance composed of the seven constituents (*dhātu*), and because tastes and so forth are qualities, and because the distinction between a quality and its possessor is established, tastes and the other qualities must have a substance as their locus.

Therefore, it should not be said that [taste] is distinct from the six tastes because it consists of the seven *dhātus*, for it is essentially composed of substance (*dravya*) and taste (*rasa*). The tastes situated within the body transform into the form of the *dhātus*. Since these *dhātus* are based upon substance and are qualities of substance, no distinction is perceived between them, just as with color and other qualities. A substance possessing taste is the object of the gustatory sense-organ; a substance possessing color is the object of the visual sense-organ.

The substance of taste (*rasadravya*) is a substance possessing both form and taste due to similarity. The *dhātu* (tissue) is indeed a modification of the six tastes; thus, the seven [tastes] are not perceived by a single sense organ. That which is of the same genus as them is found among the tastes that are of the same genus as the seven *dhātus*. Remaining within, they nourish the *dhātu* itself. For example, the sweet juice residing within a stalk of sugarcane, wherever it exists through the process of division, takes up the sweet juice inherent therein and, by dividing the substance produced from that association, creates the taste.

Immediately thereafter, having abandoned that sweet taste, one perceives the substance associated with it as distinct from it and as its substrate, just as one perceives color and other qualities. [Objection: Is this not like the case of "the sword has become blue," where there is no separate substance? [Reply: In the case of "the blue pot," the blue color residing in the pot appears as a constituent part of another substance. Since there is no substance apart from the taste here, in these cases as well, visual perception arises characterized by their status as elements (*dhātu*), their distinct forms, and their respective specific qualities.

In the same way, they are called "saline," "pungent," and "astringent," just like their substrates and so forth. They reside within the limbs of the body; therefore, they are called "tastes" (*rasas*) and so on. It should not be said that the body consists of seven constituent elements (*dhātus*), for the elements themselves consist of taste, and the body is a substance whose essence is taste because it is enveloped by the seven elements. For that reason, it appears as a single entity with the shape of a broad base and belly. The sweet taste transforms into the form of semen and phlegm (*kapha*). The sour taste transforms into the form and appearance of marrow.

The salty taste transforms into the form of the unstable element (asthi). The bitter taste transforms while assuming the form of a modification of fat (medas). The pungent taste transforms into the form of the marrow element (majjā-dhātu). The astringent taste appears as the form of the plasma and blood elements (rasa-asṛg-dhātu). Therefore, although they are designated separately, it cannot be said that they manifest the tastes and so forth, just like their substrates and other factors. Having reached the interior of the body from their external locations, those respective tastes dissolve into the corresponding elements of their own kind.
And they nourish those respective elements; the meaning is that, without doubt, a substance characterized by pure qualities and possessing many flavors brings about firmness of the body.

Now, one might object: when the wind-element (pavana-bhūta), provoked by the consumption of substances with [opposite] tastes and desiring to dry up the tissues of rasa and blood, seeks to alleviate its own provocation, there exists a single substance possessing an astringent taste (kaṣāya-rasa). To claim that an astringent taste can counteract the provocation of the wind-element in the tissues of rasa and blood is improper; thus, the previous commentary on the aphorism is not withstands scrutiny. Anticipating this objection, he says: "That [blood], accompanied by wind, increased by wind, and conditioned by the qualities of wind—dryness and lightness—is located within the rasa and blood. (34)

The meaning of this is as follows: it can be stated that tastes belonging to the same genus (*sajātīya*) as the astringency (*kaṣāyatva*) produced by a specific substance-conjunction are not obstructors of the causes of the transformation of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). This is because they possess the nature of being substances that oppose and obstruct those [causes] which are of the same genus as them. However, by possessing qualities such as the nature of heat (*uṣṇa-svabhāva-guṇa*) which promotes the flow of the blood constituent (*rasāsṛg-dhātu*), and by possessing the quality of lightness (*laghutva-svabhāva-guṇa*), it causes the drying up (*śoṣaṇa*) of the blood constituent.

Therefore, by consuming the substance of air (pavana) situated in the external region, [the wind], being characterized by specific tastes and qualities produced therein, causes the drying up of the bodily constituents (dhātus). All of this is understood through this statement; nor is there any contradiction with the preceding sūtra. In this matter, scripture itself is the authority.

The six tastes generate the seven constituent elements (dhātus) because they pervade the tastes; for there exists a relationship between the tastes and the elements characterized by their mutual manifestation. Since no distinction is perceived due to the fact that the various types of taste arise from the elements born of the taste-blood (*rasāsṛg-dhātu*), the elements themselves are indeed of an acidic nature. Thus, because the specific bodies correspond to the specific elements, the distinctions produced by the differences in taste are generated by the cognition dependent upon them.

The distinction between substances is likewise perceived; for wherever there is a perception of an abundance of taste, it is precisely therein that an abundance of those respective substances is perceived in those particular trees. Thus, one perceives through the distinction of their respective essences: "This tree is characterized by a sweet taste," "This tree is characterized by a salty taste," and "This tree is characterized by an astringent taste. The meaning is that this is established by the common consensus of many people, as in the expression, "These possess bodies."

[Objection: Is it not the case that the *dhātus* of muscle (*māṃsa*) and fat (*medas*), which reside in the locations of the *pitta* disorder, depend upon sweet taste (*svādurasa*)? Therefore, it is impossible to state that sweet taste has the power to pacify the provocation of *pitta*; there would be a contradiction, because the tastes (*rasas*) are of the nature of the *dhātus*, and the *dhātus* reside in the muscle which itself resides in the [taste]. Thus, it is improper to say that the *dhātus*—which are of the nature of taste and reside in those disorders—can pacify the provocation of the disorder. With this underlying sentiment, he says: "Pitta... "Because it is the substratum of *pitta*, following after the *pitta*, muscle, and fat dependent upon it, it causes the bones to become soft. (35)

Because it is dependent on *pitta*, the *rasa* of the *dhātus* of flesh (*māṃsa*) and fat (*medas*)—due to their being sweet, bitter, and astringent—possesses a quality that opposes the *pitta* residing therein. It cannot be said that pure sweet, pure bitter, or pure astringent tastes [themselves] oppose it, because they are of the nature of the tastes dependent upon those [tissues]. However, since it is appropriate to speak of their opposition to the provocation of *pitta*, and because they are dependent on *pitta*, it follows that *pitta* is subordinate to them; thus, *pitta* is dependent on the tastes.

When there is an aggravation of *pitta*, because only a substance possessing that [corresponding] taste can alleviate it, *pitta* is dependent on the sweet taste (*svādurasa*). Thus, residing in the tissues of muscle and fat (*māṃsa-medas*), it establishes the qualities of softness and bulkiness. Now, one might object: "Diseases caused by the three *doṣas* combined are incurable. To this we reply: the state of being an effect produced by the aggravation of those *doṣas* is caused by disorders arising from unwholesome tastes (*rasavirasādhīnajanya-vikāra-hetuka*), because it is a substance that brings about the effects of increasing or decreasing the *doṣas*. Therefore, he describes the effect based on other *doṣas* suitable for the application of the action associated with the aggravation of astringents (*kaṣāya*)—beginning with the word "slow" (*manda*).
[The humors] are located in the bones, marrow, and fat, possessing qualities of being slightly warm and so forth, equal, increased, or diminished. || 36 ||

The meaning is as follows: *pavanatva* (the state of being wind) is the delimitor of the possession of dull qualities (*mandaguṇavattva*); *pittatva* (the state of being bile) is the delimitor of the possession of hot qualities (*uṣṇaguṇavattva*); and the state of being the substratum of those diminished or increased qualities is the delimitor of the other humors, *kapha*. Such being the case, by bringing together the totality of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) extending even to the *majjā* tissue, it causes the increase of disease and brings that patient to the very brink of death.

Now, one might object: since the diseases descend through the humors (*doṣas*) until they reach the marrow-element (*majjā-dhātu*), and because when there is a totality of humors affecting all the elements, the vital winds (*vāyu*) originating from the life-force (*prāṇa*) residing in the five elements cease to circulate and consequently exit the body, that living being (*jīva*) becomes separated from the body; for the humors have fulfilled their function merely by that much, as there is no further necessity for them to perform the function of entering the semen-element (*śukla-dhātu*). [Response: This is not so. Even if the humors have reached the marrow-element, the life-force (*jīva*) does not depart from the body. For it is observed that even when the humors are extremely aggravated, the life-force remains within the body. Furthermore, the life-force does not depart due to the mere descent of the humors, but rather due to the simultaneous occurrence of the following: the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyus*), the depletion of merit (*puṇya*), and the total obstruction of the channels (*srotas*) by the humors. Moreover, the life-force does not depart because of the absence of the circulation of the winds, but rather because of the presence of the circulation of the winds. Indeed, the life-force remains in the body as long as the winds continue to circulate. And the winds circulate as long as the life-force remains in the body. Therefore, the life-force does not depart from the body merely upon the descent of the humors. Consequently, the life-force is not separated from the body by the departure of the winds. Thus, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, the humors do not cause the life-force to depart from the body, because the life-force is dependent upon the wind (*vāyu*). Since the wind is the primary factor for the maintenance of the life-force, the life-force does not depart from the body merely through the action of the humors. Nor is there any necessity for the humors to enter the semen-element to perform their function, for their function is fully accomplished by their mere descent. Thus, the objection is refuted.
