Furthermore

Therefore, since counting seven elements would be useless due to a lack of justification, he says "adoṣa" (without fault) out of this underlying intention: "They are the movers of the non-defiled elements, the followers of the sequence of the tastes, the stabilizers, the digesters of sap, and the movers of the final element. (37)

The state of being a "cook" (pacanatva) belongs to that which performs this function; it is the state of the humors (doṣas) acting as the movers of the final element (the fire). They are called "movers" (pracārakas) because they move about. The function of nourishing the white element (śukladhātu) is caused by the consumption of pure and sweet tastes; it is not a function of drying up. The term "absence of morbidity" (adoṣatva) means the absence of the action of provoking the humors—which follows the movement of the non-morbid elemental tastes—and the absence of their increase. He summarizes the stated meaning with the verse beginning "bhūta": "Due to the union with the digestion of tastes that are contrary to the equalizing digestion by the fire which is the cause of the elements born from previous matter, there is a reversal. (38)

Regarding the phrase *bhūtapūrvapadārthajātā*: that which has the five elements (*pañcabhūta*) as its prior [cause] is so described. It is both "formerly arisen" (*bhūtapūrva*) and a "substance" (*padārtha*); thus, the body, being composed of the five elements, is intended here as the substance. The "born from that" (*tajjātāḥ*) are the bodily constituents (*dhātavaḥ*). The fire that serves as their cause—that fire performs "cooking in equal flavor" (*samarasapacana*), meaning it cooks by dividing [the food] into essence (*sāra*) and waste (*kiṭṭa*). From that, there arises a refinement (*saṃskāra*) born from eating substances possessing pure essence; from that, the constituents flourish. They nourish [the body].

The body increases; the intended meaning is that for those who enjoy freedom from disease, virility increases. One becomes possessed of the sensory faculties. Regarding the application of incompatible substances, tastes, or digestive transformations: the disease born from the digestion of unpalatable food acts as an agent contrary to the bodily constituents (*dhātus*). As it develops in this manner, it becomes a state of disorder (*viparyaya*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the knowledge of the forms (*ākāra*) of the elements is preceded by the knowledge of their transformations (*vikāra*), since when there is knowledge of the absence of those transformations and the absence of their effects, there arises knowledge of the sequence of creation and dissolution? Furthermore, the knowledge of the absence of effects such as "bad taste" (*virasa*) is caused by the absence of transformations to be accomplished; for it depends upon the substance which serves as the cause for the absence of the effects of those transformations. According to the logic of the *Nyāya* system—namely, "whatever is not thus is not thus, just like a jar"—once the negative inference (*vyatirekānumāna*) is established in this manner, the aforementioned method of knowing the process of withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*) would be redundant. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Six. [The first of the six lotuses is] the Mūlādhāra. (39)

The meaning of this Sūtra is established as follows: the sour taste is presided over by the foundational lotus (*ādhāra-padma*). The water element (*ambu-tattva*) possesses the sweet taste. The fire element (*anala-tattva*) is characterized by the quality of saltiness combined with the pungent taste. The air element (*vāyu-tattva*) is distinguished by the quality of the bitter taste. And the ether element (*ākāśa-tattva*) consists of the astringent taste. These lotuses consist of the five elements and are composed of the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) of plasma, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, and semen. The thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-padma*), which is the support of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, is the generator of the lotus of the ether element (*ākāra-tattva*).

That [wind] is the producer of the lotus of the wind-element; that [fire] is the producer of the lotus of the fire-element; that [water] is the producer of the lotus of the water-element; and that [earth] is the producer of the lotus of the earth-element. Having become a modification possessing a taste contrary to its own kind—sour—the earth-element dissolves into the water-element. The water-element, whose nature is sweet taste, having become a modification possessing a taste contrary to its own kind—sweet—dissolves into the fire-element.

The fire-element (*tejas-tattva*), characterized by the quality of the salty taste (*lavaṇa-rasa*) which is internalized within the bitter taste, becomes a morbid transformation of the salty taste and dissolves into the air-element (*vāyu-tattva*). The air-element, characterized by the quality of the bitter taste, being afflicted by diseases produced from the consumption of food that has lost its bitter flavor, dissolves into the space-element (*ākāśa-tattva*). The space-element, consisting of the astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*), being afflicted by ailments born from the consumption of food that has lost its astringent flavor, dissolves of its own accord. This is the process of dissolution (*saṃhāra-krama*).

The essences residing in each respective lotus give rise to diseases produced by the consumption of substances of that same class which are devoid of essence; thus, they serve as instruments for the process of dissolution. Keeping this meaning in mind, the lotus situated at the base of the six lotuses effects the destruction of the body within each respective body, preceded by the destruction of those respective lotuses—this is the sense.

Now, it may be objected: the five sense organs are modifications of the five elements; likewise, the six tastes, the seven constituents (dhātus), and so forth. In that regard, having treated taste and blood as one, this [body] is said to consist of the six tastes. Thus, by treating taste and blood as one because there is no distinction between the tastes and the constituents (dhātus), it has been explained accordingly. Therefore, just as the sense organs and their objects are modifications of the five great elements, it must be stated that the tastes and the rest are likewise modifications of the elements.

Therefore, the enumeration of six tastes would be redundant, because the salty taste, being contained within the pungent taste, is the generator of the bone element (*asthidhātu*). Up to this point, it is only the channels (*sirā*) that convey the colors; [the tongue] residing within the elements acts as the sustainer of both sides, thereby nourishing the ten-petaled lotus and the hexagonal wheel which is the support for the thousand-petaled lotus. Through the unification of the salty and pungent tastes, the bone element, consisting of the ten-petaled lotus, is brought to fulfillment and increases.

One should console [the disciple] in this way: "Because it is unperceived within the center of the six-cornered wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*) which supports the thousand channels (*sahasrasirā*)—the very foundation that awakens all phonemes—and because it is produced from nectar (*amṛta*), up to this point only the channels that awaken the phonemes possess its nourishment and no others. This is due to its being contained within the vital constituents (*dhātu*), and because the lotuses that awaken those respective phonemes are supported by the thousand channels, owing to their connection with the channels of nectar."

Because the six-cornered wheel—which generates the bone-element consisting of fire produced primarily from salt—has the nature of being devoid of the habit of bringing nectar, [the author], due to this lack of satisfaction, says: "Iḍā.
It sprinkles the nectar that has entered the channels of the winds filled by the iḍā and piṅgalā. || 40 ||

That [process] has as its cause the filling of the retention-breath (*kumbhaka*) which awakens the hexagonal wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*) consisting of the air filled by the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*. Having enveloped the nectar from the lotus at the head filled by the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, it fills those vessels; because the substance of the hexagonal wind-wheel is thus manifested, there is a simultaneous movement of the substances fire and wind. Since the effect of igniting the fire by the wind filled by the *piṅgalā* is a manifesting wind (*vyañjanānila*), the meaning is that it is the cause for the appearance of the wheel through the filling of the wind.

Now, one might object: "Is it not to be considered that [the goddess] sprinkles nectar after filling the jar of the abdomen with the breath of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka)? For the six-cornered wheel (ṣaṭkoṇacakra) is situated below Kuṇḍalī, and it is taught that the performance of the act of filling pertains only to the lotuses located above Kuṇḍalī. To avoid this incongruity—that there would be no description of the sprinkling of nectar by the winds of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels of Kuṇḍalī—the author says: "By the back," and so forth. "She increases by means of the regions of the back, thighs, belly, shanks, penis, generative organ, and so on. (41)

The hexagonal wheel (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*), which has the form of the bone-element (*asthidhātu*) produced from salt and pungent substances, is situated below the region of Kuṇḍalinī; therefore, like the back-wheel and like the belly above it, it expands during the process of digestion by means of the thousand channels (*sahasrasirā*). Since these [channels] also expand through the conjunction with the movement of the winds of inhalation and exhalation, it is established that inhalation and exhalation have this nourishing activity as their cause; thus, the meaning is that it expands like the wheels of the back and the belly.

Because there would be no possibility of contact with the arrival of nectar (*amṛta*) for the marrow-element (*majjā-dhātu*) contained within the bone-element (*asthi-dhātu*), its status as the sustainer of nectar would not be tenable; due to this incongruity, he says: "From the navel... [verse 42].
From below the navel, the lotus consisting of the *kuṇḍalī* and other elements, a thousand-petaled lotus surrounded by five thousand channels (*sirā*), was born.

Because the elements of lymph, blood, flesh, and fat situated below the *kuṇḍalī*, as well as the winds of inhalation and exhalation, lack the capacity for tactile contact, there is no occasion for the relationship of "the nourished and the nourisher" (*upajīvyopajīvaka*). Since the activity that nourishes them is indispensable, the hundred-petaled lotus enveloped by five thousand channels was produced for the purpose of nourishing those elements and the lotuses; the meaning is that without this [lotus], there would be no capacity to nourish, and thus the lotus serving as their support was produced.

To explain how the function of increasing the white element (*śukladhātu*)—which is nourished by the sweet taste inherent in the marrow element (*majjādhātu*)—is consistent, he says: "In the abdomen... (*jaṭhareti*).
It appears as the basin for the fire of the stomach. || 43 ||

The meaning is that, because it serves as the support for the collection of digestive bile (*pācakapittakalā*)—which has manifested from the gastric fire (*jaṭharāgni*) and performs the function of digestion—and because it possesses the capacity for the act of flaming by acting as a basin-like support (*ālavāla*) for the kindling of the bile-constituent in the form of the gastric fire, it indeed shines as a basin-like receptacle, serving as the foundation for all the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) from the soles of the feet up to the crown of the head within the white constituent (*śukladhātu*).

Regarding how the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*) consist of the six tastes, and how the tastes—sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent—serve as nourishment for the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), he says: "The sweet... [etc.].
Agitating the sweet taste, it shines by its own radiance in the place of the white element (*śukladhātu*). || 44 ||

A substance possessing a sweet taste, while being digested by the digestive bile (*pitta*), increases as the white tissue (*śukladhātu*) due to the influence of the functional impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the action of that digestive bile. When indigestion occurs from the consumption of substances with an astringent taste, an aggravation of the wind humor (*pavana*) arises. This aggravation of the wind humor, having entered the white tissue, performs the function of drying up the semen. That unwholesome substance, being digested by the digestive bile, causes a disorder of the lymph-chyle (*rasa*) and blood tissues.

The locus of the white constituent (*śukladhātu*) is the space-element (*gaganabhūta*). It is the fire (*tejas*) established as a substance characterized by an abundance of the qualities of the space-element. Because this fire is endowed with the refinement produced by the digestive process of the bile-constituents (*pittakalāpa*), the quality of the form of the white constituent shines forth; this is the meaning. When indigestion occurs due to the consumption of substances that are either sweet-tasting or devoid of taste, it causes a disorder of the blood constituent (*asṛgdhātu*). If that is not remedied, diseases such as diarrhea caused by water-waste (*jalamala*) arise; this is the meaning.

The increase of the white constituent (śukladhātu) shines by means of its fiery nature due to the abundance of substances possessing a salty taste; and the increase of the transformation of the plasma and blood constituents (rasāsṛgdhātu) shines by its own fiery power due to the abundance of this [same] unwholesome taste—this is the meaning.

Now, indeed, as long as the food containing the sweet taste has been eaten, it remains in the region of the phlegm (kapha) and the heart, undergoing a transformation into a sweet state; thereafter, having entered the receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya), it undergoes an acid transformation and, being cooked by the digestive bile (pācakapitta), increases the marrow tissue (majjādhātu), which is a substance naturally possessing an acid taste.

Having extracted the morbid humors residing in the *dhātu*s, [the body] bestows upon them the qualities of the predominant taste conditioned by time, ripening, digestion, species, and substrate. Then, that substance of sour taste (*amlarasa*) causes a disorder of the muscle tissue (*māṃsadhātu*). From that, afflictions such as the provocation of *kapha*, cough, swelling, anemia, and erysipelas arise. For the purpose of pacifying the provocation of those diseases born from that *doṣa*, one should consume substances possessing a pungent taste (*kaṭurasa*).

The meaning is that, while being digested by the *rasapācaka-pitta* which suppresses the provocation of diseases born from those [vitiated] humors, it reaches the state of the white element (*śukladhātu*); consequently, we experience conditions such as vertigo, fainting, and consumption.

Now, it may be argued that as long as the food containing tastes remains merely in the region of phlegm (*kapha*) and has reached the heart, that consumed food becomes sweet; however, upon entering the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), it turns sour and, while being cooked by the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*), is unable to undergo digestion according to the specific distinctions of each substance.

The effect of sweet taste (*madhurarasakārya*) and the effect of the transformation of sour taste (*āmlarasavikārakārya*) are as follows: immediately after entering the path of the throat, having encountered the sweet taste produced from the previous meal, it reaches the region of phlegm (*kapha*) located in the heart and partakes of that sweet taste. Thereafter, producing a transformation of sour taste, it enters the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), undergoes further digestion, and partakes of that subsequent taste. Because there is a sense of incongruity as to how a substance of extremely sweet taste increases the white constituent (*śukladhātu*), he says "sour" (*āmla*):
while digesting the sour taste, it shines by its own radiance in the location of the marrow constituent (*majjādhātu*). || 45 ||

While digesting a substance with an acidic taste (*āmlarasa*), the digestive bile (*pitta*) bestows the specific qualities prescribed by the rules for each respective item until the very first substance of the meal has been digested. Although that [acidic] taste undergoes a change into another taste due to the influence of the condition (*upādhi*) produced by the process of digestion over time, it does not bestow the qualities of those adventitious tastes. Even when consuming food containing a mixture of all tastes, that digestive bile digests the various substances possessing those respective tastes by distinguishing them one after another. That very taste then yields its own fruit, which is dependent upon the qualities of the other tastes.

A substance with such sour taste (*amlarasa*) increases the marrow tissue (*majjādhātu*). It cures disorders of the wind (*pavana*) associated with that tissue. That same sour-tasting substance does not, however, produce a disorder of the muscle tissue (*māṃsadhātu*). When indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) occurs due to the consumption of substances with improper tastes, diseases specific to each respective tissue arise. A substance with a predominantly windy (*anila*) sour taste nourishes the marrow tissue, because it is a sour-tasting substance that brings about the manifestation of the wind element and its derivatives.

A substance possessing an acidic taste (*amlarasa*) that brings about the perception of wind (*anila*), earth (*bhūta*), and other elements, causes a disorder of the muscle tissue (*māṃsadhatu*) while simultaneously acting as an aid to the drying of the muscle tissue; this is because it is a substance [that performs these functions]. By means of this inference (*anumāna-pramāṇa*), it is understood that a windy substance containing an acidic taste yields two results: it strengthens the marrow tissue (*majjādhatu*) and causes a disorder of the muscle tissue. Furthermore, it is understood that a substance whose taste is incompatible with the muscle tissue causes the wasting away of the muscle tissue.

Such is the process of the arising of all elements (*bhūta*). In this very same way, the process of the dissolution of all elements is also to be understood. We maintain that up to the point where there is mutual nourishment of the elements, there is likewise mutual destruction of those very elements. Where the nourishment of the elements by the *rasas* (tastes/flavors) is perceived, that alone should be known as the process of creation (*sṛṣṭikrama*). Where the sole function of these very *rasas* is perceived to be the drying up of the elements, that alone should be understood as the process of dissolution (*saṃhārakrama*).

In the same way, the defects (doṣas), impurities (malas), and fluctuations (calas) produce their respective mutual effects and create a distinct creation; that very same [principle] brings about the destruction of the creation. Therefore, it creates itself by means of itself. The state of being destroyed by its own making resides in the self alone. The meaning is that, for both of these, the constituents (dhātus) are to be understood as nothing other than the tastes (rasas).

[Objection: Surely there are many substances with sweet taste, such as stalks of sugarcane and the like; similarly, there are many trees possessing a sour taste. Now, while it may be possible to say that a sweet taste nourishes the *śukla-dhātu* (semen) and a sour taste nourishes the *majjā-dhātu* (marrow), this tree possesses a salty taste and is thus fit for medicinal use. Since this has not been observed [in other contexts], how can one maintain that a substance with a salty taste nourishes the *dhātus*? Anticipating this doubt, he says—beginning with "lavana": "Digesting the salty taste, it shines by its own luster in the place of the *asthi-dhātu* (bone-tissue). (46)

Although this salt-tasting substance is not conventionally designated as a "salt-tasting tree" among the categories of wholesome items or in medicinal formulations, the fact that the nourishment of all bodily constituents (*dhātu*) by means of all tastes is impossible without the salty taste, establishes the presence of the salty taste in salt substances; for it is capable of effecting the digestion of the substances that produce food fit for consumption.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is well known that the element of bone, being of the nature of a saline substance, is identical with the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*), because salt has entered into the effects of that submarine fire which is a transformation of ocean water.

Salt is the cause of diseases of the fat (*medas*) tissue, because it is a substance that dries up the fat element (*medodhātu*). The salty taste (*lavaṇarasa*) nourishes the bone element (*asthidhātu*), because it is a substance of the same nature as fire and because it assists all tastes. For this very reason, when the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*) digests the salty taste, it assumes the essential form of the bone element and carries its entire burden. Consuming substances associated with the salty taste bestows strength upon the bone element; indeed, by virtue of possessing a combination of all tastes, it nourishes all the bodily elements (*dhātus*).

Therefore, salt taste possesses the power to strengthen all six tastes; for even when consuming substances that possess other pure tastes, there is no digestion in the absence of salt taste. Regarding the statement that the word *śuci* denotes saltiness: salt taste causes a disorder of the fat tissue (*medas-dhātu*), because it is a substance whose salt taste is produced from salty water. The meaning is that such a vitiated substance causes the depletion of the bone tissue (*asthi-dhātu*).

Now, it may be argued that when indigestion occurs from consuming substances possessing an astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*), a disorder of the wind (*pavana-vikāra*) arises, which causes the depletion of the white constituent (*śukla-dhātu*). To alleviate that provocation of the wind, the consumption of substances with a sweet taste (*svādu-rasa*) is prescribed as the rule. Therefore, when a disorder of the white constituent has arisen, the consumption of substances with a sweet taste is enjoined. Conversely, when indigestion occurs from consuming substances with a pungent taste (*kaṭu-rasa*), a provocation of the wind arises that produces a disorder of the marrow constituent (*majjā-dhātu*).

For the purpose of pacifying the provocation of *vāta* caused by such [food], the consumption of substances with sour taste (*amlarasa*) is prescribed. When indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arises from the consumption of substances with salty taste (*lavaṇarasa*), and when indigestion arises from the consumption of substances with bitter taste (*tiktarasa*), the provocation of *vāta* occurs; for the purpose of pacifying that provocation, the consumption of substances with salty taste is prescribed. When indigestion arises from the consumption of substances with pungent taste (*kaṭurasa*), the provocation of *vāta* occurs, and it causes the nourishment of the *pitta* disorder and the white constituent (*śukladhātu*).

In that state, fainting, giddiness, drowsiness, loss of appetite, and a piercing pain throughout the limbs arise. When indigestion occurs due to the consumption of substances with unwholesome tastes—which cause the provocation of wind (*pavana*) and bile (*pitta*) and manifest these qualities—the manifestation of dual humoral defects (*dvandva-doṣa*) takes place. In this regard, the consumption of sweet-tasting substances serves as a remedy, whereas the effect of consuming bitter-tasting substances would be ineffective; anticipating this objection, he says: "Bitter... [Verse 47].
Digesting the bitter taste, it shines by its own brilliance in the seat of the fat tissue (*medas-dhātu*).

The digestive bile (*pācakapitta*), which possesses a bitter taste, performs digestion and removes disorders of the bile located within the fat tissue (*medodhātu*). By its own radiance—the very brilliance produced by the digestive bile—it shines forth in its own place. When indigestion occurs due to the consumption of bitter tastes, the resulting disease causes the depletion of the bone tissue (*asthidhātu*). The meaning is that an aggravation of the bile (*pittaprakopa*) arises through the salty taste, which is antagonistic to that bile.

Now, it may be objected that when indigestion occurs due to the consumption of substances possessing an acidic taste (*amlarasa*), an aggravation of phlegm (*kapha*) is observed; therefore, the rule is the consumption of substances with a pungent taste (*kaṭurasa*) for the purpose of alleviating that aggravation. Furthermore, the state of being a substance possessing a smell characterized by an acidic taste is the defining characteristic (*avacchedaka*) of earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*). Earth is produced from water-substances because it is a moist substance; by virtue of being so produced, it possesses coldness and heaviness. This is because the aggravation of phlegm, as defined by these characteristics, is produced by contact with the substance of earth.

Even the consumption of substances antagonistic to that [kapha] is a cause for the provocation of kapha. Keeping in mind the intention that the provocation of kapha is averted precisely by the consumption of pungent-tasting substances, he says: "Pungent...
[Verse 48]. Digesting the pungent taste, it shines with its own brilliance in the seat of the muscle tissue (*māṃsa-dhātu*).

Because it exists everywhere and because its capacity to remove the provocation of *kapha*—which itself causes the provocation of *pavana* (vāta)—has been observed many times, it is impossible to say that it causes the provocation of *pavana*. To explain: when the provocation of *pavana* located within the channels of the vessels (*sirā*) inside the porous [body] is destroyed, the provocation of *kapha* occurs; thus, it must be stated that when a substance with an abundance of pungent (*kaṭu*) taste reaches the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), it removes that provocation of *kapha*.

For the wise, the world itself is the teacher in all activities. When a piercing pain in the head is manifested, the application of substances with pungent taste (*kaṭurasavaddravya*) there serves to alleviate that headache. Furthermore, when indigestion arises from a weak digestive fire (*analamantha*), pain is produced in the abdomen; in that case, the consumption of substances with pungent taste acts as the remedy. When there is indigestion of the rasa (*rasājīrṇa*), the provocation of the wind (*pavanaprakopa*) occurs in all limbs due to bathing in cold water; in that case, fomentation (*svedana*) through contact with fire and other means serves to alleviate fevers caused by undigested matter (*āmajvara*) and similar ailments.

In that regard, the cessation of the provocation of *pavana* (vata) occurs when the movement of the wind within the channels of its vessels is obstructed; for since the muscle tissue (*māṃsa-dhātu*) is everywhere seized by *kapha*, when there is a provocation of *kapha*, it causes the obstruction of the movement of *pavana*. Therein, pain also arises. In such a case, the remedy is either a substance that counteracts the effects of the provoked *pavana*, or a substance that counteracts the provocation of the *kapha* that produced those effects.

In this regard, since it is impossible to effect the cessation of that provocation of the wind (*pavana*) without consuming substances possessing a bitter taste (*kaṭu-rasa*) which counteract such provocation, the opponents' intended meaning is that a substance with a bitter taste should be prescribed as the means for reversing the effects of the provoked wind. [This is incorrect] because [the bitter substance] is not the cause of the aggregate of factors that produce disease; rather, the statement that "a substance with a bitter taste counteracts the provocation of the wind" is merely a figurative designation.

The meaning is that pungent taste (*kaṭurasa*) functions as a cause by way of eliminating undigested matter (*ajīrṇa*), *āmadoṣa*, *pitta*, poison (*viṣa*), and worms (*krimi*), which arise from the consumption of tastes that are contrary to those [which produce them]. This is because the function of pungent taste is fulfilled solely by the removal of the defects caused by worms. For it is impossible to eliminate the effects of the increase of wind (*pavana*)—which is the result of the excess of phlegm (*kapha*) that causes the provocation of the muscle tissue (*māṃsadhātu*)—without first removing its cause.

Therefore, what must be performed is precisely the provision of the collection of factors that counteract the aggravation of *kapha*, which in turn brings about the cessation of the effects of the provocation of *vāta*. The meaning is that the provision of those factors consists specifically in the consumption of substances possessing a pungent (*kaṭu*) taste.

Now, one might object: when indigestion arises from consuming substances that possess an excess of the quality of sweet taste, it causes a disorder of the *rasa* and blood tissues (*dhatu*). From that, diseases originating from such intake—namely water-diarrhea, dysentery caused by *mahāmala*, chronic diarrhea (*grahaṇī*), hemorrhagic fever (*raktapitta*), and blood-wind (*raktavāyu*)—occur. Keeping in mind that the consumption of substances possessing an astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*) is the remedy for these, he says:
"Astringent... [Verse 49]. Digesting the astringent taste, it shines with its own brilliance within the seats of the *rasa* and blood tissues.

When a substance with an astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*) has been consumed and reaches the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*), its digestion is carried out by the digestive bile (*pācaka-pitta*). By means of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) produced by that digestion, it removes the disorder of the tissues of plasma and blood (*rasa-asṛk-dhātu*). The consumption of substances possessing an astringent taste serves as the cause for that removal; thus, it appears that "I am capable" through a power consisting of the totality of factors (*sāmagrī*) that counteracts the disorder of the plasma and blood tissues. In this context, it is established that [the self] "shines by its own brilliance" (*svatejasā bhāti*).

The meaning is that from the consumption of food with a bitter taste, when indigestion occurs, it causes a disorder in the movement of the white constituent (śukladhātu); and when the wind (vāyu) located in that [constituent] becomes provoked, diseases produced by the derangement of that constituent arise—namely, the disease of fainting (mūrchā), the disease of hiccup (hikkā), the disorder of vertigo (bhrama), blood-wind (raktavāyu), sores (śobhā), trembling of the limbs (aṅgakampa), epilepsy (apasmāra), and twitching of the feet (pādasphuraṇa).

But surely, both the sequence of creation and the sequence of dissolution have been set forth; the order of the origination of the five elements and their order of dissolution have been made known. This being so, one might argue that by means of the instrument of inference—namely, "the perceived world consists of bodies because it possesses breath and so forth, and thus this entire world consists of bodies because its nature is that of the manifested universe"—the production of bodies from one's own limbs should be stated. In that case, when the causal complex for producing a body is present, the effect of a body would arise eternally.
Because it is impossible for that effect to arise in the absence of the causal complex that produces the body, [the author], expressing this dissatisfaction, says: "sakala...
etc. A lotus named the Triangle (trikoṇa), which is the support of all essences (rasa) and so forth, situated at the navel-lotus, was produced as the petal of the thumb. || 50 ||

That which is called the "petal of the thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhadala*) is the support for all tastes; it consists of the six tastes and the seven bodily constituents (*dhātus*). It is the substratum for the five letters of the *ka*-group preceded by the vowel *a*. Because it serves as the foundation for the arising of the body composed of the five elements, it is described as "the support for all tastes. This lotus situated below the navel, distinguished by the measure of a thumb, is the triangular lotus—[as stated in the scripture]:
"The Person is the size of a thumb, and he rests upon the thumb."

Thus, according to the sacred scripture (*śruti*), that which serves as the substratum for both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is what brings about the generation of progeny; for it is by virtue of being their locus that they reside therein, and the blood itself is the essence (*rasa*). For this very reason, it has been correctly established that [the triangle] is the substratum of the body, because of the existence of the scriptural passage: "He is indeed the essence; for having obtained the essence, he becomes blissful. In that very place, there is also a three-cornered lotus belonging to the *puruṣa*.

In the seed-syllable (*bīja*), there are two lower corners; above them is a single supporting upper corner, which consists of Kāmagiri, is characterized by the Śakti who is Rudra, and has Kāmeśvara as its presiding deity. This upper corner, endowed with such qualities, is situated above the two lower corners. On the right side of the lower corner is Jālandhara-pīṭha, consisting of the Sūryacakra and having Uḍḍiyāṇa as its presiding deity; the other left corner is Pūrṇagiri-gahvara-pīṭha, consisting of the Somacakra and characterized by the Śakti who is the Supreme Brahman. [This constitutes] the lotus of the triangle (*trikoṇapadma*).

Through the union of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, the bliss of experiencing joy is perpetually felt. Woman is *prakṛti*; man, however, is *īśvara*. The bliss of their union is experienced at all times; for this very reason, it is said to be the substratum of all flavors (*rasa*). The triangular lotus (*trikoṇapadma*) of all living beings is the locus of all flavors, because it is the sole support for the pleasure that causes procreation. That which is not so is not so, like a jar; thus, it is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that this [lotus] is the locus of all flavors.

Just as a region of the earth is designated as possessing a sour taste because it is the locus for the manifestation of the sprouts of living beings, we therefore maintain that [the body] consists of all tastes. Because it is the locus that serves as the cause for the generation of progeny, the male organ (*meḍhra*) also appears triangular. Above that, the male organ is a single triangle formed by the transformation of the two triangles situated within the two seeds (testicles) and presided over by those two seeds. Therefore, the claim that the "triangular lotus" (*trikoṇapadma*) is recognized in all men is incorrect.

It should not be suspected that for those whose bodies are born from eggs and lack a penis—which is the lotus of the two seeds—the triangular lotus is also absent; for the fact of being produced from a seed (*bīja*) is common to both, and it is established in all scriptures that they are "egg-born" (*aṇḍaja*). Even though, by direct observation, there is an absence of the penis (the modification of the triangle) and the seeds in egg-born beings, the fact that the body is produced from a seed is the same for both. For this very reason, some maintain that what is designated as the "internal embryo" (*peśī*) belongs to egg-born beings;
the meaning is that the state of being egg-born is common to the bodies of egg-born beings.

Now, since all the lotuses situated within the body serve as the substratum for all phonemes (*varṇa*), it appears that their sole purpose is merely to indicate those phonemes. In that case, because the triangular lotus (*trikoṇapadma*) is not counted [among them], why does the lotus that is the cause of procreation not manifest? If that were so, then since the triangular lotus exists at all times throughout the entire extent of the body, there would be the production of offspring at every moment.

One should not raise the objection that procreation is never observed to occur apart from the union of a man and a woman; for the body, composed of the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*), is the progenitor of another body. Therefore, the meaning is that [the new body] arises within the triangular lotus. The sense organ (*indriya*) is the cause for the production of offspring, but it is not the producer of the *varṇas* (castes), because it serves as the substratum for external karmic functions. Consequently, the intended meaning is that the statement explaining the birth of offspring is applicable at all times, and thus [your previous argument] is incorrect.

The meaning is that it is observed that [beings] proceed from the conviction that this triangular lotus (*trikoṇapadma*) is the means for producing all pleasure, even for the bodies of large-bodied ants. Now, one might object: "The triangular lotus alone is not the cause of procreation, because the white element (*śukladhātu*) itself is the cause of the effect of procreation; its function is fulfilled merely by being the substratum [of that element], since the effect of procreation is impossible without the sowing of seeds which produce sprouts. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Therefore... "Therefore the body was born; therefore the limbs shine forth in the body. (51)

Therefore, according to the manner previously stated, when there is union with a male, the function of procreation is possible for women; otherwise, even though the *meḍhra* of the "branch-body" (*śākhā-śarīra*) is the cause of procreation, that would not be possible because that *meḍhra* is also a branch-body. Thus, from the location of the two concluding sūtras, the triangular place is also the cause of procreation, and likewise the *meḍhra* is the cause of procreation because that *meḍhra* is also a branch-body.

Therefore, because the phrase "therefore" (tasmāt) appears in both concluding sūtras, the location of the triangle is also a cause for the production of progeny; likewise, since the penis is also a cause for the production of progeny, the concluding word "therefore" is recited in both sūtras as well.
Thus ends the commentary on the fifth question of Āyurveda, composed by Yogānandanātha; it is well-known, approved by great men, a word-by-word exposition, and a benefactor to the world.
It is completed.
Mahādeva reveals this state of its majesty; through its manifestations, there has been a constant empire over the enemies of speech.
May that Dakṣa, who excels even the fair-eyed one in bestowing abundant wealth and knowledge through his side-long glances, grant auspiciousness to us every day— O Kāmākṣī!
Janaka is Śaṅkara himself, and my mother is Sarvamaṅgalā;
since they are both intent upon my protection, what cause for deliberation is there, and whence could there be fear?
It was offered into the presence of the feet of the Lord of All.
Now begins the sixth question: The salty taste makes the bones firm.
The salty taste is devoid of flavor and softens the bones. 2.
The bitter taste increases fat. 3.
The taste that is both bitter and flavorless destroys fat. 4.
The pungent taste (ūṣaṇa-rasa) bestows an abundance of the flesh constituent (māṃsa-dhātu). 5. The pungent-unsavory taste (ūṣaṇa-virasa) bestows a deficiency of the flesh constituent. 6.
The astringent taste (kaṣāya-rasa) bestows an abundance of the blood constituent (asṛk-dhātu). 7.
The virasa-kaṣāya increases the rasa and asṛk that have emerged; 8.
*asṛk* itself is *rasa*; 9.
*asṛk* itself is *rasāsṛk*. 10.
Due to the combination with incompatible substances, it becomes tasteless;
it causes irregular digestion;
and it remains undigested. 11–13.
Therefore, the digestive fire becomes irregular.
(14) The fire that is produced from the rasa digests that very rasa. (15) The dosha follows the course of the rasa. (16)
Disease follows from the humors; 17. the bodily constituents follow from disease; 18. the humors circulate within the bodily constituents; 19.

The first three [qualities] subdue the provocation of the wind (*pavana*), follow its essence, and nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). Because the first three lack the state of having a single taste (*virasaikatābhāva*), the diseases associated with them follow that same nature.
Those born from the provocation of the wind (*pavana*) are incurable.
(23) A disease born from the first [element] kills immediately; (24) one born from the second [element] kills after four days. (25)
The third [period] lasts six nights.
Among those, on the eighth day, the wine becomes single-flavored, then flavorless, and finally life-destroying.
On the tenth day, it becomes flavorless from its original state.

On the fourteenth day, it becomes tasteless compared to other tastes. On the eighteenth day, that which was once of two tastes, then one taste, and then tasteless, [reaches its end]. The three bitter [tastes] increase the circulation of fat, flesh, and blood.
The tastes become tasteless and provide an unevenness of flavor.

(32) When the three pungent tastes occasionally become tasteless, they manifest many qualities of flavor one by one; the digestive fire (*anala*) that produces these various other tastes does not cease for twenty-one days. (33) Those respective diseases are easily curable. (34)

A substance that has become tasteless from its original bitter taste becomes curable within sixteen days. (35) A substance that has become tasteless from its original bitter taste, or possesses one different taste, or has become entirely tasteless, becomes curable within eleven days. (36) A substance possessing an excessive taste is the cause of disease. (37)

Those tastes which are consumed in excess as food for the humors (doṣas) generate those very humors. (38) As long as there is indigestion (ajīrṇa), so long is there disease. (39) When it has been digested (jīrṇa), the time [of health] returns. (40)
Cow's ghee cures fevers caused by the combination of sweet tastes and other factors,
removes all diseases,
while goat's and sheep's ghee destroy diseases of children.
Earth, water, fire, and lotus possess a sweet taste that subdues *pitta*.
(44) A sour taste resulting from digestion (*pākāmla-rasa*) follows the nature of wind (*pavana*) and cures diseases of the eyes.
(45) Indeed, a sweet taste resulting from perfect digestion (*siddha-pāka*) subdues wind (*pavana*). (46)
A substance possessing a sweet post-digestive taste (vipāka) and a salty flavor (rasa) cures diseases caused by vāta.
[47] A substance that is sweet in its seed, salty, and sour removes all types of vāta disorders.
[48] A substance whose seeds are sour, which is salty in its stalks, and whose leaves are sweet, etc., wards off vāta covered by pitta. [49]
The substance of the salty-seed, sweet and sour-bodied tree removes diseases caused by wind (vāta) obstructed by phlegm (kapha).
(50) The tree with a sour body, resembling astringent taste, is the remover of all ailments.
(51) Astringent taste is the cause for the destruction of the white-bodied [disease]. (52)
The sweet taste destroys the final element (semen) and eliminates the agent of its destruction.
[53] The sour taste, like pungent flavor, nourishes, awakens the marrow, and removes wind; it destroys the diseases arising from that [wind].
[54] Like bitter flavor, it dries the bones and cures ailments. [55]
The salty taste (lavaṇa-rasa) removes diseases situated within;

it counteracts the disorders of the fat tissue (medas-dhātu) caused by the specific qualities of the salty taste. 56–57. A bitter seed, a pungent branch, and a body [of a plant] [act as follows]: for one suffering from indigestion and fever born from the morbid humors (rasa) of a multitude of phlegmatic diseases (kapha-roga), this [remedy] brings relief within seven days. 58.
As long as the essence of one taste has not yet been digested, it becomes another taste;
that respective taste is the remedy for that respective disease, and thus it becomes balanced. 59–61.

Undigested sour taste caused by pitta becomes a different taste after six nights; that taste generates that specific doṣa. Undigested salty taste caused by kapha becomes a different taste after nine nights.

That taste produces that specific *doṣa*. (65) Fever also occurs from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) caused by tasteless food. (66) That which is sweet in taste but digested by a fire of tastelessness is caused by *vāta*; that which is astringent in taste is caused by *vāta*; that which is sour in taste or bitter in taste is caused by *pitta*; and those tastes which correspond to the respective *doṣas* serve as their remedies. (67)
Only fire is the means of cessation.
(68) Humans possess the discernment between what is digested and what is undigested on their tongues.
(69) Taste is perceived within one's own hollowed palms. (70)
Wherever the *rasas* (nutrient essences) are located, there they manifest.
Therefore, the digestive bile (*pācakapitta*) digests the food;
the wind (*anila*) digests the tissues (*dhātus*).
That itself is fever. (74) There occurs a depletion of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). (75) For bile is heat; there is no fever without heat. (76)
Astringent, bitter, and sweet [tastes] are pacifiers of pitta.

When the digestive fire blazes in its own proper place, then food becomes a provider of the bodily constituents (dhātus), and the fire remains healthy. At that time, both diet and lifestyle promote the nourishment of the bodily constituents.

Taste, blood, sweet, flesh, sour, fat, salty, bone, bitter, marrow, pungent, semen, and astringent are the opposites [of one another]. (80) Sweet, marrow, and sour increase the blood and rasa elements; salty, fat, bitter, flesh, pungent, and astringent tastes increase the blood and rasa elements. (81) A disorder (*vikāra*) is simply the defect (*doṣa*) arising from the causes that provoke the humors (*doṣa*). (82)
When one observes a disorder in the limbs, then one should apply a remedy that prevents such disorder.
Water is cooling and removes heat.
Substances that sustain the bodily constituents (*dhātu*), possess a pleasant taste, and are beneficial against diseases of wind (*anila*) and fire (*anala*) are medicinal.
That which is characterized by a predominance of a particular taste possesses the qualities of that predominant taste.
83 Drinking water in the morning purifies diseases located in the stomach and removes all ailments.
87 Milk alleviates the movement of bile, phlegm, and wind, and destroys asthma, cough, and fever. 88
Cow's milk increases the bodily constituents (dhātus). Goat's milk cures asthma and cough. Camel's milk subdues phlegm and bile.
Human [milk] destroys all defects and wards off fevers caused by the derangement of the humors (sannipāta).
92 The group beginning with *kaṭukā* (bitter herbs) removes diseases such as blood disorders, decoctions, and ailments arising from the obstruction of phlegm in the body.
93 It possesses a uniform potency throughout all places, times, and bodies, and it destroys diseases located within the various bodily constituents (*dhātu*). 94
Thus ends the sixth inquiry of Āyurveda.
Now begins the seventh inquiry:
A substance that possesses a single body [and a single purpose] is a single medicine. (1)

That which possesses a bitter taste removes diseases produced by that [vitiation] of the *rasa* tissue. That which possesses a pungent taste destroys the *māṃsa* (muscle) tissue; the sour taste destroys those [diseases] consisting of that [muscle] tissue. By means of sweet tastes which destroy diseases caused by the destruction of the *rasa* and *rakta* (blood) tissues, there arises blood and wind (*vāyu*) that destroys those [sweet tastes], due to their being contrary to them through astringent tastes. 4.
5. That which possesses the essence appropriate to its substance, whose primary taste follows its flavor, and which belongs to that same class while imparting qualities that counteract other tastes;

6. Those substances possessing the essence appropriate to the elements present within them, belonging to that same class, and residing in other substances, produce desires corresponding to their respective flavors;
7. Wind is generated by out-of-order, flavorless, and irregular elemental tastes, which causes the drying up of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
In the water element (*apas*), there is a sweet taste that is devoid of virulence; it generates the wind (*pavana*) produced from that constituent (*dhātu*).

As long as it is associated with a single astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*), it counteracts [the wind]. The wind produced by the final stage of the pure sweet taste residing in the first constituent (*dhātu*), moving within the bitter constituent (*tikta-dhātu*), is manifold and is offered in many ways.
The sweet taste, accompanied by the natural and morbid forms of wind and sour taste, is a subduer of wind (*anilahara*).

When substances that are mild, sweet, moderate-sour, or excessively salty are consumed in combination, they obstruct the impurities at the end of the channels, resulting in hemorrhoids and diseases such as bodily wind (vāta). (11) Through substances with deficient sourness, moderate salinity, or excessive sourness, conditions such as asthma, cough, vomiting, and belching are observed, as well as ailments like abdominal distension perceived by the senses. (12) Just as trees on earth follow the qualities of the water and sap they receive, so too do plants that possess alkaline or sweet-tasting juices remove the humors of bile and wind from the body's fluids and blood. (13)

Whatever substance follows the essence of another substance—that seed which possesses both that essence and another essence—the oil produced from it increases that very substance until it yields its essential fruit; it subdues the wind (vāyu) and nourishes all the bodily constituents (dhātus). Whatever is born from the union of the essence of one substance with the pungent quality of another substance, or from the smoke caused by the production of one substance from another, follows the properties of fire (analaguṇa).
That which possesses the qualities of moisture, heat, light, and the essence of the earth element; it alleviates phlegm and wind, provokes bile, and awakens the *mūlādhāra*.

(15) Wine made from the juice of trees (*āsava*) consists of roots, husks, single seeds, stalks, and so forth; it is suitable for the bodily winds, removes all defects, and provides nourishment to dormant tissues.
(16) [Substances] that are short are light. Substances that undergo transformation over time (*kālapāka*) become increasingly heavy as they progress. (17)
Likewise, those called by the names of white, black, red, and smoky bestow qualities of heavy, medium, and light respectively;
they remove disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm in that same order.
The varieties of form produced from the earth—namely inferior, mediocre, and superior—are distinguished by their color as being of one, two, or three hues respectively.
Grain is distinguished by differences in color and other qualities.
There are nine types of grain.
Grain bestows nourishment, depletion, or equilibrium upon the seven constituent elements (dhātus) and the three humors (doṣas), according to whether its qualities are inferior, middling, or superior.
In this way, there are these priyaṅgu grains for me; 24. and śyāmāka grains for me; 25. and nīvāra grains for me; 26. one should know that it is the same for uddālaka grains.
The first three [types] nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*);
the others cause their depletion.

*Uddālaka* has a sweet taste; it removes the provocation of *vāta*. Due to its various classifications such as "large" and so forth, it bestows qualities as previously described and eliminates unstable and chronic disorders.
30. Those [flavors] which have become the nature of nectar through an excessive movement arising from the sequence of the initial movement of the wind, serve to dry up their respective qualities.
31. The sour taste, which possesses the qualities of the essence of the earth and the water purified by the nectar that has emerged upon the first departure of the wind, becomes flavorless.
32. And this [sour taste] appears as either deficient or excessive in relation to one another.

The sense of smell does not take as its object that which has been rendered an effect by the movement of the intermediate wind. (33) Through the movement of the humors (*doṣa*), it does not take that as its object. (34) Earth possesses fragrance. (35)
The sweet essence appropriate for the season of Madhu and Mādhava removes the disease of *ariṣṭa*. 36.

Madhu and Mādhava are the two spring seasons (*vāsantika-ṛtu*). 37. Due to the transgression of the sequence of the emergence of the second element and its sweet taste, it becomes devoid of flavor (*virasa*). 38.
Its essence nourishes the final constituent; the quality produced by it causes transformation. 39.
The water-impurity shines as the *aja-lajaṃbula*. 40.
As long as the causes and effects that are to be removed and the removers [of those causes] persist, [the cycle continues]. 41.

Swelling produced by causes other than those that normally produce it indicates a fatal sign (ariṣṭa). 42. The inability to eat food and the like, along with diarrhea and wandering about, indicates that one’s life has reached its end. 43. When the movement of the vital essence (ojas) occurs without its characteristic sound, it signifies a state consisting of the time of death. 44.
[The tree] on the body has a taste like astringent and sourness.
(45) The experience of objects that are not [proper] objects destroys its effects. (46) Medical treatment is preceded by the knowledge of what is curable and what is incurable. (47)
One should consider oneself a wise man who knows the rules regarding the essential matters;
one should be vigilant in medical treatment; and one should abandon what is incurable. 48–50.
One should apply oneself to the goals to be accomplished. (51) Helping others leads to merit.
(52) And those are the *vartakas*. (53)
In this way, one should perform the protection of the nameless.

(54) Just as the pure elements are filled with the nectar of wind, the essences are also reverters [of disease]. (55) Those [diseases] which are not produced by causes that dry up the elements, and which are not caused by desire, are to be cured. (56)

As long as the period of experiencing indigestion lasts, and as long as the digestive fire remains overwhelmed by *āma*, for that long the fever persists. (57) It is *āma* itself that causes the transformation of the digestive fire.
(58) Struck by *āma*, the fire burns outwardly and produces fever. (59)
At whatever time there is a [specific] condition, it is the regulator. 60.
Indigestion, fatal signs, loss of appetite, swelling, diarrhea, and the impairment of all the sense organs are observed. 61.
Wherever these tastes reside, from the transformation of taste into blood, one substance appears as another substance. 62.
*Śobhāñjana* is the medicine for *prabhā*.

(63) The juices that arise in summer, due to moving through the space of the atmosphere and the wind, and due to the observation of the five winds, produce disorders by being supported by the astringent and bitter tastes which possess the qualities of the celestial wind (*gaganānila*). (64) Because they undergo a wondrous drying out when released from their movement through the wind, those tastes are removed; the taste that opposes them is what restores balance. (65)
From the first [word], the word *vibhūtodbhava* is heard as another word. (66) One appears as many. (67) Blue, yellow, and grasses are seen in deep sleep. (68)
Seeing buffaloes, snakes, and donkeys;
[seeing] spirits, ghosts, and piśācas—
these are the signs indicating impending death.
The sweet taste (*madhurarasā*) arises from the two elements [earth and water] and is caused by the humor of phlegm (*kaphadoṣa*). 72.
Those possessing the qualities and tastes of space and wind have pungent tastes (*kaṭurasāḥ*), which remove the phlegm produced by the savory taste (*svādurasā*). 73.
Just as that which dries up the first two elements, so too does that which pertains to the eye (*akṣuṣa*) perceive it even once. 74.

The elements (dhātus) that arise from a predominance of a particular primary element (bhūta) increase the qualities (guṇas) predominant in that same element; that which has inferior qualities is a depleter [of them]. Furthermore, those [diseases] born from these [elements] are curable. 75–77.
The digestive fire digests very slowly. 78. The fire of indigestion is worse than the fire of digestion. 79. It increases the bodily elements of fire and wards off misfortune. 80.

Through the retention of the vital breath (*pavana-dhāraṇā*), those essences arising from their respective core substances become the totality of flavors born from the element of fire; yet, because they obstruct the path leading to the nectar (*amṛta*), they become tasteless.
(81) It does not shine for the sake of manifestation, nor does it come within the range of perception. (82) The moon, fire, and stars shine as luminous bodies. (83)
A sky with a low asterism appears like a cause for the misfortune of the year; 84.
diseases born from that [asterism] are incurable. 85. Substances possessing moisture and sweet taste are the removers of those respective predicted misfortunes. 86.
Possessing the sweet flavor of a marvelous occurrence, it reverses the transformations occurring in the white constituent (*śukladhātu*).
(87) Such is the procedure for physical omens (*ariṣṭa*) among those who are healthy. (88) For children, [the duration is] one month. (89)
Half a day [is the duration] for one month.
(90) Those [fevers] born from disorders of wind and bile, from aversion to food, or from [other] morbidities are incurable.
(91) A fever born from a swelling disorder caused by a corruption of wind and phlegm is fatal. (92)

Fever arising from disorders of phlegm and bile, born of diarrhea, is destructive to the body. (93) Fever arising from disorders of bile and wind, born of phlegm-disorders and lack of appetite, is a destroyer of life. (94) Fever arising from disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm, born of disorders of all the sense organs, is destructive to the body. (95)

For those diseases arising from suppression of natural urges, overeating, or trauma, which are provoked internally, eating little and consuming tasteless substances are sometimes observed [as remedies].
Or rather, they desire [these] for the sake of the unseen (adṛṣṭa).
Thus ends the seventh inquiry of Āyurveda.
Now begins the eighth question. 1. They desire the consumption of the essence day by day. 2. He who goes to the unperishing is the remover of disease.

The taste arising from the earth element is the sweet-tasting rasa that activates the sense organ of taste and removes astringent tastes associated with rasa. 3. The meat-arising taste produced from the water element is pungent and corrupts swelling (śvayathu). 4. The bitter rasa arising from the fire element is the fat-arising [taste] that removes water-based impurities and diarrhea. 5.

That which arises from wind and spirits, possessing an internal salty and sour taste, cures diseases of the rasa and blood tissues. (6) The white-flowered variety destroys diseases located in the muscle tissue.
(7) The yellow-flowered variety is the destroyer of disorders residing in the fat tissue. (8)
Blue flowers destroy disorders of the joints, marrow, and the bodily constituents (dhātus).
Substances possessing many flowers remove diseases caused by deficient semen and loss of strength.
The essences of fruits are produced from seeds born of red flowers.
Those produced from seeds born of white flowers are *sārasārakas*.
(12) Those produced from seeds born of yellow flowers are *patrasārakas*.
(13) Those produced from seeds born of bulbs are *kandasārakas*. (14)
Those produced from seeds and generated by seeds are the "seed-essences" (bījasāraka). (15) Those produced from flowers and generated by flowers are the "flower-essences" (puṣpasāraka).

(16) That which is produced from yellow flowers removes the downward-flowing transformation of the white constituent (śukladhātu) and its natural state, and, like something possessing a sweet taste, it nourishes the final constituent. (17)

Trees that produce white flowers and yield juices from those flowers remove all wind disorders (vāta). (18) Trees with white flowers alleviate bile disorders (pitta). (19) Trees with yellow flowers destroy diseases caused by phlegm (kapha). (20)
Trees bearing blue flowers strike down diseases caused by the conjunction of dualities;
likewise, those with a single branch and many leaves do so.
Those born individually from the earth appear in a red form. 21–23.
24. Those born from the production of fire are of a middle nature characterized by yellow. 25. There are many composite parts possessing yellow radiance.
26. Substances in which air predominates do not shine like those that are devoid of qualities, deficient in qualities, or lacking all qualities.
Among those of golden complexion and those with the appearance of wind, there may be one who possesses more than one [of these] among many colors.
(27) This same rule applies to those of each single type who have been born many times.
(28) One who knows the causes of the disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm as they are understood through the forms of those elements becomes a seeker of long life. (29)

Preceded by the knowledge of the power of the *doṣas*, [it is understood that] the wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*) located below the navel, above it, and in the heart—whether combined or uncombined, and whether complete or incomplete—are the producers of diseases.

(30) The tastes (*rasa*) situated in specific locations are born from those respective elements (*bhūta*); they nourish the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). (31) In their natural, unaltered state, they nourish those constituents. (32)
Likewise, there are those born from the conjunction of semen and blood;
those caused by the mother's food and drink; and those diseases arising from substances. These are the natures of the womb, long-entrenched, and by them they revolve; by them they increase.
By that, the world is overcome.
At the time of the union of semen and blood, the natural conditions of the womb arise, caused by the food consumed by the mother; [the embryo] is enveloped by these and grows by them.
(36) Likewise, in the body, [it grows] by means of substances that cause emaciation and substances that cause nourishment.

(37) As many diseases as arise from the transformations of bodily desires, those born of mental afflictions, or those born of external injury—as many as they may increase, so many diseases arising from various substances, caused by the transformation of the constituent parts, come into being. (38)

Those who have previously experienced tastes and developed diseases from consuming various such tastes develop diseases from those very same tastes [in this life]. (39) Their constituent elements (*bhūta*) and elemental parts increase through substances born of causes that are of the same genus as the disease.
(40) Distinctions such as seeing, touching, and speaking are observed. (41)

Diseases of Vāta, Kapha, and Pitta are traditionally held to arise respectively from arid, marshy, and intermediate regions; they are produced by those [humors] and treated with medicines derived from those same elements, according to the methods prescribed in the medical treatises.
(42) Medicine is of two types: that which purifies and that which pacifies. (43) The Doshas are said to be the primary factors in this regard. (44)
By these, the purification of the body is the medicine.
(45) By these, food that purifies the body is the medicine. (46) It is beneficial for the procedures of upper and lower enemas. (47)
In that regard, there are restorative treatments such as oils, ghees, and electuaries for reversal [of disease].

(48) A physician who possesses knowledge of the distinctions among substances that are the objects of the treatise [is successful]. (49) A patient who is capable of utilizing all medicinal remedies shall become free from disease. (50)
When these [humors] are displaced from their order, they cause disorders; 51.
disease is that which produces disorders through irregular movement; 52. one is free from disease when the humors move in equilibrium. 53.
Day by day, one should meditate upon the Self alone.

(54) Having risen in the morning, one should perform the worship of the chosen deity. (55) One should determine [the nature of that deity] through its form, characteristics, and the attainment of its state of repose. (56)
The humors follow the seasons;
one should administer medicine in accordance with the season.
One should perform the internal cleansing of the teeth with bitter substances, milk, and fresh twigs, among others.
Beholding Locanā [is] 60;
anointing with oil from head to foot [is] 61; massage [is] a destroyer of phlegm. 62.
Washing with water that is comfortably warm [is prescribed]. 63. Thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath preceded by a formal resolve (saṅkalpa). 64.
For those who are unable [to perform the full ritual], there are ten types of baths. 65.
When there is impurity, life perishes. 66.
The qualification for pure action. 67. Medicine for one desiring long life. 68.

A person has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundred faculties; he becomes firmly established in both life and his faculties. (69) Observing the intentions of others, one should act while remaining concealed. (70) Those actions which are blameless should be practiced. (71)
Those which are irreproachable should be practiced by you,
and not others;
those which are our good deeds [should be followed].
Whosoever are the Brahmins superior to us, you must comfort them by offering them a seat.
(75) One should give with faith; (76) one should not give without faith. (77)
It should be given out of prosperity;
it should be given out of modesty;
it should be given out of fear.
The gift should be given with full awareness;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth.
Therefore, through engagement with the objects of the senses, a singular happiness is experienced.
Preceded by the causes of dharma, artha, and kāma, the middling [path] is the goal of all human pursuits; let it be revealed to the wise. 84–86.
One should neither oppress nor excessively indulge the senses;
thus always.
One should not harm any living beings.
In the morning, one should observe the absence of any disorder;
having voided excrement and urine, with a pure mind,
one perceives all beings as equal to one's own body.
One should worship the gods, Brahmins, cows, and supplicants; 93.
possessing conduct regulated by the prescribed rules, one enjoys 94.
long life, health, sovereignty, fame, and eternal worlds. 95.
The sun, wind, fire, stars, and so forth, established by the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), circulate.
96 The Wheel of Time bestows various forms of happiness. 97 That Time creates everything. 98
He is the nourisher of the entire world;
99 he alone is the cause of destruction; 100 he is the one eternal controller. 101
Knowing this,
he makes the world consist of food;
by the power of time and karma, he bestows various fruits.
Thus ends the eighth inquiry of Āyurveda;
now begins the ninth inquiry: [beings] of diverse forms and diverse limbs. 1.
Time possesses manifold methods: it causes the growth of both the stationary and the moving;
it carries the minuteness of the minute.
The great becomes greater.
The six flavors, impelled by time,
produce the perception of qualities and defects when caused by irregular timing.

That which yields contradictory results and arises from the ripening of uneven digestion [is such a time]. 8. The duration of time in which two units of strength are pierced by a needle is a *lava*. 9. Thirty *lavas* constitute a *tṛṭi*. 10.
Two *tṛṭis* constitute one *kāla*; 11. two *kālās* constitute one *mātrā*; 12. eighteen *mātrās* constitute one *kāṣṭhā*. 13.
Thirty *kāṣṭhās* make one *kalā*;
thirty *kalās* make one *kṣaṇa*;
six [of these] make one *nāḍikā*.
Two *nāḍikās* constitute one *muhūrta*. Four of those make one *yāma*.
Four *yāmas* make one day.
Likewise, *niśā* means night;
*aharniśam* means day and night;
and *pañcadaśāhaḥ* means a fortnight (*pakṣaḥ*).
Two fortnights constitute a month;
two months constitute a season;
three seasons constitute a solstice.
The year consists of six seasons and twelve months.
That year is the regulator of strength.
It produces time in the form of days, fortnights, months, seasons, years, and solstices.
Due to the variation in taste, various fruits produce different effects for one another.
Due to the variation in substance, many kinds of beings have existed for a long time and are difficult to comprehend.
In the season of Madhu and Mādhava, the sweet taste appeared.
Madhu and Mādhava are the two spring seasons (vāsantika-ṛtu).

Sweet taste destroys wind (pavana), though it is a cause for the provocation of phlegm (kapha-prakopa). Thereafter, the excessively sweet taste destroys bile (pitta) while also causing the provocation of phlegm.
The sweet [taste] appears as bitter during digestion;
by that very process, the white element increases,
acting as the producer of its pure qualities.
The seven bodily constituents flourish when they are in their natural state. When there is no such disorder, semen is impelled by honey-like [sweetness].
For its maintenance, the consumption of sweet food is the remedy. 38–40.
At that time, there was the mutual embrace of the limbs of women and men.
(41) For men of all castes, their respective beloveds were their nourishers.
(42) At each respective time, it shone forth as possessing its corresponding aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). (43)
That substance which possesses a similar taste is nourishing.
At the time of the *śukra* and *śuci* months, the sour taste (*amlarasa*) appeared.
*Śukra* and *śuci* are the two summer seasons (*graiṣmāvṛtu*).

Sour taste (amlarasa) provokes vāyu (anilaprakopakāraka). [47] Excessive sour substances cause the provocation of pitta (pittaprakopanāśana). [48] It becomes the cause for the provocation of kapha (kaphaprakopahetu). [49]
That which is not yet supported must be nourished.

(50) By means of food, drink, condiments, and conversation, as well as garlands, sandalwood, and the like appropriate to the time, one should provide medicine. (51) One should administer these according to the season itself. (52)
Through the conjunction of the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya, the salty taste is produced.
Nabhas and Nabhasya are the two rainy-season months.
It nourishes the bone constituent (*asthi-dhātu*) and performs its specific functions according to the requirements of that particular time.

Having observed that [the patient] is free from any morbid change, one should employ this [treatment]. (56) Having voided feces and urine, with a purified internal organ, (57) salt destroys wind caused by phlegm and bile. (58)
Salt with deficient or excessive salinity destroys phlegm and wind, but produces bile.
(59) Due to the conjunction of the months of Īṣa and Ūrja, the bitter taste appeared.
(60) Īṣa and Ūrja are the two autumnal seasons. (61)
It is bitter and sweet in its post-digestive effect (pāka).
That which possesses a deficient or excessive bitter taste destroys pitta and kapha, but produces vāta. Thus, the provocation of the doṣas occurs due to these causes.
Due to the conjunction of the months of Sahas and Sahasya, a pungent taste appears.
Sahas and Sahasya are the two winter seasons.
Pungent and extremely pungent [tastes] destroy phlegm and wind, while producing bile.
It became the source of the flesh-element (māṃsa-dhātu).
Through the conjunction of the seasons of *tapas* and *tapasya*, the astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*) appeared.
*Tapas* and *tapasya* are the two winter seasons (*śaiśira-ṛtu*).

Due to the excessive obstruction of the downward-moving wind (apāna) situated in the stomach (āmāśaya), and because of the congestion caused by the filling of the vessels that impel it, as well as the provocation of the wind moving along its own path due to that obstruction, abdominal tumors (gulma) and other ailments arise.
[71] There are pains in the abdomen, heart, throat, nose, and head.
[72] Therefore, one should expel the food, drink, and wind that have filled [the body]. [73]
The obstruction of food situated in the receptacle of digested matter (*pakvāśaya*) without excessive pressure [is recommended];
by that very means, the *doṣas* increase.
The obstruction of urine when the reservoir of water (*jalāśaya*) is full is the cause of diseases resulting from that obstruction.
Their suppression causes obstruction in the vessels and channels, pain, enlargement of the intestines, indigestion, and diseases of the eyes and ears (77).
Suppression of hunger causes weakness of the eyes, abdomen, head, and sense organs (78).
It is caused by smelling alkaline substances, pungent tastes, or añjana, as well as by bowing down or gazing at the sun (79).
From the absence of the alleviation of hunger, there arise burning sensations, vertigo, deafness, and abdominal pain. 80.
The same applies to thirst. 81.
From burning, weakness of the sense organs occurs. 82.
From laziness and excessive yawning, fever arises. [83] From oil massage and body rubbing, [fever arises]. [84] From the obstruction of phlegm, dyspnea arises. [85]
Loss of appetite, dyspnea, alcoholism, hiccup, and heart disease arise from the disappearance [of the breath] during yawning.
Itching, anemia, fever, leprosy, erysipelas, and diseases of the corrupted bowels arise from its disappearance.
Pleasant speech is the remedy for inducing sleep.
By suppressing blood from a wound, one incurs the disorders of *śoṣa*, *pāṇḍu*, and fever.
By suppressing vomiting, one causes delusion, dizziness, loss of appetite, and extreme weakness of the *vāyu*.
The remedy is to induce both upward and downward evacuation.

By knowing the time for the release of the final element and bringing about its cessation, one becomes capable of enduring heat and longevity. Diarrhea, dysentery, skin diseases, and heart ailments arise [if this is not done].
Thus ends the ninth inquiry of Āyurveda.
Now begins the tenth question.

Performing actions that are contrary to the time and the state of well-being while one is on the path of the bodily winds causes the destruction of the body. (1) Medicine is that which is produced from substances that nourish those [winds]. (2)
Performing the duties appropriate for that specific time;
ensuring that the seasonal juices produced are nourishing;
and observing [the patient's condition] day after day for any change.
One should nourish those things that are wholesome and appropriate. 6.
Examining and cleansing the substances that assist in that [process] nourishes the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). 7.
It removes impurities and filth. 8.
Through its connection with the constituents of earth, it bestows qualities favorable to all tastes;
through its connection with substances possessing a sweet taste, it increases semen;
and it promotes the growth of the watery element.
Water that has been boiled for too long and becomes excessively sour in taste excites the digestive fire (*pacana-pitta*) and removes [the heat].

Two finger-breadths above the anus and likewise two finger-breadths from the penis,
