Kuṇḍalinī exists in the form of eight constituent elements (prakṛtis), like a sleeping serpent.
Thus ends the tenth question of Āyurveda.
Now begins the eleventh question.
[The purpose is] for the attenuation of the afflictions and for the movement of the breath within the body. 1.
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions. 2. Ignorance is the field for the others—whether they be dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active. 3.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the eternal, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self.
(4) Self-identity (*asmitā*) is the apparent oneness of the powers of the seer and the seeing. (5) Attachment (*rāga*) is that which clings to pleasure. (6)
Aversion is that which lies latent within suffering. 7. The clinging to life (abhiniveśa) is an instinctive flow that persists even in the wise man, being so deeply rooted. 8.
These [five afflictions], when subtle, are to be abandoned by the process of involution (pratiprasava). 9.
The fluctuations [of the mind] are to be abandoned by meditation (dhyāna).
(10) The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions (kleśa) and is to be experienced in either the present or a future birth.
(11) When that root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. (12)

These have joy and sorrow as their fruits, because they have merit and demerit as their causes. (Yoga Sūtra 2.14) For the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering, due to the sufferings of change, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the fluctuations of the *guṇas*. (Yoga Sūtra 2.15) Suffering that has not yet come is to be avoided. (Yoga Sūtra 2.16)

The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned (suffering). 16. The "seen" consists of the elements and the senses, characterized by illumination, activity, and inertia; it exists for the purpose of experience and liberation. 17.
The stages of the gunas are the specific, the non-specific, the mere-indicative, and the unindicative. 18.
The Seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, he is the witness of the mental modifications.
(19) The nature of the object of perception exists solely for his sake.
(20) Although it has perished for one whose purpose is fulfilled, it has not perished, because it is common to others. (21)
Conjunction is the cause for the perception of the essential nature of both the self and the Lord. Ignorance is the cause of that conjunction.
From the absence of that [ignorance], there is the absence of conjunction; this cessation is the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the seer from that [object].
Unshakable discriminative discernment is the means to liberation.
(25) His wisdom has seven stages of culmination.
(26) From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there arises the light of knowledge up to discriminative discernment. (27)

The eight limbs are: restraint (yama), observance (niyama), posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). 28. Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints (yamas). 29. These, when not limited by species, place, time, or circumstance, and practiced universally, constitute the Great Vow (mahāvratam). 30.
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas). 31.
When there is obstruction by perverse thoughts (vitarka), one should cultivate their opposites.
32. Perverse thoughts consist of non-violence and so forth, whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved, and whether motivated by greed, anger, or delusion...
The cultivation of the counteragent consists in the realization that intentional acts—whether mild, moderate, or intense—result in endless suffering and ignorance.
(33) When non-violence is firmly established, hostility ceases in its presence. (34) When truthfulness is firmly established, one becomes the locus for the fruits of action. (35)
When non-stealing is firmly established, there is the appearance of all kinds of jewels. When celibacy is firmly established, there is the attainment of vigor.
When non-possessiveness is stabilized, there is the awakening to the nature of one's births.
From purity comes a sense of revulsion toward one's own body and non-contact with others;
[these lead to] purification of the mind, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the senses, and fitness for the vision of the Self.
From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness. (39–41)
The perfection of the faculty of the body arises from austerity that destroys impurity; 42. communion with one’s chosen deity arises from study; 43.
the perfection of samādhi arises from devotion to the Lord. 44.
Posture (āsana) is that which is firm and pleasant. [It is achieved] through the relaxation of effort and by attaining the infinite.
Thereafter, there is no affliction from the dualities.
When that [pratyāhāra] exists, the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation is prāṇāyāma.
(YS 2.48) It has external, internal, and stationary modes; it is regulated by place, time, and number, and is thus long and subtle.
(YS 2.49) The fourth [type] transcends both the external and internal objects. (YS 2.50)
From that, the veil over the light is destroyed;

(51) and there is fitness of the mind for the concentrations (dhāraṇās). (52) Pratyāhāra is the imitation by the senses of the nature of the mind itself when they are not in contact with their own objects. (53)
Thereafter, [the chapter] on those whose senses are under supreme control.
Thus ends the eleventh inquiry of Āyurveda;
now begins the twelfth inquiry.
Concentration (dhāraṇā) is the binding of the mind to a single place. Meditation (dhyāna) is the one-pointed flow of cognition toward that object.
Samādhi is that same [meditation] when it shines forth as the object alone, as if devoid of its own form.
The three together constitute *saṃyama*.
(4) From mastery over that, there arises the light of wisdom. (5) Its application is upon the stages [of meditative concentration]. (6)
The triad [of seat, posture, and breath-control] is internal compared to the preceding [five];
even that is external to one who is seedless.

The transformation of cessation is the sequence of the mind at the moment of cessation, characterized by the suppression of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of outward activity and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation.

The transformation of that [mind] into a state of peaceful flow occurs through mental impressions (saṃskāra). 10. The transformation of the mind as samādhi is the waning of all-objectedness and the arising of one-pointedness. 11.
The transformation of the mind’s one-pointedness is the equality of the subsided and the arisen cognitions. 12.

By this, the transformations of properties (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*) in the elements and the sense organs have been explained. (13) The substratum (*dharmī*) conforms to its properties, whether they are subsided, arisen, or unmanifested. (14) A difference in sequence is the cause for a difference in transformation. (15)
Through *saṃyama* on the three transformations, there is knowledge of the past and the future.
(YS 3.16) Because of the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is confusion; through *saṃyama* on their distinction, there is knowledge of the cries of all beings.
(YS 3.17) From the direct perception of *saṃskāras*, there is knowledge of previous births. (YS 3.18)
The supernormal power of knowing the minds of others is a type of cognition based on conditions.
(19) That [knowledge] does not possess an objective support (*sālambana*), because [the other's mind] has not become an object for it.

(20) Through *saṃyama* upon the body and its form, when the capacity to be perceived by them is suppressed, there occurs invisibility (*antardhāna*) due to the lack of contact between the eye and light. (21)

Karma is of two kinds: that which is subject to external influence (*sopakrama*) and that which is not subject to external influence (*nirupakrama*). Through *saṃyama* upon these, there arises knowledge of the time of one's departure from the body (*aparāntajñāna*), or [such knowledge may arise] from portents (*ariṣṭas*).
(YS 3.22) Powers arise from *saṃyama* upon friendliness and the other [virtues].
(YS 3.23) From *saṃyama* upon powers, one attains the power of an elephant. (YS 3.24)
Through the application of light to the process of movement, there is knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the remote.
(YS 3.25) Through saṃyama on the sun, there is knowledge of the worlds. (YS 3.26) On the moon, there is knowledge of the arrangement of the stars. (YS 3.27)
28. Knowledge of their movement in the *dhruva* [cakra]. 29. Knowledge of the bodily array in the *nābhicakra*. 30. Cessation of hunger and thirst in the *kaṇṭhakūpa*.
Stability in the *kūrma* channel;
31. perception of the perfected ones (*siddhas*) in the light at the crown of the head; 32. or, through intuitive insight (*prātibha*), everything [is known]. 33.

In the heart is the perception of the mind. (YS 3.34) Experience is the non-distinction of the cognitions of the sattva and the puruṣa, which are absolutely distinct. From saṃyama on the object as such, there arises knowledge of the puruṣa. (YS 3.35) Thence arise the supernormal powers of intuition, hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell. (YS 3.36)
These are obstacles to concentration (*samādhi*), but they are accomplishments (*siddhi*) upon emergence from it.
(37) Through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind, there is entry into another's body.
(38) Through mastery over the *udāna* breath, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and so forth, as well as the power of departure [from the body]. (39)
From mastery over the *samāna* breath, there is radiance.
(40) From *saṃyama* on the connection between the ear and space, there is divine hearing.
(41) From *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and from the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of lightness like that of cotton, there is movement through space. (42)
The external non-conceptualized state is the "Great Bodilessness" (*mahāvideha*); from that follows the destruction of the veil of illumination. 43.
Through *saṃyama* on the gross form, the essential nature, the subtle, the inherence, and the purposefulness [of the elements], there is mastery over the elements. 44.
From that, the manifestation of the powers such as atomization (*aṇimā*), the perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by their properties. 45.
Perfection of the body consists in beauty, grace, strength, and adamantine compactness.
(46) Through *saṃyama* upon the perception, the essential nature, self-sense, inherence, and purposefulness [of the senses], there is mastery over the senses.
(47) From that, there arise swiftness like the mind, the state of having no physical organs, and mastery over *pradhāna*. (48)
For one who possesses only the discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there arises sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience.

(49) From dispassion toward even that [omniscience], upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). (50) When addressed by those who dwell in the higher realms, one should avoid attachment and pride, because of the risk of falling back into undesirable states. (51)
Through *saṃyama* on moment and its sequence, knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arises.

(Yoga Sūtra 3.52) Because of the lack of distinction in terms of genus, characteristic, and location, there is no discernment of difference between two similar things; from that [knowledge], their perception occurs. (Yoga Sūtra 3.53) Knowledge born of discrimination is illuminating, has all things as its object, has all modes as its object, and is non-sequential. (Yoga Sūtra 3.54)

When there is equality of purity between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is isolation (*kaivalya*). (55) Perfections arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative concentration (*samādhi*). (56) The transformation into another species occurs through the influx of primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (57)
The external sign is not the motivator of the *prakṛtis*; rather, it is the removal of their obstruction, like a farmer [using water].
(58) Emanation-minds arise from the mere state of "I-am-ness" (*asmitāmātra*).
(59) Among many minds, there is one mind that acts as the motivator for the differentiation of their activities. (60)
Among these, that which is born of meditation is without latent residue (anāśaya).
For the yogi, karma is neither white nor black; for others, it is of three kinds.
Even when separated by birth, place, or time, there is immediate succession because memory and its latent impressions (saṃskāra) are of a single nature.
Their beginninglessness is due to the eternity of the aspiration (*āśis*).
(64) Because they are comprised by cause, fruit, basis, and object, in the absence of these, they are absent.
(65) The past and the future exist in their own nature (*svarūpa*) because of the distinction of the time-periods (*adhvan*) of phenomena (*dharma*). (66)
These manifest and subtle [objects] consist of the gunas.
(67) The reality of an object consists in its unity through transformation. (68) Since there is identity of the object but diversity of minds, the paths of these two are distinct. (69)
Furthermore, an object does not depend solely on a single moment of consciousness; otherwise, what would happen to that object when it is not being cognized?
Because the mind depends upon the coloring by that object, the object is either known or unknown.
However, the fluctuations of the mind are always known to their master, the Puruṣa, because the Puruṣa is unchanging.
It does not have that [external object] as its own appearance, because it is something seen. (73) Furthermore, both cannot be determined at the same time.
(74) If [the object] were seen by another mind, there would be the over-extension of the intellect [to infinite regress], as well as a confusion of memory. (75)
The perception of one's own intellect occurs when the incorporeal [mind] assumes the form of that [object].
Thus ends the twelfth question in the Āyurveda Sūtra;
now begins the thirteenth question.

1. *Kṣaya* (wasting) is the diminution of all the defects residing in the channels (*sirāpatha*), which are caused by a weak digestive fire produced by various actions that dehydrate the *dhātus* and have multiple objects as their effects; it is also the increase or decrease of all the defects belonging to parasites (*krimi*).
2. The substance that counteracts and nourishes [the body] therein is the medicine (*bheṣaja*).
3. The symptoms (*lakṣaṇa*) are likewise [to be understood].
And one should cause it to be turned back by those who are suitable; 4. a substance produced from many causes performs many functions; 5.
one should perform the protection of that which is nameless; 6.

For Brahmā has declared that undigested matter (*āma*) is indeed the primary cause of all diseases. Herein are observed the disorders of the channels (*sirā*) afflicted by *āma*, bile, poison, and worms; the disorders of the blood constituent (*rasa* and *asṛk-dhātu*) resulting from the consumption of substances rich in the quality of odor (*gandha*), as well as earthy substances and those with deficient tastes.

In the case of *āmaja-jvara* (fever born of undigested matter) caused by the consumption of substances with deficient or contrary tastes, fasting and drying agents (*viśoṣaka-dravya*) are the remedies. 10.
From that, swellings, anemia, diarrhea, hemorrhoids, skin diseases, internal hemorrhaging, and urinary disorders are observed to arise.

11. It follows many diseases and precedes many diseases; for this reason, a substance with deficient or contrary tastes among the six tastes causes the destruction of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) according to its specific application. 12.

For *rasa* (plasma) is indeed blood; *rasa* is truly that [essence]. Having obtained *rasa*, one indeed becomes blissful. 13. Semen is sweet; marrow is sour; bone is salty; fat is bitter; flesh is pungent. Those with an astringent taste nourish the elements of *rasa* and blood. 14. *Rasa* and blood are sweet; flesh is sour; fat is salty; bone is bitter; marrow is pungent; semen has an astringent taste and is devoid of flavor (*virasa*). Those that are flavorless destroy the elements of *rasa* and blood. 15.
Whichever tastes are produced from those respective elements, they nourish those very same elements.

(16) The great tastes (*mahārasa*), consisting of the five elements, arise from the substratum of mercury, secondary minerals, metals, and so forth; these great tastes, which eliminate specific major diseases, consist of tastes directed toward their respective functions and are characterized by the processes of digestion (*jāraṇā*) and infusion (*bhāvanā*). (17) One should not cause mercury to die (*mārayet*) unless it has been digested (*jārita*). (18)
The processed essences (*rasa*) bestow health, devotion, and liberation.

(19) The *soma-rasa* essences, when cooked along with bile and poison, eliminate the disorders of wind and bile caused by the movement of wind and bile residing in the blood, flesh, fat, and marrow, as well as fever, delusion, drowsiness, pain, and burning sensations. (20) The pure essences (*śuddha-rasa*), when cooked together with the nectar of dead metals (*mṛtaloha-amṛta*), eliminate the aggravation of drowsiness, burning, and emaciation caused by the dual action of wind and bile following disorders in the fat and bone, as well as those arising from the digestion of essences, undigested matter (*āma*), bile, poison, worms, throat-thorns, hunchbackedness, white limbs, and red tongues. (21)

As long as the defects of *āma* resulting from the undigested state of the scent-wind (*gandhapavana*) are externally visible; as long as the defects of *pitta* resulting from the *āma* caused by the undigested state of that which is other than scent (*gandhetara*) prevail within the body; and as long as the defects that generate *pitta* resulting from the *āma* caused by the undigested state of the scent-wind are observed externally—for that long, there exists the ignorance regarding specific scents, as well as the defects of the wind (*pavana*) arising from the *āma* produced by indigestion caused by the three humors (*doṣa-traya*).
22. The specific *āma* resulting from indigestion caused by the consumption of substances with unwholesome tastes is a defect of *pitta*.
23. A defect of *pitta* is not produced by that [ignorance] alone. 24. [This is] a defect of *pitta*.
The external humors (doṣas) situated outside cause disorders of the teeth;
[25] they are presided over by the fifty phonemes and, according to their respective application, increase those specific body parts.
[26] The external fire blazes in the location of the fire. [27]
Fire is established in my speech; speech is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the Immortal; the Immortal is in Brahman.
(28) The initiator of speech sets ablaze the channels and arteries.
(29) Wind is established in my breath; breath is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the Immortal; the Immortal is in Brahman. (30)

Or rather, the sun enters the fire at evening; therefore, the fire is not seen from afar. May the sun impel my sight. The sun is established in my eyes; the eye is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman.
(31) One should eat food that does not cause modifications of the mind.
(32) Substantial food that possesses flavor causes freedom from disease in the head and gladdens all the senses. (33)

The mind-substance (manodravya) of disagreeable coloration is supported by the five vital breaths (prāṇas). 34. The Moon is seated in my mind; the mind is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the Immortal; the Immortal is in Brahman. 35.
The water-substance nourishes the entire body. 36.
Water is indeed semen. Water is supported in my semen; semen is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. Thus, he places semen within that semen.
(37) The earth, which nourishes the entire body, is devoid of fragrance and devoid of taste.
(38) Earth is supported in my body; the body is in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman. (39)
As long as there is a substance possessing flavor, it is a producer of health.
As long as there is hair, so long do they bear bodies.

The plants have entered into King Soma; the earth has entered his body. The herbs and trees are stationed in my body hairs; the body hairs are in the heart; the heart is in me; I am in the immortal; the immortal is in Brahman.

Indra is established in my strength; strength in the heart; the heart in me; I in the immortal; the immortal in Brahman. 43 As far as there are hairs on the body, so far are there bodies—this is the manifestation. Through Parjanya, herbs and trees are produced. Parjanya is established in my head; the head in the heart; the heart in me; I in the immortal; the immortal in Brahman. 44 The wrath impelled by the Lord of the Forest arises. Īśāna is established in my wrath; wrath in the heart; the heart in me; I in the immortal; the immortal in Brahman. 45
The knowledge of Āyurveda is preceded by the knowledge of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
Thus ends the thirteenth inquiry concerning Āyurveda.
Now begins the fourteenth inquiry.
The foot-lotus, which is the nature of the Aśvinī constellation, is enveloped by thirty-seven channels (*sirā*); it is the support for the vowel *a* and the foundation of the entire body.

(1) The knee-lotus, which is the form of the Bharaṇī asterism, rests upon thirty-seven channels; it is born from the vowel *i* and performs the functions of movement and the actions of coming and going.
(2) The shank-lotus, presided over by the Kṛttikā lunar mansion, is enveloped by thirty-seven channels; it rests on the vowel *u* and serves as the support for the mobile body. (3)
The lotus of the penis, having the form of the Rohiṇī constellation, is enveloped by thirty-seven channels (sirās) and rests upon the vowel Ṛ;
it is the cause of procreation. The lotus of the thighs, which supports the channels and awakens the vowel Ṛ, sustains the moving body. 4.

The form of the Mṛgaśiras constellation, supported by thirty-seven vessels, is the lotus located in the region that indicates the sound *lṛ* and sustains the reservoir of water-impurities. (5) The nature of the Ārdrā constellation, supported by thirty-seven vessels, is the lotus in the region of the back that makes known the sound *e* and produces extreme pleasure. (6) The indicator of the Punarvasu lunar mansion, supported by thirty-seven vessels, is the lotus that sustains the sound *ai* and produces the pleasure of sexual union. (7)

The form of the Tiṣya star is covered by thirty-seven channels; it rests upon the navel-lotus of the vowel *o*, causes the movement of the breath-wind, and consists of the constellation Āśleṣā. It is covered by thirty-seven channels, serves as the support for the vowel *au*, has its lotus coiled at the navel, and effects the movement of the wind. (8–9) The form of the Makhā constellation consists of thirty-seven hanging channels; it is the lotus covering the navel that makes known the resonance of the syllable *am*, and it brings about the digestive bile (*pācaka-pitta*). (10)

The lotus of the two testicles, which has the form of the *phalgunī* constellation, supports thirty-seven channels, indicates the letter *kha*, and nourishes the basin for the sprouts of the seven constituents (*dhātu*). 11.

The lotus of the line of body hair, which is of the nature of the *uttaraphalgunī* constellation, supports thirty-seven channels, indicates the letter *kha*, and is the cause of the bliss of emission (*visarjana*). 12.

The lotus of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, which is of the nature of the *phalgunī* constellation, supports thirty-seven channels, indicates the letter *kha*, and illuminates all latent dispositions (*āśaya*). 13.

The lotus situated on the right wing, which represents the constellation Hasta, is supported by thirty-seven vessels, indicates the letter *ga*, and is the cause of the formation of the womb (*garbhāśaya*).

(14) The lotus situated on the left wing, which has the form of the constellation Citrā, is enveloped by twenty-seven vessels, makes known the letter *gha*, and is the cause of the fully developed womb.

(15) The lotus of the right hand, which represents the lunar mansion Svāti, is supported by thirty-seven vessels, indicates the letter *ṅa*, and makes known the various distinct vowels present within that body. (16)

The left lotus-hand, which has the form of the Viśākhā constellation, is supported by thirty-seven veins, indicates the letter *cha*, and makes known the distinction between the voices of men and women. (17) The right arm-lotus, which consists of the Anūrādhā constellation, is enveloped by thirty-seven veins, indicates the letter *cha*, and supports the upper body. (18) The left arm-lotus, which has the form of the Rohiṇī constellation, is enveloped by thirty-seven veins and supports the upper body. (19)
The lotus of the right arm, having the form of the constellation Citrā, supporting thirty-seven channels and indicating the syllable *ja*, is beneficial for all ritual activities.
(20) The lotus of the left arm, having the form of the constellation Āṣāḍhā, enveloped by thirty-seven channels and signifying the syllable *jha*, is beneficial for all ritual activities.
(21) The lotus of the right forearm, consisting of the constellation Āṣāḍhā, supporting thirty-seven channels and illuminating the syllable *ña*, indicates skill in hand gestures. (22)
The lotus of the left forearm, consisting of the Śroṇā constellation, enveloped by thirty-seven veins, awakened by the phoneme *ṭa*, and indicative of manual dexterity; 23.

The lotus of the right palm, consisting of the Śraviṣṭhā constellation, enveloped by thirty-seven veins, awakened by the phoneme *ṭha*, and indicative of the knowledge of all gestures (*sarvārthābhinaya*); 24.

The lotus of the left palm, consisting of the Śatabhiṣak constellation, supported by thirty-seven veins, awakened by the phoneme *ḍa*, and the cause of the knowledge of all gestures (*sarvārthābhinayajñāna*). 25.

The throat-lotus, which consists of the *proṣṭhapadā* constellation, is enveloped by thirty-seven channels; it manifests the phoneme *ḍha* and makes known the various distinctions of vowels based on those respective phonemes. 26. The neck-lotus, which consists of the *proṣṭhapadā* constellation, is enveloped by thirty-seven channels; it manifests the phoneme *ṇa* and serves as the support for the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*). 27.

The heart-lotus, which consists of the *proṣṭhapadā* constellation, is enveloped by thirty-seven channels; it awakens the phoneme *ta* and is the cause of knowledge consisting of volition and effort. 28.

The asterism Revatī has the form of a constellation and is enveloped by thirty-seven channels; it is the indicator of the letter *tha* and is the lotus consisting of the head-lotus, which makes known the knowledge of the letters residing in the thousand channels.
(29) There are sixty nāḍīs in a day and night. (30) Fifteen days constitute a fortnight (*pakṣa*). (31)
Two fortnights constitute a month;
two months constitute a season;
three seasons constitute a solstice.
The year consists of six seasons and twelve months. 35.
Aśvinī is fever. 36. Bharaṇī is dysentery. 37.
Kṛttikā is dysentery; Rohiṇī is disorders of hemorrhoids;
Mṛgaśīrṣa is indigestion.
In Ārdrā, there is a gentle breeze;
in Punarvasū, cholera;
in Tiṣya, loss of appetite.
Āśleṣā is jaundice; Maghā is labored breathing; Phalgunī is cough.
Phalgunī: skin disease (kuṣṭha); 47. Hasta: urinary disorder (meha); 48. Citrā: abdominal disease (kukṣiroga); 49.
In Svātī, there is eye disease;
in Viśākhā, ear disease; in Anūrādhā, nasal disease. 50, 51, 52.
Rohiṇī: epilepsy. 53. Vicṛti: consumption. 54. Pūrvāṣāḍhā: leprosy and urinary stones. 55.
Uttarāṣāḍhā causes skin diseases and disorders of vomiting; Śroṇā causes heart disease; Śraviṣṭhā causes wind disorders.
Śatabhiṣaj: diseases of bile (pitta). 59. Proṣṭhapada: diseases of phlegm (kapha). 60. Proṣṭhapada: alcoholism (madātyaya). 61.
Revatī is the wound. 62.

Fevers caused by the corruption of undigested food (āmadoṣa), bile (pitta), poisons, and worms—arising from the influence of specific times when the moon is in conjunction with the constellation Aśvinī and associated with malefic planets—are observed. 63.
Medicinal plants that cover the entire network of vessels (sirā) which indicate the [patient's] complexion are the removers of the provocation of fever. 64.
That which removes indigestion, āma-pitta, poison, and worms is indeed the medicine.
(65) The administration of medicinal herbs, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, and worship of the deities are the means of removal.
(66) "Where the medicinal herbs have gathered together like kings in an assembly, that Brahmin is called a physician, a slayer of demons, a dispeller of disease. (67)
Compounds prepared from *kaṭurohikā*, the *gaṇa* of *caudira*, poison, mineral stones, and iron-encrusting substances (*lohapuṭa*) are effective in curing those diseases.
(68) In some cases, they are administered as decoctions; (69) in other cases, as powders and so forth. (70)
In some cases, oils, electuaries, clarified butter, and so forth [are used].
(71) There, the worship of the deity Aśvinī is the remedy.

(72) Fevers arising by virtue of the conjunction of specific lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), *viguṇi* yogas, and planetary positions are difficult to cure. Knowledge of what is to be removed and the means of removal is the appropriate remedy for them. (73)
Due to the conjunction of the time with the *bharaṇī* asterism, the *vigati* yoga, and the influence of the planets, diseases such as dysentery are observed to appear.
(74) The application of various medicinal herbs corresponding to the specific vessels and channels indicated by the letter *i* serves to eliminate them.
(75) Worship of the deity Yama is the means of their cessation. (76)

Due to the conjunction of time with planets born of adverse movements in the Kṛttikā constellation, the disease of *grahaṇī* (malabsorption) arises. (77) The application of treatments involving herbs that grow in autumn and possess vessels and stalks characterized by the vowel *u* cures the disease of *grahaṇī*. (78) The ritual procedure for praying to the deity Agni is also curative. (79)
The onset of hemorrhoids occurs due to the conjunction of time characterized by the presence of planets at the time of the Rohiṇī constellation and the Viṣṭi yoga.

(80) Any substance that removes the network of vessels and ducts indicated by the vowel *ṛ* is a remedy for the disease of hemorrhoids. (81) Prayer to Prajāpati as the presiding deity is the medicine in this case. (82)

Due to the conjunction of the time with planets born from the *mṛgaśīrṣa-viruddha-gati-yoga*, diseases of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arise. (83) The application of medicinal herbs that awaken digestion and cover all the channels and vessels is the remedy for the disease of indigestion. (84) Prayer to the deity Soma and so forth is also a remedy. (85)

Due to the conjunction of the time at which a planet is born under the *vigati* yoga of the *Ārdrā* nakṣatra, a disease of weak digestion (*mandānalaroga*) arises. The medicine for weak digestion consists of whatever substances are capable of removing the blockages in as many vessels (*sirā*) as are indicated by the phonemes *e* and *ai*.
(86) The procedure (*vidhi*) is the petitioning of the deity Rudra in the form of whatever expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are required to remove those respective evils.
(87) Thus ends the fourteenth inquiry of Āyurveda.
Now begins the fifteenth question.

Due to the conjunction of time with the movement and planetary alignment of Punarvasu, the disease Viṣūcī arises. (1) The application of herbs that cause the circulation of blood through as many vessels as are indicated by the letters *ā* and *au* serves to eliminate the disease Viṣūcī. (2)
The prayer to the deity Aditi is a remedy.
(3) Due to the specific conjunction of the Tiṣya constellation with planets arising from its transit, a disease of loss of appetite occurs.
(4) Whatever substance illuminates the complexion and pervades the channels and vessels, and whatever brings them back [to health], serves as a remedy for the disease of anorexia. (5)

The prayer to the deity Bṛhaspati is the remedy. (6) Due to the conjunction of the Aśleṣā nakṣatra, the vigati yoga, and the influence of the planets at that time, the disease of jaundice (pāṇḍvāmaya) arises. (7) The application of substances of corresponding nature—encompassing all the vessels and channels that manifest the colors [of the skin] beginning with *ka* and *kha*—is the means for curing the disease of jaundice. (8)

Due to the influence of a specific time characterized by the unfavorable transit of planets during the constellation Makhā, the disease of asthma (śvāsāmaya) arises. The remedial herbs are those that pervade as many vessels and stalks as are indicated by the letters *ga* and *gha*.

Worship of the ancestors and deities, recitation of mantras (japa), and fire offerings (homa) constitute the medicine. Due to the influence of a specific time characterized by the unfavorable transit of planets during the constellation Phalgunī, the disease of cough (kāsāmaya) comes into being.
12. The application of medicinal formulations consisting of various veins, stalks, and creepers that indicate [the patient's] complexion is a remedy for the disease of cough.
13. The ritual procedure consists of praying to the deity Aryaman.

14. Due to the influence of the time when the moon enters the constellation Phalgunī while conjoined with a planet, the disease of leprosy arises; the application of medicinal formulations consisting of various veins, stalks, and creepers that illuminate the complexion is a remedy for the disease of leprosy.
The ritual procedure consists of the prayer to the deity Bhaga.
(15) Due to the influence of the time at which the urinary disorder arises, as determined by the movement of the lunar mansion Hasta and its conjunction with planets, the disease of meha manifests.
(16) The application of medicinal herbs that cover the network of vessels, which are indicated by the letters *ja* and *jha*, brings about the cessation of the disease of meha. (17)
The prayer to the deity Savitṛ is the remedy.
(18) A disease of fainting arises by virtue of the specific time of conjunction with a planet born under the constellation Citrā.
(19) Any substance that dispels the obstruction of the channels and illuminates the five colors is the remedy for the disease of fainting. (20)
The ritual procedure consists of a prayer to Indra as the presiding deity.
(21) Due to the conjunction of time associated with the transit of the Svātī asterism and its connection with specific planetary positions, an eye disease arises.
(22) Any substance that contains the essence of the *ṭa* and *ṭha* phonemes, and which pervades all the channels and vessels, removes the eye disease. (23)
The ritual procedure for supplicating the deity Vāyu [is as follows]: 24.
Due to the influence of the time when the planet [Mars] is situated in the movement of the Viśākhā nakṣatra, ear disease arises. 25.
The application of medicinal herbs that envelop the vessels and stalks which illuminate the letters *ḍa* and *ḍha* is the remedy for its removal. 26.
The prayer to the deities Indra and Agni, which effects the ripening of those respective karmas, is the medicine.
(27) Due to the influence of the time when the planet associated with the movement of the Anurādhā nakṣatra is joined [with it], a disease of the nose arises.
(28) The application of substances consisting of as many fibers as there are channels that indicate the nine letters is the remover of nasal disease. (29)
The prayer to the deity Mitra is a means of turning [disease] back.
(30) Likewise, the application of medicinal herbs to the sheaths of the vessels that indicate the complexion and cover the nostrils removes diseases of the nose.
(31) The prayer to the deity Mitra is a means of turning [disease] back. (32)
Facial disease arises due to the influence of the time when the Rohiṇī constellation is joined with a planet at the moment of its disappearance.
(33) The application of appropriate medicinal substances, such as curd-colored *bodhaka* and fibers from lotus stalks, is the remedy for facial disease.
(34) The ritual procedure consists of praying to Indra, the presiding deity. (35)

Due to the influence of the conjunctions and times of planets that arise from contrary movements and retrograde motions, decay occurs. (36) The application of substances prepared by being enclosed within the stalks of as many lotus fibers as there are letters signifying the disease brings about the cessation of that malady. (37)
Prayer to the ancestral deities (*pitṛdevatā*) is the medicine.
(38) Due to the influence of the time when the *Aṣāḍhā* constellation is in its [specific] position and conjoined with a planet, the disease of urinary calculi (*aśmarī*) manifests.

(39) [The remedy consists of] whatever substances there may be that are indicated by the letters *ra*, *ha*, *la*, *pa*, and *pha*, which illuminate the vessels and channels, and which cause [the obstruction] to cease.

It prevents urinary calculi. 40. Prayer to the water-deities is a preventive measure. 41. Due to the influence of time characterized by the conjunction of the Aṣāḍhā constellation with the rising of the moon and the presence of malefic planets, the disease of vomiting occurs. 42.
43. It becomes covered with veins and stalks that manifest various colors; this application of medicinal herbs is the remedy.
44. The consecration by the Viśvedevas is the remedy.
45. Due to the conjunction of time with planets arising from unfavorable movements during the Śroṇā constellation, a disease of aversion (anorexia) occurs.

The application of a combination of substances appropriate for that [condition], administered through as many channels as are necessary to convey the letter *ma*, brings about the cessation of that disease.
(46) Prayer to Lord Viṣṇu is the remedy in that case.
(47) A wind-related disorder arises due to the influence of a conjunction with a time when a planet is in a retrograde motion or otherwise unfavorable during the Śraviṣṭhā asterism. (48)
A substance of that same class, enclosed within the respective channels and vessels caused by the pronunciation of excellent syllables, is a remedy for that particular disease.
(49) Prayer to the deity Vasu is a medicine. (50) A bile disorder arises through the influence of the conjunction of the planet and time produced by the movement of the Śatabhiṣaj constellation. (51)
The application of substances that counteract those [symptoms] which are enveloped by as many vessels as manifest the color of the wash-water is a remedy for the provocation of *pitta*. 52.
Prayer to Indra as the presiding deity is the medicine in that case. 53.
A phlegmatic disease (*kaphāmaya*) arises at a specific time when there is an unfavorable movement of the *proṣṭhapadā* constellation and the conjunction of planets. 54.
The preparation of a medicinal compound using as many fibers and stalks as possible from plants whose names begin with the letter *śa* removes diseases caused by *kapha*.
(55) The ritual procedure involves praying to the deity Ajaikapād.
(56) Due to the influence of the time when the moon is in conjunction with planets moving in opposition to the *proṣṭhapadā* constellation, diseases of epilepsy (*apasmāra*) arise. (57)
The application of as many substances as can be contained within a vessel covered by as many veins and stalks as indicate the same color (savarṇa) removes the disease of epilepsy. 58.
Prayer to the deity Ahirbudhnya is averter [of that disease]. 59.
Due to the influence of time, when there is a conjunction of planets arising from unfavorable movements during the Revatī asterism, a wound or disease occurs. 60.
The application of whatever substances are contained within the vessels and tubular organs that illuminate the cavities [of the body] effects the cessation of wounds and diseases.
(61) The ritual procedure consists of praying to the deity Pūṣan.

(62) Blood-bile disorders arise from the consumption of excessive substances by those whose digestive fire has been weakened, resulting in indigestion, and from the production of āma, bile, poison, worms, and disorders of the vessels. (63)
All substances that perceive qualities superior to those of water, which remove its disorders, include:

*paṭola*, *gopā* (cow’s foot), thick rain-clouds, *rohiṇī*, *keśya*, sandalwood, *tiktāvarī*, blue lotus, *yaṣṭīmadhu*, grapes, sugarcane, *padmaka*, *reṇuka*, neem, *vadhū*, *trāyantī*, *madayantī*, *vatsaka*, *mūrvā*, *priyaṅgu*, *mahatī*, *sthirāparṇī*, *balā*, banyan tree, *viśva*, *mocarasa*, and so forth—all such substances, whether in the form of powders, decoctions, oils, electuaries, or other preparations, remove the provocation of the disease of *raktapitta*.

The disorders of dyspnea and cough arise from the consumption of excessive water-based substances, resulting in indigestion, and are caused by the vitiation of the vessels due to *āmadoṣa*, *pitta*, poison, and worms.
(66) All substances that perceive the qualities of the fire element serve as remedies for those disorders.

(67) These include: vāśā, niśā, kṣudrā, amṛtā, muṇḍikā, potā, śaṭhī, kuṇḍalī, punarnavā, bhārṅgī, masī, kokilākṣa, brāhmī, jharasī, varuṇa, maṇḍūkaparṇī, arka, alarka, ārtava, tapasvinī, bhṛṅgī, suvarcalā, and bilva.

Kāśmīra, takkāri, pāṭalā, aṃśumatī, sthirā, granthi, cavya, citraka, śuṇṭhī, pacyāta, karabha, rājamāriṣa, śṛṅgī, dhātrī, vibhītaka, elā, lavaṅga, patra, nāgakeśara, dhanvayāsa, tuṣa, gandhavāri, jīraka, and dīpyaka—these are used in preparations such as powders, decoctions, oils, and electuaries. They remove disorders caused by the fiery element, such as dyspnea, cough, and the provocation of blood.
Disorders arising from the consumption of excessive fiery substances, indigestion, āma-pitta, poison, worms, and diseases of the vessels, as well as hiccups, are also treated by these. (68–69)
All substances that perceive the qualities of water and earth in their obstructive state are removers of those disorders.

(70) A decoction prepared with wood-apple (*kapittha*), long pepper (*kaṇā*), honey, salt, garlic (*rasona*), the ten roots (*daśamūla*), milk, *punarnavā*, *nirguṇḍī*, *balā*, blue lotus (*utpala*), *pittavarā*, costus (*kuṣṭha*), *kaṭuka*, *cavya*, *aśvagandhā*, and *suvarcala* is a remover of the disease of hiccups (*hidhmā*). (71) The consumption of other substances that are mutually incompatible with the constituent elements (*dhātu*) produces indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), which in turn causes undigested matter (*āma*), bile (*pitta*), poison (*viṣa*), worms (*krimi*), and disorders of the vessels (*sira*). The remedy for this is a single medicine that nourishes all the constituent elements. (72)

The ten roots (daśamūla), cloves (lavaṅga), Indian sandalwood (dāru), bhārṅgī, cāśā, vṛścika, ghanasāra, dhanvayāsa, balā, kurucaka, kola, madanamusali, haridrā, netā, aśvagandhā, jīraka, rāsnā, grapes (drākṣā), śṛṅgī, sthirā, parṇī, bhṛṅgarāja, ugrā, gokṣura, candana, utpala, yaṣṭimadhu, kaśeru, kapāta, ativiṣā, uśīra, bāluka, heṣmala, kākanāsā, kuṣṭha, mañjiṣṭhā, lākā, kākolyaka, bṛhaspati, kuṇḍalī,
arka, amṛtā, vanti, viḍaṅga, bhārṅgī, vatsaka, khadira, and āsana.

Nimba, śigru, karañja, śatabīja, bilva, rājavṛkṣa, bhallātaka, brahmaguḍūcī, ghuṣṭi, vatrī, vidārī, vibhītaka, śirīṣa, pauṣkara, dārvī, karaka, kuṣṭha, ...bījaka, kṣāra, kapittha, dīpyaka, jājī, tāra, miśi, guggulu, lākṣā, kaṭukā, and others—along with śālā, puṣpa, dhānyāka, kūṣmāṇḍa, saukumāryā, and aśvaparṇā—these, when prepared as decoctions, ghees, oils, or electuaries, take the form of remedies that cure diseases by parching the two [humors], acting upon the seven tissues (dhātus), treating emaciation (kārya), and destroying all maladies. (73) The fifteen or thirteen substances of the *paṭolādi* group, reduced to powder according to the appropriate application, destroy the disease of *raktapitta*. (74)
The twelve and thirteen substances, as appropriate, are used as decoctions to cure diseases of *rakta-pitta*.

Likewise, oils, ghees, electuaries (*lehya*), and other substances combined with honey and sugar destroy blood-related disorders. The fifteen, thirteen, and eighteen substances, as appropriate, when prepared as fine powders with honey, destroy the afflictions of asthma, cough, and consumption (*kṣaya*).
Decoctions prepared from eight, nine, ten, eleven, or thirteen substances, as appropriate, are suitable for use and alleviate dyspnea, cough, and consumption.
(78) Preparations of fifteen, seventeen, or twenty ingredients are fit for use with oils and ghees, and they destroy dyspnea, cough, and consumption.
(79) Thus ends the fifteenth inquiry of Āyurveda.
Now begins the sixteenth question.

Likewise, linctuses and other preparations combined with jaggery and similar substances, as well as the twenty-two medicinal items beginning with *kapittha*, are destroyers of the disease of hiccough. 1–2.
3. So many substances in the form of oils, clarified butter, and unctuous preparations are the removers of the disease of hiccup (*hidhmā*).

4. Whatever substance removes all those substances that cause the wasting of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) through diseases arising from indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) due to the consumption of various pure substances belonging to the respective elements (*bhūta*), that substance nourishes those respective constituents.
5. The fifteen substances beginning with the ten roots (*daśamūla*) nourish or deplete the constituent of rasa (plasma) according to their specific application.
The fifteen substances beginning with *ghana* dry up and nourish the blood constituent (*rakta-dhātu*).
(6) The fifteen substances beginning with *rāsnā*, when applied appropriately, remove diseases located in the drying constituents and the muscle constituent (*māṃsa-dhātu*).
(7) The fourteen substances beginning with *vālukā* destroy disorders of the fat constituent (*medas-dhātu*). (8)
The fifteen substances beginning with nimba remove the provocation of diseases located in the bone tissue (asthi-dhātu). 9.
The fifteen substances beginning with vidra remove the provocation of diseases residing in the marrow tissue (majjā-dhātu). 10.
The six substances beginning with jātī remove, as appropriate, the provocation of diseases located in the final tissue (śukra-dhātu).

The consumption of substances possessing qualities superior to those of the wind-element (*pavana-bhūta*) and earth-element (*bhūta*), resulting in indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), gives rise to *āma-pitta*, poison, worms, and disorders of the channels (*sirā-vikāra*), which constitute the causes of the disease of vomiting (*chardi-roga*).
(12) The remedy for the disease of vomiting consists of the consumption of as many substances as are capable of producing fire-element qualities that counteract those [causes].

(13) Powders, decoctions, oils, and electuaries composed of *śaṭha*, *dhani*, water-born [lotus], *jīraka*, *mudga*, *pāṭhā*, *kaṭuka*, *madhuka*, *pittha*, *śivā*, *amṛtā*, *marīci*, *elā*, cotton (*kārpāsa*), sandalwood (*candana*), honey (*mākṣika*), *jīraka*, cloves (*lavaṅga*), bark (*tvak*), *kesara*, *priyaṅgu*, and camphor (*śaśi*), when combined in appropriate proportions, destroy the disease of vomiting. (14)

The consumption of substances that increase skin, flesh, and fat, which are heavy, excessively oily, and of poor taste, and which—due to indigestion—give rise to undigested matter (*āmā*), bile (*pitta*), poison, and worms, thereby causing disorders of the vessels and provoking the disease of hemorrhoids (*gudāṅkura*), is [counteracted] by the consumption of substances that destroy those respective ailments. 15.

Svarjikā, niśā, vāntī, musalī, śirīṣa, kaṇā, tuttha, jīrṇi, veṇu, arka, snuh, bhallātaka, karañja, vakula, dhātrī, vibhītaka, abhayā, yavānī, bilva, punarnavā, śirīṣa, liha, saindhava, marica, sūraṇa, cavya, jīraka, vajravallī, mūrvā, apāmārga, daśamūla, lavaṅga, kesara, muragī, mohā, bhīru, brāhmī, ghoṣā, kuṣṭha, hiṅgu, saindhava, bhārgī, rāsnā, madhūka, vacā, śirīṣa, dhātu, mayūraka, uśīra, pāṭhā, duḥsparśā, siddhārtha, and palāṇḍu.

Substances consisting of earth, matured aromatics, ghee, oil, and electuaries are destroyers of diseases of the anal folds (hemorrhoids). [16] The consumption of substances containing excessive dhātus that produce incompatible tastes as ordained by nature causes indigestion, which in turn generates āma, pitta, poison, and worms; therefore, the consumption of substances that counteract all such incompatible items prevents the diarrhea caused by the depletion of the essence of the rasa-dhātu. [17] Hence, [the remedy consists of] viṣaghnī, vyoṣa, divine pāṭhā, abhayā, kuṭaja, ajājī, ajamoda, mocarasa, dhātu, ciribilva, tinduka, dāḍima, padmaphalinī, marica, dhavikā, jājī, guṇṭhi, triṇī, yavaśūka, and kapi...

Tamarind, mango, rose-apple, vijayā, bījā, foamy fruit, cumin, *kola*, *cavya*, *citraka*, pomegranate, *ghuṇapriya*, seeds of *vatsaka*, *yaṣṭi*, *trutṛṭika*, *aiḍarya*, *śarapuṅkha*, garlic, asafoetida, *dhātrī*, *vibhītaka*, *granthi*, *talapoṭaka*, *titīra*, and substances possessing a salty taste—all such items, in the form of powders, decoctions, ghees, oils, or electuaries, are curatives for the diseases of diarrhea and chronic dysentery (*atisāra-grahaṇī*). 18.

The substance consisting of the water element (*ambubhūtadravya*), which possesses an acidic taste (*amlarasa*) characterized by an abundance of the quality of passion (*rajo-guṇa*), perceives its own sweet taste (*svādurasopalambhaka*) as coexisting with qualities superior to those of earth and the other elements; it is the destroyer of diseases caused by indigestion (*ajīrṇāmayanivartaka*).

(19) Pathyā, dhātrī, akṣa, punarnavā, hiṅgu, śarapuṅkha, vyāghrī, durālabhā, pūgīphala, tamāla-kṣāra, jambīra, arka, snuhī, śigru, parvaka, ugragandha, karañja, khadira, agni, śrīparṇī, śrībhāna, jayā, and āgneya—these, in the form of powders, decoctions, and electuaries (*cūrṇa-kvātha-leha-rūpa*), are the removers of diseases caused by indigestion. (20)

A substance possessing a sweet taste (*svādurasavat*) with a predominance of earthy qualities (*pārthivaguṇādhika*) is that which removes the disease of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) arising from the consumption of substances that produce an acidic taste (*amlarasa*) which is co-located with a substance whose fiery element (*agnibhūta*) is predominant.

(21) Furthermore, substances possessing a pungent taste (*kaṭurasavat*), such as *viśvadeva*, *kusumbha*, *kaṭukā*, *pippalī*, *rasona*, *dīpyaka*, *karañja*, *punarnavā*, *yavānī*, *jīraka*, *hiṅgu*, *vatsaka*, *vasuka*, *pathyā*, *ajagandhā*, *suragī*, *jātīphala*, *tālīśa*, *poṭaka*, *kaṭukā*, *barbara*, *kuṣṭha*, and *yāvasaka*, when prepared in the form of powders (*cūrṇa*), decoctions (*kvātha*), pastes (*kalka*), and so forth, remove all types of indigestion and the disease of ama. (22)

A substance possessing a bitter taste (*tiktarasa*), which functions to kindle the wind-element (*pavana-bhūta*) that is predominant in the wind-disorder caused by indigestion (*ajīrṇa*), undigested food (*āma*), and bile-fever (*pitta-jvara*)—arising from the consumption of substances whose tastes are co-located with the water, air, and earth elements—does not alleviate the impairment of the digestive fire (*agnimāndya*). 23.

Pāṭhā, karañja, anala, śarapuṅkhā, punarnavā, nimba, laśuna, yavānī, carabandhana, dīpyaka, jīraka, bilva, ativiṣā, vacā, saindhava, viśva, cavya, naitala, rāsnā, mṛtā, atasī, bhṛṅga, kuberākṣa, lodhra, kavaca, māṃsī, elā, tālapatrikā, keśa, dāru, ulūka, granthi, and agni—these, prepared as powders, decoctions, ghees, oils, or electuaries, cure weak digestion and disease. (24)

A substance possessing a pungent taste (kaṭurasavat), which possesses qualities exceeding those of the space element (gaganabhūtādhikaguṇopalambhaka) and removes the disease of the *grahaṇī*—which is characterized by the presence of undigested food (*ajīrṇa*), bile (*pitta*), and poison (*viṣa*) arising from the consumption of substances that produce heat and astringency co-located with the space, air, and earth elements—is the remedy for *grahaṇī* disease. 25.

Ginger, vatsaka, talapoṭa, mango, arjuna, vaṭa, aśvattha, bilva, badara, garlic, viśvā, āṅgerukī, nāgabalā, ciñcā, ajamoda, rasona, dāḍima, karañja, vāśā, śukla, lodhra, vṛddhadāru, śarapuṅkhā, marica, dīpyaka, jīraka, lavaṅga, karuṇā, abhīru, nimba, kuṭaja, and others—when administered as powders, decoctions, or electuaries, these remove the disease of *grahaṇī*. 26.

A substance predominantly characterized by the qualities of fire and air, which brings about the seven types of bodily fluids (*rasa*)—arising from the consumption of all substances that cause indigestion, bile, poison, worms, and disorders of the channels (*sirā*) through their association with astringent taste (*kaṣāya-rasa*), and which is preponderant in the element of space (*gagana*)—is a remedy for the disease of cholera (*viṣūcī*).
(27) The ten substances beginning with pungent (*kaṭu*) [taste], used as a powder, decoction, or medicinal preparation, are a remedy for the diseases of asthma (*śvāsa*) and vomiting (*chardi*).
(28) The seven items beginning with sandalwood (*candana*), when employed as a powder or decoction, are remedies for the diseases of asthma and vomiting. (29)
The twelve substances beginning with svarjikā, when prepared as incense, ointment, and decoction, remove the disease of hemorrhoids (gudāṅkura).
(30) The eleven substances beginning with karañja, when employed as incense, ointment, decoction, and oil, ward off the disease of hemorrhoids.
(31) The twenty-one substances beginning with daśamūla, existing in the form of incense, ointment, decoction, oil, and electuary, remove the affliction of hemorrhoids. (32)
The twelve medicinal formulations beginning with *bhārṅgī*, existing in the forms of powders, decoctions, ghees, oils, and electuaries, are removers of the disease of hemorrhoids (*gudāṅkura*).

(33) The fifteen substances beginning with *ativiṣā*, having become preparations of powders, decoctions, and electuaries, are removers of the disorder of diarrhea (*atisāra*). (34) Similarly, the eighteen ingredients beginning with *marīca* are likewise curers of diarrhea. (35)

The ten substances beginning with *niṣṭhā* likewise cure diarrhea (36). Through the powder and decoction of the thirteen substances beginning with *pathyā*, the disease of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) is cured (37).
The thirteen items beginning with *ākrandita*, in the form of powder and decoction, are removers of the disease of indigestion (38).

The *Viśvādi* group of twelve substances, in the form of powder, decoction, and electuary, cures the diseases of indigestion (*ajīrṇa*) and ama. (39) The *Mustādi* group of twelve substances, when employed as powder and decoction, cures the diseases of indigestion and ama.
(40) The *Veṇvādi* group of fifteen substances, in the form of powder, decoction, ghee, and oil, removes the disease of weak digestive fire (*agnimāndya*). (41)

The twelve substances beginning with rock salt (saindhava) are likewise medicinal for curing the disease of weak digestion (mandāgni). 42. The seven ingredients beginning with ginger (viśva) in the form of a decoction bring about the restoration of weak digestive fire. 43.
The ten substances beginning with fresh ginger (ārdraka), in the form of a decoction or electuary (leha), cure the disease of malabsorption (grahaṇī). 44.
The twelve substances beginning with garlic (laśuna), prepared as powder, decoction, electuary, and ghee, cure the disease of weak digestive fire (mandānala).
||45|| The six substances beginning with cardamom (elā), existing in the form of powder, decoction, and processed preparations, cure the disease of weak digestive fire.
||46|| By one desiring long life, these are the means for achieving dharma, artha, and sukha.
One should show the highest respect for the instructions of Ayurveda.
Having investigated with great effort, one should constantly examine the entire body;
having examined it for ten days, one should then treat it only with wholesome [regimens].
One should not oppress the senses, nor should one indulge them excessively;
one should not engage in any undertaking devoid of the three aims of life, doing so without contradicting them.
There is an increase for all [humors] when they are equal, and the opposite occurs when they are contrary;
the accumulation, provocation, and pacification of Vāyu occur during the three seasons beginning with summer.
And [there is an increase] of pitta during the rainy season and so forth, and of kapha during the cool season and so forth.
Thus ends the sixteenth inquiry of Āyurveda.
